title: Social Science, Class 8
subject: Social Science
description: NCERT Grade 8 Social Science, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: Natural Resources and Their Use
chapters.summary: In this chapter: nature and the meaning of resources; categorising natural resources by use; renewable and non-renewable resources; distribution of natural resources and its effects.

lessons.title: Nature and the Meaning of Resources

activities.prompt: What makes a natural treasure a resource?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Nature becomes resources
activities.body: Nature includes living and non-life forms. People turn elements of Nature into resources when they use or consume them. An entity becomes a resource when people can reach it and use it. Some natural treasures cannot be reached with available technology. Natural resources are natural materials and substances that people value. A regenerative economy should live in harmony with Nature.
keyPoints: Nature has living and non-life forms.
People turn Nature's elements into resources by using them.
A regenerative economy lives in harmony with Nature.
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas about Nature and resources.

activities.prompt: Can a community use a natural treasure that is far away?
steps: Nature includes living and non-life forms in our environment.
People turn elements of Nature into resources when they use them.
It becomes a resource when people can reach and use it.
So an unreachable treasure is not yet a resource for that community.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Making resources
activities.prompt: What do people do to turn elements of Nature into resources?
options: Leave them unused
Hide them away
Use or consume
Praise them aloud
activities.explanation: People use or consume Nature's elements to turn them into resources.

activities.title: Trees and Nature
activities.prompt: Trees are natural entities even before people cut their wood.
activities.explanation: Trees are natural entities even before people cut their wood.

activities.title: Match the examples
activities.prompt: Match each example with the correct description.
pairs: Coal, petroleum, precious stones and metal ores
Trees before people cut their wood
May be culturally unacceptable to cut
activities.explanation: These pairs show examples and limits described in the lesson.

activities.title: A costly problem
activities.prompt: Which condition can stop an entity from becoming a resource?
options: Low extraction cost
High extraction cost
Easy public reach
Regular use by people
activities.explanation: A high extraction cost can also stop an entity from being a resource.

activities.title: From tree to resource
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Trees exist before people cut their wood.
People can reach and use tree elements.
activities.explanation: First, the tree exists. People then reach and use its elements, making them resources.

activities.title: A regenerative economy
activities.prompt: Which statement fits a regenerative economy?
options: It lives with Nature in harmony.
It values natural materials only.
It reaches every natural treasure.
It avoids using resources.
activities.explanation: A regenerative economy should live in harmony with Nature.

activities.prompt: A grove is sacred to local people. Why might its trees stay uncut?
options: Cutting the trees may be culturally unacceptable there.
The trees have no wood until people cut them.
The trees cannot grow while people protect them.
The trees are not natural while people protect them.

why.The trees have no wood until people cut: This wrongly thinks wood appears only after cutting.
why.The trees cannot grow while people prote: This wrongly links protection with stopped growth.
why.The trees are not natural while people p: This wrongly thinks protection makes a tree unnatural.

activities.explanation: People may protect sacred groves because cutting them is culturally unacceptable.

activities.prompt: One village can reach a treasure. Another cannot. What is the difference?
options: Only the first village can use the treasure as a resource.
Both villages can use it because natural things are resources.
Neither village can use it because Nature stays the same.
The second village has no Nature around its treasure.

why.Both villages can use it because natural: This confuses a natural entity with a usable resource.
why.Neither village can use it because Natur: This wrongly assumes equal access in different places.
why.The second village has no Nature around: This wrongly thinks being unable to reach something removes Nature.

activities.explanation: An entity becomes a resource when people can reach and use it.

activities.prompt: A map shows buried coal far from any road. What can the map tell us?
options: It shows the coal's place, but not whether people can reach it.
It proves every person can reach and use the coal.
It shows the coal is already an easy natural resource.
It shows the coal formed only after people found it.

why.It proves every person can reach and use: This wrongly treats a marked place as guaranteed access.
why.It shows the coal is already an easy nat: This wrongly assumes a location also proves low extraction cost.
why.It shows the coal formed only after peop: This wrongly links a treasure's finding with its formation.

activities.explanation: A map can show location, but access may still be missing.

activities.prompt: A team can reach and use a new natural material. Why can they use it as a resource?
options: People value it and can reach and use it.
It became a resource before people knew it existed.
Every natural material is always ready for use.
Its name decides whether it can become a resource.

why.It became a resource before people knew: This wrongly thinks value and use are unnecessary.
why.Every natural material is always ready f: This wrongly assumes all natural materials are already resources.
why.Its name decides whether it can become a: This wrongly believes names decide a material's status.

activities.explanation: Reach and use matter because resources need human use.

activities.prompt: People can reach a natural treasure, but extracting it costs too much. How will they view it?
options: They may not treat it as a resource yet.
They must treat it as a resource at once.
They cannot regard it as a natural treasure.
They can use it freely despite the high cost.

why.They must treat it as a resource at once: This wrongly ignores the high cost of extraction.
why.They cannot regard it as a natural treas: This wrongly thinks high cost removes natural value.
why.They can use it freely despite the high: This wrongly assumes reachability removes every cost.

activities.explanation: A high extraction cost can stop an entity from being a resource.

lessons.title: Categorising Natural Resources by Use

activities.prompt: How can we sort natural resources by the ways we use them?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Resources and Their Uses
activities.body: Air, water and food are resources essential for life. People get essential resources from air, water, rivers, ponds and soil. People cannot make the air they breathe or the water they drink. People make physical objects from Nature’s gifts. India’s geographical diversity gives it many natural resources.
keyPoints: Air, water and food are essential for life.
People get essential resources from air, water, rivers, ponds and soil.
People make physical objects from Nature’s gifts.
activities.explanation: Natural resources give us essentials and help us make physical objects.

activities.prompt: People use air, water, food, rivers, soil, coal and sunlight. How can these natural resources be grouped?
steps: Air, water and food support life, so they form a life-needs group.
Nature’s gifts make objects or provide energy, so they form other use groups.
Renewability gives another grouping, because it checks if resources can be renewed.
Thus, resources can be grouped by use and by renewability.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Essential Resources
activities.prompt: Which group contains only resources that are essential for life?
options: Air, water and food
Coal, petroleum and wind
Sunlight, soil and gas
Rivers, ponds and objects
activities.explanation: Air, water and food are essential resources for life.

activities.title: Resources From Nature
activities.prompt: People cannot make the air they breathe or the water they drink.
activities.explanation: Air and water come from Nature. People cannot make them.

activities.title: Resources and Their Roles
activities.prompt: Match each item with its role in the lesson.
activities.explanation: People get resources from soil. Coal provides energy, while air and water cannot be made by people.

activities.title: Natural Energy
activities.prompt: Coal, petroleum, natural gas, sunlight and wind can provide ______.
activities.hint: These are all natural energy sources.
activities.explanation: Energy is essential to modern life and production.

activities.title: Returning to Health
activities.prompt: A damaged thing must return to its original healthy state. What is this process called?
options: Restoration
Regeneration
Production
Categorisation
activities.explanation: Restoration means returning something to its original healthy state.

activities.title: Restoration or Regeneration?
activities.prompt: Regeneration means returning a damaged place to its original healthy state.
activities.explanation: That describes restoration. Regeneration means Nature can create new life and the conditions for thriving.

activities.prompt: People cannot make the air they breathe or the water they drink. What must they do?
options: They get them from natural sources like rivers and soil.
They make them from Nature’s gifts in factories.
They restore them whenever their supply ends.
They create them from soil, sunlight and wind.

why.They make them from Nature’s gifts in fa: This wrongly assumes factories can make air and water.
why.They restore them whenever their supply: This confuses restoration with getting resources from nature.
why.They create them from soil, sunlight and: This wrongly treats soil and sunlight as sources of air and water.

activities.explanation: This is right because people get these resources from natural sources.

activities.prompt: One village gets water from a river. Another gets resources from soil. What do both sources do?
options: They provide some essential resources for people.
They provide energy for factories and production.
They make physical objects from Nature’s gifts.
They create new life and thriving conditions.

why.They provide energy for factories and pr: This confuses life-giving resources with energy sources.
why.They make physical objects from Nature’s: This confuses getting resources with making physical objects.
why.They create new life and thriving condit: This confuses providing resources with regeneration.

activities.explanation: This is right because rivers and soil provide essential resources.

activities.prompt: A map marks coal, sunlight and wind. What can we learn about this place?
options: It has several sources of natural energy.
It has every source of essential resources.
It can make the air and water people need.
It can restore all damaged natural resources.

why.It has every source of essential resourc: A map with these markers does not show every resource.
why.It can make the air and water people nee: The map does not mean people can make air or water.
why.It can restore all damaged natural resou: The map does not show that every resource can be restored.

activities.explanation: This is right because these sources can provide natural energy.

activities.prompt: People check if a resource is renewable. Which resource best fits this rule?
options: Soil, because Nature can create new life there.
Coal, because Nature can create new life there.
Petroleum, because Nature can create new life there.
Natural gas, because Nature can create new life there.

why.Coal, because Nature can create new life: Coal gives energy, but this does not show renewal of life.
why.Petroleum, because Nature can create new: Petroleum gives energy, but this does not show renewal of life.
why.Natural gas, because Nature can create n: Natural gas gives energy, but this does not show renewal of life.

activities.explanation: This is right because soil supports Nature’s regeneration of life.

activities.prompt: People return a damaged river to its original healthy state. Nature creates new life in soil. How do these actions differ?
options: Repairing restores the river; creating new life regenerates soil.
Repairing regenerates the river; creating new life restores soil.
Both actions return their resource to its original healthy state.
Both actions provide energy for modern life and production.

why.Both actions return their resource to it: Regeneration creates new life, not an original healthy state.
why.Both actions provide energy for modern l: Neither action here is described as a source of energy.

activities.explanation: Repairing restores health, while new life is regeneration.

activities.prompt: Factories and modern life need energy. Why might people use sunlight and wind?
options: They are natural sources that can provide energy.
They can make the air and water people need.
They can turn coal into physical objects.
They can restore every damaged natural resource.

why.They can make the air and water people n: Air and water cannot be made by sunlight or wind.
why.They can turn coal into physical objects: This wrongly says sunlight and wind create physical objects.
why.They can restore every damaged natural r: This confuses energy sources with restoration.

activities.explanation: This is right because sunlight and wind are natural energy sources.

lessons.title: Renewable and Non-renewable Resources

activities.prompt: How can we use natural resources without harming the planet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Resources
activities.body: Nature’s cycles work so there is no waste. Solar, wind, flowing water and forest timber can be renewable resources. Non-renewable resources cannot be replenished as quickly as people use them. Coal, petroleum, iron, copper and gold are non-renewable resources. People must manage renewable resources sustainably. Ecosystems filter water and prevent soil erosion.
keyPoints: Solar, wind, flowing water and forest timber can be renewable.
Coal, petroleum, iron, copper and gold are non-renewable.
Renewable resources must be managed sustainably.
activities.explanation: Renewable resources can return through cycles, while non-renewable resources cannot return as quickly.

activities.prompt: A village uses flowing water and forest timber. Its forest also filters water. How should it manage these resources?
steps: Flowing water and forest timber can be renewable resources.
The village must manage them sustainably because renewable resources need careful management.
Protecting the forest helps because ecosystems filter water and prevent soil erosion.
Therefore, the village should use both resources carefully and sustainably.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which of these can be a renewable resource?
options: Solar
Coal
Iron
Petroleum
activities.explanation: Good choice! Solar is listed as a renewable resource.

activities.prompt: Which group contains only non-renewable resources?
options: Coal, petroleum, iron and copper
Solar, wind, water and timber
Coal, iron, gold and water
Petroleum, copper, timber and wind
activities.explanation: These resources are all listed as non-renewable resources.

activities.prompt: Forest timber can be a renewable resource.
activities.explanation: Yes! Forest timber is included among renewable resources.

activities.prompt: How should people manage renewable resources?
options: Manage them sustainably
Manage them carelessly
Use them without care
Treat them as non-renewable
activities.explanation: Renewable resources must be managed in a sustainable manner.

activities.prompt: Which benefit do people receive from ecosystems?
options: Coal
Clean water
Copper
Petroleum
activities.explanation: Ecosystems give people benefits such as clean water.

activities.prompt: A storm moves soil into a stream. What should the forest do about water and soil?
options: Filter the water and hold the soil in place.
Make coal and petroleum supplies for the village.
Speed up soil movement toward the stream each day.
Use up the local water and forest timber faster.

why.Make coal and petroleum supplies for the: This mistakes non-renewable resources for benefits provided by ecosystems.
why.Speed up soil movement toward the stream: This reverses the ecosystem function that prevents soil erosion.
why.Use up the local water and forest timber: This mistakes renewable resources for a reason to use them faster.

activities.explanation: This is right because filtering water and preventing erosion are ecosystem functions.

activities.prompt: A map marks where coal and gold are found. What can the map show us?
options: Where those non-renewable resources are found.
When those resources will be used up.
How those resources can be replenished.
How forests should be managed there.

A map of locations does not show when resources will be used up.
A map of locations does not show how resources are replenished.
A map of locations does not set rules for managing forests.

activities.explanation: This is right because a location map shows where resources are found.

activities.prompt: An article says India's coal may last about fifty years. What can we safely conclude?
options: Coal is available now, but its reserves may have a time limit.
Coal will be replenished soon because nature makes no waste.
Coal can be managed like a renewable forest resource.
Coal will outlast every other resource in India.

why.Coal will be replenished soon because na: This wrongly applies nature's waste cycle to non-renewable coal.
why.Coal can be managed like a renewable for: This wrongly treats coal as renewable like forest timber.
why.Coal will outlast every other resource i: This makes an unsupported comparison with every other resource.

activities.explanation: This is right because the source gives coal a possible time limit.

activities.prompt: People remove fallen waste from a forest. What may happen to nature's cycle?
options: Waste may remain because nature cannot reuse what is removed.
The cycle may speed up because the forest is cleaner.
Forest timber may stop becoming a renewable resource.
Coal and petroleum may form inside the forest.

why.The cycle may speed up because the fores: This wrongly thinks removing waste would make nature's cycle faster.
why.Forest timber may stop becoming a renewa: This wrongly assumes waste removal changes what forest timber is.
why.Coal and petroleum may form inside the f: This wrongly thinks forest waste becomes coal and petroleum.

activities.explanation: This is right because nature's cycles reuse waste instead of leaving it.

activities.prompt: A farm needs help with its crops. Nearby homes need clean water. What can the forest provide?
options: Pollinated crops and clean water for people.
Coal and gold for nearby industries.
Soil erosion and dirty water for homes.
Petroleum and iron for farm tools.

This confuses useful resources with benefits supplied by ecosystems.
This reverses the benefits of soil protection and water filtering.
This wrongly treats mined materials as services supplied by ecosystems.

activities.explanation: This is right because ecosystems provide pollinated crops and clean water.

lessons.title: Distribution of Natural Resources and Its Effects

activities.prompt: Why can natural resources make some communities flourish while others face difficult choices?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Resources Shape Our World
activities.body: Natural resources are spread unevenly across the planet and within countries. This affects settlements, trade, relations, and conflicts. Industries near resources create local jobs. Townships grow around these industries and support other businesses. Resource development can bring costs and displace people. Threats to sacred places can lead to conflict. Trade depends on resource locations. Human skills can create special products such as Wootz steel.
keyPoints: Resources are spread unevenly.
Resource industries can create local jobs.
Development can also cause costs and displacement.
activities.explanation: Uneven resources can support development, but they can also create difficult effects.

activities.prompt: Why do some places gain jobs when natural resources are found nearby?
steps: Natural resources are unevenly spread, so villages have different resources.
A nearby industry can hire local people because it uses those resources.
As a township grows around it, other businesses can also grow.
However, people may lose homes, so resource growth can bring heavy costs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How are natural resources spread?
options: Spread evenly worldwide
Spread unevenly worldwide
Found only near cities
Limited to one country
activities.explanation: Natural resources are spread unevenly across the planet and within countries.

activities.prompt: Human knowledge and skills can turn resources into special products such as ______ steel.
activities.hint: This special steel is named in your book.
activities.explanation: Human knowledge and skills can create special products such as Wootz steel.

activities.prompt: Resource-based development never displaces people from their homes.
activities.explanation: Resource-based development can displace people from their homes.

activities.prompt: Match each resource effect with its result.
activities.explanation: Industries near resources create local jobs, while townships support other businesses. Threats to sacred places can also lead to conflict.

activities.prompt: Which statement about trade is correct?
options: Trade depends on natural resource locations.
Trade ignores natural resource locations.
Trade depends only on resource ownership.
Trade follows only political boundaries.
activities.explanation: National and international trade depend on where natural resources are located.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the resource curse and India is correct?
options: Plenty may bring wealth; India developed resource-based industries.
Plenty need not bring wealth; India developed resource-based industries.
Plenty need not bring wealth; India rejected resource-based industries.
Plenty always brings wealth; India developed resource-based industries.
activities.explanation: Plenty of resources does not automatically make a country rich. India has generally avoided the resource curse by developing resource-based industries.

activities.prompt: A skilled worker makes Wootz steel from a resource. What is added?
options: Human knowledge and skills turn the resource into a special product.
Natural resources are already special products before people use them.
Human skills remove the need for any natural resource.
The resource alone turns into steel without human skills.

why.Natural resources are already special pr: It confuses a natural resource with a specially made product.
why.Human skills remove the need for any nat: It mistakes adding skills through work for not needing a resource.
why.The resource alone turns into steel with: It ignores the human knowledge and skills used to make Wootz steel.

activities.explanation: Human knowledge and skills can turn resources into special products such as Wootz steel.

activities.prompt: A map shows northern water and southern homes. What trade is likely?
options: Water may move from the north to the south.
Water may move from the south to the north.
People may move south to find more water.
Homes may move north to match the water.

why.Water may move from the south to the nor: It reverses the direction from water resources to homes.
why.People may move south to find more water: It puts the water in the wrong place compared with the homes.
It assumes people can solve location differences by moving homes.

activities.explanation: Trade depends on where natural resources are located.

activities.prompt: A river resource lies across two countries' border. What tension may appear?
options: The countries may argue over the shared resource.
The countries may agree to ignore the resource.
Both countries may lose all resource industries.
The border may move because water is nearby.

why.The countries may agree to ignore the re: It assumes agreement can remove the effect of uneven distribution.
why.Both countries may lose all resource ind: It mistakes political tension for the loss of every industry.
why.The border may move because water is nea: It assumes borders move automatically when resources sit nearby.

activities.explanation: Political boundaries do not match resource locations, so tension can grow.

activities.prompt: A new industry threatens a sacred place. Why might people oppose it?
options: They fear conflict if the sacred place is harmed.
They expect the industry to create local jobs.
They want the township to grow more quickly.
They think the industry will protect the sacred place.

why.They expect the industry to create local: It mistakes a possible benefit for a reason to oppose the industry.
why.They want the township to grow more quic: It assumes faster township growth explains opposition to a sacred-place threat.
why.They think the industry will protect the: It reverses the meaning of a threat to the sacred place.

activities.explanation: Threats to sacred places can lead to conflict, so people may oppose them.

lessons.title: Stewardship and Resource Sustainability

activities.prompt: How can we care for Earth’s resources while meeting everyone’s needs?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Caring for Nature
activities.body: Stewardship means respecting Nature so life on Earth can continue. Irresponsible resource use causes pollution, biodiversity loss and climate change. Biodiversity loss means losing different kinds of life. Water can be taken faster than the water table can replace it. A deficit can raise costs and make water unavailable. Punjab’s groundwater is severely depleted. Improper fertiliser and pesticide use causes soil degradation. Traditional practices can help manage soil as a whole.
keyPoints: Respect Nature to sustain life on Earth.
Groundwater deficits can raise costs and make water unavailable.
Improper chemical use can cause soil degradation.
activities.explanation: Stewardship helps people use natural resources responsibly.

activities.prompt: A farmer gets free power for pumping. What happens to groundwater over time?
steps: Free power makes pumping cheap, so the farmer pumps too much.
Extraction can outpace replenishment, so the water table falls.
As groundwater declines, pumping becomes harder and more costly.
Therefore, free power must not encourage overuse of a shared resource.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Respect Nature
activities.prompt: To sustain life on Earth, people must respect which part of nature?
options: Nature
Machines
Cities
Shops
activities.explanation: The lesson says that sustaining life on Earth requires respecting Nature.

activities.title: Punjab’s Water
activities.prompt: Punjab’s groundwater resources have been severely depleted.
activities.explanation: This describes the condition of Punjab’s groundwater resources.

activities.title: Refilling Groundwater
activities.prompt: Groundwater extraction is often faster than the water table can be ______.
activities.hint: This means filled with water again.
activities.explanation: Replenished means filled with water again.

activities.title: Causes and Results
activities.prompt: Match each cause or action with its result.
pairs: Misuse of chemical fertilisers and pesticides
One of the most polluting industries
activities.explanation: Each pair links a cause or action with the result stated in the lesson.

activities.title: Water Level Initiatives
activities.prompt: What are the launched initiatives trying to achieve?
options: Lower groundwater levels
Raise groundwater levels
Create more deficits
Reduce extraction costs
activities.explanation: These initiatives aim to raise groundwater levels.

activities.title: The Groundwater Pathway
activities.prompt: Put these groundwater events in order.
activities.explanation: Too much extraction can create a deficit, raise costs and eventually make water unavailable.

activities.prompt: Free power makes pumping easy. What is the most likely result?
options: The water table falls, and pumping later costs more.
The water table rises, and pumping later costs less.
The soil improves, and pumping later costs less.
The rain increases, and pumping later costs less.

why.The water table rises, and pumping later: More pumping does not raise the water table.
why.The soil improves, and pumping later cos: Free power affects pumping, not directly soil fertility.
why.The rain increases, and pumping later co: Free power does not cause more rain.

activities.explanation: Too much pumping can exceed replenishment and raise later costs.

activities.prompt: Traditional seeds need less water. Which choice best protects groundwater?
options: Use traditional seeds and limit extra pumping.
Use high-yielding seeds and pump more often.
Use traditional seeds and pump more often.
Use high-yielding seeds and limit extra pumping.

why.Use high-yielding seeds and pump more of: High-yielding seeds need more water, so extra pumping worsens the problem.
why.Use traditional seeds and pump more ofte: Traditional seeds help, but extra pumping still harms groundwater.
why.Use high-yielding seeds and limit extra: Less pumping helps, but high-yielding seeds still need more water.

activities.explanation: Traditional seeds need less water, and less pumping protects groundwater.

activities.prompt: The government wants to raise groundwater levels. Which rule best supports this goal?
options: Require farmers to limit groundwater pumping.
Require farmers to increase groundwater pumping.
Require farmers to stop all soil care.
Require farmers to use more chemicals.

why.Require farmers to increase groundwater: More pumping can exceed replenishment and lower the water table.
Stopping soil care does not directly raise groundwater levels.
More chemicals can degrade soil and do not raise groundwater.

activities.explanation: Limiting pumping helps groundwater recover and supports rising levels.

activities.prompt: Factories can pollute nature. Which production should a stewardship plan check closely?
options: Cement production, because it is highly polluting.
Traditional soil care, because it is highly polluting.
Groundwater recharge, because it is highly polluting.
Wheat farming, because it is highly polluting.

why.Traditional soil care, because it is hig: Traditional soil care supports the soil and is not listed as polluting.
why.Groundwater recharge, because it is high: Groundwater recharge aims to raise water levels, not cause pollution.
why.Wheat farming, because it is highly poll: Wheat farming can increase water needs, but this does not show heavy pollution.

activities.explanation: Cement production is listed as one of the most polluting industries.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants long-term soil care. Which plan best supports sustainability?
options: Use traditional practices and avoid improper chemical use.
Use more chemicals and avoid traditional practices.
Use traditional practices and add more chemicals.
Use no soil care and avoid traditional practices.

why.Use more chemicals and avoid traditional: Improper chemicals can damage soil, so avoiding traditional practices is unwise.
why.Use traditional practices and add more c: Traditional practices help, but adding chemicals may still damage soil.
why.Use no soil care and avoid traditional p: Avoiding all soil care gives up holistic management of the soil.

activities.explanation: Traditional practices support holistic care, while improper chemicals degrade soil.

lessons.title: Wise Use, Sustainable Farming and Renewable Energy

activities.prompt: How can farms grow healthy food while caring for the Earth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Farming with Care
activities.body: Vṛikṣhāyurveda combines vṛikṣha, meaning tree, with ayurveda, the science of life or health. It suggests natural pest repellents and useful plant combinations. Crop rotation and mixed cropping maintain soil health. Pema’s family used compost, neem, and garlic repellents. Their farm thrived after about five years. Sikkim became completely organic in 2016. Wise choices include renewable energy, fair resource access, and care for nature.
keyPoints: Natural repellents and useful plant combinations
Crop rotation and mixed cropping maintain soil health
Stewards restore and regenerate natural resources
activities.explanation: These ideas connect healthy farming, clean energy, and careful stewardship.

activities.prompt: Pema’s crops face pests and tired soil. How can she follow Vṛikṣhāyurveda?
steps: Add compost, because Pema’s family used it on the farm.
Use neem and garlic repellents, because natural repellents help against pests.
Rotate and mix crops, because these practices maintain soil health.
Together, these wise choices can help Pema’s farm thrive.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Does Ayurveda Mean?
activities.prompt: In Vṛikṣhāyurveda, what does ayurveda mean?
options: The science of life or health
Only the science of trees alone
The study of many farm tools
The work of many crop sellers
activities.explanation: Ayurveda means the science of life or health.

activities.title: Healthy Soil
activities.prompt: Crop rotation and mixed cropping help maintain ______ health.
activities.hint: Healthy crops need healthy ground.
activities.explanation: Crop rotation and mixed cropping maintain soil health.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea to the correct example or role.
pairs: Natural repellent used by Pema’s family
Basic resources that need fair access
People who restore and regenerate resources
activities.explanation: Pema’s family used neem and garlic repellents. People should prefer renewable energy and act as fair stewards.

activities.title: Choose a Better Energy Source
activities.prompt: Put the energy shift in the order stated.
activities.explanation: The lesson says to move from non-renewables to renewable energy whenever possible.

activities.title: A Fairer Future
activities.prompt: A town has unfair access to basic resources. What should its people do?
options: Regenerate resources as stewards
Always use non-renewable sources
Use natural resources carelessly
Keep basic resources unfair
activities.explanation: People must act as stewards who restore and regenerate natural resources.

activities.title: Farmers’ Income
activities.prompt: What change did farmers in Sikkim experience on average?
options: A twenty per cent income growth
A fifty per cent income fall
A twenty per cent income fall
No change in farmers’ incomes
activities.explanation: Farmers’ incomes in Sikkim grew by twenty per cent on average.

activities.prompt: Vṛikṣhāyurveda links trees with health. Which farm plan best follows it?
options: Grow one crop repeatedly and leave soil health uncared for.
Mix crops but replace natural plant mixtures with empty fields.
Use natural plant mixtures and rotate crops to maintain soil health.
Use plant combinations but stop rotating crops for soil health.

why.Grow one crop repeatedly and leave soil: This wrongly repeats one crop and ignores soil health.
why.Mix crops but replace natural plant mixt: This replaces useful plant mixtures instead of using them.
why.Use plant combinations but stop rotating: This keeps plant combinations but wrongly drops crop rotation.

activities.explanation: This follows both natural mixtures and crop practices for soil health.

activities.prompt: A farm uses compost, neem repellents, and crop rotation. What may happen?
options: The farm may thrive after about five years, like Pema’s.
The soil may weaken because crop rotation changes the crops.
Pests may vanish forever because neem repellents are used.
The farm may stay weak because compost cannot support it.

why.The soil may weaken because crop rotatio: Crop rotation maintains soil health, so it does not weaken it.
why.Pests may vanish forever because neem re: Natural repellents manage pests but do not mean every pest vanishes forever.
why.The farm may stay weak because compost c: This wrongly assumes compost cannot support the family’s farm.

activities.explanation: Pema’s farm became thriving after about five years using similar methods.

activities.prompt: Farmer incomes in Sikkim grew twenty per cent on average. What can we conclude?
options: Every farmer gained exactly twenty per cent across the whole state.
The average fell, even though most farmers gained much more.
The average rose, but every farmer may not have gained.
Farm incomes stayed equal because twenty per cent means no change.

why.Every farmer gained exactly twenty per c: An average rise does not mean every farmer gained exactly that amount.
why.The average fell, even though most farme: The stated average rise contradicts the claim that it fell.
why.Farm incomes stayed equal because twenty: This wrongly treats twenty per cent growth as no change.

activities.explanation: A twenty per cent average rise allows different gains for different farmers.

activities.context: A community lives beside a forest and uses water, air and soil from the surrounding environment. The forest has trees that are sacred to the community, so cutting their wood is culturally unacceptable. Another part of the forest contains a natural treasure that people cannot reach with available technology. The community therefore values what it can use while leaving the unreachable treasure and the sacred trees undisturbed.
activities.prompt: If new technology allows people to reach and use the previously unreachable treasure, what should happen to its classification?
options: It should become a natural resource.
It should remain only a natural entity because people did not create it.
It should remain outside the resource category because its extraction cost is unknown.
It should count as a less obvious material, but not as a natural resource.

why.It should remain only a natural entity b: Natural origin alone does not prevent an entity from becoming a resource.
why.It should remain outside the resource ca: An unknown cost is not the same as a cost high enough to prevent use.
why.It should count as a less obvious materi: Less obvious natural materials can still be natural resources.

activities.explanation: People can reach and use it, so it meets the condition for becoming a resource.

activities.context: A community lives beside a forest and uses water, air and soil from the surrounding environment. The forest has trees that are sacred to the community, so cutting their wood is culturally unacceptable. Another part of the forest contains a natural treasure that people cannot reach with available technology. The community therefore values what it can use while leaving the unreachable treasure and the sacred trees undisturbed.
activities.prompt: Technology now allows people to reach the treasure, but extraction is so costly that they still cannot use it. What follows?
options: The treasure may remain outside the resource category because the cost prevents use.
The treasure must become a resource because reachability has been solved.
The treasure becomes a resource if people value it, even when they cannot use it.
The treasure is no longer a natural treasure once people reach it.

why.The treasure must become a resource beca: Reachability is important, but people must also be able to use the entity.
why.The treasure becomes a resource if peopl: Valuing something without being able to use it does not make it a resource.
why.The treasure is no longer a natural trea: Reaching an entity does not remove its natural origin.

activities.explanation: A high extraction cost can stop an entity from becoming a resource.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Water, air and soil are natural resources.
Reason (R): They are natural materials and substances that people value.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why people value and use them as natural resources.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): An unreachable natural treasure cannot become a resource with the technology currently available.
Reason (R): A high extraction cost can also stop an entity from being a resource.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but cost is a separate barrier from the inability to reach the treasure.

activities.prompt: Explain why a natural entity does not automatically become a natural resource.
activities.answer: An entity does not automatically become a resource simply because it exists in Nature. Trees are natural entities even before people cut their wood. People turn elements of Nature into resources when they use or consume them, and an entity becomes a resource when they can reach it and use it. Some natural treasures cannot be reached with available technology, while a high extraction cost can also prevent an entity from being a resource. Therefore, natural existence and human use are different ideas: a resource is also a natural material or substance that people value.
points: Natural entities exist before people use them.
An entity must be reachable and usable to become a resource.
Technology and extraction cost can prevent use.
People value natural materials and substances that become resources.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community gets drinking water from a river, breathes air, and uses soil to grow food. A worker makes physical objects from soil, while another worker uses coal to provide energy for production. The same place also has sunlight and wind. India’s geographical diversity gives the community many different natural resources, so planners must choose how each resource should be used and restored.
activities.prompt: If the community could no longer obtain coal, what could happen next?
options: Production would have to stop because coal is the only possible source of natural energy.
Production could continue by using food, because essential resources can provide energy.
Production could continue by using another natural energy source, such as sunlight or wind.
Production could continue by using physical objects, because making objects provides energy.

why.Production would have to stop because co: Natural energy comes from several sources, not only coal.
why.Production could continue by using food,: Food is essential for life but is not listed as a natural energy source.
why.Production could continue by using physi: Physical objects are made from Nature’s gifts but do not thereby become energy sources.

activities.explanation: Sunlight and wind can provide energy for production.

activities.context: A community gets drinking water from a river, breathes air, and uses soil to grow food. A worker makes physical objects from soil, while another worker uses coal to provide energy for production. The same place also has sunlight and wind. India’s geographical diversity gives the community many different natural resources, so planners must choose how each resource should be used and restored.
activities.prompt: Why should planners protect the community's river water instead of expecting it to be replaced?
options: Because water is essential for life and people cannot make the water they drink.
Because rivers are the only source of natural energy.
Because soil can be changed into drinking water whenever it is needed.
Because food can replace water when people need essential resources.

why.Because rivers are the only source of na: Rivers provide essential resources but are not energy sources.
why.Because soil can be changed into drinkin: People cannot make the water they drink from soil.
why.Because food can replace water when peop: Food and water are both essential resources, so one does not remove the need for the other.

activities.explanation: Water is essential, and people cannot make their drinking water.

activities.context: A community gets drinking water from a river, breathes air, and uses soil to grow food. A worker makes physical objects from soil, while another worker uses coal to provide energy for production. The same place also has sunlight and wind. India’s geographical diversity gives the community many different natural resources, so planners must choose how each resource should be used and restored.
activities.prompt: What should planners do if they want the soil to regenerate rather than merely be restored?
options: Return the soil to its original healthy state and stop there.
Use coal to add energy to the soil.
Make physical objects from the soil instead of supporting life.
Allow Nature to create new life and the conditions for thriving in the soil.

why.Return the soil to its original healthy: Returning the soil to its earlier healthy state describes restoration.
Coal can provide energy, but this does not describe creating new life.
why.Make physical objects from the soil inst: Making objects uses soil but does not describe regeneration.

activities.explanation: Regeneration means Nature can create new life and the conditions for thriving.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Sunlight and wind can provide energy for production.
Reason (R): Natural energy comes from several different sources.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Sunlight and wind are among the several natural energy sources that can provide energy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): People can make the air they breathe and the water they drink.
Reason (R): Air and water are essential resources for life.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Air and water are essential, but people cannot make the air they breathe or the water they drink.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between restoration and regeneration.
activities.answer: Restoration and regeneration describe two different processes. Restoration means returning something to its original healthy state. Regeneration means that Nature can create new life and the conditions for thriving. If damaged soil is returned to its former healthy condition, that is restoration. If Nature can then produce new life and the conditions needed for it to thrive in that soil, that is regeneration. The main difference is that restoration focuses on recovering a healthy condition, while regeneration focuses on Nature creating new life and supporting its growth.
points: Restoration returns something to its original healthy state.
Regeneration means Nature creates new life.
Regeneration also includes creating conditions for thriving.
Restoration recovers a condition, while regeneration creates new life.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community uses solar energy for some of its needs and obtains timber from a forest. It also uses coal to run machines. Residents want the forest to provide timber for future generations, and they are worried that the coal supply may not last as long as it is being used. They ask planners to decide how energy and forest resources should be managed.
activities.prompt: If the community continues using coal at the same rate, what is most likely to happen to its coal reserves?
options: They will be used more quickly than they can be replenished.
They will be replenished as quickly as they are used.
They will remain unchanged despite continued use.
They will become renewable because coal is widely used.

why.They will be replenished as quickly as t: This wrongly treats coal as a resource that can be quickly replenished.
why.They will remain unchanged despite conti: This wrongly ignores the effect of continued use on reserves.
why.They will become renewable because coal: This wrongly confuses regular use with the type of resource.

activities.explanation: Coal cannot be replenished as quickly as people use it.

activities.context: A community uses solar energy for some of its needs and obtains timber from a forest. It also uses coal to run machines. Residents want the forest to provide timber for future generations, and they are worried that the coal supply may not last as long as it is being used. They ask planners to decide how energy and forest resources should be managed.
activities.prompt: What should planners do to make sure the forest continues providing timber?
options: Manage the forest's timber in a sustainable manner.
Harvest as much timber as possible immediately because forest timber is renewable.
Allow repeated overuse because nature's cycles can replenish the timber.
Ignore sustainable management because nature's cycles mean that there is no waste.

why.Harvest as much timber as possible immed: Renewable does not mean that unlimited immediate use is wise.
why.Ignore sustainable management because na: Nature's cycles working without waste does not remove the need for management.

activities.explanation: Renewable resources such as forest timber must be managed sustainably.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Coal is a non-renewable resource because it cannot be replenished as quickly as people use it.
Reason (R): Coal belongs to the non-renewable group because its use is faster than its replenishment.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason explains why coal is non-renewable.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): India's coal reserves may last for about another fifty years.
Reason (R): Coal is renewable because it can be replenished as quickly as people use it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement about India's reserves is true, but the reason is false because coal is non-renewable.

activities.prompt: How do ecosystem functions benefit people, and why should renewable resources be managed sustainably?
activities.answer: Ecosystems perform functions such as filtering water and preventing soil erosion. People receive benefits from these functions, including clean water and pollinated crops. Some resources, such as forest timber and flowing water, can be renewable because nature's cycles can replenish them. However, renewable resources must still be managed in a sustainable manner. Doing so helps their supply continue through nature's cycles and supports the ecosystem functions that provide clean water and pollinated crops.
points: Identifies filtering water and preventing soil erosion as ecosystem functions.
Names clean water and pollinated crops as benefits for people.
Explains that some resources can be renewable through nature's cycles.
States that renewable resources must be managed sustainably.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A resource-rich region lies near a political boundary, while a resource-poor area lies far from resource-based industries. A company establishes a resource-based industry near the resource and employs local people. A township grows around it, and shops and other businesses begin to serve workers. However, homes are cleared for the expansion. The company also sells the resource through national and international trade. Local leaders fear that outside traders and neighboring political authorities may compete for control of the resource.
activities.prompt: Because the resource does not match the political boundaries, what is a likely result?
options: Political disputes may increase because the resource lies across different political boundaries.
Trading the resource will settle the boundary issue because trade makes political differences unimportant.
The resource-poor area will develop the same industries because resources are actually spread evenly.
Local employment will decline because industries cannot create jobs near natural resources.

why.Trading the resource will settle the bou: Trade does not necessarily remove political competition.
why.The resource-poor area will develop the: Natural resources are not spread evenly.
why.Local employment will decline because in: Resource-based industries can create local employment.

activities.explanation: Resources that cross political boundaries can create tension.

activities.context: A resource-rich region lies near a political boundary, while a resource-poor area lies far from resource-based industries. A company establishes a resource-based industry near the resource and employs local people. A township grows around it, and shops and other businesses begin to serve workers. However, homes are cleared for the expansion. The company also sells the resource through national and international trade. Local leaders fear that outside traders and neighboring political authorities may compete for control of the resource.
activities.prompt: How should local leaders weigh the company's plan?
options: Jobs and business growth should be considered together with displacement costs.
Local employment should be ignored because displacement is the only lasting effect.
Business growth proves that displacement cannot be a long-term cost.
Displacement shows that resource-based industries create no benefits for a township.

why.Local employment should be ignored becau: Displacement is one important cost to consider.
why.Business growth proves that displacement: Business growth does not remove all long-term costs.
why.Displacement shows that resource-based i: The same industries can employ people and support a township.

activities.explanation: Resource industries bring benefits as well as costs.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Natural Resources and Their Use

activities.prompt: Which statement best describes natural resources?
options: Natural materials that people value.
Materials made only by industries.
Any object found in a forest.
Products bought from a market.
activities.explanation: Natural resources are natural materials and substances that people value.

activities.prompt: A tree becomes a resource only after people cut its wood.
activities.explanation: Trees are natural entities even before people cut their wood.

activities.prompt: Filtering water and preventing soil erosion are ______ functions.
activities.hint: Name the kind of function mentioned in your lesson.
activities.explanation: Filtering water and preventing soil erosion are ecosystem functions.

activities.prompt: Why may some natural treasures not be resources?
options: People cannot reach them with available technology.
People do not value them at all.
People cannot store them for long.
People use them too quickly.
activities.explanation: Some treasures cannot be reached with available technology. High extraction costs can also stop use.

activities.prompt: Uneven resource distribution affects settlements, trade, relations and conflicts.
activities.explanation: Natural resources are spread unevenly. Their uneven distribution affects these parts of life.

activities.prompt: Put these groundwater steps in order.
activities.explanation: Fast extraction can create a deficit. This can raise costs and eventually make water unavailable.

activities.prompt: What did Pema’s family use on their farm?
options: Compost and neem and garlic repellents.
Chemical fertilisers and plastic sheets.
Coal and petroleum for field power.
High-yielding wheat and paddy seeds.
activities.explanation: Pema’s family used compost and natural repellents made from neem and garlic.

activities.prompt: Plenty of natural resources automatically makes a country rich.
activities.explanation: The natural resource curse means plenty of resources does not automatically make a country rich.

activities.prompt: _____ knowledge and skills can turn resources into special products such as Wootz steel.
activities.hint: Think about what people learn and practise.
activities.explanation: Human knowledge and skills can turn resources into special products such as Wootz steel.

chapters.title: Reshaping India’s Political Map
chapters.summary: In this chapter: medieval india and new invasions; the delhi sultanate: rule, conflict and resistance; resistance and the vijayanagara empire; the mughals: expansion, rule and decline.

lessons.title: Medieval India and New Invasions

activities.prompt: What drew invaders and travellers to India across the mountains?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Medieval India and New Invasions
activities.body: “Medieval” was first used for a period in European history. In this book, it means the 11th to 17th centuries. A new era began in India in the early 11th century. An invasion is an attack from outside. Invasions beyond the Hindu Kush changed India’s political map. The number was unusual. Many invaders were Central Asian, including Turkic and Afghan groups. Some wanted riches, territory, or to force religious beliefs.
keyPoints: Medieval means the 11th to 17th centuries in this book.
Invasions from beyond the Hindu Kush changed India’s political map.
Some invaders wanted riches, territory, or religious control.
activities.explanation: These points introduce medieval India and the changes linked to new invasions.

events.label: A new era in India’s history began
The Delhi Sultanate was formed after King
The Musunuri confederacy expelled Muhammad bin
Timur’s forces launched a devastating attack
Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle
A coalition of Deccan Sultanates defeated

activities.title: Walk through time

tasks.say: Move to when this happened: The Delhi Sultanate was formed after King.
Go forward to the last event.
tasks.then: The latest event here is from 1565 CE.

activities.takeaway: Put events in order, and remember that BCE years count down towards 1 CE.
activities.explanation: Put events in order, and remember that BCE years count down towards 1 CE.

activities.prompt: A child sees a map of crossing places and a timeline of important dates. The child asks why neither gives every answer. How should the teacher explain this?
steps: Maps show places crossed by armies, traders, and travellers, so they help picture movement.
Many outside invasions changed India's political map, so crossing places help reveal this change.
Timelines show only important reference dates, so they do not list every event.
Historians disagree about the medieval ending, so the child should expect limits and use both tools as guides.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where was the word first used?
activities.prompt: Where was the word “medieval” first used?
options: For a period in European history.
For a period in Indian history.
For a map of Indian trade routes.
For a study of Central Asian peoples.
activities.explanation: The word was first used for a period in European history.

activities.title: Match the Clues
activities.prompt: Match each clue to its correct match.
pairs: Places crossed by armies and travellers
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an idea with the matching lesson detail.

activities.title: The Medieval Period
activities.prompt: In this book, the medieval period runs from the ______ to the 17th centuries.
activities.hint: Use the first century named for this period.
activities.explanation: Yes. The medieval period runs from the 11th to the 17th centuries.

activities.title: Why Are Maps Useful?
activities.prompt: Why do the maps help you in this lesson?
options: See places crossed by armies and travellers.
See every date in India’s long history.
See the exact end of medieval India.
See how the word medieval began.
activities.explanation: The maps help you picture places crossed by armies, traders and other travellers.

activities.title: What Do We Know About the Invasions?
activities.prompt: Which pair of statements about the invasions is correct?
options: Many invaders were Central Asian, and their number was unusual.
Most invaders were local, and their number was ordinary.
All invaders came from the same group, and every invasion was local.
Some invaders came only for trade, and their number was ordinary.
activities.explanation: Correct. Many invaders were Central Asian, and the large number of invasions was unusual.

activities.prompt: Medieval was first used for European history. In this book, it means the 11th to 17th centuries. A student calls it an Indian word. What is the best correction?
options: It first described European history; this book uses it for India.
It first described India; Europe later began using it.
Central Asia first created it, and Europe later used it.
It only describes periods after India's medieval era ended.

why.It first described India; Europe later b: This reverses the word's first use and later spread.
why.Central Asia first created it, and Europ: This wrongly gives Central Asia the word's first use.
why.It only describes periods after India's: This wrongly limits the book's period to after the 11th century.

activities.explanation: This correctly joins Europe's first use with this book's use for India.

activities.prompt: Some historians disagree about India's medieval ending. Timelines show important reference points. How should a student read one?
options: It gives key reference points but may not settle the ending.
It proves one exact and universally agreed ending date.
It shows every event from all medieval centuries.
It identifies every place crossed by travellers.

why.It proves one exact and universally agre: Important reference dates do not prove one agreed ending.
why.It shows every event from all medieval c: A timeline marks reference points, not every medieval event.
why.It identifies every place crossed by tra: The fact about travellers belongs to maps, not timelines.

activities.explanation: Reference points can guide study without settling a disputed ending.

activities.prompt: Outside invasions changed India's political map. A government has a rule against such changes. An invading group wants territory. What does the chapter suggest?
options: The invasion can still change India's political map.
The rule must turn every invasion into a peaceful visit.
The group will care only about beliefs, not territory.
The political map will remain unchanged in every place.

why.The rule must turn every invasion into a: This wrongly assumes a government rule can erase the chapter's pattern.
why.The group will care only about beliefs,: This wrongly makes beliefs the group's only purpose.
why.The political map will remain unchanged: This assumes political change cannot follow outside invasion.

activities.explanation: This applies the stated link between outside invasions and political change.

lessons.title: The Delhi Sultanate: Rule, Conflict and Resistance

activities.prompt: Why did the Delhi Sultanate rise, clash, and face resistance?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding the Delhi Sultanate
activities.body: The Delhi Sultanate began after King Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated in 1192. Five foreign dynasties of Turkic–Afghan origin ruled it. The Mamluks were also called the Slave dynasty, while the Khiljis were also called Khaljis. The Sultanate faced political instability and tried to expand. Campaigns raided villages and cities and took wealth. Succession could be bloody. Local groups also resisted its advance.
keyPoints: Formed after Prithviraj Chauhan’s defeat in 1192
Five Turkic–Afghan dynasties ruled the Sultanate
Expansion, raids, instability, and resistance marked its rule
activities.explanation: This card connects the Sultanate’s rulers, campaigns, conflict, and resistance.

activities.prompt: A ruler wants a large army, while villagers fear losing their goods. How are these connected?
steps: Raids took wealth from villages and cities.
That wealth gave the Sultanate money.
The money helped pay for its large army.
So raids could support the army, even though people feared them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which name was also used for the Mamluks?
options: Slave dynasty
Khilji dynasty
Lodi dynasty
Hoysala kingdom
activities.explanation: The Mamluks were also called the Slave dynasty. This was another name for the same group.

activities.prompt: Match each group with its description in the lesson.
activities.explanation: These pairs show alternative names and two important facts about the Sultanate.

activities.prompt: What did the Sultanate combine?
options: Political instability and territorial expansion
Stable rule and reduced military spending
Peaceful successions and halted campaigns
Equal power and no territorial expansion
activities.explanation: The Sultanate faced political instability while trying to expand its territory. Both features shaped its rule.

activities.prompt: Timur invaded northwestern India from ______.
activities.hint: This was the region from which Timur entered India.
activities.explanation: Timur invaded northwestern India from Central Asia. His forces later attacked Delhi.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct time order.
items: The Lodis established the last dynasty
activities.explanation: Timur’s attack came before his withdrawal. The Lodis then established the last dynasty.

activities.prompt: Which leader conquered kingdoms during the Sultanate’s southward expansion?
options: Malik Kafur
Ala-ud-din Khilji
King Prithviraj Chauhan
Timur
activities.explanation: Malik Kafur conquered several kingdoms during the southward expansion. Ala-ud-din Khilji led northern and central campaigns.

activities.prompt: Soldiers take goods from a village. Why might the ruler welcome this?
options: The money can help pay for the Sultan's large army.
The money can make the village safe from attacks.
The money can stop the ruler from making campaigns.
The money can show that the village supports the raid.

why.The money can make the village safe from: This reverses the effect because raids did not make villages safer.
why.The money can stop the ruler from making: This reverses the effect because taking goods did not stop campaigns.
why.The money can show that the village supp: This confuses who loses wealth because raids took goods from villagers.

activities.explanation: This is right because wealth from conquest helped pay for the large army.

activities.prompt: A map shows two regions with resistance. What does it tell us?
options: Where the Sultan's advance met strong resistance from local powers.
Where the five foreign dynasties first came from.
When the Mamluks later received the Slave dynasty name.
Who ended the Sultanate after Timur later withdrew.

why.Where the five foreign dynasties first c: This confuses a map of resistance with a map of dynasty origins.
why.When the Mamluks later received the Slav: This confuses resistance with a later name for the Mamluks.
why.Who ended the Sultanate after Timur late: This confuses resistance with a later change of dynasty.

activities.explanation: This is right because the east and south resisted the Sultan's advance.

activities.prompt: A new sultan wins the throne through fighting. Campaigns continue. What fits?
options: Violent power changes and campaigns often happened together.
New rulers always ended campaigns after winning the throne.
Territorial expansion always began after peaceful successions.
Military campaigns always produced peaceful successions everywhere.

why.New rulers always ended campaigns after: This wrongly assumes that every violent change ended campaigns.
why.Territorial expansion always began after: This reverses the pattern because instability and expansion happened together.
why.Military campaigns always produced peace: This confuses campaigns with peaceful successions, which were not typical.

activities.explanation: This is right because instability and territorial expansion happened together.

activities.prompt: Soldiers enter a village. Families hide money. Why would they do this?
options: They expect the raid to carry away their wealth.
They expect the raid to leave their village richer.
They expect the raid to protect every house.
They expect the raid to make soldiers stop campaigning.

why.They expect the raid to leave their vill: This reverses the effect because raids took wealth instead of adding it.
why.They expect the raid to protect every ho: This misunderstands raids because they threatened villages rather than protected them.
why.They expect the raid to make soldiers st: This confuses the result of a raid with an end to military campaigns.

activities.explanation: This is right because military raids carried wealth away from villages.

activities.prompt: A map shows a path from Central Asia to Delhi. What can we learn?
options: Timur's forces attacked Delhi after entering northwestern India.
Timur began the first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.
The Mamluks came from villages in eastern India.
The Lodis ruled before Timur entered northwestern India.

why.Timur began the first dynasty of the Del: This mistakes an invader for the founder of the Sultanate.
why.The Mamluks came from villages in easter: This confuses the Mamluks' later name with Timur's place of origin.
why.The Lodis ruled before Timur entered nor: This reverses the order because the Lodis came after Timur withdrew.

activities.explanation: This is right because Timur invaded from Central Asia and then attacked Delhi.

activities.prompt: After Timur withdraws from Delhi, which claim fits the sequence?
options: The Lodis will establish the last Sultanate dynasty.
The Mamluks will establish the last dynasty after Timur.
The Khiljis will establish the last dynasty from Central Asia.
Timur will establish the last dynasty after withdrawing.

why.The Mamluks will establish the last dyna: This confuses an earlier dynasty with the dynasty established later.
why.The Khiljis will establish the last dyna: This confuses the Khiljis with Timur's place of origin.
why.Timur will establish the last dynasty af: This confuses the invader with the dynasty established after withdrawal.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Lodis established the last dynasty after Timur withdrew.

lessons.title: Resistance and the Vijayanagara Empire

activities.prompt: How could local rulers and mighty empires resist powerful invaders?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different Powers Fought Delhi
activities.body: Resistance means trying to stop another power from ruling you. The Delhi Sultanate failed to conquer Kalinga. The Musunuri Nayakas joined more than 75 chieftains against the Sultanate. Their confederacy, a joined group, drove out an army from Warangal around 1330–1336. The Hoysalas also defeated attacks and stayed independent. Harihara and Bukka Raya then founded Vijayanagara by rejecting Delhi’s authority.
keyPoints: Delhi could not conquer Kalinga.
The Musunuri Nayakas united more than 75 chieftains.
The Hoysalas stayed independent before the empire absorbed their kingdom.
activities.explanation: Resistance grew through military defence, united groups, and rulers claiming their own authority.

activities.prompt: Several small teams face one enemy team. How can they resist together?
steps: They should cooperate because united groups can face the same enemy.
Delhi failed to conquer Kalinga, showing that resistance could succeed.
The Musunuri confederacy united over 75 chieftains against the Sultanate.
It later expelled Delhi’s army from Warangal, showing united action could resist.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which power failed to conquer the Eastern Ganga kingdom of Kalinga?
options: Vijayanagara Empire
Delhi Sultanate
Bahmani Sultanate
Hoysala kingdom
activities.explanation: Kalinga remained unconquered because the Delhi Sultanate failed against it.

activities.prompt: The Hoysala kingdom was later absorbed into the ______ Empire.
activities.hint: Think of the empire that later included the Hoysala kingdom.
activities.explanation: The Hoysala kingdom later became part of the Vijayanagara Empire.

activities.prompt: Match each ruler or group with the event linked to them.
pairs: Built the Sūrya temple at Konark
Led the empire at its peak
activities.explanation: Narasimhadeva built Konark; the others united, founded, or led the empire.

activities.prompt: Why were Portuguese traders treated well in Vijayanagara?
options: The king wanted their horses
They wanted to join its army
They supplied temple builders
They gave the king spices
activities.explanation: The king wanted the traders’ horses, so he treated them well.

activities.prompt: Put the stages of the Bahmani Sultanate’s story in the correct order.
items: It rose in the mid-14th century.
It controlled much of the Deccan.
It broke into five Deccan Sultanates.
activities.explanation: It rose, controlled much of the Deccan, and later split into five states.

activities.prompt: What happened at the Battle of Talikota in 1565?
options: The Musunuri Nayakas expelled an army.
Portuguese traders received horses from the king.
A Deccan coalition defeated Vijayanagara.
The Hoysalas defeated a Delhi Sultanate attack.
activities.explanation: A coalition of Deccan Sultanates won at Talikota in 1565.

activities.prompt: Narasimhadeva I won victories and built the famous Sūrya temple. What can we understand about his rule?
options: It combined military strength with cultural achievement.
It focused only on war and ignored all culture.
It supported culture but showed no military strength.
It used temple building to avoid every military action.

why.It focused only on war and ignored all c: This mistake treats military strength as excluding cultural achievement.
why.It supported culture but showed no milit: This mistake ignores the victories that showed his military strength.
why.It used temple building to avoid every m: This mistake thinks building a temple meant avoiding military action.

activities.explanation: This is right because his victories and temple show both strengths.

activities.prompt: Delhi failed to conquer Kalinga. Later, over 75 chieftains expelled its army from Warangal. What does this show?
options: Local resistance could stop Delhi’s advances in more than one place.
Delhi won in Kalinga but failed only at Warangal.
Kalinga and Warangal were ruled by the same confederacy.
Delhi failed in both places because one copied the other’s method.

why.Delhi won in Kalinga but failed only at: This mistake reverses what happened in Kalinga.
why.Kalinga and Warangal were ruled by the s: This mistake assumes both places had the same rulers.
why.Delhi failed in both places because one: This mistake assumes one place copied the other’s method.

activities.explanation: Both Kalinga and Warangal stopped Delhi’s advance through resistance.

activities.prompt: The Hoysalas defeated several Delhi attacks and later joined the Vijayanagara Empire. How did their kingdom change?
options: It stayed independent first, then became part of the empire.
It joined the empire first, then became independent again.
It remained outside the empire and kept the same status.
It forced the empire to leave the south instead.

why.It joined the empire first, then became: This mistake reverses the order of independence and absorption.
why.It remained outside the empire and kept: This mistake ignores the later joining of their kingdom.
why.It forced the empire to leave the south: This mistake turns absorption into an expulsion of Vijayanagara.

activities.explanation: This is right because they stayed independent before being absorbed.

activities.prompt: A map shows Vijayanagara fighting Bijapur, Golconda and Odisha. Another source names Krishnadevaraya as its peak ruler. What do they show together?
options: Vijayanagara fought several powers and reached its greatest height.
Vijayanagara fought one power and reached its greatest height.
Vijayanagara fought several powers but never reached its greatest height.
Vijayanagara reached its greatest height before fighting any powers.

why.Vijayanagara fought one power and reache: This mistake reduces several fighting powers to only one.
why.Vijayanagara fought several powers but n: This mistake ignores the empire’s peak under Krishnadevaraya.
why.Vijayanagara reached its greatest height: This mistake puts the peak before the listed battles without support.

activities.explanation: The sources show several battles and a peak under one ruler.

activities.prompt: A king wants foreign traders to bring him horses. What policy should he choose?
options: Treat the traders well and welcome them to trade.
Treat them badly so they cannot meet other kings.
Keep them away because their horses are not useful.
Take their horses but refuse them any friendly treatment.

why.Treat them badly so they cannot meet oth: This mistake thinks being cruel would bring more horses.
why.Keep them away because their horses are: This mistake ignores that the king wanted their horses.
why.Take their horses but refuse them any fr: This mistake separates getting horses from treating traders well.

activities.explanation: This is right because the king wanted the traders’ horses.

activities.prompt: The Bahmani Sultanate rose in the mid-14th century. It broke into five Deccan Sultanates. Later, Deccan Sultanates defeated Vijayanagara. What sequence does this show?
options: The Deccan powers first divided, then joined against Vijayanagara.
The Deccan powers first joined, then divided against Vijayanagara.
The Deccan powers divided and never fought Vijayanagara again.
The Deccan powers joined Delhi and divided Vijayanagara five times.

why.The Deccan powers first joined, then div: This mistake reverses the order of division and joining.
why.The Deccan powers divided and never foug: This mistake ignores the later defeat of Vijayanagara.
why.The Deccan powers joined Delhi and divid: This mistake mixes the Deccan powers with Delhi and Vijayanagara.

activities.explanation: The five states later joined together to defeat Vijayanagara.
