lessons.title: The Mughals: Expansion, Rule and Decline

activities.prompt: What secrets lie behind the Mughals’ rise, rule, and decline?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Mughal Empire began
activities.body: Babur won the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. His victory relied on gunpowder, artillery and matchlock guns. It ended the Delhi Sultanate and began the Mughal Empire. Babur wrote the Baburnama, his autobiography. Humayun struggled to hold his father’s empire together. Sher Shah Suri founded the Sur Empire. Himu briefly ruled Delhi. Akbar combined conquest, tolerance and reforms. He abolished jizya and supported sulh-ikul, meaning “peace with all”.
keyPoints: Babur won the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
The victory began the Mughal Empire.
Akbar supported sulh-ikul, meaning “peace with all”.
activities.explanation: This lesson follows the Mughal rulers from Babur’s victory to Aurangzeb’s rule.

activities.prompt: A child sees old guns in a museum and asks why they changed a whole empire.
steps: Babur’s gunpowder weapons helped him defeat Ibrahim Lodi in 1526.
That victory ended the Delhi Sultanate and began the Mughal Empire.
Yet his Baburnama described him as brutal and ruthless.
So, winning power did not mean ruling gently.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Reforms, expansion and weakening
activities.body: Sher Shah Suri founded the Sur Empire and introduced lasting reforms. Himu captured Delhi and briefly ruled it before Akbar defeated him. Akbar combined conquest with political strategies, tolerance and reforms. He abolished jizya and promoted sulh-ikul, meaning “peace with all”. Aurangzeb’s rule saw the empire’s greatest geographical expansion. His wars drained the treasury and weakened Mughal administration.
keyPoints: Sher Shah Suri introduced lasting reforms.
Akbar combined conquest with tolerance and reforms.
Aurangzeb’s wars weakened Mughal administration.
activities.explanation: Mughal power grew widely, but costly wars later weakened its administration.

activities.prompt: Babur’s victory ended the Mughal Empire.
activities.explanation: Good try! His victory ended the Delhi Sultanate and began the Mughal Empire.

activities.prompt: Which weapon helped Babur at the First Battle of Panipat?
options: Delhi Sultanate
Matchlock guns
Mughal Empire
Baburnama
activities.explanation: Babur’s victory relied heavily on gunpowder, artillery and matchlock guns.

activities.prompt: Match each ruler with an event from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a ruler with an event described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Babur wrote an autobiography called the _______.
activities.hint: It is the name of Babur’s autobiography.
activities.explanation: The Baburnama is the name of Babur’s autobiography.

activities.prompt: What happened because of Aurangzeb’s wars?
options: They weakened Mughal administration
They strengthened Mughal administration
They increased the treasury
They repaired Mughal administration
activities.explanation: Aurangzeb’s wars drained the treasury and weakened the Mughal administration.

activities.prompt: The Mughal Empire reached its greatest geographical expansion under Aurangzeb.
activities.explanation: The Mughal Empire reached its greatest geographical expansion under Aurangzeb.

activities.prompt: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. His victory relied heavily on gunpowder, artillery and matchlock guns. What helped him win?
options: His gunpowder weapons gave him a strong military advantage.
His enemies had no effective weapons against his army.
His victory ended the Delhi Sultanate and began the Mughal Empire.
His own autobiography later described him as a kind ruler.

why.His enemies had no effective weapons aga: This wrongly assumes the enemy had no weapons.
why.His victory ended the Delhi Sultanate an: This confuses the victory's result with its military cause.
why.His own autobiography later described hi: This mistakes an autobiography for praise of Babur's character.

activities.explanation: Right: These weapons helped Babur win, as the facts state.

activities.prompt: A map shows the Mughal Empire at its greatest geographical expansion under Aurangzeb. His wars also drained the treasury and weakened the Mughal administration. What can we conclude?
options: The empire covered more land, but its administration was weaker.
The empire covered less land, but its administration was stronger.
The empire had strong finances, but it covered less land.
The empire was small, strong, and free from war.

why.The empire covered less land, but its ad: This wrongly reverses both the map's size and the administration's strength.
why.The empire had strong finances, but it c: This wrongly treats strong finances as a fact about Aurangzeb.
why.The empire was small, strong, and free f: This wrongly ignores both the map's size and the effect of wars.

activities.explanation: Right: Greatest expansion and weaker administration happened under Aurangzeb.

lessons.sceneAlt: A Mughal folio shows Babur crossing the River Saun in an ink illustration from the Baburnama.
lessons.sceneCaption: Babur crosses the River Saun in this 1598 ink folio from the illustrated Baburnama.

sceneCredit.text: Babur crossing the River Saun, Folio of Babur Nama by Jaganath, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Jaganath

lessons.title: Resistance to the Mughals

activities.prompt: Who stood up against the Mughals, and how did they do it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Many Forms of Resistance
activities.body: Resistance came from many communities. Peasants rebelled against harsh treatment and heavy exploitation. Tribal groups fought annexation and taxes. Rani Durgavati led a large army. Maharana Pratap refused Mughal authority and used guerrilla warfare. The Ahoms organised labour, public works and defence. Sikh Gurus taught equality, stood by their faith and organised defence. Maharaja Ranjit Singh united Sikh confederacies and founded a powerful Sikh Empire.
keyPoints: Peasants and tribal groups fought harsh treatment, annexation and taxes.
Rani Durgavati led an army, while Maharana Pratap refused Mughal authority.
The Ahoms and Sikh Gurus organised defence in different ways.
activities.explanation: Different communities resisted the Mughals in many ways.

activities.prompt: A village faces harsh treatment and heavy taxes. How can people resist?
steps: Peasant communities rebelled because the burden had become too harsh.
The Jat rebellion showed that many fighters could challenge the Mughal army.
Tribal groups fought back against annexation and taxes.
With Bhil help, Pratap showed that local knowledge could strengthen guerrilla resistance.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did many peasant communities do during resistance to the Mughals?
options: Rebelled against harsh treatment
Moved to the Aravalli hills
Fought as Mughal soldiers
Formed the Ahom paik system
activities.explanation: Many peasant communities rebelled because they faced harsh treatment and heavy exploitation.

activities.prompt: During one Jat rebellion, 20,000 men fought valiantly against the Mughal army.
activities.explanation: The lesson tells us that 20,000 men fought valiantly during one Jat rebellion.

activities.prompt: Rani Durgavati led an army of 20,000 soldiers and ______ elephants.
activities.hint: Think about the elephants in her army.
activities.explanation: Rani Durgavati led 20,000 soldiers and 1,000 elephants.

activities.prompt: Match each leader with the action described in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each leader took a different step in teaching, defending faith or organising Sikh forces.

activities.prompt: How did the Bhils support Maharana Pratap?
options: Supported him as archers
Refused him all support
Created the Ahom paik system
Founded a powerful Sikh Empire
activities.explanation: The Bhils supported Pratap as archers. They also shared their knowledge of the terrain.

activities.prompt: Which statement shows two different forms of resistance in the lesson?
options: Pratap founded the Ahom system; Nanak led Durgavati’s army.
Durgavati formed the paik system; Pratap united Sikh confederacies.
Hargobind accepted Mughal authority; Ranjit Singh led Jat rebels.
Pratap used guerrilla warfare; Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa.
activities.explanation: Pratap used guerrilla warfare against the Mughals. Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa for justice and defence.

activities.prompt: Pratap used guerrilla warfare, while Durgavati led soldiers. What is the contrast?
options: Pratap used the hills; Durgavati led a large army.
Durgavati used the hills; Pratap led a large army.
Both used guerrilla warfare in the same open fields.
Both led armies of twenty thousand fighting men.

why.Durgavati used the hills; Pratap led a l: This swaps the two leaders' methods of resistance.
why.Both used guerrilla warfare in the same: This wrongly treats Durgavati as a guerrilla fighter.
why.Both led armies of twenty thousand fight: This wrongly gives Pratap Durgavati's army size.

activities.explanation: Pratap fought from the hills, while Durgavati led soldiers and elephants.

activities.prompt: Ahom men served for land rights. How did this build state strength?
options: It created public works and a large standing force.
It created a permanent army and no public works.
It removed all public duties from able-bodied men.
It left the state with neither labour nor soldiers.

why.It created a permanent army and no publi: This confuses a standing force with a permanent army.
why.It removed all public duties from able-b: This wrongly says public works needed no public service.
why.It left the state with neither labour no: This wrongly assumes the system removed labour and defence.

activities.explanation: The paik system built public works and a large standing force.

activities.prompt: A map shows Aravalli hills near Mewar. How did they aid Pratap?
options: Bhils helped Pratap use guerrilla warfare in the hills.
The Mughals used Bhil guides to find Pratap.
Bhils used their terrain knowledge for Mughal rulers.
Bhil support ended Pratap's resistance in the hills.

why.The Mughals used Bhil guides to find Pra: This wrongly assumes Bhils guided the Mughal army.
why.Bhils used their terrain knowledge for M: This reverses who the Bhils supported.
why.Bhil support ended Pratap's resistance i: This wrongly assumes Bhil knowledge ended the resistance.

activities.explanation: Bhil support and terrain knowledge helped Pratap use guerrilla warfare.

activities.prompt: Guru Gobind Singh formed the Khalsa. Why did this strengthen Sikh resistance?
options: It united Sikhs around justice and defending their faith.
It gave every Sikh a permanent post in government.
It encouraged Sikh communities to leave their faith.
It replaced Sikh teaching with service to Mughal rulers.

why.It gave every Sikh a permanent post in g: This wrongly treats the Khalsa as a government jobs system.
why.It encouraged Sikh communities to leave: This wrongly assumes the Khalsa weakened Sikh faith.
why.It replaced Sikh teaching with service t: This wrongly claims the Khalsa served Mughal rulers.

activities.explanation: The Khalsa united Sikhs around justice and defence of faith.

lessons.sceneCaption: Rani Durgavati prepares for the Battle of Narrai in a fresco-secco painting by Beohar Rammanohar Sinha.

lessons.title: Administration and People’s Lives

activities.prompt: How did rulers shape the everyday lives of people in medieval India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Empire Was Organised
activities.body: The Delhi Sultanate’s government centred on the sultan, who held absolute authority. A council of ministers assisted him and controlled departments. Akbar divided major work among officials. His ministers served in twelve subahs. Officers maintained troops and animals by rank under mansabdari. Village self-government continued. Agriculture formed the economy’s foundation, and rulers often took one-fifth of the harvest.
keyPoints: The sultan held absolute authority.
Different officials handled major work.
Village self-government continued under Mughal rule.
Agriculture formed the economy’s foundation.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how rulers organised authority, officials, village life and revenue.

activities.prompt: A peasant sells grain and pays trade tax. He also gives one-fifth of the harvest. Why is his income low?
steps: Trade taxes weighed heavily on peasants, because they paid the largest share.
The peasant’s income came from farming, because agriculture was the economy’s foundation.
Rulers often took one-fifth of the harvest, because this supplied land revenue.
So trade tax and land revenue leave the farmer with less income.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Sultan’s Authority
activities.prompt: Which statement best describes the sultan’s power?
options: The sultan held limited authority.
The sultan held absolute authority.
The sultan served under village councils.
The sultan worked as a village official.
activities.explanation: Good choice. The sultan held absolute authority, while ministers only assisted him.

activities.title: The Iqta System
activities.prompt: Under the iqta system, nobles collected taxes from ______ territories for the sultan.
activities.hint: These territories were given to nobles.
activities.explanation: Good try. Assigned territories gave nobles tax-collecting duties for the sultan.

activities.prompt: A council of ministers assisted the sultan and controlled the Sultanate’s departments.
activities.explanation: Correct. The council assisted the sultan and controlled the Sultanate’s departments.

activities.title: Roles and Responsibilities
activities.prompt: Match each description with its matching detail.
activities.explanation: Great matching. Each pair links a role with its duty or payment.

activities.title: The Burden of Trade Taxes
activities.prompt: Who bore the heaviest burden of trade taxes?
options: Peasants bore the heaviest burden.
Peasants were freed from trade taxes.
Trade taxes were paid by nobles.
Trade taxes no longer affected farmers.
activities.explanation: You are right. Trade taxes burdened the peasantry most heavily.

activities.title: Payment for Mansabdars
activities.prompt: How were mansabdars usually paid?
options: Often as land assignments.
Often as military ranks.
Often as village offices.
Often as trade grants.
activities.explanation: Correct. Mansabdars were usually paid with land assignments called jagirs.

activities.prompt: The sultan held final authority. His council helped run departments. What does this show?
options: The sultan led; ministers assisted with departments.
Ministers led; the sultan obeyed their advice.
The council replaced the sultan and made every decision.
Departments worked without any ruler or minister.

why.Ministers led; the sultan obeyed their a: This wrongly treats assistants as leaders who replaced the sultan.
why.The council replaced the sultan and made: This wrongly ignores the sultan’s absolute authority.
why.Departments worked without any ruler or: This wrongly removes both the sultan and ministers from government.

activities.explanation: The sultan had absolute authority, while ministers assisted him.

activities.prompt: Akbar assigns ministers to twelve regions. Why would this help manage the government?
options: To divide government work across many regions.
To let one minister control the whole government.
To remove ministers from all regional duties.
To give each region its own separate sultan.

why.To let one minister control the whole go: This wrongly imagines one minister controlled all regional work.
why.To remove ministers from all regional du: This wrongly treats regional posts as duties ministers no longer held.
why.To give each region its own separate sul: This wrongly assumes each region became a separate sultanate.

activities.explanation: Akbar divided work among officials serving in twelve subahs.

activities.prompt: A noble receives assigned land. What does the iqta system require?
options: Collect taxes there for the sultan.
Keep all taxes for his own use.
Give the land to local peasants.
Lead the sultan’s council of ministers.

This wrongly lets the noble keep the sultan’s taxes.
This wrongly treats assigned land as a gift to peasants.
This wrongly mixes a noble’s duty with council membership.

activities.explanation: Under iqta, nobles collected taxes from assigned territories for the sultan.

activities.prompt: A high-rank mansabdar receives a jagir. What must he provide?
options: Troops and animals matching his rank.
More trade goods for the local market.
Taxes from villages for the sultan.
Money for every village council.

This confuses military duties with the ruler’s trade work.
This confuses a mansabdar’s duty with an iqta noble’s tax duty.
This wrongly treats village councils as mansabdars’ main duty.

activities.explanation: His rank set troop and animal duties; jagirs usually paid him.

activities.prompt: Villagers manage local matters. Rulers also survey land for revenue. Which situation fits Mughal rule?
options: Village self-government continued alongside systematic land surveys.
Village councils replaced the ruler and surveyed every field.
Land surveys ended local government and created twelve subahs.
Mughal officials removed both village work and revenue surveys.

why.Land surveys ended local government and: This wrongly links land surveys to ending local government and creating subahs.
why.Mughal officials removed both village wo: This wrongly assumes Mughal officials removed both village work and land surveys.

activities.prompt: How does this book use the word “medieval,” and why can students not mark one universally accepted end date for medieval India?
activities.answer: In this book, “medieval” refers to the 11th to the 17th centuries, although the word was first used for a period in European history. Historians do not agree on when medieval India ended, so students cannot mark one universally accepted final date. The chapter presents a new era beginning in the early 11th century and examines political changes from the 13th century onwards. Its timelines identify important reference points rather than claim to list every event, while its maps help readers picture the places crossed by armies, traders, and other travellers.
points: Medieval is defined here as the 11th to the 17th centuries.
The word was first used for a period in European history.
Historians disagree about India's medieval end date.
Timelines mark only important reference points.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After King Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated in 1192, the Delhi Sultanate was formed and ruled by five foreign dynasties of Turkic–Afghan origin. Its rulers often combined political instability with territorial expansion. Campaigns raided villages and cities, carried away wealth, and helped pay for a large army, while successions could be bloody and violent. Later, Timur invaded from Central Asia and his forces devastated Delhi; after he withdrew, the Lodis established the last dynasty.
activities.prompt: The Sultanate needs to maintain a large army while continuing expansion. What should its rulers expect campaigns to do?
options: Seize resources from settlements so that conquests help maintain a large fighting force.
Take control of territory without harming settlements or removing resources.
Gather resources, then reduce the fighting force that conquests supported.
Avoid further campaigns because internal disorder makes expansion pointless.

why.Take control of territory without harmin: Campaigns harmed settlements and carried away wealth.
why.Gather resources, then reduce the fighti: Conquered wealth supported rather than reduced the army.
why.Avoid further campaigns because internal: The Sultanate continued expanding despite instability.

activities.explanation: Raiding and taking wealth supplied resources for the large army.

activities.context: After King Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated in 1192, the Delhi Sultanate was formed and ruled by five foreign dynasties of Turkic–Afghan origin. Its rulers often combined political instability with territorial expansion. Campaigns raided villages and cities, carried away wealth, and helped pay for a large army, while successions could be bloody and violent. Later, Timur invaded from Central Asia and his forces devastated Delhi; after he withdrew, the Lodis established the last dynasty.
activities.prompt: If new sultans repeatedly succeed one another through bloody and violent successions, what condition in the case is most likely to worsen?
options: Internal disorder at the centre of the Sultanate.
Greater stability at the centre of the Sultanate.
The end of resistance to the Sultanate’s advance.
A complete halt to attempts to expand territory.

why.Greater stability at the centre of the S: Violent successions did not produce greater stability.
why.The end of resistance to the Sultanate’s: The case does not connect them with resistance ending.

activities.explanation: Bloody successions were linked to political instability.

activities.context: After the Musunuri Nayakas brought together more than 75 chieftains, their confederacy expelled Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s army from Warangal around 1330–1336. In the south, the Hoysalas defeated several Delhi Sultanate attacks and remained independent. Harihara and Bukka Raya then rejected Delhi’s authority and founded the Vijayanagara Empire. The Bahmani Sultanate later broke into five Deccan Sultanates, while Vijayanagara reached its peak under Krishnadevaraya.
activities.prompt: If the Musunuri Nayakas had brought together far fewer than 75 chieftains against the Sultanate, what would most likely have happened?
options: Their resistance would probably have been weaker because fewer chieftains would be united.
Their resistance would probably have been stronger because a smaller group could make faster decisions.
Their resistance would probably have been unchanged because the number of chieftains made no difference.
Their resistance would probably have been stronger because fewer chieftains would create less confusion.

why.Their resistance would probably have bee: A smaller group might still resist, but this overlooks the importance of united support.
The success of more than 75 chieftains shows that their numbers mattered.
This overlooks the strength provided by bringing many chieftains together.

activities.explanation: A large alliance strengthened resistance against the Sultanate.

activities.context: After the Musunuri Nayakas brought together more than 75 chieftains, their confederacy expelled Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s army from Warangal around 1330–1336. In the south, the Hoysalas defeated several Delhi Sultanate attacks and remained independent. Harihara and Bukka Raya then rejected Delhi’s authority and founded the Vijayanagara Empire. The Bahmani Sultanate later broke into five Deccan Sultanates, while Vijayanagara reached its peak under Krishnadevaraya.
activities.prompt: If Vijayanagara’s authority expanded into the southern region where the independent Hoysala kingdom was located, what result would be supported by the history?
options: The Hoysala kingdom would eventually be absorbed into the Vijayanagara Empire.
The Hoysala kingdom would become one of the five Deccan Sultanates.
The Hoysala kingdom would remain permanently independent because it had defeated earlier attacks.
The Hoysala kingdom would defeat Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota.

why.The Hoysala kingdom would become one of: The Deccan Sultanates arose from the breakup of the Bahmani Sultanate.
why.The Hoysala kingdom would remain permane: Earlier victories did not prevent later absorption into Vijayanagara.
why.The Hoysala kingdom would defeat Vijayan: The Deccan Sultanate coalition, not the Hoysalas, defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota.

activities.explanation: The Hoysala kingdom was later absorbed into Vijayanagara.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Muhammad bin Tughlaq founded the Vijayanagara Empire.
Reason (R): Harihara and Bukka Raya rejected Delhi’s authority and founded the Vijayanagara Empire.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because Harihara and Bukka Raya, not Muhammad bin Tughlaq, founded Vijayanagara.

activities.prompt: Explain how the resistance of the Musunuri confederacy and the Hoysalas showed that the Delhi Sultanate’s power was limited.
activities.answer: The Musunuri confederacy showed resistance through united action. The Musunuri Nayakas brought together more than 75 chieftains against the Sultanate, and the confederacy expelled Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s army from Warangal around 1330–1336. The Hoysalas also resisted Delhi, but their situation was different: they defeated several Delhi Sultanate attacks and remained independent in the south. The Musunuri example therefore emphasizes the strength of a large alliance, while the Hoysala example shows how repeated military victories helped a southern kingdom keep its independence.
points: More than 75 chieftains were united against the Sultanate.
The Musunuri confederacy expelled Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s army from Warangal.
The Hoysalas defeated several Delhi Sultanate attacks.
Both examples show successful resistance and the limits of Delhi’s power.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A class is preparing a role-play about how Mughal rule changed over time. In the first scene, Babur faces Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, and students must explain why his side has an important battle advantage. After Babur dies, Humayun struggles to hold the empire together. Later scenes show Akbar combining conquest with tolerance and reforms, while Aurangzeb’s wars put heavy pressure on the treasury and administration.
activities.prompt: If the role-play removes the military technology that helped Babur win, which prediction about the battle is best supported?
options: Babur’s victory would probably have been harder to secure.
Babur’s victory would probably have been easier to secure.
Babur’s victory would probably have been secured just as easily.
Babur’s victory would probably have required no military advantage.

why.Babur’s victory would probably have been: Removing an important advantage would not make victory easier.
Heavy reliance means its absence would affect the outcome.
why.Babur’s victory would probably have requ: The weapons were important to his success.

activities.explanation: Babur relied heavily on these weapons.

activities.context: A class is preparing a role-play about how Mughal rule changed over time. In the first scene, Babur faces Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, and students must explain why his side has an important battle advantage. After Babur dies, Humayun struggles to hold the empire together. Later scenes show Akbar combining conquest with tolerance and reforms, while Aurangzeb’s wars put heavy pressure on the treasury and administration.
activities.prompt: If Humayun had inherited an empire that was already firmly united, which result would be most reasonable?
options: His main difficulty after inheriting power would probably have been reduced.
His main difficulty after inheriting power would probably have increased.
His main difficulty after inheriting power would probably have remained unchanged.
His main difficulty after inheriting power would probably have disappeared at once.

why.His main difficulty after inheriting pow: Uniting it further would add difficulty, not remove it.
His recorded difficulty would probably have changed.
A smaller problem would not vanish immediately without any effort.

activities.explanation: A united empire would make control easier.

activities.context: A class is preparing a role-play about how Mughal rule changed over time. In the first scene, Babur faces Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, and students must explain why his side has an important battle advantage. After Babur dies, Humayun struggles to hold the empire together. Later scenes show Akbar combining conquest with tolerance and reforms, while Aurangzeb’s wars put heavy pressure on the treasury and administration.
activities.prompt: If Aurangzeb had reduced the wars that harmed the empire, which result would be most reasonable?
options: Less financial and administrative strain would probably have resulted.
More financial and administrative strain would probably have resulted.
A geographically smaller Mughal Empire would probably have resulted.
A quicker weakening of the Mughal administration would probably have resulted.

why.More financial and administrative strain: Reducing such wars would remove some of the pressure.
why.A geographically smaller Mughal Empire w: Fewer wars would not necessarily make the empire smaller.
why.A quicker weakening of the Mughal admini: Reduced wars would tend to lessen, not increase, administrative strain.

activities.explanation: Those wars drained the treasury and weakened administration.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Mughal Empire began after Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
Reason (R): Babur’s victory relied heavily on gunpowder, artillery and matchlock guns.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both are true, but the weapons explain how Babur won rather than why his victory marked the beginning of the empire.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Aurangzeb’s wars weakened the Mughal administration.
Reason (R): Those wars drained the treasury.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Draining the treasury helped cause the administrative weakening.

activities.prompt: Explain how Babur’s military advantage and his written account together give a mixed picture of the founder of the Mughal Empire.
activities.answer: Babur’s victory at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 relied heavily on gunpowder, artillery and matchlock guns. These weapons helped him defeat Ibrahim Lodi, end the Delhi Sultanate and begin the Mughal Empire. However, Baburnama does not present him only as a successful ruler. It also describes him as a brutal and ruthless conqueror. Thus, the military details explain why he achieved power, while his autobiography reveals that his conquests could be harsh.
points: Explains the importance of gunpowder, artillery and matchlock guns.
Links the victory with the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of the Mughal Empire.
Identifies Baburnama as Babur’s autobiography.
Explains that the autobiography also portrays him as brutal and ruthless.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community follows the Ahom paik system. Able-bodied men perform labour or military service in return for land rights. The Ahoms maintain public works and a large standing force without establishing a permanent army. When leaders consider how to meet public obligations and prepare for danger, they must decide how duties should be shared among eligible men without weakening either responsibility.
activities.prompt: The leaders believe that every able-bodied man must stop all public work and join a permanent army. What correction should they make?
options: Use the paik system to combine labour or military service with land rights, while maintaining a standing force rather than a permanent army.
Choose labour service only and end all military service under the paik system.
Create a permanent army and give up the public works supported by the community.
Remove the standing force because military service alone should meet every community obligation.

why.Choose labour service only and end all m: Paik service may include labour or military duty, so choosing only labour is incomplete.
why.Create a permanent army and give up the: The Ahoms maintained public works as well as a standing force.
why.Remove the standing force because milita: Military service is only one part of the system; removing the standing force would weaken defence.

activities.explanation: The system links able-bodied men's service with land rights and does not require a permanent army.

activities.context: A community follows the Ahom paik system. Able-bodied men perform labour or military service in return for land rights. The Ahoms maintain public works and a large standing force without establishing a permanent army. When leaders consider how to meet public obligations and prepare for danger, they must decide how duties should be shared among eligible men without weakening either responsibility.
activities.prompt: Why can the Ahom arrangement support both community obligations and defence?
options: Land rights alone remove the need for able-bodied men to perform any service.
Public works replace military service whenever danger increases.
Because service is tied to land rights, while public works and defence are maintained by a large force that does not require a permanent army.
A standing force is identical to a permanent army and therefore fulfils every obligation by itself.

why.Land rights alone remove the need for ab: Land rights are given in return for service, so they do not remove the need to serve.
why.Public works replace military service wh: Public works and military service are separate responsibilities within the arrangement.
why.A standing force is identical to a perma: The Ahoms maintained a large standing force without establishing a permanent army.

activities.explanation: This explanation connects land rights, public works, the standing force and the absence of a permanent army.

activities.context: A community follows the Ahom paik system. Able-bodied men perform labour or military service in return for land rights. The Ahoms maintain public works and a large standing force without establishing a permanent army. When leaders consider how to meet public obligations and prepare for danger, they must decide how duties should be shared among eligible men without weakening either responsibility.
activities.prompt: If the community neglects public works but continues military service under the paik system, what result would most likely follow?
options: The community may retain its standing force and land rights, but the public works supported by the system could suffer.
All land rights would immediately disappear because the community neglected public works.
The standing force would automatically become a permanent army.
Military service would no longer be connected with land rights.

why.All land rights would immediately disapp: The system links service with land rights, but it does not state that public works must also continue.
why.The standing force would automatically b: A standing force does not automatically change into a permanent army.
why.Military service would no longer be conn: The stated connection between service and land rights remains unless the arrangement itself changes.

activities.explanation: Neglecting one responsibility need not remove service-based land rights or the standing force.

lessons.title: Who Were the Marathas?

activities.prompt: How did Marathi songs and devotion become a path to political power?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Marathas and Their Cultural Foundation
activities.body: The Marathas came from the Deccan plateau, especially present-day Maharashtra. They spoke Marathi. It had a rich literary history since the 12th century. In the 13th century, the Yadava dynasty ruled most of Maharashtra. Later, Delhi's Khilji Sultanate defeated it. Saints preferred bhakti, meaning devotion to the divine. Their songs, poetry and social work built a cultural foundation. This later helped the Marathas organise as political power.
keyPoints: The Marathas came from the Deccan plateau.
Marathi literature and bhakti strengthened their shared culture.
Their cultural foundation helped them organise politically.
activities.explanation: These ideas trace the Marathas from their home to their later political power.

events.label: Marathi had a rich and continuous literary history
During the 13th century, most of Maharashtra
Chhatrapati Shivaji was born
Shivaji was crowned at Raigad
Under Mahadji Shinde, the Marathas recaptured Delhi

activities.title: Walk through time

tasks.say: Move to when this happened: During the 13th century, most of Maharashtra.
Go forward to the last event.
tasks.then: The latest event here is from 1771 CE.

activities.takeaway: Put events in order, and remember that BCE years count down towards 1 CE.
activities.explanation: Put events in order, and remember that BCE years count down towards 1 CE.

activities.prompt: A child sees Marathi devotional poems shared by many people. How could this help the Marathas organise later?
steps: Since the 12th century, Marathi literature gave the Marathas a shared base.
Saints used ordinary people's languages, so devotion could spread widely.
Translating holy texts into Marathi let people share the same devotion.
This cultural foundation later helped the Marathas organise as a political power.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which place was the Marathas' home region?
options: The Deccan plateau
Present-day Delhi
The Yadava dynasty
The Khilji Sultanate
activities.explanation: The Marathas came from the Deccan plateau, especially present-day Maharashtra.

activities.prompt: Match each name with its correct detail.
pairs: Rich literary history since the 12th century
Ruled most of Maharashtra in the 13th century
activities.explanation: These details connect the Marathas' homeland, language and early political history.

activities.prompt: Marathi had a rich and continuous literary history since the ______ century.
activities.hint: Choose the century named in your lesson.
activities.explanation: Marathi's rich and continuous literary history began in the 12th century.

activities.prompt: What did bhakti mean?
options: Devotion to the divine
Rule by a dynasty
Defeat of a kingdom
A literary history
activities.explanation: Bhakti meant devotion to the divine or to a particular deity.

activities.prompt: Put these developments in the order given by the lesson.

Yadava rule over most of Maharashtra in the 13th century
Defeat of the Yadava dynasty by the Khilji Sultanate

activities.explanation: The literary history came first, followed by Yadava rule and its later defeat.

activities.prompt: Which important texts did some saints translate into Marathi?
options: The Upaniṣhads and the Bhagavad Gītā
The Upaniṣhads and Marathi devotional songs
The Bhagavad Gītā and Yadava dynasty rule
The Yadava dynasty and Khilji Sultanate rule
activities.explanation: Some saints translated the Upaniṣhads and the Bhagavad Gītā into Marathi.

activities.prompt: Marathi had a rich literary history since the 12th century. How could this culture help Marathas gain political power later?
options: Their shared culture helped them organise as a political power.
Their rich literary history stopped them from organising politically.
Their shared language led them to organise only religious ceremonies.
Their literary history was the only way they organised politically.

why.Their rich literary history stopped them: This mistake thinks a literary history prevents political organisation.
why.Their shared language led them to organi: This mistake confuses political organisation with only religious ceremonies.
why.Their literary history was the only way: This mistake treats literature as the only possible way to organise.

activities.explanation: This is right because culture later helped the Marathas organise politically.

activities.prompt: A source lists Marathi translations of the Upaniṣhads and Bhagavad Gītā. What does this show about the Marathas' religious culture?
options: Saints brought important sacred texts into Marathi.
Saints stopped using Marathi for sacred poetry.
Only devotional songs, not sacred texts, used Marathi.
Sacred texts were translated from Marathi into other languages.

why.Saints stopped using Marathi for sacred: This mistake says translation ended Marathi's use for devotional poetry.
why.Only devotional songs, not sacred texts,: This mistake thinks only songs, rather than sacred texts, used Marathi.
why.Sacred texts were translated from Marath: This mistake reverses the direction of the translation.

activities.explanation: This is right because the saints translated important texts into Marathi.

activities.prompt: Some Maratha saints sing devotional songs and help neighbours organise. What best explains their behaviour?
options: They joined devotion with work for social organisation.
They treated social organisation as a replacement for devotion.
They helped organise people but rejected all devotion.
They used devotion only for private matters, not community life.

why.They treated social organisation as a re: This mistake treats devotion and social work as separate choices.
why.They helped organise people but rejected: This mistake thinks social organisation required rejecting devotion.
why.They used devotion only for private matt: This mistake believes devotion could not support community life.

activities.explanation: This is right because bhakti is devotion and saints also organised society.

activities.prompt: Bhakti meant devotion to the divine. The Marathas' culture included saints from across India. They wrote in ordinary people's languages. Why did this help their teaching reach people?
options: Ordinary people could understand the songs and poems more easily.
Only trained experts could understand the ordinary-language songs.
The songs were meant to keep ordinary people away from devotion.
Writing in ordinary languages made devotion harder for people to follow.

why.Only trained experts could understand th: This mistake assumes only trained experts could understand the songs.
why.The songs were meant to keep ordinary pe: This mistake treats the songs as a way to keep people away.
why.Writing in ordinary languages made devot: This mistake thinks ordinary languages made devotion harder to follow.

activities.explanation: This is right because ordinary-language songs were easier for people to understand.

activities.title: Shivaji’s Early Rise
activities.body: Shivaji was born in 1630 in the Bhonsle clan. He grew up in his jāgīr at Pune under Jijabai and trusted officials. Shahji served the Deccan sultanates and was often away from his family. Pune suffered from constant fighting among the Deccan sultans. At sixteen, Shivaji began campaigns, captured forts, and developed his vision of Swarājya. He used guerrilla warfare and defeated Afzal Khan’s army at Pratapgad.
keyPoints: Shivaji was born in 1630 in the Bhonsle clan.
He grew up in his jāgīr at Pune.
He used guerrilla warfare and captured forts.
activities.explanation: These events show how Shivaji grew from childhood to a powerful leader.

He captured forts because this strengthened his hold over the Pune region.
Together, steady guidance and stronger control helped his early plans for Swarājya grow.

Shivaji’s vision of Swarājya grows over the years.
activities.explanation: The order moves from Shivaji’s birth to his campaigns and growing vision.

activities.prompt: What happened after Shivaji and his advisers persuaded Afzal Khan to meet them at Pratapgad?
options: Shivaji left Pratapgad; both armies stayed safe.
The meeting failed; both armies went home.
Afzal Khan took forts; Marathas withdrew.
Shivaji killed Afzal Khan; hidden Marathas routed the army.
activities.explanation: Shivaji killed Afzal Khan, and hidden Marathas routed the Khan’s army.

activities.prompt: Shivaji’s father was often away. How could this shape his childhood?
options: Jijabai and trusted officials became his main guides.
Deccan sultans became his main guides at home.
Afzal Khan became his main guide during childhood.
Hidden Marathas became his main guides while he grew.

why.Deccan sultans became his main guides at: This confuses rulers involved in fighting with his trusted guides.
why.Afzal Khan became his main guide during: This confuses a later opponent with the people who guided him.
why.Hidden Marathas became his main guides w: This confuses soldiers hidden for battle with his childhood guides.

activities.explanation: Shivaji grew up under Jijabai and trusted officials in Pune.

activities.prompt: A map marks forts captured by Shivaji around Pune. What can we reasonably infer from the map?
options: His captured forts helped strengthen his hold over Pune.
His captured forts helped weaken his hold over Pune.
His captured forts lay only outside the Deccan region.
His captured forts show that fighting in Pune had ended.

why.His captured forts helped weaken his hol: This reverses the effect of capturing forts.
why.His captured forts lay only outside the: A map of forts near Pune does not place them only elsewhere.
why.His captured forts show that fighting in: Stronger control does not mean that all fighting in Pune had ended.

activities.explanation: Capturing forts strengthened his control over the Pune region.

activities.prompt: At a school game, a small team faces a much bigger team. Which plan follows guerrilla warfare?
options: Move fast and use surprise to attack the bigger team.
Stay still and wait for the bigger team to attack.
Gather many players and move slowly toward their goal.
Leave the game because the bigger team looks stronger.

why.Stay still and wait for the bigger team: This uses waiting and lack of surprise, the opposite of guerrilla tactics.
why.Gather many players and move slowly towa: This relies on size and slow movement rather than small, fast groups.
why.Leave the game because the bigger team l: This gives up before using the speed and surprise of guerrilla warfare.

activities.explanation: Guerrilla warfare uses speed and surprise against larger armies.

activities.prompt: Shivaji and his advisers brought Afzal Khan to Pratapgad. Why was this meeting useful for Shivaji?
options: Hidden Marathas could surprise and defeat the Khan’s army.
The meeting gave every Maratha a place in the army.
The meeting made the Deccan sultans stop their fighting.
The meeting allowed Shivaji to lead the Khan’s army.

why.The meeting gave every Maratha a place i: This misreads a battle meeting as a way to join the army.
why.The meeting made the Deccan sultans stop: This mistakes one battle meeting for an end to wider fighting.
why.The meeting allowed Shivaji to lead the: This mistakes defeating a commander for taking command of his army.

activities.explanation: Hidden Marathas routed the Khan’s army after Shivaji killed him.

activities.prompt: Shivaji began military campaigns at sixteen, but his vision of Swarājya grew over years. What does this order show?
options: Military action began before his kingdom vision was fully formed.
Military action began only after his kingdom vision was complete.
His kingdom vision began before any military action started.
Military action and his kingdom vision began at the same time.

why.Military action began only after his kin: This reverses the order between early campaigns and the later vision.
why.His kingdom vision began before any mili: This reverses the order between the early campaigns and the growing vision.
why.Military action and his kingdom vision b: This treats a vision that grew over years as fully present at the start.

activities.explanation: The campaigns started at sixteen, while the vision grew over years.

lessons.sceneCaption: A historical illustration from M. V. Dhurandhar’s series on Shivaji’s life shows his journey on horseback to Purandar.

lessons.title: The Navy, the Mughals and the Coronation

activities.prompt: How did a daring leader outsmart a mighty empire and win a crown?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: From Navy to Crown
activities.body: Shivaji established the Maratha Navy. Its exploits became legendary. He raided Shaista Khan’s camp at night with few soldiers. He sacked Surat, sparing religious places. He conceded defeat at Purandar Fort and made a treaty. Aurangzeb held him under house arrest. Shivaji and Sambhaji escaped in baskets of gifts. Shivaji was crowned at Raigad in 1674 with full Vedic rites. His southern expansion gave the Marathas great strategic depth.
keyPoints: Shivaji established the Maratha Navy.
He avoided religious places during the sack of Surat.
Shivaji and Sambhaji escaped in baskets of gifts.
Shivaji was crowned at Raigad in 1674.
activities.explanation: These events trace Shivaji’s Navy, Mughal conflict, escape and coronation.

activities.prompt: Shivaji is under house arrest. How can he get free and become a crowned ruler?
steps: First, he must leave because house arrest stops him acting freely.
He and Sambhaji escape by hiding in baskets of gifts.
After escaping, he is crowned at Raigad with full Vedic rites.
Only then can he begin his conquest of the South.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Founder of the Navy
activities.prompt: Who established the Maratha Navy?
options: Shivaji
Aurangzeb
Sambhaji
Shaista Khan
activities.explanation: Shivaji established the Maratha Navy. Its exploits later became legendary.

activities.title: The Coronation Year
activities.prompt: Shivaji was crowned at Raigad in ______ with full Vedic rites.
activities.hint: Enter the year of his coronation.
activities.explanation: Shivaji was crowned at Raigad in 1674 with full Vedic rites.

activities.title: Match the People and Events
activities.prompt: Match each left item with the correct right item.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a person with an event from the lesson.

activities.title: After Purandar Fort
activities.prompt: What did Shivaji do after conceding defeat at Purandar Fort?
options: Placed Aurangzeb under house arrest
Stopped trade with Mughal ports
Made a Mughal peace treaty
Attacked religious places in Surat
activities.explanation: Shivaji had to concede defeat and make a treaty with the Mughals.

activities.title: The Escape Sequence
activities.prompt: Put these escape events in the order they happened.
items: Aurangzeb placed Shivaji under house arrest.
Shivaji and Sambhaji hid in baskets of gifts.
activities.explanation: House arrest came first. They then hid in gift baskets and escaped.

activities.title: Shivaji’s Last Days
activities.prompt: What claimed Shivaji’s life when he was fifty?
options: A battle
A shipwreck
A fever
A prison fire
activities.explanation: A fever claimed Shivaji’s life when he was fifty.

activities.prompt: A map gives Raigad a crown and Surat crossed swords. What can a reader learn?
options: Raigad means crowning; Surat means a sack.
Raigad means a sack; Surat means crowning.
Both marks show house arrest at those places.
Both marks show treaties made at those places.

why.Raigad means a sack; Surat means crownin: This reverses the symbols attached to the two places.
why.Both marks show house arrest at those pl: This mistakes house arrest for a map event.
why.Both marks show treaties made at those p: This mistakes a treaty for a map event.

activities.explanation: The crown and crossed swords match the events at those places.

activities.prompt: After his conquest of the South began, the Marathas gained strategic depth. What does this mean?
options: They could act from a deeper and stronger position.
They had won one larger naval battle.
They no longer had any need for the Navy.
They had become governors within the Mughal Empire.

This confuses expansion with one large naval victory.
why.They no longer had any need for the Navy: This wrongly treats expansion as making the Navy useless.
why.They had become governors within the Mug: This confuses Maratha expansion with Mughal rule.

activities.explanation: Southern expansion gave the Marathas great strategic depth.

activities.prompt: Shivaji and Sambhaji hid in baskets of gifts. Why could this help them escape house arrest?
options: The baskets could conceal them while they left the court.
The baskets could carry weapons for a large battle.
The gifts could make Aurangzeb release them.
The baskets could move them through a naval battle.

why.The baskets could carry weapons for a la: This wrongly treats the baskets as weapons carriers.
why.The gifts could make Aurangzeb release t: This wrongly thinks the gifts caused their release.
why.The baskets could move them through a na: This wrongly links the baskets to a naval battle.

activities.explanation: The baskets could conceal them while they left the court.

lessons.title: The Marathas after Shivaji

activities.prompt: Who led the Marathas after Shivaji, and what challenges did they face?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Changes after Shivaji
activities.body: After Shivaji’s death, Sambhaji became Chhatrapati. Rajaram became Chhatrapati and fled to Gingee. The Marathas often had the upper hand against the Mughals. Aurangzeb died without defeating them. The state decentralised as chiefs gained more power. The Peshwa, or prime minister, gained influence. Bajirao I and Nanasaheb Peshwa helped expansion across India. After defeat at Panipat in 1761, the Marathas recovered. Under Mahadji Shinde, they took Delhi again in 1771.
keyPoints: Sambhaji and Rajaram held the Chhatrapati position.
The chiefs gained more power as the state decentralised.
The Peshwa gained great influence over the Chhatrapati.
The Marathas expanded, suffered defeat and recovered.
activities.explanation: The Chhatrapati was the position held by Sambhaji and Rajaram.

activities.prompt: After Shivaji's death, how could the Marathas keep leaders while the Peshwa and chiefs gained more power?
steps: Sambhaji became Chhatrapati, so a new leader followed Shivaji.
Rajaram also became Chhatrapati, so leadership continued even when he fled.
The state became decentralised, so chiefs gained more power.
The Peshwa gained influence, so the ruler and chiefs both held power.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Imagine you are a guide. Who became the Chhatrapati after Shivaji’s death?
options: Rajaram
Sambhaji
Aurangzeb
Bajirao I
activities.explanation: Sambhaji became the Chhatrapati after Shivaji’s death.

activities.prompt: After their disastrous defeat at Panipat in ______, the Marathas soon recovered.
activities.hint: Think of the year of the defeat.
activities.explanation: The Marathas suffered a disastrous defeat at Panipat in 1761. They soon recovered.

activities.prompt: Match each person or office with the correct information.
activities.explanation: Each pair links a leader or office with information from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
activities.explanation: The defeat came first, followed by recovery. Delhi was taken again in 1771.

activities.prompt: According to the lesson, what helped make the Maratha state decentralised?
options: The Peshwa lost all influence
The chiefs gained more power
The state gained one stronger chief
The Mughals gained control of the state
activities.explanation: The Maratha state became decentralised as the chiefs gained more power.

activities.prompt: Which statement is fully supported by the lesson?
options: Aurangzeb defeated the Marathas and took Delhi.
Chiefs gained more power as the state decentralised.
Bajirao I alone helped the Marathas expand across India.
The British took more India from the Mughals.
activities.explanation: Chiefs gained more power as the state decentralised. The other statements conflict with the lesson.

activities.prompt: Fact: Sambhaji became Chhatrapati after Shivaji's death. Rajaram became Chhatrapati and fled to Gingee. What can we conclude?
options: The Marathas kept leaders, including one who fled to Gingee.
The Marathas lost leadership after Shivaji died.
Rajaram ruled before Sambhaji held the title.
Rajaram ruled after Maratha power had ended.

why.The Marathas lost leadership after Shiva: This treats one succession as the end of Maratha leadership.
why.Rajaram ruled before Sambhaji held the t: This reverses the order of Sambhaji and Rajaram.
why.Rajaram ruled after Maratha power had en: This assumes Maratha power ended before Rajaram ruled.

activities.explanation: Both successions show that Maratha leadership continued after Shivaji.

activities.prompt: Fact: Peshwa Bajirao I and Nanasaheb Peshwa helped expansion across India. Which map change supports this?
options: Maratha control appears at Lahore, Attock and Peshawar.
Maratha control disappears from every labelled place.
Maratha control appears only in one nearby village.
Maratha control remains inside one small region.

why.Maratha control disappears from every la: This shows contraction, which does not support expansion.
why.Maratha control appears only in one near: This shows a small area, not expansion across India.
why.Maratha control remains inside one small: This shows no wider reach, so it cannot support expansion.

activities.explanation: Those places show Maratha control spreading across a wide area.

activities.prompt: Fact: The Marathas suffered a disastrous defeat at Panipat in 1761. They soon recovered. Under Mahadji Shinde, they recaptured Delhi in 1771. What does this show?
options: Maratha power could recover after a great defeat.
Maratha power ended after the defeat at Panipat.
The defeat at Panipat caused Delhi to fall.
Delhi was always outside Maratha control.

why.Maratha power ended after the defeat at: This mistakes one disastrous defeat for the end of Maratha power.
why.The defeat at Panipat caused Delhi to fa: This reverses the sequence, because Delhi was later recaptured.
why.Delhi was always outside Maratha control: This ignores the recapture of Delhi under Mahadji Shinde.

activities.explanation: Recovery and the recapture of Delhi show that defeat did not end Maratha power.

activities.prompt: Fact: Tarabai led large-scale attacks into Mughal territories. Aurangzeb died without subduing the Marathas. Why did Mughal success fail?
options: Maratha attacks and battle strength blocked Mughal success.
Maratha attacks ended all Mughal territory.
Maratha leaders soon stopped fighting the Mughals.
The Mughals controlled every battle with the Marathas.

why.Maratha attacks ended all Mughal territo: This confuses attacking Mughal territory with destroying all of it.
why.Maratha leaders soon stopped fighting th: This contradicts the continued Maratha struggle with the Mughals.
why.The Mughals controlled every battle with: This reverses who usually had the upper hand in battles.

activities.explanation: Large attacks and frequent upper hand support this explanation.

activities.prompt: The British took more India from the Marathas than from the Mughals. What was the stronger British opponent?
options: The Marathas were stronger than the Mughals.
The Mughals were stronger than the Marathas.
The British faced only one Indian power.
The British faced no Maratha opposition.

why.The Mughals were stronger than the Marat: This reverses which power lost more territory to the British.
This confuses a stronger opponent with having only one opponent.
This ignores the British taking India from the Marathas.

activities.explanation: Taking more India from the Marathas makes them the greater opponent.

lessons.title: Maratha Administration

activities.prompt: How did Shivaji organize a strong kingdom that could protect its people and grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Marathas Were Governed
activities.body: Shivaji made the Maratha administration more centralised. This means power was organised under a central government. Eight ministers helped him govern. Officials received salaries from the state treasury, the government's money store. The state also supported soldiers' widows. Marathas collected chauth and sardeshmukhi as taxes. Forts protected the state. A panchāyat, a local group, delivered justice. Ships carried trade to overseas ports.
keyPoints: Shivaji organised a centralised administration.
Officials received salaries and soldiers' widows received pensions.
Forts, local justice, taxes, and overseas trade supported the state.
activities.explanation: These features show organised government, support for people, defence, and trade.

activities.prompt: A Maratha ruler has many officials, local disputes, and a soldier’s widow who needs help. How should he organise these needs?
steps: Use the eight ministers to help, because Shivaji’s administration was centralised.
Pay officials from the treasury, because every government official received a salary.
Use the panchāyat for justice, because it was the main local body.
Give the widow a pension, because Shivaji supported soldiers’ widows.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Shivaji introduce for the Maratha kingdom?
options: a centralised administration
a fully decentralised system
an administration without ministers
an army without government officials
activities.explanation: Shivaji introduced a relatively centralised administration for his kingdom.

activities.prompt: Shivaji gave pensions to the ______ of soldiers who died in battles.
activities.hint: Think about the women whose husbands had died.
activities.explanation: Shivaji gave pensions to the widows of soldiers who died in battles.

activities.prompt: Match each part of Maratha administration with its role.
activities.explanation: Each pair links a person or institution with its role in Maratha administration.

activities.prompt: Why were forts important to the Maratha state?
options: They collected taxes in every village.
They helped the state survive invasions.
They replaced every government official.
They delivered justice in every village.
activities.explanation: Forts were the core of the state and helped it survive invasions.

activities.prompt: Match each part of Maratha administration with its correct role.
pairs: Carried goods to Yemen, Oman and Malaysia
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a leader, institution, trade link, or force with its role.

activities.prompt: Which statement best shows support for officials and soldiers' families?
options: Officials were paid, and soldiers' widows paid taxes.
Forts were paid, and soldiers' widows led administration.
Officials were paid, and soldiers' widows were supported.
Taxes were paid, and government officials received no salary.
activities.explanation: Government officials received salaries, while soldiers' widows received pensions.

activities.prompt: Shivaji’s aṣhṭa pradhāna manḍala had eight ministers to help him. When kingdom work grows, how should ministers and local panchāyats divide work?
options: Panchayats take local cases; ministers help run the kingdom.
Panchayats run the kingdom; ministers take local cases.
Ministers settle local cases; panchayats run the kingdom.
Both groups ignore the ruler and rule separate kingdoms.

why.Panchayats run the kingdom; ministers ta: This wrongly swaps the central and local duties.
why.Ministers settle local cases; panchayats: This wrongly swaps the central and local duties again.
why.Both groups ignore the ruler and rule se: This wrongly makes central administration independent of the ruler.

activities.explanation: This is right because ministers helped centrally while panchayats delivered local justice.

activities.prompt: Kanhoji Angre led the Marathas to victory in many naval battles. Why could this strength help maritime trade?
options: It could remove the need for ships to carry goods.
It could make every foreign port collect Maratha taxes.
It could protect merchant ships carrying goods overseas.
It could make inland forts carry goods to the sea.

why.It could remove the need for ships to ca: This wrongly thinks naval strength removes the need for merchant ships.
why.It could make every foreign port collect: This wrongly treats naval power as a tax-collecting power.
why.It could make inland forts carry goods t: This wrongly mixes inland forts with ships carrying sea goods.

activities.explanation: This is right because strong naval power can protect trade ships.

activities.prompt: Forts were the core of the Maratha state and helped it survive invasions. If danger grows, what should the ruler protect first?
options: Village judges, because forts cannot help against invasions.
The navy only, because land forts had no defensive role.
Merchant ships, because forts protect only overseas trade.
The forts, because they are the state’s core defence.

why.Village judges, because forts cannot hel: This wrongly thinks forts had no role against invasions.
why.The navy only, because land forts had no: This wrongly treats the navy as a replacement for land forts.
why.Merchant ships, because forts protect on: This wrongly limits forts to overseas trade.

activities.explanation: This is right because forts were central to surviving invasions.

activities.prompt: A shopkeeper must pay the Maratha taxes called chauth and sardeshmukhi. What should he expect this money to support?
options: The running of the Maratha state and its government.
Only the private wealth of every tax collector.
The ending of official salaries and state treasury work.
A separate military command for every local judge.

why.Only the private wealth of every tax col: This wrongly imagines that taxes become collectors’ private wealth.
why.The ending of official salaries and stat: This wrongly thinks taxes replace regular salaries from the treasury.
why.A separate military command for every lo: This wrongly turns local judges into military commanders.

activities.explanation: This is right because state taxes helped support the government and its work.

activities.prompt: A map shows Maratha trade routes to Yemen, Oman and Malaysia. Kanhoji Angre won many naval battles. What combined picture do these facts create?
options: Maratha sea power ended trade with all overseas ports.
Overseas trade was replaced by forts and local justice.
Maratha sea power supported trade with several overseas ports.
Naval victories showed that overseas ports needed local forts.

why.Maratha sea power ended trade with all o: This wrongly treats naval strength as a reason to stop trade.
why.Overseas trade was replaced by forts and: This wrongly replaces maritime trade with land administration.
why.Naval victories showed that overseas por: This wrongly extends the role of forts to distant overseas ports.

activities.explanation: This is right because naval strength and trade routes supported sea trade.

lessons.sceneCaption: The Maratha Empire expanded across India between 1674 and 1702.

lessons.title: Cultural Revival and the Maratha Legacy

activities.prompt: How did Maratha leaders revive culture and transform India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Language, Religion, and Culture
activities.body: Shivaji promoted Marathi by commissioning the Rājya-Vyavahāra-Koṣha. This treatise reduced foreign loanwords in Marathi diplomatic language. His seal carried a Sanskrit inscription, instead of the usual Persian one. He was a devout Hindu, yet he respected other religions. Shivaji helped revive ancient Indian culture and values.
keyPoints: Shivaji commissioned a work to promote Marathi.
The work reduced foreign loanwords in diplomatic Marathi.
His seal used Sanskrit instead of Persian.
He respected other religions.
He helped revive ancient Indian culture and values.
activities.explanation: These points show Shivaji's support for language, religion, and culture.

activities.prompt: Why did Shivaji change the words on his seal and diplomatic writing?
steps: Shivaji wanted to revive ancient Indian culture and values.
His Sanskrit seal inscription showed this wish through official symbols.
He commissioned the Rājya-Vyavahāra-Koṣha because he wanted Marathi promoted.
So language choices helped build Maratha identity through cultural revival.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Maratha Legacy
activities.body: The Maratha legacy includes what Marathas left behind. Ahilyabai Holkar governed the state wisely for thirty years after losing her family. Tarabai organised armies that invaded Mughal territories in northern India. The Thanjavur Marathas created a rich culture full of new ideas. Serfoji II supported many talented musicians in Thanjavur.
keyPoints: Wise government, military action, and cultural growth marked Maratha rule.
Ahilyabai Holkar governed wisely for thirty years after losing her family.
Thanjavur's culture grew with new ideas and talented musicians.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows many parts of the Maratha legacy.

activities.title: Shivaji's Seal
activities.prompt: Shivaji's seal carried the usual Persian inscription instead of a Sanskrit one.
activities.explanation: His seal carried a Sanskrit inscription instead of the usual Persian one.

activities.title: Maratha Actions
activities.prompt: Match each person or group with their action.
pairs: commissioned a work to promote Marathi
created a rich culture with new ideas
activities.explanation: Each action comes from the lesson. Ahilyabai Holkar also governed for thirty years after losing her family.

activities.title: The Royal Seal
activities.prompt: Which inscription did Shivaji's seal carry?
options: Persian inscription
Marathi inscription
Sanskrit inscription
no inscription
activities.explanation: The lesson says his seal used Sanskrit instead of Persian. The Persian inscription was the usual one.

activities.title: Shivaji's Language Work
activities.prompt: Put the stages of Shivaji's language work in order.
items: The work aims to promote Marathi.
The work reduces foreign loanwords in Marathi diplomatic language.
activities.explanation: Shivaji commissioned the work. It promoted Marathi and reduced foreign loanwords.

activities.title: Language on the Seal
activities.prompt: Shivaji's seal carried a ______ inscription instead of the usual Persian one.
activities.hint: This language was named in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Shivaji's seal carried a Sanskrit inscription instead of the usual Persian one.

activities.title: Power and Cultural Growth
activities.prompt: Which choice best shows Maratha challenges to Mughal power and Maratha cultural growth?
options: Challenged Mughal dominance and built a rich culture
Preserved Mughal dominance and stopped cultural growth
Changed only the seal and avoided Maratha rule
Supported no armies and rejected cultural growth
activities.explanation: Maratha rule challenged Mughal dominance and created the largest Indian empire. The Thanjavur Marathas also built a rich culture with new ideas.

activities.prompt: An official seal shows Sanskrit words where Persian words are usual. What does this choice suggest?
options: Shivaji used an Indian language for official identity.
Shivaji followed Persian seal customs without any change.
Shivaji rejected every foreign word in all Marathi writing.
Shivaji used his seal only for private family matters.

why.Shivaji followed Persian seal customs wi: This mistake assumes a changed seal means Persian customs stayed unchanged.
why.Shivaji rejected every foreign word in a: This mistake treats one official choice as a ban on every foreign word.
why.Shivaji used his seal only for private f: This mistake confuses an official seal with a private family object.

activities.explanation: This is right because Sanskrit appeared on Shivaji’s own seal.

activities.prompt: Diplomatic letters use many foreign loanwords. Shivaji orders fewer of them. Why?
options: To make Marathi stronger in official communication.
To make Marathi rely more on foreign language.
To keep foreign words out of everyday family talk.
To turn Marathi into the language of Persian courts.

why.To make Marathi rely more on foreign lan: This mistake reverses the effect because fewer loanwords mean less foreign dependence.
why.To keep foreign words out of everyday fa: This mistake mixes diplomatic language with everyday family talk.
why.To turn Marathi into the language of Per: This mistake mistakes the goal of promoting Marathi for promoting Persian.

activities.explanation: This is right because fewer loanwords strengthened Marathi in diplomatic use.

activities.prompt: A map shows Maratha armies entering Mughal territory in northern India. What does the map suggest?
options: Tarabai’s armies challenged Mughal control in northern India.
Tarabai’s armies helped the Mughals keep northern control.
Tarabai’s armies entered the area only for peaceful travel.
Tarabai’s armies had no aim to challenge Mughal rule.

why.Tarabai’s armies helped the Mughals keep: This mistake assumes an invasion was meant to protect Mughal rule.
why.Tarabai’s armies entered the area only f: This mistake treats a military invasion as only peaceful travel.
why.Tarabai’s armies had no aim to challenge: This mistake ignores the direct challenge shown by the invasion.

activities.explanation: This is right because Tarabai’s armies invaded Mughal territories in northern India.

activities.prompt: After losing her family, Ahilyabai Holkar governs wisely for thirty years. What does this show?
options: She accepted responsibility and kept good government.
She waited for family help before governing at all.
She linked wise rule to gaining a new family.
She treated state duties as less important than family.

why.She waited for family help before govern: This mistake assumes personal loss made public responsibility disappear.
why.She linked wise rule to gaining a new fa: This mistake wrongly links wise rule to replacing a lost family.
why.She treated state duties as less importa: This mistake wrongly makes family loss more important than state duties.

activities.prompt: If the bhakti saints had not written devotional works or translated texts, what would most likely have happened?
options: The Marathas’ shared cultural foundation would have been weaker, making political organisation harder.
Political organisation would have become easier because the group would have had fewer shared cultural ideas.
The Marathi literary tradition would have become continuous because fewer devotional works were produced.
The cultural foundation would have remained unchanged because political organisation does not depend on literature or awareness.

why.Political organisation would have become: More shared ideas would support organisation, not weaken it.
why.The Marathi literary tradition would hav: Continuous history requires continuing literary activity.
why.The cultural foundation would have remai: Literature and awareness helped build the foundation.

activities.explanation: The lack of literature and awareness would weaken the foundation.

The Marathi literary tradition would weaken because sacred texts were made available in an ordinary language.

why.The Marathi literary tradition would wea: Using an ordinary language does not weaken literature.
why.Social and political awareness would bec: Devotional work and social awareness could exist together.
why.The Marathas would lose their language i: Writing in Marathi strengthened, rather than weakened, language identity.

activities.context: The Marathas came from present-day Maharashtra on the Deccan plateau and were identified with Marathi. Marathi had a continuous literary history since the 12th century. activities.prompt: After the Yadava dynasty was defeated, which development best explains how the Marathas could still organise as a political power?
options: They built on a shared Marathi cultural foundation strengthened by bhakti, literature, and social and political awareness.
They had no shared cultural foundation because the Yadava dynasty’s defeat ended Marathi cultural life.
They organised politically only because they had defeated the Khilji Sultanate.
They organised politically by turning away from Marathi and abandoning the saints’ social work.

why.They had no shared cultural foundation b: Their cultural life continued after the dynasty’s defeat.
why.They organised politically only because: The facts do not say that the Marathas defeated the Khilji Sultanate.
why.They organised politically by turning aw: Turning away from Marathi would remove an important basis of their strength.

activities.explanation: Their cultural foundation supported later organisation.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Marathas’ cultural foundation helped them organise as a political power.
Reason (R): Marathi’s continuous literary history and the saints’ social and political awareness gave this foundation substance.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the literary and social activities explain the foundation for political organisation.

activities.prompt:

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Marathas’ cultural foundation helped them organise as a political power.
activities.answer: The Marathas shared a cultural foundation built around Marathi. The language had a continuous literary history since the 12th century, while saints following bhakti wrote devotional works in ordinary people’s languages and translated important texts into Marathi. Some saints also worked for social organisation and political awareness. These activities connected the Marathas through a shared language, traditions, and awareness of social and political issues. Therefore, when this foundation later helped them organise as a political power, they already had a common cultural basis on which to build.
points: Marathi had a continuous literary history since the 12th century.
Bhakti saints wrote and translated important works in Marathi.
Some saints worked for social organisation and political awareness.
The shared cultural foundation supported later political organisation.

activities.context: At sixteen, Shivaji began campaigns from his jāgīr at Pune, where he had grown up under Jijabai and had learned to trust officials. Constant fighting among the Deccan sultans was causing suffering in the Pune region. By capturing forts, Shivaji sought to strengthen his hold there. activities.prompt: Why was life in the Pune region difficult during Shivaji’s early years?

Jijabai had stopped trusting the officials in Pune.
Shivaji’s campaigns immediately removed every cause of suffering.
Shahji’s absence meant that Pune had no government at all.
