why.Shivaji’s campaigns immediately removed: His early campaigns did not end all the fighting immediately.
why.Shahji’s absence meant that Pune had no: Shahji’s absence did not mean that no one governed Pune.

activities.explanation: Constant conflict among the Deccan sultanates caused the region’s suffering.

activities.prompt: After strengthening his position around Pune, what long-term aim should guide Shivaji’s next steps?
options: Establish a sovereign kingdom called Swarājya.
Continue serving the Deccan sultanates and reject a kingdom of his own.
Divide his jāgīr among trusted officials and give up central control.
Restore his jāgīr to Shahji and end all military campaigns.

activities.prompt: How did guerrilla warfare help Shivaji defeat larger armies, as shown at Pratapgad?
activities.answer: Shivaji’s guerrilla warfare suited a smaller force because it did not depend on meeting a larger army in one direct contest. Small groups could move with speed and use surprise to defeat larger armies. At Pratapgad, Shivaji and his advisers had persuaded Afzal Khan to meet them. Shivaji killed Afzal Khan, and hidden Marathas then routed the Khan’s army. Thus, secrecy, a swift and unexpected attack, and the removal of the opposing leader helped the smaller force gain victory.
points: Guerrilla warfare used small groups.
Speed and surprise were its main advantages.
Shivaji killed Afzal Khan at Pratapgad.
Hidden Marathas routed the Khan’s army.

activities.prompt: How did Shivaji’s actions at Surat show that military success could be combined with restraint, and how did his later expansion strengthen the Marathas?
activities.answer: During the sack of Surat, Shivaji showed restraint by sacking the wealthy city while being careful not to attack religious places. This meant that military success and protection of religious sites could occur together. His later expansion followed his coronation at Raigad: he began his conquest of the South, and that expansion gave the Marathas great strategic depth. Restraint at Surat therefore limited his conduct during the sack, while the southern conquest increased Maratha strength.

activities.prompt: How did the Marathas expand across India, and what happened after their defeat at Panipat?
activities.answer: The Marathas expanded across India with help from Peshwa Bajirao I and Nanasaheb Peshwa. Their reach included Lahore, Attock and Peshawar. chapters.title: The Colonial Era in India
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what colonialism meant and why india was attracted; the portuguese, dutch and french establish footprints; the british move from trade to rule; famines and the drain of india’s wealth.

lessons.title: What Colonialism Meant and Why India Was Attracted

activities.prompt: Why did India attract the attention of faraway European powers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Colonialism and India
activities.body: Colonialism means one country taking control of another region and settling there. It can be traced back to great empires of the 1st millennium BCE. Europe’s expansion began in the 15th century. European powers wanted resources, markets and trade routes. They also wanted to convert indigenous populations to Christianity and explore unknown lands. Before Europeans sailed to India, India was a vibrant economic and cultural powerhouse. Colonisation caused loss of independence and harm.
keyPoints: Colonialism means control and settlement by another country.
European expansion involved trade, religion and scientific inquiry.
India was prosperous before European powers arrived.
activities.explanation: This lesson explains colonialism, its motives, and India's earlier strength.

events.label: The Age of Colonialism began with Europe’s expansion
Goa became the capital of the Portuguese colony
The Portuguese established the Inquisition in Goa
The Dutch arrived in India
The French opened their first Indian trading post

tasks.then: The latest event here is from 1770 CE.

activities.explanation: Put events in order, and remember that BCE years count down towards 1 CE.

Thus colonisation brought gains but also exploitation and lost independence.

lessons.title: The Portuguese, Dutch and French Establish Footprints

activities.prompt: How did European traders find their way into India's trading world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Portuguese, Dutch and French Footprints
activities.body: Da Gama reached Kappad near Kozhikode in May 1498. Goa became the colony’s capital in 1510. Portuguese ships needed cartaz permits, or permissions to sail, in the Arabian Sea. They set up an Inquisition in Goa in 1560. Dutch traders arrived in the early 17th century and focused on commerce. France’s first trading post opened at Surat in 1668. Dupleix trained Indian soldiers and called them sepoys. France lost ground to Britain.
keyPoints: Portuguese milestones include Kappad in 1498, Goa in 1510 and the Inquisition in 1560.
Dutch activity focused on commerce in the early 17th century.
French activity included Surat in 1668, sepoys, indirect rule and French losses.
activities.explanation: This lesson traces the main actions of the Portuguese, Dutch and French in India.

activities.prompt: A Portuguese ship has reached India, but its captain still wants to sail in the Arabian Sea. Why can’t he sail freely, and what should he do?
steps: The Portuguese reached India in May 1498, because Vasco da Gama arrived at Kappad near Kozhikode.
The captain still needs a cartaz permit, because Portuguese ships required one in the Arabian Sea.
He must get it before sailing, because the permit was needed for navigation there.
Therefore, the ship should wait for the permit before continuing its Arabian Sea journey.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Dupleix and French Rule
activities.body: The French opened their first trading post at Surat in 1668. Dupleix trained Indian soldiers in European military methods and called them sepoys. He developed indirect rule. This meant rulers were chosen by the French. Later, the French lost ground to the British. They were reduced to Pondicherry and a few smaller enclaves.
keyPoints: The French first trading post opened at Surat in 1668.
Dupleix trained Indian soldiers in European military methods.
Indirect rule used rulers chosen by the French.
activities.explanation: These points describe French trading, military and ruling methods.

options: May 1510
May 1498

May 1668
activities.explanation: The lesson dates his arrival at Kappad to May 1498.

activities.prompt: Portuguese ships needed a cartaz permit to navigate in the Arabian Sea.
activities.explanation: A cartaz permit was needed for navigation in the Arabian Sea.

activities.hint: Look for the year linked with Goa.
activities.explanation: Goa became the Portuguese colony’s capital in 1510.

options: His power comes through being chosen by the French.
His power comes through choosing the French rulers.
The French choose no rulers when they use indirect rule.
Local rulers hold power without any French choosing.

why.His power comes through choosing the Fre: This reverses the choice: the French chose the ruler, not the other way.
why.The French choose no rulers when they us: This misunderstands indirect rule, which used rulers chosen by the French.
why.Local rulers hold power without any Fren: This misses the French role in choosing each indirect ruler.

activities.explanation: This is right because the system worked through rulers chosen by the French.

activities.prompt: The French lost ground to the British and were reduced to Pondicherry and a few smaller enclaves. A map shows French areas shrinking. What does this map support?
options: The map supports the French having less territory.
The map supports the French having more territory.
The map shows the French losing only one large area.
The map shows the French gaining all British areas.

why.The map supports the French having more: This reverses the result, since the French lost ground and became smaller.
why.The map shows the French losing only one: This misses the few smaller enclaves left after French losses.
why.The map shows the French gaining all Bri: This wrongly claims French gains in British areas.

activities.explanation: This is right: shrinking French areas match their loss of ground.

lessons.title: The British Move from Trade to Rule

activities.prompt: How could a trading company gain control over an entire country?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: From Trading Company to Ruler
activities.body: The East India Company began in trade. Queen Elizabeth I gave it a royal charter, meaning permission. Special powers allowed a private army, meaning own soldiers. The Company built coastal trading footholds in India. Agents used military support in conflicts. Clive and Mir Jafar betrayed Bengal’s Nawab. It became a kingmaker, helping rulers gain power. Residents sat at Indian courts. Subsidiary alliances, or agreements, brought Britain control of large territories.
keyPoints: Trade began before territorial control.
Royal permission and military power helped expansion.
Residents and subsidiary alliances strengthened British control.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows how trading power grew into political and territorial control.

activities.prompt: Shop gets an army, picks a leader, and rules towns. What changed?
steps: Trade came first, because the Company began as a trading company.
It gained an army, because charter powers included raising a private army.
It used that army, because agents entered conflicts between local rulers.
It gained rule, because kingmaker power brought control of larger territories.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the English East India Company first begin as?
options: a trading company
a private army
a royal Resident
a subsidiary alliance
activities.explanation: The Company began as a trading company. Its trading work later supported its move towards rule.

activities.prompt: Why did British agents use military support?
options: To enter conflicts between local rulers.
To build coastal trading footholds.
To place Residents at Indian courts.
To receive a royal charter.
activities.explanation: British agents used military support to enter conflicts between local rulers. This helped them extend their influence.

activities.prompt: Match each person or group with the correct action.
pairs: gave a royal charter and powers
were placed at courts of Indian rulers
activities.explanation: These links show how trade, permission, soldiers and court officers supported British power.

activities.prompt: Clive plotted with Mir Jafar to betray the ______ of Bengal.
activities.hint: This title belonged to the ruler in Bengal.
activities.explanation: Clive and Mir Jafar planned to betray the Nawab of Bengal. Their plot helped weaken Bengal’s ruler.

activities.prompt: How did the Company use its position as kingmaker?
options: End its role as kingmaker.
Gain control over larger territories.
Stop placing Residents at courts.
Abandon its coastal footholds.
activities.explanation: The Company used its kingmaker position to gain control over larger territories. This greatly strengthened British power.

activities.prompt: Put the steps in the order they developed.
items: Receive a royal charter and special powers
Build trading footholds along India's coast
Use military support in local conflicts
Gain control through the position of kingmaker
activities.explanation: This order shows the movement from trading company to territorial power. Each step strengthened the next.

activities.prompt: A football club first sold shirts. Later, it gained special powers and an army. What happened next?
options: It kept only selling shirts along the coast.
It used military help in fights between local leaders.
It ended all trade along the entire coast.
It stayed only a small local sports team.

why.It kept only selling shirts along the co: This matches how military support helped agents enter conflicts between local rulers.
why.It ended all trade along the entire coas: This mistake thinks stronger powers would stop coastal trade.
why.It stayed only a small local sports team: This mistake treats private military powers as ordinary team membership.

activities.explanation: This mistake keeps the Company in its early trading role.

activities.prompt: At first, the Company traded along India's coast. Later, it helped rulers gain power. What best describes the change?
options: Trade contacts helped the Company gain wider political control.
Trading posts ended when the Company entered politics.
The Company gained power without entering local conflicts.
Local rulers gained wider control from Company support.

why.Trading posts ended when the Company ent: This mistake reverses the move from trade toward political control.
why.The Company gained power without enterin: This mistake ignores military support in conflicts between rulers.
why.Local rulers gained wider control from C: This mistake gives the Company's support to the local rulers.

activities.explanation: Coastal footholds and local conflicts helped the Company gain wider control.

activities.prompt: A map marks early trading footholds along India's coast and British-controlled areas. What can we infer?
options: Coastal trade was an early step toward wider British rule.
British rule began far away from India's coast.
Trading footholds and wider rule were completely unrelated.
The Company directly ruled every coastal trading foothold.

why.British rule began far away from India's: This mistake places British rule away from the early coastal footholds.
why.Trading footholds and wider rule were co: This mistake separates the trading stage from the rule-making stage.
why.The Company directly ruled every coastal: A map cannot show whether every foothold was ruled directly.

activities.explanation: Early coastal footholds helped lead to control over larger territories.

activities.prompt: Clive plotted with Mir Jafar to betray the Nawab of Bengal. Why would this help the Company?
options: It let the Company act as kingmaker and gain wider control.
It helped the Nawab keep control from the Company.
It made the Company give up its Bengal gains.
It showed local rulers could defeat the Company's army.

why.It helped the Nawab keep control from th: This mistake makes the Nawab the winner of the Company's plot.
why.It made the Company give up its Bengal g: This mistake confuses political gain with giving up Company control.
why.It showed local rulers could defeat the: This mistake thinks the Company's army lost because of the plot.

activities.explanation: Clive's betrayal helped the Company use kingmaker power for wider control.

activities.prompt: At a school election, one group backs a candidate who becomes leader. It then guides the leader's choices. What does this resemble?
options: The Company acting as kingmaker and gaining wider control.
The Company acting only as a trader with coastal footholds.
The Company raising a private army for coastal trade.
The Company ending its role in local rulers' courts.

why.The Company acting only as a trader with: This mistake limits the Company to its early trading role.
why.The Company raising a private army for c: This mistake treats the private army as the Company's main role.
why.The Company ending its role in local rul: This mistake reverses the Company's continued role at rulers' courts.

activities.explanation: Backing a leader and then guiding choices resembles gaining wider control.

lessons.title: Famines and the Drain of India’s Wealth

activities.prompt: How did British rule affect India’s wealth and its people?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How British Policies Worsened Famine
activities.body: In Bengal, crop failure and harsh Company taxation caused a catastrophic famine in 1770–1772. The Company increased land tax even while people suffered from famine. Its agents took maximum revenue but spent very little on governance or development. The British administration continued exporting grain during the Great Famine of 1876–1878. The free-market policy allowed food prices to rise, making famines worse.
keyPoints: Crop failure and harsh Company taxation caused the Bengal famine
Maximum revenue was collected while development spending stayed very low
Free-market policies raised food prices during famine
activities.explanation: These policies increased suffering while taking more from people who were already struggling.

activities.prompt: If food is sent out of a hungry country, why can that make a famine worse?
steps: The British administration kept exporting grain during the 1876–1878 famine.
This took food away from hungry people in India.
The free-market policy let food prices rise, making food harder to buy.
Together, these policies made the famine worse.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Wealth Taken from India
activities.body: Famine deaths during British rule are estimated at 50 to 100 million. According to Adams, stolen Indian wealth helped finance Britain’s Industrial Revolution. One estimate puts India’s drained wealth at 45 trillion U.S. dollars. The estimate covers 1765 to 1938. Indians were also charged for British spending on railways, telegraphs and wars. These facts show how British rule harmed India through famine and lost wealth.
keyPoints: Famine deaths during British rule: 50 to 100 million
Adams linked stolen Indian wealth to Britain’s Industrial Revolution
One wealth estimate: 45 trillion U.S. dollars
activities.explanation: The lesson connects the loss of life with the large drain of India’s wealth.

activities.prompt: The Company increased land tax while Bengal was suffering from famine.
activities.explanation: The Company increased land tax even while Bengal was suffering from famine. Both details happened together.

activities.prompt: Up to ______ million Indians died during the Great Famine of 1876–1878.
activities.hint: Use the death estimate for the Great Famine.
activities.explanation: The lesson gives 8 million as the death estimate for the Great Famine of 1876–1878.

activities.prompt: Match each event or period with its related fact.
pairs: Crop failure and harsh Company taxation
activities.explanation: Each fact belongs with the event or period on the left. This checks your understanding of the famines.

activities.prompt: What happened under the free-market policy during famine?
options: Food prices fell, and famines eased.
Food prices stayed steady during famine.
Food prices rose, and famines worsened.
Food exports stopped during famine.
activities.explanation: The free-market policy allowed food prices to rise. Higher food prices made famines worse.

activities.prompt: What did Adams say about stolen Indian wealth?
options: It helped finance Britain’s Industrial Revolution.
It stopped Britain’s Industrial Revolution.
It raised food prices across Britain.
It reduced Britain’s spending on wars.
activities.explanation: Adams said stolen Indian wealth helped finance Britain’s Industrial Revolution. This was his stated view.

activities.prompt: Between 1765 and 1938, one estimate puts India’s drained wealth at 50 trillion U.S. dollars.
activities.explanation: The lesson gives 45 trillion U.S. dollars. The estimate covers 1765 to 1938.

activities.prompt: A shop raises rice prices after free-market rules allow it. What is likely to happen?
options: More families will find rice harder to buy.
Most families will suddenly have more food.
Rice sellers will have less rice to sell.
Every family will pay the same lower price.

why.Most families will suddenly have more fo: This wrongly assumes more people can suddenly buy food.
why.Rice sellers will have less rice to sell: This confuses higher prices with less food being available.
why.Every family will pay the same lower pri: This thinks free-market rules keep food prices low.

activities.explanation: This is right because free-market rules allowed food prices to rise.

activities.prompt: The Company raised land tax during Bengal’s famine. British officials exported grain during the 1876–1878 famine. What do both actions show?
options: Both actions made hunger worse during each famine.
Both actions quickly ended the food shortage.
Both actions gave poor families more support.
Both actions lowered land taxes for poor families.

why.Both actions quickly ended the food shor: This reverses the effect; both actions did not end shortages.
why.Both actions gave poor families more sup: This mistakes harmful government actions for help.
why.Both actions lowered land taxes for poor: This treats one measure as the only cause and misses grain exports.

activities.explanation: This is right because higher taxes and exports harmed hungry families.

activities.prompt: Imagine a government takes maximum revenue but spends little on governance or development. Which outcome fits the Company’s approach?
options: Farmers pay more while the government helps them little.
Farmers pay less while the government fixes every farm.
Farmers pay more and receive much more government help.
Farmers pay less and receive no help from government.

why.Farmers pay less while the government fi: This assumes taking more revenue lowers what farmers pay.
why.Farmers pay more and receive much more g: This confuses weak public spending with strong support.
why.Farmers pay less and receive no help fro: This treats low spending as a sign of low tax collection.

activities.explanation: This is right because maximum revenue meant taking more while spending little.

activities.prompt: The Company kept raising land tax while Bengal was starving. Why might its agents have done this?
options: They wanted maximum revenue, even during famine.
They wanted to give every farmer more food.
They wanted to end the famine with free markets.
They wanted to spend more on local development.

why.They wanted to give every farmer more fo: This confuses collecting land tax with distributing food.
why.They wanted to end the famine with free: This wrongly treats free markets as famine relief.
why.They wanted to spend more on local devel: This confuses collecting revenue with spending on development.

activities.explanation: This is right because the agents took maximum revenue while spending very little.

activities.prompt: Adams says stolen Indian wealth helped finance Britain’s Industrial Revolution. Another source estimates a 45 trillion U.S. dollars drain from 1765 to 1938. What do these sources together suggest?
options: India’s loss helped Britain’s Industrial Revolution grow.
India’s loss stopped Britain’s Industrial Revolution.
India’s loss was the only cause of industrial growth.
India kept all its wealth during British rule.

why.India’s loss stopped Britain’s Industria: This reverses the effect of the wealth taken from India.
why.India’s loss was the only cause of indus: This mistakes one contribution for the only cause.
why.India kept all its wealth during British: This wrongly treats the wealth drain as wealth kept in India.

activities.explanation: This is right because stolen Indian wealth helped finance Britain’s Industrial Revolution.

lessons.title: Colonial Rule Changes Indian Life

activities.prompt: How did colonial rule change the way Indians lived and worked?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Colonial Rule Changed India
activities.body: Before the 18th century, India was famous for manufacturing textiles. British trade policies then damaged much of this industry. Colonial courts ignored customary laws, meaning local legal customs. They also used a foreign language and legal system. English education gained prestige, while traditional schools slowly disappeared. Britain also made India supply raw materials for British industry. These changes reshaped work, learning and government in India.
keyPoints: British duties harmed India's textile industry.
Colonial rule changed government, courts and education.
India became a supplier of raw materials for British industry.
activities.explanation: These changes reshaped India's economy, education and identity.

activities.prompt: A cloth seller sees British cloth priced lower. Why do Indian textile businesses suffer?
steps: British duties made Indian textiles cost more than British goods.
British goods stayed cheap because their tariffs were low.
Indian sellers then found it harder to sell their cloth.
These policies ruined much of India’s textile industry.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What was India especially famous for manufacturing before the 18th century?
options: Legal rules and courts
English schools and books
Textiles and cloth
Raw materials and production
activities.explanation: India was famous for manufacturing, especially textiles, before the 18th century.

activities.prompt: Match each colonial change with its effect.
pairs: Much of the textile industry was ruined
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how a colonial change affected Indian life.

activities.prompt: British courts ignored customary laws and used a foreign ______ and legal system.
activities.hint: They used something for communicating in court.
activities.explanation: British courts ignored customary laws and used a foreign language and legal system.

activities.prompt: What did British rule make India become for British industry?
options: A centre of English education
A supplier of raw materials
A centre of British legal rules
A centre of textile manufacturing
activities.explanation: Britain transformed India into a supplier of raw materials for British industry.

activities.prompt: Macaulay wanted Indians to remain English in blood and colour but Indian in taste.
activities.explanation: Macaulay wanted Indians to be Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste.

activities.prompt: Put these developments in their historical order.
items: India was famous for textile manufacturing before the 18th century
Britain placed heavy duties on Indian textiles
Much of India's textile industry was ruined
activities.explanation: Heavy duties came before much of India's textile industry was ruined.

activities.prompt: Britain taxes Indian cloth heavily, but keeps British goods cheap. What will happen to Indian textile sellers?
options: Indian cloth becomes harder to sell, so textile businesses may shrink.
Indian cloth becomes easier to sell, so more textile businesses open.
British cloth becomes costly, so Indian cloth sells better everywhere.
Cloth prices stay the same, so textile businesses grow safely.

why.Indian cloth becomes easier to sell, so: This reverses the effect of heavy duties on Indian textiles.
why.British cloth becomes costly, so Indian: This wrongly makes British goods costly, but their tariffs were low.
why.Cloth prices stay the same, so textile b: This ignores the heavy duty and assumes prices stayed unchanged.

activities.explanation: Heavy duties raise Indian cloth prices while British cloth stays cheap.

activities.prompt: A map shows raw materials going from India to Britain. What does this mainly show?
options: Britain made India a supplier for British industry.
Britain made India a leading maker of finished goods.
India’s textile industry became Britain’s main supplier.
Britain ended India’s role in world trade.

why.Britain made India a leading maker of fi: This confuses a raw-material supplier with a maker of finished goods.
why.India’s textile industry became Britain’: This reverses the direction of supply between India and Britain.
why.Britain ended India’s role in world trad: This wrongly assumes that supplying Britain meant ending world trade.

activities.explanation: The map shows India supplying raw materials to British industry.

activities.prompt: English education gains prestige, while traditional schools slowly disappear. What might explain both changes?
options: People valued English education, so they left traditional schools.
People disliked English education, so they joined traditional schools.
People valued traditional schools, so English education lost prestige.
People valued courts, so they turned courts into schools.

why.People disliked English education, so th: This reverses why people left traditional schools.
why.People valued traditional schools, so En: This reverses the prestige English education gained.
why.People valued courts, so they turned cou: This confuses legal change with the growth of education.

activities.explanation: Macaulay wanted English tastes, and English education gained prestige.

lessons.sceneCaption: This flag map shows the territory of British India under colonial rule.

lessons.title: Resistance, Rebellion and the Colonial Legacy

activities.prompt: What can the past teach us about resistance and the colonial legacy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Colonial Rule and Resistance
activities.body: Colonial rule brought resistance across India. The Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion began after the 1770 Bengal famine. British policies restricted the movements of sannyasis and fakirs. British expansion into forests and hills disrupted many tribal communities. Planters forced Bengal peasants to grow indigo. Cartridge rumours helped trigger the Great Rebellion of 1857. It spread widely, but British violence crushed it. European rule meant subjugation and exploitation. Colonial rulers also stole thousands of Indian statues, paintings, jewels and manuscripts.
keyPoints: British land, taxation and crop policies harmed people.
The Great Rebellion spread widely but faced brutal suppression.
Colonial rule involved exploitation and theft from India.
activities.explanation: These events show colonial subjugation, exploitation and theft.

activities.prompt: A fakir cannot travel because British land and tax rules block him. Why might he join resistance?
steps: British land and taxation policies restrict sannyasi and fakir movement.
The fakir cannot travel freely, so these rules limit his choices.
The Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion began after Bengal's terrible famine of 1770.
Therefore, blocked travel after a terrible famine helps explain his resistance.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: After the Famine
activities.prompt: Which rebellion began after the terrible famine of 1770?
options: Santhal Rebellion
Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion
Kol Uprising
Great Rebellion
activities.explanation: The Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion began in Bengal after the terrible famine of 1770.

activities.title: The Famine Year
activities.prompt: The Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion began after the terrible famine of ______.
activities.hint: Use the year connected with the Bengal famine.
activities.explanation: The terrible famine of 1770 came before this rebellion began.

activities.title: Match Each Rebellion
activities.prompt: Match each rebellion with the correct place, leader or year.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a rebellion with its place, leaders or year.

activities.title: What Planters Forced
activities.prompt: What did European planters force many Bengal peasants to grow?
options: Allow them to grow food crops
Force them to grow indigo
Remove restrictions on their movements
Stop forest expansion near villages
activities.explanation: European planters forced many Bengal peasants to grow indigo instead of food crops.

activities.title: Events in Time Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in time order, from earliest to latest.
activities.explanation: The dates place the famine first and the Great Rebellion last.

activities.title: Why the Rebellion Failed
activities.prompt: Why did the Great Rebellion fail?
options: They had united command and clear plans.
They defeated British forces everywhere.
They lacked united command and clear plans.
They stopped it from spreading widely.
activities.explanation: The sepoys lacked unified command and a consistent strategy. This weakness helped the rebellion fail.

activities.prompt: A sepoy's letter mentions greased cartridges and anger. What can we infer?
options: Some sepoys join the Great Rebellion after hearing the rumour.
The letter proves every sepoy joined the Great Rebellion.
The letter proves British rule had become a civilising mission.
The letter shows Bengal peasants had to grow indigo.

why.The letter proves every sepoy joined the: This overstates one source by claiming every sepoy joined.
why.The letter proves British rule had becom: This wrongly treats colonial rule as a civilising mission.
why.The letter shows Bengal peasants had to: This mixes the cartridge rumour with the forced indigo policy.

activities.explanation: says these rumours helped trigger the Great Rebellion.

activities.prompt: A map marks rebels across northern and central India. It also marks captured cities. Why did the revolt fail?
options: Different rebel groups lacked one command and one clear plan.
The British refused to use systematic and extremely brutal violence.
The revolt lacked important cities, so it could not spread.
Colonial rule was so civilising that sepoys willingly surrendered.

why.The British refused to use systematic an: This reverses, which describes extremely brutal British violence.
why.The revolt lacked important cities, so i: The map shows important cities were captured, so this is wrong.
why.Colonial rule was so civilising that sep: This wrongly assumes colonial rule was civilising and sepoys accepted it.

activities.explanation: says they lacked unified command and a consistent strategy.

activities.prompt: British land and tax rules block a fakir's travel. What does it show?
options: It restricts people's freedom rather than civilising them.
It gives every group equal freedom and equal rights.
It protects tribal communities from all outside expansion.
It ends resistance because people welcome such limits.

why.It gives every group equal freedom and e: This assumes British rule gave equal freedom, which the facts reject.
why.It protects tribal communities from all: This confuses British expansion with protection of tribal communities.
why.It ends resistance because people welcom: This wrongly assumes people welcomed restrictions and stopped resisting.

activities.explanation: Facts 6.2 and 6.11 show restriction and exploitation, not civilising rule.

activities.prompt: European planters force Bengal peasants to grow indigo, not food. Why might peasants resist?
options: The forced policy reduces food growing and takes control.
Indigo gives them more food and makes work easier.
Food crops would weaken every village and every family.
Peasants want colonial planters to control all farming.

why.Indigo gives them more food and makes wo: This wrongly treats indigo as more food and easier work.
why.Food crops would weaken every village an: This wrongly suggests food crops harmed communities.
why.Peasants want colonial planters to contr: This confuses resistance with support for planter control.

activities.explanation: shows farmers lost food crops and faced forced planting.

activities.context: Before European powers began sailing to India, India’s agriculture, manufacturing and trading networks had made it a vibrant economic and cultural powerhouse. European travellers took note, and India produced at least one-fourth of the world’s GDP. Later, European trading parties sought permission to settle and control territory. Their countries competed for wider influence and valued access to resources, markets and trade routes, while some also pursued conversion to Christianity.
activities.prompt: If the European parties receive permission to settle and control Indian territory, what is the most likely result according to the lesson?
options: India would lose independence, face resource exploitation, and have traditional ways of life damaged.
India would keep full independence, and the European settlers would avoid resource exploitation.
India would remain independent at first, but its traditional ways of life would be strengthened by settlement.
India would face loss of independence, but resource exploitation and disruption of traditional life would not follow.

why.India would keep full independence, and: Colonial control does not guarantee that exploitation will be avoided.
why.India would remain independent at first,: Colonisation is presented as damaging traditional ways of life.
why.India would face loss of independence, b: Loss of independence did not prevent harmful exploitation and disruption.

activities.explanation: This matches the effects of colonial settlement.

activities.context: Before European powers began sailing to India, India’s agriculture, manufacturing and trading networks had made it a vibrant economic and cultural powerhouse. European travellers took note, and India produced at least one-fourth of the world’s GDP. Later, European trading parties sought permission to settle and control territory. Their countries competed for wider influence and valued access to resources, markets and trade routes, while some also pursued conversion to Christianity.
activities.prompt: Why was settlement in India especially appealing to European countries that were competing with one another?
options: They wanted greater global influence and access to resources, markets and trade routes.
They valued scientific knowledge but did not want territorial expansion.
They wanted wider influence, but they did not expect colonies to help them gain resources or markets.
They wanted trade, but scientific inquiry was the only thing that made territorial expansion useful.

why.They valued scientific knowledge but did: Scientific inquiry was one motive, not the only one.
why.They wanted wider influence, but they di: Colonial expansion did provide access to resources and markets.
why.They wanted trade, but scientific inquir: Economic access and influence were important motives for expansion.

activities.explanation: Competition encouraged expansion, influence and economic access.

activities.context: Before European powers began sailing to India, India’s agriculture, manufacturing and trading networks had made it a vibrant economic and cultural powerhouse. European travellers took note, and India produced at least one-fourth of the world’s GDP. Later, European trading parties sought permission to settle and control territory. Their countries competed for wider influence and valued access to resources, markets and trade routes, while some also pursued conversion to Christianity.
activities.prompt: If one European power cannot persuade local people to convert to Christianity, what would it most likely do next?
options: It may still pursue expansion because economic gain and wider influence were also motives.
It must stop expanding immediately because conversion was its only motive.
It will continue only if scientific inquiry replaces all interest in resources and markets.
It will expand for influence but can avoid every harmful effect on local people.

why.It must stop expanding immediately becau: Conversion was powerful, but it was not the only motive.
why.It will continue only if scientific inqu: Scientific inquiry did not replace the economic motives.
why.It will expand for influence but can avo: Colonial expansion could still harm local people.

activities.explanation: Other motives remained even without conversion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Competition between European countries encouraged territorial expansion and global influence.
Reason (R): European powers established colonies across Africa, Asia, the Americas and other regions.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but establishing colonies does not explain why competition encouraged expansion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): European powers expanded overseas partly to gain access to resources, markets and trade routes.
Reason (R): Colonial expansion gave European powers access to resources, markets and trade routes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why overseas expansion was attractive to European powers.

activities.prompt: Explain why India was attractive to European powers that came to explore and establish colonies.
activities.answer: India was attractive because it was already a vibrant economic and cultural powerhouse. It produced at least one-fourth of the world’s GDP, and European travellers noted its agriculture, manufacturing and extensive trading networks. These features offered European powers valuable resources, markets and trade routes. Competition among European countries also encouraged them to expand and increase global influence. Conversion to Christianity and scientific inquiry gave further reasons for exploration and settlement.
points: India was an economic and cultural powerhouse.
India produced at least one-fourth of the world’s GDP.
European travellers noted agriculture, manufacturing and trade networks.
European powers sought resources, markets, trade routes and wider influence.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A captain’s ship reached Kappad near Kozhikode in May 1498. Later, the Portuguese made Goa the capital of their colony in India. Before entering the Arabian Sea, his crew obtained a cartaz permit. Goa’s administration began using the Inquisition in 1560. Dutch traders focused on commerce. French power depended on Indian soldiers trained by Dupleix and on rulers chosen by him. British pressure later caused the French to lose ground, leaving them Pondicherry and a few smaller enclaves.
activities.prompt: Why is Goa important in the case beyond being the Portuguese arrival point?
options: It became the centre of Portuguese colonial administration.
It was where the French opened their first trading post.
It was where Dupleix trained Indian soldiers.
It was where the Dutch conducted their main commerce.

why.It was where the French opened their fir: The French opened their first trading post at Surat.
why.It was where Dupleix trained Indian sold: Dupleix trained Indian soldiers using European military methods.
why.It was where the Dutch conducted their m: The Dutch focused mainly on commerce.

activities.explanation: Goa became the capital of the Portuguese colony in India.

activities.context: A captain’s ship reached Kappad near Kozhikode in May 1498. Later, the Portuguese made Goa the capital of their colony in India. Before entering the Arabian Sea, his crew obtained a cartaz permit. Goa’s administration began using the Inquisition in 1560. Dutch traders focused on commerce. French power depended on Indian soldiers trained by Dupleix and on rulers chosen by him. British pressure later caused the French to lose ground, leaving them Pondicherry and a few smaller enclaves.
activities.prompt: If British pressure causes the French to lose ground, which result follows?
options: The French take over Portuguese positions in Goa.
The French remain spread across many Indian territories.
The French are reduced to Pondicherry and a few smaller enclaves.
The Dutch take over all French trading posts.

why.The French take over Portuguese position: The Portuguese maintained Goa as their colonial capital.
why.The French remain spread across many Ind: The French lost ground to the British.
why.The Dutch take over all French trading p: The Dutch focused on commerce rather than taking French trading posts.

activities.explanation: The French were reduced to Pondicherry and a few smaller enclaves.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Dupleix’s strategy combined military preparation with indirect political control.
Reason (R): He trained Indian soldiers in European military methods and developed indirect rule through rulers chosen by the French.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains both parts of the assertion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Portuguese established the Inquisition in Goa because Goa had become their capital in 1510.
Reason (R): Goa became the capital of the Portuguese colony in India in 1510.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both dates and locations are correct, but the facts do not establish that becoming the capital caused the Inquisition to be established.

activities.prompt: Explain how the Portuguese presence in India developed from the first arrival to colonial control in Goa.
activities.answer: Vasco da Gama arrived at Kappad near Kozhikode in May 1498, beginning the Portuguese presence in India. By 1510, Goa had become the capital of the Portuguese colony, so the arrival had developed into a settled colonial centre. Ships also needed cartaz permits to navigate in the Arabian Sea. In 1560, the Portuguese established the Inquisition in Goa. The sequence therefore shows the Portuguese moving from arrival to a capital and then exercising stronger institutional control.
points: Names Vasco da Gama, Kappad, Kozhikode and May 1498.
Explains Goa’s importance as the colonial capital from 1510.
Includes the cartaz permit and the Inquisition established in 1560.
Shows a progression from arrival to organised colonial control.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Along India’s coast, the English East India Company had established a trading foothold. Its royal charter gave the Company special powers, including its own private army. When a dispute broke out between local rulers, British agents used military support and entered the conflict. Later, Clive plotted with Mir Jafar to betray the Nawab of Bengal. The Company then used its position as kingmaker to enlarge its control. Under subsidiary alliances, the British also placed Residents in the courts of Indian rulers.
activities.prompt: Suppose a ruler agrees to a subsidiary alliance and accepts a British Resident at the court. What is the most likely result?
options: Britain would gain control over a large territory while keeping administrative costs low.
The ruler would keep complete control because the Resident could only observe.
The Company would need to run the entire territory directly to gain any influence.
The Resident would replace the ruler and collect all the territory’s revenue.

why.The ruler would keep complete control be: The arrangement gave Britain political control, not merely observation.
why.The Company would need to run the entire: Direct administration would not be necessary to gain influence.
why.The Resident would replace the ruler and: Residents were placed in courts rather than replacing rulers.

activities.explanation: This is the direct result described for subsidiary alliances.

activities.context: Along India’s coast, the English East India Company had established a trading foothold. Its royal charter gave the Company special powers, including its own private army. When a dispute broke out between local rulers, British agents used military support and entered the conflict. Later, Clive plotted with Mir Jafar to betray the Nawab of Bengal. The Company then used its position as kingmaker to enlarge its control. Under subsidiary alliances, the British also placed Residents in the courts of Indian rulers.
activities.prompt: Why were British agents able to enter conflicts between local rulers?
options: They could use the Company’s military power to support a side and strengthen the Company’s position.
They were following the charter’s instruction to end all fighting between rulers.
The Company wanted to avoid any political involvement in local disputes.
The agents could enter only after the Company had already become kingmaker.

why.They were following the charter’s instru: The charter granted powers, but no instruction to end all fighting.
why.The Company wanted to avoid any politica: Their use of military support shows that they did become involved.
why.The agents could enter only after the Co: They entered conflicts before using their kingmaker position.

activities.explanation: The Company had the power to raise its own private army.

activities.context: Along India’s coast, the English East India Company had established a trading foothold. Its royal charter gave the Company special powers, including its own private army. When a dispute broke out between local rulers, British agents used military support and entered the conflict. Later, Clive plotted with Mir Jafar to betray the Nawab of Bengal. The Company then used its position as kingmaker to enlarge its control. Under subsidiary alliances, the British also placed Residents in the courts of Indian rulers.
activities.prompt: If the Company were no longer allowed to raise its own private army, what would most likely happen?
options: British agents would have less military strength for entering conflicts between rulers.
British agents would gain stronger support from local rulers because they had no soldiers.
The Company would immediately lose every coastal trading foothold.
The Company could still use the same military support because its charter would be unchanged.

why.British agents would gain stronger suppo: Local rulers would not necessarily support agents more strongly.
why.The Company would immediately lose every: Trading footholds would not all disappear immediately.
why.The Company could still use the same mil: The loss of this special power would weaken the Company’s military support.

activities.explanation: Removing the private army would reduce the military strength available to agents.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The royal charter gave the English East India Company important special powers.
Reason (R): One of those powers was raising its own private army.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The second statement directly identifies a special power granted by the royal charter.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Clive’s plotting with Mir Jafar contributed to the Company gaining a kingmaker position.
Reason (R): The British placed Residents in the courts of Indian rulers under subsidiary alliances.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the placement of Residents does not explain Clive’s plotting.

activities.prompt: Explain why the English East India Company moved from trade to political rule in India.
activities.answer: The Company began as a trading company and established early footholds along India’s coast. Its royal charter granted special powers, including the right to raise a private army. British agents then used military support to enter conflicts between local rulers. Clive’s plot with Mir Jafar helped the Company use its position as kingmaker to gain wider control. Finally, Residents placed in courts under subsidiary alliances helped Britain control large territories at low administrative cost. Trade therefore provided the starting point, while military intervention, political influence and alliances turned commercial presence into rule.
points: The Company began with coastal trading footholds.
Its royal charter granted military and other special powers.
Military support and Clive’s plot helped create political influence.
Subsidiary alliances brought control over large territories at low cost.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In Bengal in 1770–1772, crop failure and harsh Company taxation combined with a catastrophic famine. Even while people were suffering, the Company raised land tax. Its agents collected maximum revenue but spent very little on governance or development. The episode shows how a company could worsen hardship and take wealth without helping the people affected. A student asks what could have reduced suffering and what the revenue-taking policy produced.
activities.prompt: If the Company had kept land tax unchanged instead of increasing it during the famine, what would most likely have happened?
options: Some suffering might have been reduced because people would have retained more money.
The famine would have ended immediately and permanently.
The Company would no longer have needed revenue from Bengal.
Food prices would have fallen to their lowest possible level.

why.The famine would have ended immediately: An unchanged tax cannot guarantee an immediate end to a famine.
why.The Company would no longer have needed: The Company’s need for revenue would not necessarily have disappeared.
why.Food prices would have fallen to their l: The facts do not show that unchanged tax would produce the lowest food prices.

activities.explanation: Keeping the tax unchanged would have avoided an additional burden.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Colonial Era in India

activities.prompt: Which meaning best describes colonialism?
options: One country takes control of another and settles there.
One country shares equal power with another region's rulers.
Two countries exchange goods but never send people to settle.
Colonialism means local rulers keep all political control.
activities.explanation: Colonialism means one country taking control of another region and settling there.

activities.prompt: The Age of Colonialism began with Europe's expansion from the 15th century.
activities.explanation: European expansion from the 15th century began this age.

activities.hint: His arrival near Kozhikode happened in May.
activities.explanation: Vasco da Gama arrived at Kappad near Kozhikode in May 1498.

activities.prompt: Match each historical detail with its correct name.
activities.explanation: These details connect early European powers with their Indian activities.

activities.prompt: Put these events in time order.

Goa became the Portuguese colonial capital in 1510.
The Portuguese established the Inquisition in Goa in 1560.

chapters.title: Universal Franchise and India’s Electoral System
chapters.summary: In this chapter: universal adult franchise; making voting accessible and fair; the election commission and the scale of elections; voting process and the model code of conduct.

lessons.title: Universal Adult Franchise

activities.prompt: How does India make sure every adult’s voice is heard?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Is Universal Adult Franchise?
activities.body: Universal adult franchise gives voting rights to every adult Indian citizen, except people found guilty of certain serious crimes. Citizens aged 18 and above have this right. Each person has one vote, and every vote counts equally. It does not discriminate based on caste, creed, sex, education or wealth. Voters must register in the constituency, or voting area, where they want to vote.
keyPoints: Every adult citizen has one equally valuable vote.
Citizens aged 18 and above have voting rights.
Voting rights do not depend on caste, creed, sex, education or wealth.
activities.explanation: This system gives equal voting rights without discrimination.

activities.prompt: A rich adult and a poor adult live in the same constituency. Both are registered. How should their votes count?
steps: Both can vote because every adult citizen has one vote.
Each vote must count equally because wealth must not change its value.
They may vote in that constituency because both are registered there.
So their votes must count equally, with no extra vote for wealth.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Can Vote?
activities.prompt: Who has the right to vote in India?
options: Every Indian citizen aged 18 and above
Only Indian citizens aged 21 and above
Only Indian men aged 18 and above
Only wealthy Indian citizens aged 18 and above
activities.explanation: India gives voting rights to every citizen aged 18 and above.

activities.title: When Did the Voting Age Change?
activities.prompt: India lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 in ______.
activities.hint: This was the year of the voting age change.
activities.explanation: India lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 in 1988.

activities.title: Voting Before Independence
activities.prompt: Before Independence, around what per cent of Indians could vote?
options: Around 13 per cent
Around 18 per cent
Around 21 per cent
activities.explanation: Before Independence, only around 13 per cent of Indians could vote.

activities.title: Match the Voting Rules
activities.prompt: Match each person to the voting rule that applies.
pairs: Person wanting to vote in a constituency
Must be registered in that constituency
Person guilty of certain serious crimes
Had voting rights from universal franchise's beginning
activities.explanation: These pairs show equal votes, registration, crime rules and women's rights.

activities.title: Which Situation Follows the Rules?
activities.prompt: Which situation follows the voting rules?
options: A citizen is blocked from voting because they are wealthy.
A woman is blocked from voting because of her sex.
An 18-year-old citizen registers in the constituency and votes.
A citizen votes without registering in the constituency.
activities.explanation: Registration and no discrimination are key parts of universal adult franchise.

activities.title: Voting Milestones
activities.prompt: Put these voting milestones in time order.
items: Before Independence: around 13 per cent could vote
2024: over 968 million voters were eligible in the Lok Sabha election
activities.explanation: The milestones move from pre-Independence limits to the 1988 change and 2024 election.

activities.prompt: An adult has more money than another adult in the same constituency. Both are registered and eligible to vote. How should their votes count?
options: Each person's vote should have equal value.
The richer person's vote should have more value.
The poorer person's vote should have more value.
Only the richer person's vote should be counted.

why.The richer person's vote should have mor: This mistake assumes that more money gives a stronger vote.
why.The poorer person's vote should have mor: This mistake assumes that less money gives a stronger vote.
why.Only the richer person's vote should be: This mistake leaves out one eligible adult's vote.

activities.explanation: This is right because all votes have equal value.

activities.prompt: An adult wants to vote elsewhere but is registered in another area. What must the adult do before voting there?
options: Register in the area where they wish to vote.
Vote there without registering in that area.
Give two votes because they know two areas.
Choose a vote with less value to stay registered.

why.Vote there without registering in that a: This mistake assumes that local registration is not needed.
why.Give two votes because they know two are: This mistake wrongly gives extra votes for knowing two areas.
why.Choose a vote with less value to stay re: This mistake assumes that people can choose a vote's value.

activities.explanation: This is right because voters must register where they wish to vote.

activities.prompt: One adult was found guilty of a certain serious crime. What should be true about this person's voting right?
options: The person cannot vote because of that conviction.
The person may vote if registered in the same area.
The person may vote only in a different constituency.
The person's vote may count less than all other votes.

why.The person may vote if registered in the: This mistake treats the crime rule as only a registration issue.
why.The person may vote only in a different: This mistake assumes that conviction changes the voting place.
why.The person's vote may count less than al: This mistake assumes that conviction lowers a vote instead of removing it.

activities.explanation: This is right because such convictions stop a person from voting.

lessons.title: Making Voting Accessible and Fair

activities.prompt: How can voting be made easier and fairer for everyone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways to Make Voting Easier
activities.body: The Election Commission of India has introduced new ways to make voting easier. Election officials travel to remote places so citizens can vote. In 2024, elderly people and people with disabilities could vote from home. Support also includes postal voting, Braille voter cards and app-based help for voters.
keyPoints: Officials travel to remote places.
Some voters could vote from home in 2024.
Braille cards and app-based help support voters.
activities.explanation: These supports help different voters take part.

activities.prompt: Neha received a ballot paper printed in Braille. How can she vote while the class election stays private and fair?
steps: Neha can read the Braille ballot, so it gives her access to voting.
A secret ballot can keep her choice private from others.
Privacy helps keep the voting process fair.
Therefore, Braille access and a secret ballot support fair voting.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Selecting Representatives Fairly
activities.body: The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe an old and transparent way of selecting representatives. A boy publicly drew candidate names randomly from a sealed pot. In a class election, Ms Usha served as Election Officer. A class representative connects students with school authorities. A secret ballot kept voting private and fair.
keyPoints: The Uttaramerur method used a sealed pot.
A class representative connects students and school authorities.
The secret ballot kept voting private and fair.
activities.explanation: These examples show different ways to select representatives.

activities.title: Who Introduced New Voting Ways?
activities.prompt: Who has introduced new ways to make voting easier?
options: The Election Commission of India
Election officials
Ms Usha
A class representative
activities.explanation: The Election Commission introduced these new ways for easier voting.

activities.prompt: Election officials travel to remote places so citizens can vote.
activities.explanation: Officials travel to remote places so citizens can vote there.

activities.title: Ms Usha's Role
activities.prompt: What did Ms Usha do in the class election?
options: Served as Election Officer
Acted as a class representative
Received a Braille ballot paper
Drew names from a sealed pot
activities.explanation: Ms Usha served as the Election Officer for the class election.

activities.title: Match Voting Roles and Actions
activities.prompt: Match each person or voting method with its role or action.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a role or action described in the lesson.

activities.title: Why Was the Method Transparent?
activities.prompt: Why did the Uttaramerur method make selecting representatives transparent?
options: Names were drawn randomly from a sealed pot
Officials travelled to remote places
People voted from home in 2024
Postal voting served a particular group
activities.explanation: The boy publicly drew candidate names randomly from a sealed pot.

activities.prompt: Ms Usha received a ballot paper printed in Braille.
activities.explanation: Neha received the ballot paper printed in Braille.

activities.prompt: The Election Commission introduced new ways to make voting easier. A citizen lives in a remote place. Which method helps this citizen?
options: Send election officials to the remote place.
Keep all voting services at the main office.
Ask the citizen to find another representative.
Stop voting help until the citizen can travel.

why.Keep all voting services at the main off: This leaves a remote citizen without the needed voting help.
why.Ask the citizen to find another represen: The fact says officials travel, not that citizens find representatives.
why.Stop voting help until the citizen can t: This makes voting harder instead of making it easier.

activities.explanation: Officials travel to remote places so citizens there can vote.

activities.prompt: The 2024 rule allowed elderly people and people with disabilities to vote from home. One elderly voter cannot travel easily. Which plan follows this rule?
options: Let the elderly voter vote from home instead of travelling.
Make the elderly voter travel even though home voting is allowed.
Allow only the disabled voter to vote from home.
Use a sealed-pot draw for the elderly voter.

why.Make the elderly voter travel even thoug: It ignores the home-voting choice for elderly people.
why.Allow only the disabled voter to vote fr: The rule included elderly people as well as people with disabilities.
why.Use a sealed-pot draw for the elderly vo: The sealed-pot draw was an old method for choosing representatives.

activities.explanation: This follows the 2024 home-voting rule for elderly people.

activities.prompt: Postal voting is available to a particular group of voters. Two voters are outside that group. Which plan follows the rule?
options: Do not use postal voting for voters outside the stated group.
Use postal voting for every voter to make voting easier.
Let outside voters use home voting without checking the rule.
Let outside voters join the old random name draw.

why.Use postal voting for every voter to mak: This ignores the group limit for postal voting.
why.Let outside voters use home voting witho: Home voting in 2024 had its own elderly and disability groups.
why.Let outside voters join the old random n: The random draw selected old representatives, not voting methods.

activities.explanation: Postal voting is available only to the stated particular group.

activities.prompt: Neha received a ballot paper printed in Braille. Braille voter cards and app-based help were also made possible. What do these facts show?
options: Braille and app support can make voting easier for different voters.
Braille and app support are both required for every voter.
Braille is allowed, but app support was never made possible.
Printed ballots are the only support because privacy needs print.

why.Braille and app support are both require: These are support choices, not requirements for every voter.
why.Braille is allowed, but app support was: The facts say that app-based help was made possible.
why.Printed ballots are the only support bec: Privacy comes from the secret ballot, not from printed ballots.

activities.explanation: The facts offer both Braille and app help to support voters.

activities.prompt: Ms Usha served as the Election Officer for the class election. The class representative connects students and school authorities. The secret ballot keeps choices private. A student has both a concern and a vote. What should happen?
options: The representative passes the concern, while the secret ballot hides the choice.
The representative marks the ballot, while Ms Usha keeps the concern.
The representative hides the ballot, while Ms Usha passes the concern.
The ballot chooses the representative, while the concern stays hidden.

why.The representative marks the ballot, whi: The representative's bridge role is about school concerns, not marking ballots.
why.The representative hides the ballot, whi: The secret ballot, not the representative, should protect each choice.
why.The ballot chooses the representative, w: The facts do not say that the ballot chooses the class representative.

activities.explanation: The representative carries concerns, and the secret ballot protects choices.

lessons.title: The Election Commission and the Scale of Elections

activities.title: The Election Commission and the Scale of Elections
activities.body:
India is a parliamentary democracy.

State Election Commissions manage elections to local bodies.

The Election Commission of India is an independent constitutional body.
keyPoints: The Election Commission of India was established in 1950.
India’s first general elections were held in 1951–1952.
activities.explanation: Now try some questions.

activities.prompt: How does India make sure every vote is organized and counted fairly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.prompt: When a town holds a local body election, who should organise it properly?
steps: Local body elections need organised management for voters.
The State Election Commission manages elections to local bodies.
Therefore, it is the right body to organise the town's election.
This gives the election a clear and proper manager.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Manages Local Elections?
activities.prompt: Which body manages elections to local bodies?
options: The Election Commission of India
State Election Commissions
A group of teachers
The Model Code of Conduct
activities.explanation: State Election Commissions manage local body elections. The Election Commission manages the wider electoral process.

activities.title: The Year of Establishment
activities.prompt: The Election Commission of India was established in ______.
activities.hint: This was the year the Commission was established.
activities.explanation: The Election Commission of India became an independent constitutional body in 1950.

activities.title: Bodies and Their Work
activities.prompt: Match each body or group with its role.
activities.explanation: Each body or group has a clear role. Together, they help elections take place across India.

activities.title: Reserved Constituencies
activities.prompt: How many Lok Sabha constituencies are reserved altogether for scheduled castes and scheduled tribes?
options: 84 constituencies
47 constituencies
131 constituencies
activities.explanation: There are 84 reserved for scheduled castes and 47 for scheduled tribes. Together, they make 131.

activities.title: Groups With Reserved Seats
activities.prompt: Which pair correctly names the groups with reserved Lok Sabha constituencies?
options: Scheduled castes and scheduled tribes
Teachers and other election workers
State Election Commissions and local bodies
The Commission and the Model Code
activities.explanation: Some Lok Sabha constituencies are reserved for scheduled castes and scheduled tribes.

activities.title: Who Runs Which Elections?
activities.prompt: State Election Commissions manage general elections across India.
activities.explanation: State Election Commissions manage local body elections. The Election Commission manages the wider electoral process.

activities.prompt: India is a parliamentary democracy. Which rule helps make elections trustworthy?
options: An independent Election Commission works under the Constitution.
The Prime Minister personally controls every polling station in India.
Political parties choose all members of the Election Commission.
State governments decide how all national votes are counted.

why.The Prime Minister personally controls e: This wrongly makes the Prime Minister the Commission's controller.
why.Political parties choose all members of: This wrongly gives political parties power over Commission members.
why.State governments decide how all nationa: This wrongly gives counting decisions to state governments.

activities.explanation: Independence helps keep the Commission separate from the government.

lessons.title: Voting Process and the Model Code of Conduct

activities.prompt: What happens between checking your identity and casting your vote?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Voting Is Checked
activities.body: Polling officers help at elections. First, an officer checks your name and identity proof. Next, another officer marks your finger and takes your signature. Another checks your finger and the small chit. You press a button on an electronic voting machine. You can check the VVPAT slip. It makes a physical record and can help with verification or recounting. The Model Code of Conduct helps keep elections free and fair.
keyPoints: Polling officers check the voter’s details in order.
VVPAT makes a physical record for possible verification or recounting.
The Model Code of Conduct helps keep elections free and fair.
activities.explanation: The Model Code of Conduct helps keep elections free and fair.

activities.prompt: A candidate gives a gift to influence a voter and uses a government car. What should happen?
steps: The gift should be refused because influencing voters with gifts is punishable.
The government car should not be used because election use is forbidden.
The candidate should show discretion and restraint because elections must stay fair.
Both actions should stop so the election stays free and fair.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The First Polling Officer
activities.prompt: What does the first polling officer do?
options: Checks your name and identity proof
Marks your finger and takes your signature
Checks your finger and the chit
Presses the voting machine button
activities.explanation: The first polling officer checks the voter’s name and identity proof.

activities.title: Checking the Voter
activities.prompt: The first polling officer checks your name and ______ proof.
activities.hint: This proof identifies the voter.
activities.explanation: The first polling officer checks your name and identity proof.

activities.title: Match Each Action
activities.prompt: Match each person with the correct action.
pairs: Presses the electronic voting machine button
activities.explanation: Each person has one action in the voting process.

activities.title: The VVPAT Record
activities.prompt: Why is the VVPAT paper record useful?
options: It helps with verification or recounting
It marks the voter’s finger
It checks the voter’s identity
It takes the voter’s signature
activities.explanation: The paper record can help with verification or recounting if there is a dispute.

activities.title: Order of Checks
activities.prompt: Put the polling officer actions in the correct order.
items: Check the voter’s name and identity proof
Mark the voter’s finger and take the signature
Check the voter’s finger and the chit
activities.explanation: The first, second and third officers perform these actions in this order.

activities.title: Rules for Candidates
activities.prompt: What should a candidate do during elections?
options: Use government resources for election purposes
Give gifts to influence voters
Show discretion and restraint
activities.explanation: Candidates must show discretion and restraint. Giving gifts to influence voters is punishable.

activities.prompt: An election result is disputed. The VVPAT paper record can be checked. What might it help to do?
options: Verify the vote or recount it.
Choose the candidate who received more gifts.
Decide which polling officer made a mistake.
Stop the Model Code from being followed.

why.Choose the candidate who received more g: This wrongly assumes gifts decide a disputed election.
why.Decide which polling officer made a mist: This wrongly treats officer duties as the purpose of recounting.
This wrongly assumes recounting works against the Model Code.

activities.explanation: The paper record can help with verification or recounting after a dispute.

activities.prompt: A candidate uses a government van to carry campaigners. What should the candidate do with the van?
options: Stop using it because government resources cannot be used.
Keep using it because campaigners need free transport.
Keep using it because voters may support the candidate.
Keep using it because it travels through many areas.

why.Keep using it because campaigners need f: This wrongly assumes free transport is allowed for campaigners.
why.Keep using it because voters may support: This wrongly assumes candidate support allows election use.
why.Keep using it because it travels through: This wrongly assumes travel distance changes the rule.

activities.explanation: Government resources cannot be used for election purposes.

activities.prompt: One voter accepts a gift for supporting a candidate. Another refuses the same gift. Why should the second voter refuse?
options: Because giving gifts to influence voters is punishable.
Because gifts are needed for fair campaigns.
Because every candidate gives gifts to supporters.
Because voting gifts are checked after counting.

why.Because gifts are needed for fair campai: This wrongly assumes small gifts cannot influence voters.
why.Because every candidate gives gifts to s: This wrongly treats gifts as a sign of a fair campaign.
why.Because voting gifts are checked after c: This wrongly assumes all candidates give gifts to supporters.

activities.explanation: Giving gifts to influence voters is punishable.

activities.prompt: A candidate shouts at voters and uses a government office for meetings. What should the candidate change?
options: Show restraint and avoid using the government office.
Keep shouting and use the office for more meetings.
Give gifts and invite more people to meetings.
Press the voting button and check each slip.

why.Keep shouting and use the office for mor: This wrongly treats shouting and office use as normal campaigning.
why.Give gifts and invite more people to mee: This wrongly assumes gifts can replace discreet campaigning.
why.Press the voting button and check each s: This wrongly mixes candidate conduct with the polling process.

activities.explanation: Right because restraint and no government election use follow the Model Code.
