lessons.title: Elections at Every Level

activities.prompt: How do votes turn into leaders at every level of Indian democracy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Elections Work
activities.body: India’s general elections are called the ‘Festival of Democracy’. You vote at national, state and local levels. India uses First-Past-the-Post, so the candidate with the most votes wins. A party, or a group of parties called a coalition, with a Lok Sabha majority forms the national government. The majority party’s state leader becomes chief minister. People elected to state assemblies are called Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs).
keyPoints: Voting happens at national, state and local levels
The candidate with the most votes wins
A Lok Sabha majority forms the national government
activities.explanation: Your votes help choose representatives at different levels.

activities.prompt: No party has a Lok Sabha majority. Two parties join. Can they form the national government?
steps: No party has a majority, so no party can form the government.
The two parties join, so their seats work together.
A party or coalition with a majority forms the national government.
Therefore, the joined parties form the government if they have a majority.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Festival of Democracy
activities.prompt: What are India’s general elections called?
options: Festival of Elections
Festival of Government
Festival of Democracy
Festival of Votes
activities.explanation: General elections in India are known as the ‘Festival of Democracy’.

activities.title: Members of Parliament
activities.prompt: People elected to the Lok Sabha are called Members of ______.
activities.hint: The full name starts with ‘Members of’.
activities.explanation: These elected representatives are called Members of Parliament.

activities.title: State Assembly Members
activities.prompt: What are people elected to state assemblies called?
options: Members of Parliament
Members of State Assembly
Members of National Assembly
Members of Legislative Assembly
activities.explanation: They are called Members of the Legislative Assembly, or MLAs.

activities.title: Elections and Responsibility
activities.prompt: Match each group or role with the correct detail.
pairs: Leader of a state’s majority party
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how elections and majority lead to important offices.

activities.title: The Winning Candidate
activities.prompt: Which candidate wins under India’s First-Past-the-Post system?
options: The candidate with the fewest votes
The candidate with the most votes
The candidate chosen by a party
The candidate chosen by citizens
activities.explanation: Under First-Past-the-Post, the candidate with the most votes wins.

activities.title: Elected by an Electoral College
activities.prompt: Which offices are elected by an electoral college?
options: The Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
The President and Vice President
The Prime Minister and President
The Chief Minister and President
activities.explanation: Both the President and Vice President are elected by an electoral college.

activities.prompt: A result chart shows one group has a Lok Sabha majority. Who should form the national government?
options: The group with a Lok Sabha majority.
The group with the most votes.
The group with the fewest seats.
The group whose leader won most votes.

Most votes do not always mean a Lok Sabha majority.
Fewest seats cannot give a group a majority.
Popular votes for a leader do not decide who forms the government.

activities.explanation: It has a majority, so the rule says it forms the government.

activities.prompt: No party wins a Lok Sabha majority. Two parties join. What can they do?
options: Form the government if they have a majority.
Form the government because they won most votes.
Choose the President without any electoral college.
Elect all Rajya Sabha members by direct voting.

why.Form the government because they won mos: Most votes do not always give the coalition a majority.
why.Choose the President without any elector: This confuses government formation with choosing the President.
why.Elect all Rajya Sabha members by direct: This confuses direct voting with indirect Rajya Sabha elections.

activities.explanation: If their seats make a majority, they can form the national government.

activities.prompt: One election uses First-Past-the-Post. Another elects the President. How are the winners chosen?
options: The first uses most votes; the President uses transferable votes.
The first uses transferable votes; the President needs most votes.
Both winners need more votes than all rivals together.
Both winners are chosen by state assemblies.

why.The first uses transferable votes; the P: This swaps the two separate voting methods.
why.Both winners need more votes than all ri: It treats a majority requirement as the rule for both elections.
why.Both winners are chosen by state assembl: It confuses electoral colleges with state assemblies.

activities.explanation: Most votes decide the first; transferable votes decide the President.

activities.prompt: Most Rajya Sabha members are chosen by MLAs. Why is voting indirect?
options: MLAs vote for most members, so citizens act through them.
Citizens directly vote for every Rajya Sabha member.
The President personally elects every Rajya Sabha member.
All members are chosen in state assembly elections.

why.Citizens directly vote for every Rajya S: This confuses indirect election with direct citizen voting.
why.The President personally elects every Ra: This confuses the President’s nominations with elections by MLAs.
why.All members are chosen in state assembly: This confuses electing members with choosing them in assemblies.

activities.explanation: Most members are elected by MLAs from state assemblies.

activities.prompt: One party has a state assembly majority. Who becomes the chief minister?
options: The leader of that majority party.
The candidate with the most national votes.
The leader of the largest Rajya Sabha group.
The Lok Sabha member with the most votes.

why.The candidate with the most national vot: National election votes do not choose a state chief minister.
why.The leader of the largest Rajya Sabha gr: Rajya Sabha members do not lead state assembly majorities.
why.The Lok Sabha member with the most votes: Lok Sabha members belong to the national level.

activities.explanation: The leader of the majority party becomes chief minister.

activities.prompt: Both offices are chosen indirectly. What common method chooses their holders?
options: An electoral college elects both leaders.
Only the President uses an electoral college.
State assemblies directly elect both leaders.
MLAs directly elect both office holders.

why.Only the President uses an electoral col: This wrongly treats only one leader as indirectly elected.
why.State assemblies directly elect both lea: State assemblies do not directly elect either leader.
MLAs elect most Rajya Sabha members, not these leaders.

activities.explanation: An electoral college elects both the President and Vice President.

lessons.title: Challenges and Responsible Voting

activities.prompt: What makes voting a powerful choice, and how can we make it fair?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Voting Wisely and Responsibly
activities.body: Responsible voting starts with proper information. Media, education and awareness campaigns should work together. They should help young people understand the importance of voting wisely. The right to vote is also a responsibility. Voter awareness is an important part of this right. All eligible voters should be able to participate. Money’s growing influence and voter apathy are challenges. Indian democracy needs vigilant and aware voters.
keyPoints: Proper information supports thoughtful, responsible choices.
Media, education and awareness campaigns should work together.
Voting is both a right and a responsibility.
activities.explanation: Good information, awareness and responsibility help voters choose wisely.

activities.prompt: Two friends are eligible to vote. One supports a candidate because of money. What should they do?
steps: Proper information helps because it supports thoughtful and responsible choices.
Voting is a responsibility because voters must choose responsibly.
Media, education and awareness campaigns should work together to build understanding.
Therefore, voters should question money, learn more, and vote responsibly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What should awareness efforts help young people understand?
options: The need to ignore information
The importance of voting wisely
The value of staying away
The power of election money
activities.explanation: These efforts should help young people understand why voting wisely matters.

activities.prompt: All eligible voters should be able to participate in elections.
activities.explanation: Every eligible voter should have the chance to participate.

activities.prompt: The right to vote is also a ______.
activities.hint: It means you have a duty when you vote.
activities.explanation: Voting gives people a right, but they must use it responsibly.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its partner from the lesson.
pairs: Helps young people understand wise voting
activities.explanation: The Commission conducts elections. Campaigns guide young voters. Money creates challenges.

activities.prompt: What helps voters make thoughtful choices?
options: Less information
More election money
Proper information
Fewer campaign voices
activities.explanation: Voters need proper information to make thoughtful and responsible choices.

activities.prompt: Which action best helps Indian democracy meet its challenges?
options: Stay uninformed about choices
Remain passive during elections
Allow money to shape choices
Become vigilant and aware
activities.explanation: Indian democracy needs vigilant and aware voters to meet its challenges.

activities.prompt: A voter hears only a campaign promise. Why seek more information?
options: The promise may not give facts for a thoughtful choice.
Campaign promises always contain complete voter information.
More information can make the vote seem more exciting.
A voter does not need facts when choosing a candidate.

why.Campaign promises always contain complet: This wrongly assumes campaign promises always give complete information.
why.More information can make the vote seem: This confuses useful information with excitement.
why.A voter does not need facts when choosin: This ignores the need for proper information before voting.

activities.explanation: Proper information helps voters make thoughtful and responsible choices.

activities.prompt: Voters know little about voting. How should media, education and campaigns help?
options: Together they should help young people understand voting wisely.
They should use money to decide what voters must learn.
Only cities need help to understand voting wisely.
They should wait for apathy to teach voters how to vote.

why.They should use money to decide what vot: This mistakes money influence for useful voter education.
why.Only cities need help to understand voti: This wrongly limits voter awareness work to cities.
why.They should wait for apathy to teach vot: This treats apathy as a teacher instead of a challenge.

activities.explanation: Working together helps young people understand the importance of voting wisely.

activities.prompt: A map shows polling places across India. What does this mainly show?
options: The Election Commission conducts elections across the country.
Only city voters can take part in Indian elections.
Voter apathy is the biggest problem in every place.
The map shows that every voter in India feels responsible.

why.Only city voters can take part in Indian: A map cannot show that only city voters can vote.
why.Voter apathy is the biggest problem in e: Polling places alone cannot prove the same problem everywhere.
why.The map shows that every voter in India: A map shows places, not voters’ feelings or responsibility.

activities.explanation: Polling places across the country show that elections are held nationally.

activities.prompt: An eligible voter cannot reach the polling place. What should happen?
options: Election arrangements should let this voter participate.
The voter should give up voting because rules matter.
Only money should decide whether this voter participates.
The voter should wait until the next city election.

why.The voter should give up voting because: This mistakes following rules for denying someone a right.
why.Only money should decide whether this vo: This gives money power over voter participation.
why.The voter should wait until the next cit: This leaves an eligible voter out without helping participation.

activities.explanation: All eligible voters should be able to take part in elections.

activities.prompt: Campaigns spend more money. What concern should aware voters notice?
options: Money may have growing influence over voters and choices.
Money always gives every voter the same result.
More campaign money proves all voters are vigilant.
Campaign money means cities have no voter apathy.

why.Money always gives every voter the same: This wrongly treats money as a guarantee of equal results.
why.More campaign money proves all voters ar: This confuses spending money with being watchful.
why.Campaign money means cities have no vote: This confuses campaign money with the problem of voter apathy.

activities.explanation: The growing influence of money in elections is a known challenge.

activities.prompt: City voters feel unheard and skip voting. Why is this a problem?
options: Democracy needs vigilant voters, and apathy weakens participation.
Apathy proves that elections in cities work perfectly.
Skipping votes makes money influence elections weaker.
People should vote only after campaigns give them money.

why.Apathy proves that elections in cities w: Low participation does not prove that elections work perfectly.
why.Skipping votes makes money influence ele: Not voting does not remove the challenge of money influence.
why.People should vote only after campaigns: This turns money influence into a rule for responsible voting.

activities.explanation: Apathy reduces participation, so democracy needs vigilant and aware voters.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Universal franchise is a cornerstone of Indian democracy.
Reason (R): Every adult citizen has one vote, and all votes have equal value.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Giving equal voting power to every adult citizen helps make universal franchise a foundation of democracy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Elections for the Lok Sabha, state assemblies and local bodies follow universal franchise.
Reason (R): A voter must be registered in the constituency where they wish to vote.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Registration is a voting procedure, but it does not explain why the three types of elections follow universal franchise.

activities.prompt: How does universal franchise work in India, and what changes did the lowering of the voting age bring?
activities.answer: Universal franchise gives every eligible adult citizen one vote, and all votes have equal value. It does not discriminate on grounds such as caste, creed, sex, education or wealth. India lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 in 1988, so every Indian citizen aged 18 and above has the right to vote. Before Independence, only around 13 per cent of Indians could vote. Women in India also had voting rights from the beginning of universal adult franchise, showing that sex was not a ground for exclusion.
points: Every eligible adult citizen has one vote.
All votes have equal value.
The voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 in 1988.
Before Independence, only around 13 per cent could vote.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a class election, Ms Usha served as the Election Officer and students used a secret ballot. Neha received a ballot paper printed in braille. The class representative acted as a bridge between students and school authorities. One student asked whether these arrangements could keep the election accessible and fair while protecting voters' choices.
activities.prompt: If school authorities change the class meeting time without telling students, what should the class representative do next?
options: Keep the change within the class until the next election.
Take over the Election Officer role and announce the new time.
Choose a new class representative without asking the other students.
Inform classmates about the change and pass their concerns to the administrators.

why.Keep the change within the class until t: Keeping the change secret would prevent the representative from acting as a bridge.
why.Take over the Election Officer role and: Ms Usha held the Election Officer role, while the class representative communicated with students.
why.Choose a new class representative withou: The representative should pass on concerns rather than make the decision alone.

activities.explanation: Informing students and communicating their concerns fulfils the bridge role.

activities.context: During a class election, Ms Usha served as the Election Officer and students used a secret ballot. Neha received a ballot paper printed in braille. The class representative acted as a bridge between students and school authorities. One student asked whether these arrangements could keep the election accessible and fair while protecting voters' choices.
activities.prompt: If the class replaced its secret ballot with the public draw used in the old Uttaramerur method, what would happen?
options: The random draw would be transparent, but the private character of the class voting method would be lost.
The public draw would hide the selection because the pot was sealed.
The public draw would remove randomness because students could see and influence it.
The change would have no effect because sealed pots make voting private.

why.The public draw would hide the selection: The pot was sealed before the names were drawn, but the drawing itself was public.
why.The public draw would remove randomness: A public drawing could still be random.
why.The change would have no effect because: Keeping a pot sealed did not make the public drawing of names private.

activities.explanation: The public random draw was transparent, while the secret ballot kept voting private.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In 2024, elderly people and people with disabilities could vote from home.
Reason (R): Postal voting was available to every voter in the country.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Postal voting was available to a particular group, not every voter.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The introduction of new voting methods helped make home voting possible for elderly people and people with disabilities.
Reason (R): The Election Commission introduced new ways to make voting easier.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The new methods provided an easier way for elderly people and people with disabilities to vote from home.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the old Uttaramerur method of selecting representatives and the secret ballot used in the class election.
activities.answer: In the Uttaramerur method, a boy publicly drew candidate names randomly from a sealed pot. This was an old and transparent way to select representatives because the drawing was public. In the secret ballot, voters choose privately, and the process keeps voting private and fair. The main difference is that the old method made the selection visible, while the secret ballot protects each voter's choice from public view. Random drawing and secrecy are therefore separate features.
points: The Uttaramerur method involved a public random draw from a sealed pot.
The method is described as old and transparent.
The secret ballot keeps voting private and fair.
The main difference is public selection versus private voting.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student sees teachers working as part of the election process. The student is told that the Election Commission of India manages elections across India and helps enforce the Model Code of Conduct. The student learns that this is a mammoth task because elections take place at different times but follow a regular cycle. The student also wonders how reserved Lok Sabha constituencies and State Election Commissions fit into the election system.
activities.prompt: In the case, who should take responsibility for an election to a local body?
options: The state election authority assigned to local-body elections
The national election authority, regardless of the type of election
The teachers mentioned in the case
The workers who assist with the national electoral process

why.The national election authority, regardl: This ignores the specific role of State Election Commissions.
why.The teachers mentioned in the case: Teachers help run the process but are not the deciding authority.
why.The workers who assist with the national: Workers assist the process but do not manage local elections.

activities.explanation: State commissions are assigned local-body elections.

activities.context: A student sees teachers working as part of the election process. The student is told that the Election Commission of India manages elections across India and helps enforce the Model Code of Conduct. The student learns that this is a mammoth task because elections take place at different times but follow a regular cycle. The student also wonders how reserved Lok Sabha constituencies and State Election Commissions fit into the election system.
activities.prompt: Why is the work described in the case a mammoth task?
options: Elections occur at different times, and many workers help run the process.
All elections occur on one day, so very few workers are needed.
Only local-body elections follow a regular cycle.
Only reserved constituencies need election workers.

why.All elections occur on one day, so very: The elections do not all occur on one day.
why.Only local-body elections follow a regul: The regular cycle applies to elections generally.
why.Only reserved constituencies need electi: Election workers are needed beyond reserved constituencies.

activities.explanation: Different election times and many workers make the task large.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Managing elections across India is a mammoth task.
Reason (R): Elections take place at different times but follow a regular cycle.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The need to manage elections at different times helps explain why the task is mammoth.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Election Commission of India was established in 1950.
Reason (R): India's first general elections were held before the Commission was established.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The Commission was established in 1950, before the first general elections of 1951–1952.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Election Commission of India was established in 1951.
Reason (R): India's first general elections were held in 1951–1952.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The establishment year was 1950, while the first general elections were held in 1951–1952.

activities.prompt: Explain why managing elections across India is a mammoth task.
activities.answer: Managing elections across India is a mammoth task because elections take place at different times while following a regular cycle. The Election Commission has to manage the electoral process throughout the country, which includes helping enforce the Model Code of Conduct. Many workers, including teachers, help run the election process, showing that elections require work by many people. The Commission must also deal with the scale of elections across India. All these responsibilities make the work very large.
points: Elections happen at different times.
The regular electoral cycle continues across the country.
Many workers, including teachers, help run elections.
The Commission manages the process and helps enforce the Model Code.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a polling station, a voter gave identity proof. The first officer checked the name; the second marked the finger and took a signature; the third checked the finger and chit. The voter pressed the machine button and examined the printed VVPAT slip. This slip made a physical record of the electronic vote. If a dispute arose, the record could help with verification or recounting.
activities.prompt: After the third polling officer checks the voter’s finger and chit, what should the voter do next?
options: Operate the voting machine’s button and then look at the printed slip.
Return to the second officer so that the finger is marked and signed again.
Ask the third officer to press the machine button instead of the voter.
Skip the electronic machine and ask the third officer to record the vote on the chit.

why.Return to the second officer so that the: The second officer’s checks are already complete.
why.Ask the third officer to press the machi: The voter must operate the machine.
why.Skip the electronic machine and ask the: The chit is checked, not used to record the vote.

activities.explanation: This is the correct casting and checking stage.

activities.context: At a polling station, a voter gave identity proof. The first officer checked the name; the second marked the finger and took a signature; the third checked the finger and chit. The voter pressed the machine button and examined the printed VVPAT slip. This slip made a physical record of the electronic vote. If a dispute arose, the record could help with verification or recounting.
activities.prompt: If a candidate offers the voter a gift to influence the vote, what should the voter do?
options: Refuse the gift because giving gifts to influence voters is punishable.
Accept the gift because candidates may give gifts during an election.
Accept the gift secretly because candidates need not show restraint.
Accept the gift because the Model Code applies only to government resources.

why.Accept the gift secretly because candida: Secrecy does not make it acceptable.
why.Accept the gift because the Model Code a: The Code has broader election rules.

activities.explanation: Influencing voters with gifts is punishable.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Model Code of Conduct helps keep elections free and fair.
Reason (R): Government resources cannot be used for election purposes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the restriction on government resources does not explain how the Code helps keep elections free and fair.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The VVPAT slip leaves only an electronic record and no physical record of the vote.
Reason (R): VVPAT produces a physical record of the electronic vote.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because VVPAT does produce a physical paper record.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Universal Franchise and India’s Electoral System

activities.prompt: Which age gives a citizen the right to vote in India?
options: 18 years old
21 years old
After becoming a chief minister
After joining a political party
activities.explanation: The voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 in 1988. Every citizen aged 18 and above can vote.

activities.prompt: Universal franchise treats adult citizens equally, whatever their caste, creed, sex, education or wealth.
activities.explanation: Universal franchise does not discriminate on grounds such as caste, creed, sex, education or wealth.

activities.prompt: A voter must be registered in the ______ where they wish to vote.
activities.hint: Choose the electoral area word from the lesson.
activities.explanation: A voter must register in the constituency where they wish to vote.

activities.prompt: Match each group with its elected name or role.
activities.explanation: Lok Sabha members are Members of Parliament. State assembly members are Members of Legislative Assembly.

activities.prompt: Put the voting steps in the correct order.
items: The first officer checks the voter’s name and identity proof.
The second officer marks the voter’s finger and takes a signature.
The third officer checks the voter’s finger and the chit.
The voter presses the button on an electronic voting machine.
activities.explanation: The officers complete checks in their numbered order. The voter then casts the vote.

activities.prompt: What is one important task of the Election Commission of India?
options: Choosing every state chief minister
Managing the electoral process
Selecting every Lok Sabha candidate
Deciding who may join a political party
activities.explanation: Managing the electoral process is one important Commission task.

activities.prompt: Government resources can be used for election purposes.
activities.explanation: Government resources cannot be used for election purposes.

activities.prompt: The ______ produces a physical record of the electronic vote.
activities.hint: Use the short name from your book.
activities.explanation: VVPAT produces a physical record. It can help with verification or recounting if there is a dispute.

activities.prompt: Which pair correctly identifies two challenges to Indian democracy?
options: Equal votes and universal franchise
Postal voting and Braille cards
Money’s influence and voter apathy
Regular cycles and remote polling
activities.explanation: Growing money influence and voter apathy are challenges. Indian democracy needs vigilant and aware voters.

chapters.title: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive
chapters.summary: In this chapter: introduction and composition of parliament; presiding officers and constitutional functions; lawmaking and accountability; executive functions and checks on power.

lessons.title: Introduction and Composition of Parliament

activities.prompt: How does your voice become the laws that shape our country?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Parliament
activities.body: Parliament is India's supreme body for making laws. It has the President and two houses. The Lok Sabha is also called the House of the People. People directly elect representatives who become Lok Sabha members. A majority group of elected representatives forms the government. The government works with the consent of the people. Rajya Sabha members are chosen indirectly by an electoral college. Two houses together form a bicameral system.
keyPoints: People directly elect Lok Sabha members.
A majority group forms the government.
Parliament has the President and two houses.
Rajya Sabha members are chosen indirectly.
activities.explanation: This introduction shows how Parliament, its houses, and the government are connected.

activities.prompt: You vote for representatives. Why does the majority group form the government?
steps: The people directly elect representatives who become Lok Sabha members.
The elected group with a majority forms the government.
Voting matters because the elected majority determines which group forms the government.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which body makes laws for the country?
options: Parliament
The President
Each state government
The Lok Sabha alone
activities.explanation: Parliament is the supreme body that makes laws for the country.

activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct answer.
activities.explanation: These pairs show Parliament's role, its two houses, and their membership.

activities.prompt: What is a Parliament with two houses called?
options: Bicameral system
Unicameral system
Federal system
Judicial system
activities.explanation: A Parliament with two houses is called a bicameral system.

activities.prompt: The Constitution allows the Lok Sabha to have a maximum of ______ members.
activities.hint: Think about the maximum number given in your book.
activities.explanation: The Constitution allows the Lok Sabha to have a maximum of 550 members.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Elected representatives form a majority group
The majority group forms the government
The government works with the people's consent
activities.explanation: Elections begin the process that leads to government formation and public consent.

activities.prompt: How are seats in both Houses related to the states?
options: Based on each state's population
Based on each state's area
Based on each state's cities
Based on each state's rivers
activities.explanation: The number of seats in both Houses is based on each state's population.

activities.prompt: One lawmaking body has two houses. Another has one house. Which body uses a bicameral system?
options: The body with two houses uses it.
The body with one house uses it.
The body with elected members uses it.
The body with nominated members uses it.

This mistake confuses a one-house body with a two-house body.
This mistake thinks elected members determine the number of houses.
This mistake thinks nominated members determine the number of houses.

activities.explanation: This is right because a two-house Parliament uses a bicameral system.

activities.prompt: State A has a larger population than State B. Seats in both Houses are based on each state’s population. How should their seats compare?
options: State A should have more seats in both Houses.
State B should have more seats in both Houses.
State A should have more seats only in the Lok Sabha.
State B should have more seats only in the Rajya Sabha.

why.State B should have more seats in both H: This mistake reverses the population rule.
why.State A should have more seats only in t: This mistake applies the population rule to only one House.
why.State B should have more seats only in t: This mistake applies the population rule to only one House.

activities.explanation: This is right: larger population means more seats in both Houses.

activities.prompt: Lok Sabha members are directly elected by people. Rajya Sabha members are chosen indirectly by an electoral college. What difference does this show?
options: People choose Lok Sabha members more directly.
People choose Rajya Sabha members more directly.
Both Houses choose all members in the same way.
Neither House gives people any choosing power.

why.People choose Rajya Sabha members more d: This mistake reverses direct and indirect choosing.
why.Both Houses choose all members in the sa: This mistake ignores the different choosing methods in the Houses.
why.Neither House gives people any choosing: This mistake thinks people have no choosing power in either House.

activities.explanation: This is right because people directly elect Lok Sabha members.

activities.prompt: A plan gives the Lok Sabha more than 550 members. The Constitution allows a maximum of 550 members. What must happen for the plan to follow this rule?
options: The Lok Sabha must reduce its membership to the maximum.
The Lok Sabha may keep all extra members.
The Lok Sabha must remove every elected member.
The Lok Sabha must remove every nominated member.

why.The Lok Sabha may keep all extra members: This mistake treats the maximum as if it can be crossed.
why.The Lok Sabha must remove every elected: This mistake thinks the rule removes every elected member.
why.The Lok Sabha must remove every nominate: This mistake thinks the rule removes every nominated member.

activities.explanation: Above 550 breaks the maximum rule, so this is right.

lessons.sceneCaption: Barack Obama addresses members of both houses in a joint session of India’s Parliament at New Delhi’s Old Parliament House.

lessons.title: Presiding Officers and Constitutional Functions

activities.prompt: How does Parliament guide debate, create laws, and keep our government working smoothly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Who Presides over Parliament?
activities.body: Each House of Parliament has a presiding officer. This officer keeps debates orderly. Lok Sabha members elect the Speaker. The Speaker conducts sessions and lets members speak. The Speaker also helps maintain discipline. The Vice President of India chairs the Rajya Sabha.
keyPoints: Each House has a presiding officer.
Lok Sabha members elect the Speaker.
The Vice President chairs the Rajya Sabha.
activities.explanation: These officers help members speak and keep debates orderly.

activities.prompt: A Lok Sabha debate becomes so noisy that members cannot hear one another. What should happen next?
steps: Lok Sabha members elect a Speaker because each House needs a presiding officer.
The Speaker lets members speak because members must have a chance to speak.
The Speaker helps maintain discipline because debates must stay orderly.
Therefore, the Speaker should guide the debate and keep it orderly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Conducts Lok Sabha Sessions?
activities.prompt: Who do Lok Sabha members elect to conduct its sessions?
options: President
Speaker
Vice President
Council of Ministers
activities.explanation: Lok Sabha members elect the Speaker. The Speaker conducts its sessions.

activities.title: The Rajya Sabha Chair
activities.prompt: The Vice President of India chairs the Lok Sabha.
activities.explanation: The Vice President of India chairs the Rajya Sabha.

activities.title: Match the Role and Duty
activities.prompt: Match each person or group with its role.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a role given in the lesson.

activities.title: The Ministers’ Responsibility
activities.prompt: The ministers are collectively responsible to the ______ Sabha.
activities.hint: Choose the House whose members elect the Speaker.
activities.explanation: The ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

activities.title: Members and the Union Executive
activities.prompt: Which group is part of the Union Executive and chosen from Parliament’s members?
options: Council of Ministers
Lok Sabha
Presiding officer
Rajya Sabha
activities.explanation: The Council of Ministers is part of the Union Executive. It is chosen from among Parliament’s members.

activities.title: From Law to Enforcement
activities.prompt: Put these stages in order.
items: The Union Executive gives effect to legislative powers
activities.explanation: Parliament makes laws. The Union Executive gives effect to them and helps ensure enforcement.

activities.prompt: A Lok Sabha debate becomes noisy and members interrupt each other. What should the Speaker do next?
options: Let members speak and help keep the debate orderly.
Choose a new Speaker from outside Parliament.
Give the debate to the President to control.
Ask the Council of Ministers to write the debate rules.

why.Choose a new Speaker from outside Parlia: This is wrong because Lok Sabha members elect the Speaker.
why.Give the debate to the President to cont: This is wrong because the President is part of the Union Executive.
why.Ask the Council of Ministers to write th: This is wrong because Council of Ministers members cannot write the debate rules.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Speaker lets members speak and maintains discipline.

activities.prompt: Parliament has made a law. Which body must make sure the law is enforced?
options: The Union Executive, because it must make sure laws are enforced.
Parliament alone, because making a law also means enforcing it.
The President alone, because one person should enforce every law.
The Vice President alone, because the presiding role includes enforcement.

why.Parliament alone, because making a law a: This is wrong because it mixes Parliament’s legislative and executive work.
why.The President alone, because one person: This is wrong because the President is part of the Union Executive.
why.The Vice President alone, because the pr: This is wrong because the Vice President is part of the Union Executive.

activities.explanation: This is right because enforcement is Parliament’s executive responsibility.

activities.prompt: Parliament makes laws, while the Union Executive enforces them. Why must Parliament follow separation of powers?
options: So each branch keeps its own constitutional role.
So Parliament can make laws and enforce them together.
So the President can make all laws for Parliament.
So the Council of Ministers can vote on every law.

why.So Parliament can make laws and enforce: This is wrong because it joins Parliament’s legislative and executive roles.
why.So the President can make all laws for P: This is wrong because the Union Executive gives effect to Parliament’s powers.
why.So the Council of Ministers can vote on: This is wrong because ministers’ collective responsibility is separate from Parliament’s legislative role.

activities.explanation: This is right because separation of powers keeps the branches’ roles separate.

lessons.sceneCaption: Bala Ram Choudhary with Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.

lessons.title: Lawmaking and Accountability

activities.prompt: How does a bill become law, and who keeps the government accountable?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How a Bill Becomes Law
activities.body: A bill is a draft of a proposed law. It is introduced in Parliament before becoming law. Its clauses explain specific details. MPs read a bill before discussing it. An act brings a law into force. Parliament checks government work through committees, Question Hour, and the annual budget.
keyPoints: A bill is introduced in Parliament before becoming law.
An act brings a law into force.
Parliament checks government work in several ways.
activities.explanation: Parliament makes laws and keeps the government accountable.

activities.prompt: A student sees a draft bill and says, “This is already law, so it must be followed.” Why is the student confused?
steps: A bill is only a draft of a proposed law, so the student has confused a proposal with law.
The bill must be introduced in Parliament before it can become law.
A law is brought into force through an act, so the draft has clear stages.
Therefore, the student's draft proposal is not yet a law in force.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Parliament Holds the Government Accountable
activities.body: Standing Committees examine government activities and ask questions. During Question Hour, ministers justify their actions and decisions. Parliament approves and monitors government spending through the annual budget. The government must give Parliament correct information on time. The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers implement and enforce laws.
keyPoints: Standing Committees examine government activities.
Ministers must justify their actions during Question Hour.
Parliament checks spending through the annual budget.
activities.explanation: Different parliamentary checks help make the government answerable.

activities.prompt: What is a bill?
options: An annual budget
A draft proposed law
An official notice
A set of clauses
activities.explanation: A bill is the draft of a law that Parliament will consider.

activities.prompt: A bill becomes law before Parliament introduces it.
activities.explanation: Parliament introduces a bill before it becomes law.

activities.prompt: During Question Hour, ministers must ______ their actions and decisions.
activities.hint: Think about what ministers do when Parliament asks about their work.
activities.explanation: Ministers must explain and defend their actions and decisions.

activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct term.
activities.explanation: Each term has a clear role in lawmaking or official communication.

activities.prompt: Parliament wants to check government spending. Which action should it take?
options: Read bills before discussion
Collect bill clauses
Announce legal documents
Approve and monitor spending
activities.explanation: The annual budget lets Parliament approve and monitor government spending.

activities.prompt: A Money Bill can begin only in the Lok Sabha.
activities.explanation: A Money Bill deals with financial matters and can begin only in the Lok Sabha.

activities.prompt: A financial bill is ready. It is not placed in the Lok Sabha. What must happen before it can begin?
options: It must begin in the Lok Sabha instead.
It may begin anywhere without any special starting rule.
It must begin only after Question Hour has ended.
It must begin only after the Gazette has printed it.

why.It may begin anywhere without any specia: This mistake ignores the special starting rule for money bills.
why.It must begin only after Question Hour h: This mistake mixes a money bill's starting rule with Question Hour.
why.It must begin only after the Gazette has: This mistake mixes a money bill's starting rule with publication.

activities.explanation: A money bill deals with money and can begin only in the Lok Sabha.

activities.prompt: A government activity is not being explained well. What should a Standing Committee do?
options: Approve the annual budget for government spending.
Ask questions about the government's activities.
Bring a new government activity into force.
Read the clauses of a proposed bill.

why.Approve the annual budget for government: This mistake gives the committee Parliament's spending-checking role.
why.Bring a new government activity into for: This mistake treats the committee as if it could create an act.
This mistake confuses committee questions with the bill reading done by MPs.

activities.explanation: A Standing Committee examines government activities and asks questions.

lessons.sceneCaption: The old Indian Parliament building viewed from Rashtrapathi Bhavan Junction.

lessons.title: Executive Functions and Checks on Power

activities.prompt: How does power work in India—and who makes sure leaders don’t overstep?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Who Leads and Who Checks?
activities.body: The President is the nominal Executive head, meaning the formal head. The President appoints the Prime Minister and other ministers. The Prime Minister is the actual executive authority. The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers and coordinates ministries. In certain political crises, the President can choose to use discretionary powers. The Legislature makes laws, while the Executive enforces them. The Judiciary can step in when the Executive violates the Constitution.
keyPoints: The President is the nominal Executive head.
The Prime Minister is the actual executive authority.
The Judiciary can step in if the Executive violates the Constitution.
activities.explanation: Each branch has a role, and some branches check the power of others.

activities.prompt: A new law is made, but it is not being followed. Who should make it work, and when can judges step in?
steps: The Legislature watches the Executive, so it should ask about the delay.
Ministers should act because civil servants help implement laws under them.
The Executive enforces laws, while the Judiciary checks constitutional violations.
So the Legislature oversees, ministers act, and judges step in for breaches.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Actual Executive Authority
activities.prompt: Who is the actual executive authority in India’s Parliamentary system?
options: The President
The Prime Minister
The Legislature
The Judiciary
activities.explanation: The Prime Minister is the actual executive authority in India’s Parliamentary system.

activities.title: The Formal Executive Head
activities.prompt: The ______ is the nominal head of the Executive.
activities.hint: This person appoints the Prime Minister.
activities.explanation: The President is the nominal head and appoints the Prime Minister.

activities.title: Roles in Government
activities.prompt: Match each part of government to its role.
pairs: Makes laws and oversees the Executive
activities.explanation: Each part has a different duty. Their work supports government and checks its power.

activities.title: A Check on Executive Power
activities.prompt: What happens if the Executive violates the Constitution?
options: The Judiciary can step in.
Civil servants can make laws.
The Legislature can enforce laws.
The President can ignore it.
activities.explanation: The Judiciary can step in when the Executive violates the Constitution.

activities.title: From Appointment to Enforcement
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: The President appoints the Prime Minister
The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers
activities.explanation: First, the President appoints the Prime Minister. Later, the Legislature makes laws, and the Executive enforces them.

activities.title: Two Important Roles
activities.prompt: In certain crises, who can use discretionary powers, and who coordinates ministries?
options: The President; the Prime Minister
The Prime Minister; the President
The Legislature; the Judiciary
The Judiciary; the Legislature
activities.explanation: The President can use discretionary powers during certain political crises. The Prime Minister coordinates different ministries.

activities.prompt: Most bills came from the government, according to a report. What does this show?
options: Government usually introduces bills; Parliament makes laws.
Government makes laws; Parliament usually introduces bills.
Government appoints judges; Parliament introduces most bills.
Government appoints ministers; Parliament makes all laws.

why.Government makes laws; Parliament usuall: This swaps bill introduction with the Legislature's law-making role.
why.Government appoints judges; Parliament i: This confuses the Judiciary's checking role with executive appointments.
why.Government appoints ministers; Parliamen: This confuses presidential appointments with legislative lawmaking and overstates it.

activities.explanation: The report matches government bill introduction and Parliament's lawmaking role.

activities.prompt: Two ministries disagree about implementing a law. What should the Prime Minister do?
options: Coordinate their work so both follow one plan.
Appoint one ministry's head as the actual executive authority.
Wait for the Legislature to coordinate their daily work.
Ask the Judiciary to settle which ministry should exist.

why.Appoint one ministry's head as the actua: This confuses coordinating ministries with holding actual executive authority.
why.Wait for the Legislature to coordinate t: This mistakes the Legislature's oversight role for ministry coordination.
why.Ask the Judiciary to settle which minist: The Judiciary checks constitutional violations, not the organisation of ministries.

activities.explanation: The Prime Minister coordinates the work of different ministries.

activities.prompt: During a political crisis, discretionary powers may be used. Who remains India's actual executive authority?
options: The President, leading the Council of Ministers.
The Prime Minister, leading the Council of Ministers.
The Prime Minister, introducing most bills in Parliament.
The President, introducing most bills in Parliament.

why.The President, leading the Council of Mi: This mistakes the President's nominal role for leadership of the Council.
why.The Prime Minister, introducing most bil: This mistakes bill introduction for actual executive authority.
why.The President, introducing most bills in: This mistakes discretionary crisis powers for actual executive authority.

activities.explanation: The Prime Minister leads the Council and remains the actual executive authority.

activities.prompt: First, one party has a majority. Later, two parties form a coalition. Who should the President appoint each time?
options: President's choice first, then coalition leader.
Oldest minister first, then majority-party leader.
Majority-party leader first, then coalition leader.
Civil servant first, then coalition leader.

why.President's choice first, then coalition: This mistakes personal preference for the required appointment rule.
why.Oldest minister first, then majority-par: This uses age, which the appointment rule does not mention.
why.Civil servant first, then coalition lead: This treats civil servants as the rule for choosing a Prime Minister.

activities.explanation: The rule uses the majority-party or coalition leader in each case.

lessons.title: Union and State Levels

activities.prompt: How do state governments make laws and lead their communities?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Union and State Government
activities.body: The Union List and State List contain subjects that each level can legislate on exclusively. Every state has its own legislature and executive. The state-level structure is similar to the union-level structure. Members of the Legislative Assembly formulate laws for their state. The Chief Minister is the state's actual executive authority.
keyPoints: The Union List and State List contain exclusive subjects.
Every state has its own legislature and executive.
The Chief Minister holds the state's actual executive authority.
activities.explanation: This card introduces how legislation and government work at state level.

activities.prompt: At a school debate, a friend says both levels can make the law for one subject. Is that correct?
steps: Union List subjects belong to the Union level's exclusive law-making power.
State List subjects belong to each state's exclusive law-making power.
So both levels cannot make the law for one listed subject.
Therefore, the friend's claim is wrong.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: One House or Two Houses
activities.body: A state legislature may have one house or two houses. In a unicameral legislature, there is one house. In a bicameral legislature, there are two houses. The lower house is the Vidhan Sabha. The upper house is the Vidhan Parishad. Six states have bicameral state legislatures. The remaining states have unicameral legislatures.
keyPoints: Unicameral means having one house.
Bicameral means having two houses.
Six states have bicameral state legislatures.
activities.explanation: These new words explain how state legislatures may be organised.

activities.title: The Exclusive Union List
activities.prompt: Which list contains subjects that only the Union can legislate on?
options: Subjects only the Union can legislate on
Subjects only states can legislate on
Subjects both levels must share
Subjects only the Governor can legislate on
activities.explanation: The Union List contains subjects that only the Union can legislate on.

activities.title: State Government
activities.prompt: Each state has its own legislature and executive.
activities.explanation: Every state has a separate legislature and executive.

activities.title: The State Executive Authority
activities.prompt: The chief ______ is the actual executive authority of a state.
activities.hint: The full office title has two words.
activities.explanation: The Chief Minister is the actual executive authority of a state.

activities.title: Appointing a Governor
activities.prompt: Who appoints the Governor of a state?
options: President
Chief Minister
Legislative Assembly
State executive
activities.explanation: The President appoints the Governor of a state.

activities.title: Parts of a State Legislature
activities.prompt: Match each state part with its correct name or role.
activities.explanation: The Vidhan Sabha is the lower house, and the Vidhan Parishad is the upper house.

activities.title: States with One House
activities.prompt: Six states have bicameral legislatures. What do the remaining states have?
options: Unicameral legislatures
Bicameral legislatures
Separate executives only
No state legislature
activities.explanation: Six states have bicameral legislatures. The remaining states have unicameral legislatures.

activities.title: Houses in State Legislatures
activities.prompt: Every state legislature has two houses.
activities.explanation: Six states have bicameral legislatures. The remaining states have unicameral legislatures.

activities.prompt: State A has Vidhan Sabha and Vidhan Parishad. State B has one house. Which comparison is correct?
options: State A has two houses; State B has one.
State A has one house; State B has two.
Both states have two separate houses.
Both states have only one legislative house.

This mistake reverses the number of houses in each state.
This mistake treats one lower house as two houses.
why.Both states have only one legislative ho: This mistake ignores State B's unicameral legislature.

activities.explanation: A lower and an upper house make two houses.

activities.prompt: A state has subjects on the State List. Why can it make their laws?
options: Its legislature makes laws and its executive acts.
The Union makes all those laws instead.
The state has no separate legislature.
Only its Governor can make every law.

This mistake gives Union power over State List subjects.
This mistake denies the state's own legislature.
This mistake treats the Governor as the law-making authority.

activities.explanation: The state has its own legislature and executive for State List subjects.

lessons.title: Challenges and the Role of Citizens

activities.prompt: How can citizens help Parliament solve the challenges facing our democracy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Parliament Works
activities.body: The legislature is the group that makes laws and oversees administration. It gives people a platform to discuss policies and public grievances, meaning complaints from the public. Parliament has Budget, Monsoon and Winter Sessions. During sittings, it discusses laws and questions the Executive’s decisions. Parliament usually sits for six hours each day.
keyPoints: The legislature makes laws and oversees administration.
Parliament discusses laws and questions the Executive’s decisions.
Parliament has Budget, Monsoon and Winter Sessions.
activities.explanation: This card shows how Parliament works and how citizens can help.

activities.prompt: Your class is role-playing Parliament, but members miss meetings and argue. How can the class show Parliament’s role well?
steps: The legislature makes laws and oversees administration, so these duties must be shown clearly.
It provides a platform for discussing policies and grievances, so citizens’ concerns can be heard.
Absenteeism and uncooperative behaviour can reduce effectiveness, so members must attend and cooperate.
Angry or biased debates can fail on people’s issues, so informed and fair citizens can strengthen democracy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Challenges and Citizen Action
activities.body: Legislative effectiveness can fall when representatives are absent or uncooperative. Angry or biased debates can fail to deal seriously with people’s issues. Some representatives in the Lok Sabha have faced criminal cases. Citizens help democracy grow stronger by staying informed and engaged. Public debate on digital spaces allows them to influence policy-making. Future voters can strengthen Parliament. Checks and balances protect citizens’ rights and democratic values.
keyPoints: Absenteeism and uncooperative behaviour can reduce legislative effectiveness.
Informed and engaged citizens can influence policy-making.
Checks and balances protect citizens’ rights and democratic values.
activities.explanation: These challenges show why active and responsible citizens matter.

activities.prompt: Which is NOT a Parliament session?
options: Budget Session
Monsoon Session
Winter Session
Six-hour Sitting
activities.explanation: Parliament has Budget, Monsoon and Winter Sessions.

activities.prompt: During each sitting day, Parliament usually sits for ______ hours.
activities.hint: Think about the usual length of each sitting day.
activities.explanation: Parliament usually sits for six hours on each day of a session.

activities.prompt: The legislature oversees administration as well as making laws.
activities.explanation: Yes. The legislature both makes laws and oversees administration.

activities.prompt: Which can reduce legislative effectiveness?
options: Absenteeism and uncooperative behaviour
Public debate on digital spaces
Checks and balances for citizens
Participation of future voters
activities.explanation: Absenteeism and uncooperative behaviour can reduce legislative effectiveness.

activities.prompt: Participation of future voters will have no role in strengthening Parliament.
activities.explanation: Future voters’ participation will play an important role in strengthening Parliament.

activities.prompt: Match each group or system with its role.
pairs: Discusses laws and questions the Executive’s decisions
Protect citizens’ rights and democratic values
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a group or system with the role described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Many representatives skip Parliament meetings. What is most likely to happen?
options: Lawmaking and administration oversight will become less effective.
Public grievances will be discussed more quickly.
Parliament will sit for longer each day.
The Executive will gain more control over Parliament.

why.Public grievances will be discussed more: This wrongly thinks missing members will speed up discussions.
This wrongly assumes fewer meetings will make sittings longer.
why.The Executive will gain more control ove: This wrongly assumes reduced oversight will give the Executive more control.

activities.explanation: says absenteeism can reduce legislative effectiveness.

activities.prompt: Parliament usually sits for six hours each Session day. Which comparison is fair?
options: Budget, Monsoon, and Winter Sessions share the usual sitting time.
Budget Sessions have twice the usual Winter sitting time.
Winter Sessions never include the usual six-hour sittings.
Monsoon Sessions are the only sessions with public debate.

why.Budget Sessions have twice the usual Win: This wrongly assumes Budget Sessions have a special time limit.
why.Winter Sessions never include the usual: This wrongly treats Winter Sessions as different from other Sessions.
why.Monsoon Sessions are the only sessions w: This wrongly connects public debate with only one kind of Session.

activities.explanation: gives the usual sitting time for every Session.

activities.prompt: Residents bring public grievances to the legislature. Why can this affect laws?
options: Their concerns enter the legislature’s policy discussion.
The legislature must accept every demand at once.
The Executive becomes exempt from later questions.
Future voters lose all power in Parliament.

why.The legislature must accept every demand: This mistakes hearing grievances for agreeing with every demand.
why.The Executive becomes exempt from later: This wrongly thinks discussing grievances removes later scrutiny.
why.Future voters lose all power in Parliame: This wrongly assumes giving citizens a platform weakens future voters.

activities.explanation: The legislature discusses policies and public grievances when making laws.

activities.prompt: Representatives argue angrily and ignore people’s issues. What is likely to happen?
options: Serious discussion of public issues may fail.
Public grievances will certainly be solved sooner.
Parliament will gain more checks on the Executive.
More citizens will become informed about policies.

why.Public grievances will certainly be solv: This wrongly treats angry arguments as helpful progress.
why.Parliament will gain more checks on the: This wrongly thinks conflict automatically improves checks and balances.
why.More citizens will become informed about: This wrongly assumes an unhelpful debate will inform citizens.

activities.explanation: says angry or biased debates can fail to handle issues.

activities.prompt: Students read news and discuss public issues in digital spaces. How can they help Parliament later?
options: They can influence policy now and strengthen Parliament later.
They can directly control every vote in Parliament.
They can remove all checks on government decisions.
They can end every public debate about policy.

why.They can directly control every vote in: This wrongly mistakes influence over policy for complete control.
why.They can remove all checks on government: This wrongly thinks engagement means removing checks and balances.
why.They can end every public debate about p: This wrongly thinks informed citizens want public debate to end.

activities.explanation: Facts 6.9, 6.10 and 6.11 support informed debate and future participation.
