activities.context: After the election, a group of citizens directly chose representatives, who became Lok Sabha members. A majority group of elected representatives formed the government. Parliament includes elected and nominated representatives of the people. As the supreme body making laws for the country, it controls and guides the government, which works with the people's consent. The Lok Sabha can have at most 550 members. Rajya Sabha members are chosen indirectly by an electoral college, and seats in both Houses depend on each state's population.
activities.prompt: If the people withhold their consent from the government, what should the citizens conclude?
options: A government without public consent would not meet the condition for doing its work.
A majority in Parliament makes public consent unnecessary.
Public consent is needed only while Parliament is making laws.
Nominated representatives can supply the consent that the people withhold.

why.A majority in Parliament makes public co: A majority forms the government but does not remove the consent requirement.
why.Public consent is needed only while Parl: Consent applies to government work, not only law-making.
why.Nominated representatives can supply the: Nominated representatives cannot replace consent from the people.

activities.explanation: Consent is required for the government to work.

activities.context: After the election, a group of citizens directly chose representatives, who became Lok Sabha members. A majority group of elected representatives formed the government. Parliament includes elected and nominated representatives of the people. As the supreme body making laws for the country, it controls and guides the government, which works with the people's consent. The Lok Sabha can have at most 550 members. Rajya Sabha members are chosen indirectly by an electoral college, and seats in both Houses depend on each state's population.
activities.prompt: If the population of a state changes, what should citizens expect about the allocation of seats in the two Houses?
options: The allocation will reflect the new population figures.
The allocation will remain fixed because Parliament has two Houses.
Only the Lok Sabha will change because its representatives are directly elected.
Neither House will change because an electoral college chooses Rajya Sabha members.

why.The allocation will remain fixed because: Having two Houses does not fix the number of seats in each state.
why.Only the Lok Sabha will change because i: Direct election does not remove the population basis for Lok Sabha seats.
why.Neither House will change because an ele: Indirect selection does not remove the population basis for Rajya Sabha seats.

activities.explanation: Seat numbers in both Houses are based on each state's population.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A Parliament with two Houses follows a bicameral system.
Reason (R): The Indian Parliament has the President and two Houses.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Having two Houses is what makes the system bicameral.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Lok Sabha can have more than 550 members.
Reason (R): The Constitution allows the Lok Sabha to have a maximum of 550 members.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The stated maximum of 550 means that more than 550 members is not allowed.

activities.prompt: How is the Indian Parliament organized, and how are the people connected to its two Houses?
activities.answer: The Indian Parliament has the President and two Houses, so it follows a bicameral system. The Lok Sabha, also called the House of the People or Lower House, has members directly elected by the people. Rajya Sabha members are chosen indirectly by an electoral college. Parliament includes elected and nominated representatives of the people. It is the supreme body that makes laws for the country and controls and guides the government. The government works with the consent of the people, and the number of seats in both Houses is based on each state's population.
points: The President and two Houses
Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Direct and indirect selection
Law-making, government control and people's consent
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a debate in the Lok Sabha, several members begin speaking at the same time. The Speaker restores order before the session continues. Parliament later approves a law. The Union Executive must give effect to Parliament’s legislative powers and ensure that laws are enforced. When a minister is questioned about this work, the debate concerns the ministers’ collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha.
activities.prompt: If the members continue speaking simultaneously, what should the Speaker do next?
options: Ask members to speak in turn and help them maintain discipline.
Allow every interrupting member to finish so that no view is missed.
Ask the Vice President to chair the Lok Sabha session instead.
Ask the Council of Ministers to enforce the speaking rules during the debate.

why.Allow every interrupting member to finis: Allowing simultaneous speech would prevent orderly debate.
why.Ask the Vice President to chair the Lok: The Vice President chairs the Rajya Sabha, not the Lok Sabha.
why.Ask the Council of Ministers to enforce: The Council of Ministers is not the Lok Sabha’s presiding officer.

activities.explanation: This is part of the Speaker’s responsibility for conducting sessions.

activities.context: During a debate in the Lok Sabha, several members begin speaking at the same time. The Speaker restores order before the session continues. Parliament later approves a law. The Union Executive must give effect to Parliament’s legislative powers and ensure that laws are enforced. When a minister is questioned about this work, the debate concerns the ministers’ collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha.
activities.prompt: When the Lok Sabha questions a minister about the Council’s work, what is the appropriate understanding of responsibility?
options: The Council should answer for its ministers’ work before the Lok Sabha.
Each minister should answer only for personal work because the Council is not collectively responsible.
The Council need not answer because its members are chosen from Parliament.
The Vice President should answer because the Vice President chairs the Rajya Sabha.

why.Each minister should answer only for per: Collective responsibility requires the Council to answer for its ministers’ work.
why.The Council need not answer because its: Selection from among Parliament’s members does not remove responsibility.
why.The Vice President should answer because: The Vice President’s chairing role does not replace the Council’s responsibility.

activities.explanation: The ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Lok Sabha members elect a Speaker to conduct its sessions.
Reason (R): Each House needs a presiding officer to keep its debates orderly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The need for orderly debate explains why the Lok Sabha elects a Speaker to conduct its sessions.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Council of Ministers is chosen from among Parliament’s members.
Reason (R): The ministers are individually responsible to the Lok Sabha.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The Council is chosen from Parliament’s members, but the ministers are collectively rather than individually responsible to the Lok Sabha.

activities.prompt: Explain how the presiding officers help the two Houses of Parliament conduct orderly debates.
activities.answer: Each House of Parliament has a presiding officer to keep its debates orderly. The members of the Lok Sabha elect a Speaker to conduct its sessions. The Speaker lets members speak and helps maintain discipline, allowing the session to continue in an orderly manner. In the Rajya Sabha, the Vice President of India chairs the House. Thus, each House has a presiding arrangement that helps members participate while preventing debate from becoming disorderly.
points: Each House has a presiding officer.
The Lok Sabha elects its Speaker.
The Speaker lets members speak and maintains discipline.
The Vice President chairs the Rajya Sabha.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A proposed law contains clauses explaining its specific details. MPs read the bill before discussing it in Parliament. One proposal concerns financial matters, making it a Money bill. If the bill becomes law, an act brings it into force. The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers must implement and enforce it. A Standing Committee examines government activities, asks questions, and learns that some information was not supplied correctly or on time.
activities.prompt: When the bill is introduced in Parliament, what should happen next?
options: Members would study its provisions before debating the proposal.
An act would put it into force immediately, without parliamentary discussion.
The Gazette would announce it before Parliament examines the proposal.
The government would enforce it before the bill is introduced.

why.An act would put it into force immediate: A bill must be introduced before it can become law.
why.The Gazette would announce it before Par: The Gazette announces legal documents and official information.
why.The government would enforce it before t: The government must implement and enforce laws, not enforce an unpassed bill.

activities.explanation: MPs are required to read a bill before discussing it.

activities.context: A proposed law contains clauses explaining its specific details. MPs read the bill before discussing it in Parliament. One proposal concerns financial matters, making it a Money bill. If the bill becomes law, an act brings it into force. The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers must implement and enforce it. A Standing Committee examines government activities, asks questions, and learns that some information was not supplied correctly or on time.
activities.prompt: During the Standing Committee’s examination, the government has not supplied Parliament with correct information on time. What should it do?
options: It should provide Parliament with correct information on time.
It should wait until the annual budget is approved before giving Parliament any information.
It should give only its opinion because Parliament does not need factual details.
It should stop the committee from asking questions about the matter.

why.It should wait until the annual budget i: Budget approval does not remove the duty to provide correct information.
why.It should give only its opinion because: Correct factual information is required for parliamentary scrutiny.
why.It should stop the committee from asking: The Standing Committee examines government activities and asks questions.

activities.explanation: The government must give Parliament correct information on time.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A Money bill can begin only in the Lok Sabha.
Reason (R): This special starting rule applies because a Money bill deals with financial matters.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the financial purpose of a Money bill explains its special starting rule.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a bill, a law and an act.
activities.answer: A bill is a draft of a proposed law. It is introduced in Parliament before it can become law, and its clauses explain the specific details of the proposal. Once the law exists, it is brought into force through an instrument called an act. Thus, the bill is the proposal considered by Parliament, the law is the result of that process, and the act is the instrument used to bring the law into force. The clauses help Parliament understand exactly what the proposed law contains.
points: A bill is a draft of a proposed law.
A bill is introduced in Parliament before becoming law.
Clauses give the specific details of the proposal.
An act brings the law into force.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After an election, a majority party has formed the government. The President appoints its leader as Prime Minister and appoints other ministers. The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers and coordinates the ministries. During a political crisis, the President considers using discretionary powers. The government plans to introduce a bill, while the Legislature examines it. If the Executive violates the Constitution, the Judiciary can step in.
activities.prompt: In the case, who must lead the Council of Ministers and coordinate the different ministries after the appointments?
options: The appointed Prime Minister would perform these two leadership tasks.
The President would perform them because the President is the nominal head of the Executive.
A civil servant would perform them because civil servants implement laws and policies.
The Legislature would perform them because it oversees the work of the Executive.

why.The President would perform them because: The President is the nominal head, not the actual executive authority.
why.A civil servant would perform them becau: Civil servants implement laws and policies under ministers.
why.The Legislature would perform them becau: The Legislature makes laws and oversees the Executive.

activities.explanation: The Prime Minister leads the Council and coordinates the ministries.

activities.context: After an election, a majority party has formed the government. The President appoints its leader as Prime Minister and appoints other ministers. The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers and coordinates the ministries. During a political crisis, the President considers using discretionary powers. The government plans to introduce a bill, while the Legislature examines it. If the Executive violates the Constitution, the Judiciary can step in.
activities.prompt: Suppose an Executive official violates the Constitution while carrying out responsibilities. According to the case, what should happen next?
options: The Judiciary should step in to check the violation.
The Legislature should appoint a new Prime Minister because constitutional problems affect appointments.
Civil servants should ignore the ministers and decide how to implement the laws.
The President should introduce the disputed action as a bill and ask Parliament to approve it.

why.The Legislature should appoint a new Pri: The Legislature makes laws and oversees the Executive but does not appoint the Prime Minister.
why.Civil servants should ignore the ministe: Civil servants implement laws and policies under ministers.
why.The President should introduce the dispu: The government usually introduces bills, but a constitutional violation is not corrected by passing a bill.

activities.explanation: The Judiciary can step in when the Executive violates the Constitution.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Prime Minister coordinates the work of different ministries.
Reason (R): The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Leading the Council of Ministers helps explain how the Prime Minister coordinates the different ministries.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The government usually introduces most bills placed before Parliament.
Reason (R): The Legislature has no power to make laws.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because the Legislature makes laws.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive

activities.title: Choosing Representatives
activities.prompt: Which statement about members of Parliament is correct?
options: People directly elect Lok Sabha members.
People directly elect Rajya Sabha members.
Rajya Sabha members are chosen indirectly.
Parliament has only one house.
activities.explanation: Rajya Sabha members are chosen indirectly. People directly elect Lok Sabha representatives.

activities.title: Forming the Government
activities.prompt: A majority group of elected representatives forms the government.
activities.explanation: The majority group of elected representatives forms the government.

activities.title: Actual and Nominal Authority
activities.prompt: The President is the nominal head of the ______.
activities.hint: This branch enforces laws and carries out government work.
activities.explanation: The President is nominal. The Prime Minister is the actual executive authority.

activities.title: Three Branches of Government
activities.prompt: Which sequence shows the three branches doing their main work?
options: Executive, Legislature, Judiciary
Legislature, Executive, Judiciary
Executive, Judiciary, Legislature
Judiciary, Legislature, Executive
activities.explanation: The Legislature makes laws, the Executive enforces them, and the Judiciary checks violations.

activities.title: Bill Before Law
activities.prompt: A bill becomes law before it is introduced in Parliament.
activities.explanation: A bill is introduced in Parliament before it can become law.

activities.title: Starting a Money Bill
activities.prompt: A Money Bill can begin only in the ______.
activities.hint: This House is also called the House of the People.
activities.explanation: Money Bills deal with financial matters, and the Lok Sabha is their only starting House.

activities.title: Government in a State
activities.prompt: Which statement about state-level government is correct?
options: All state legislatures have two houses.
The Governor is the state's actual executive authority.
Each state has its own legislature and executive.
The Vidhan Parishad is the lower house.
activities.explanation: Each state has its own legislature and executive. The Chief Minister is its actual executive authority.

chapters.title: Factors of Production
chapters.summary: In this chapter: production and land; labour and human capital; building human capital; capital.

lessons.title: Production and land

activities.prompt: What happens before your favorite snack reaches your hands?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How products are made
activities.body: Every product goes through a production process before it reaches the consumer. Factors of production are the resources used to make goods and services. Businesses combine these resources to create goods and services. The four factors are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Technology helps businesses produce more goods with the same or fewer resources.
keyPoints: Products pass through a production process.
Factors of production are resources used to make goods and services.
Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship are the four factors.
Technology can produce more goods with fewer resources.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand how businesses make products.

activities.prompt: Ratna’s restaurant serves tasty, good-quality food. Why must she combine different factors of production?
steps: First, Ratna chooses land and arranges money, because production needs resources.
Next, she hires workers and gets equipment, because labour and capital help make food.
Then, she plans the business, because entrepreneurship guides the other factors.
Finally, she combines these factors, because this creates the food service customers enjoy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do businesses do with factors of production?
options: They combine them to create goods and services.
They keep them apart from their products.
They use only land to create goods.
They sell them before making anything.
activities.explanation: Businesses combine different factors of production to create goods and services.

activities.prompt: In economics, land includes geographical land and ______ resources.
activities.hint: These resources come from nature.
activities.explanation: Land includes geographical land and natural resources.

activities.prompt: Match each factor of production with a related example.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a factor of production linked to Ratna's business or the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which description explains why Ratna's restaurant is popular?
options: Its food is tasty and of high quality.
Its food is cheap and of low quality.
Its food is plain and of medium quality.
Its food is raw and of poor quality.
activities.explanation: Ratna's restaurant is popular because its food is tasty and of high quality.

activities.prompt: Put this simple production story in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Businesses use factors, products pass through production, and then products reach consumers.

activities.prompt: Which choice correctly describes land and technology?
options: Land includes natural resources, while technology can reduce inputs.
Land includes hired workers, while technology must increase inputs.
Land includes business money, while technology uses only land.
Land includes bought ingredients, while technology stops production.
activities.explanation: Land includes natural resources. Technology can make more goods with fewer inputs.

activities.prompt: A maker changes to better technology but keeps its workers and materials. What will likely happen to its output?
options: It will produce more goods.
It will need many more workers.
It will produce fewer goods.
It will use more materials each time.

This confuses better technology with a need for more labour.
This reverses the effect of better technology on output.
This assumes technology needs more materials instead of the same or fewer.

activities.explanation: Technology can produce more goods with the same or fewer inputs.

activities.prompt: Before, a workshop used an old method. Now it uses better technology with the same workers and materials. How is its output likely to change?
options: It will grow because technology helps production.
It will shrink because technology reduces worker skills.
It will stay because the inputs remain the same.
It will stop because technology works only with new inputs.

why.It will shrink because technology reduce: This believes technology makes workers less effective in production.
why.It will stay because the inputs remain t: This ignores the help that technology gives to production.
why.It will stop because technology works on: This wrongly believes technology cannot work with the same inputs.

activities.explanation: Better technology can produce more goods with the same or fewer inputs.

activities.prompt: A map shows soil, forests, water, and minerals near a village. What does this tell us about the area's land?
options: The land has natural resources for production.
The land has only empty geographical space.
The area shows labour used by local workers.
The area shows capital used by local shops.

why.The land has only empty geographical spa: This mistakes natural resources for geographical land alone.
why.The area shows labour used by local work: This confuses natural resources with workers and labour.
why.The area shows capital used by local sho: This confuses natural resources with money and equipment.

activities.explanation: In economics, land includes geographical land and natural resources.

activities.prompt: A food stall needs land only for a short period. The owner can buy land or pay rent to use it. What should the owner choose?
options: Pay rent, because the stall's need is temporary.
Buy land, because renting does not count as land.
Buy land, because every stall must own its land.
Pay rent, because land cannot help production.

why.Buy land, because renting does not count: This thinks only buying land can count as using land.
why.Buy land, because every stall must own i: This believes every business must own land, which is not stated.
why.Pay rent, because land cannot help produ: This thinks land has no role in production.

activities.explanation: Paying rent lets the business use land for the needed period.

activities.prompt: Ratna has ingredients, workers, and a place. She decides what to make and plans the business. What will this decision help her do?
options: Combine factors to create useful goods and services.
Turn land and labour into natural resources.
Replace capital with extra ingredients and workers.
Stop production and serve no food at all.

why.Turn land and labour into natural resour: This confuses planning with changing natural resources.
why.Replace capital with extra ingredients a: This mistakes entrepreneurship for replacing other factors of production.
why.Stop production and serve no food at all: This believes entrepreneurship means stopping production.

activities.explanation: Entrepreneurship helps a business combine factors to create goods and services.

lessons.title: Labour and human capital

activities.prompt: What helps people turn their knowledge and skills into great work?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: People at work
activities.body: Labour is the physical and mental effort used in production. People use their knowledge, skills and decision-making abilities. These qualities help them perform jobs well. Human capital means the skills, knowledge and abilities people bring to work. Education begins with basic literacy and can build expertise. Training gives skills for a particular job. Education and training prepare people for careers. Good health helps children learn better and workers give their best.
keyPoints: Labour includes physical and mental effort.
Human capital includes specialised skills and knowledge.
Education and training prepare people for careers.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect effort, abilities, learning and health.

activities.prompt: A student can read well but cannot repair a bicycle. How can the student become ready for this job?
steps: The student has basic literacy because education develops knowledge.
The student still needs job skills because suitable knowledge and skills help good work.
Training is useful because it gives the skills required for one job.
Therefore, education and training together can prepare the student for this career.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does labour mean in production?
options: Physical and mental effort
Only physical effort
Only mental effort
Knowledge used at school
activities.explanation: Labour includes both physical and mental effort.

activities.prompt: Education gives people knowledge, beginning with basic ______.
activities.hint: It is a basic skill learned through education.
activities.explanation: Education begins by giving people basic literacy.

activities.prompt: Workers need suitable knowledge and skills to perform their jobs well.
activities.explanation: Suitable knowledge and skills help workers perform their jobs well.

activities.prompt: Match each learning or health idea with its result.
pairs: Gives people knowledge and basic literacy
Gives skills for a particular job
Helps workers give their best physically and mentally
activities.explanation: Education builds knowledge. Training builds job skills. Together, they support careers.

activities.prompt: Which work matches inventing new technologies?
options: Police officer
Production worker
Scientist
School attendee
activities.explanation: A scientist invents new technologies. A police officer maintains order.

activities.prompt: Why are education and training useful for a person's career?
options: They prepare the person to do the career well
They remove the need for suitable skills
They make every person a scientist
They ensure perfect physical health
activities.explanation: Education and training prepare people to do their careers well.

activities.prompt: A nurse knows first-aid rules but cannot use a hospital computer. What should help the nurse do the job well?
options: Training for the hospital computer system
More basic reading lessons at home
A holiday to rest after illness
Food chosen for good physical health

why.More basic reading lessons at home: Basic literacy helps learning, but it does not teach every work skill.
why.A holiday to rest after illness: Rest may help health, but it does not teach the missing work skill.
why.Food chosen for good physical health: Good health helps workers, but it does not teach computer skills.

activities.explanation: Training gives the skills needed for this particular job.

activities.prompt: After learning to read, Maya studies how to repair water pipes. Why are school learning and job training both useful?
options: School gives knowledge, while training gives job skills.
School gives job skills, while training gives basic knowledge.
School and training both give only physical strength.
School and training both develop only general literacy.

why.School and training both give only physi: Education and training develop knowledge and skills, not only strength.
why.School and training both develop only ge: Training develops expertise in a job, not only general literacy.

activities.explanation: Education gives knowledge, and training gives skills for a particular job.

activities.prompt: A child is often ill and misses school. What is most likely to happen?
options: The child may learn less because school visits are reduced.
The child may read more because school visits are reduced.
The child may need less knowledge for later work.
The child may become healthy after missing school regularly.

why.The child may read more because school v: Missing school reduces learning time, so more reading is unlikely.
why.The child may need less knowledge for la: Learning less may reduce the knowledge gained for later work.
why.The child may become healthy after missi: Illness causes missed school; missing school does not make a child healthy.

activities.explanation: Good health helps children attend school and learn better.

activities.prompt: A notice says healthy children attend school regularly. What can we reasonably expect?
options: They may learn better because they attend school more often.
They may learn worse because they attend school more often.
They will miss school more because they are healthy.
They will forget literacy because they attend school regularly.

why.They may learn worse because they attend: The notice connects good health with better learning, not worse learning.
why.They will miss school more because they: Healthy children can attend school more often, not miss it more.
why.They will forget literacy because they a: Regular attendance supports learning, so it does not cause forgetting.

activities.explanation: Regular attendance helps children learn better.

activities.prompt: A police officer keeps order. A scientist creates new technologies. What do these jobs show?
options: People can use knowledge and skills in different kinds of work.
People can use knowledge and skills in only one kind of work.
People need knowledge and skills only for making goods.
People need knowledge and skills only for keeping order.

why.People can use knowledge and skills in o: Different jobs show that human abilities are useful in many kinds of work.
why.People need knowledge and skills only fo: Keeping order is also work that needs knowledge and skills.
Inventing technologies is also work that needs knowledge and skills.

activities.explanation: Both workers use their abilities in different economic activities.

activities.prompt: A worker can do the job but makes many mistakes. Which change is most useful?
options: Get training for the skills this job needs.
Get training for a different job's skills.
Use health care instead of job training.
Use general knowledge instead of job training.

why.Get training for a different job's skill: Training for another job may not help with this work.
Health care helps health, but it does not replace job training.
why.Use general knowledge instead of job tra: General knowledge may help, but specific job skills are needed here.

activities.explanation: Training gives the skills needed to perform this job well.

lessons.sceneAlt: Postdoctoral researcher Sulalit Bandyopadhyay studies magnetic nanoparticles with his team while developing a new coronavirus test method.
lessons.sceneCaption: A researcher and his team develop a new coronavirus test in a laboratory.

lessons.title: Building human capital

activities.prompt: How can learning and teamwork help a country grow stronger?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Skills for a better future
activities.body: Human capital grows when literacy improves people’s skills and productivity. Hard work and continuous improvement can move a country forward. Kaizen is a Japanese idea meaning continuous improvement. A demographic dividend happens when a country has many young, working people. Good education, healthcare, training and skilling help young people gain from it. Indian knowledge also grew as each generation passed it on and added more over time.
keyPoints: Literacy improves skills and productivity.
Kaizen means continuous improvement.
Young people need education, healthcare, training and skilling.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how learning and steady improvement can help people and countries.

activities.prompt: A country has many young people. Why might it not gain from them at once?
steps: A large group of young, working people can create a demographic dividend.
The country must provide good education and healthcare to young people.
People also need training and skilling to gain from this advantage.
So, the country must prepare its young people before gaining the dividend.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Knowledge across generations
activities.body: Indian knowledge was not kept still. Each generation passed it to the next and added more over time. The śhilpa śhāstras recorded detailed design guidelines for artistic work. Ancient Indian shipbuilders also joined wooden planks with cords instead of nails. These examples show careful knowledge and skills being preserved and improved.
keyPoints: Each generation added more to Indian knowledge.
The śhilpa śhāstras contained detailed design guidelines.
Ancient shipbuilders used cords instead of nails.
activities.explanation: Generations preserved useful knowledge and made careful improvements.

activities.title: A Japanese idea
activities.prompt: Which idea means continuous improvement?
options: Kaizen
Demographic dividend
Human capital
Literacy rate
activities.explanation: Kaizen is a Japanese idea meaning continuous improvement. It helped Japan achieve higher standards of living.

activities.title: The result of literacy
activities.prompt: Literacy improves the skills and ______ of human capital.
activities.hint: This means how well people can work.
activities.explanation: Literacy improves both the skills and the productivity of human capital.

activities.title: Many young workers
activities.prompt: A country has many young, working people. What is this called?
options: A literacy rate
Kaizen
Human capital
A demographic dividend
activities.explanation: A demographic dividend occurs when a country has many young, working people.

activities.title: Ideas and their meanings
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its description.
pairs: passed from one generation to another
activities.explanation: Each pairing shows an important idea from the lesson.

activities.title: How knowledge grows
activities.prompt: Put these stages in the order described in the lesson.
items: One generation passes Indian knowledge to the next.
The next generation adds new knowledge.
activities.explanation: Knowledge moves between generations and grows as new learning is added.

activities.title: A strong plan
activities.prompt: Which plan best supports continuous improvement and human capital?
options: Use continuous improvement and invest in training and skilling.
Stop learning and keep all working methods unchanged.
Use continuous improvement but remove all education and training.
Avoid training because literacy does not improve productivity.
activities.explanation: Kaizen supports continuous improvement. Training and skilling help people gain from a demographic dividend.

activities.prompt: A community teaches adults to read and write well. What is likely to happen?
options: People's skills will improve, so their work will become more productive.
They will read more books, but their work will stay the same.
Their work will improve without any change in their skills.
They will gain new jobs, but their skills will not change.

why.They will read more books, but their wor: This wrongly assumes that reading does not change anyone's skills.
why.Their work will improve without any chan: This wrongly says that productivity can rise without better skills.
why.They will gain new jobs, but their skill: This confuses job changes with the skill gains that literacy brings.

activities.explanation: Literacy improves skills, and better skills improve work productivity.

activities.prompt: One team improves each day. Another checks every part and finishes on time. What do these teams show?
options: Kaizen fits the first team; German work culture fits the second.
Kaizen fits the second team; German work culture fits the first.
Kaizen fits both teams because both check their work carefully.
German work culture fits both teams because both value daily improvement.

why.Kaizen fits the second team; German work: This swaps continuous improvement with punctuality and careful work.
why.Kaizen fits both teams because both chec: This assumes that checking work is the same as continuous improvement.
why.German work culture fits both teams beca: This assumes that daily improvement is Germany's main work value.

activities.explanation: Kaizen means continuous improvement; German culture values punctuality, detail and quality.

activities.prompt: A poster says about 65 per cent of India's population is below 35. What can we conclude?
options: India has many young people who may help create a demographic dividend.
India has many workers now, so no education or healthcare is needed.
India's population is mostly old, so a demographic dividend is unlikely.
India has few young people, so the age group above 35 is larger.

why.India has many workers now, so no educat: This assumes everyone below 35 is already working and ready.
why.India's population is mostly old, so a d: This mistakes a mostly young population for a mostly old one.
why.India has few young people, so the age g: This reverses the meaning of the age information on the poster.

activities.explanation: India's large young group may help create a demographic dividend.

activities.prompt: Many young people are ready to work. What will help the country gain from this situation?
options: Good education, healthcare, training and skilling for these young people.
Older workers' pay, so no young person needs to learn new skills.
More shopping centres, because only spending can create young workers.
Less attention to young people, because they can learn without help.

why.Older workers' pay, so no young person n: This wrongly thinks young people do not need preparation for work.
why.More shopping centres, because only spen: This wrongly believes spending matters more than education and skills.
why.Less attention to young people, because: This wrongly believes young people can learn without health or training.

activities.explanation: Good education, healthcare, training and skilling help young people benefit.

activities.prompt: One team learns from mistakes and keeps improving its work. Why can this help a country move forward?
options: A culture of hard work and improvement can help a country progress.
Only finished products, not daily learning, can move a country forward.
Continuous improvement mainly helps shops, not whole countries.
A country stops moving forward when its workers keep learning.

why.Only finished products, not daily learni: This wrongly treats finished products as more important than daily learning.
why.Continuous improvement mainly helps shop: This wrongly limits the benefit of improvement to shops.
why.A country stops moving forward when its: This wrongly links regular learning with a country's lack of progress.

activities.explanation: Hard work and continuous improvement can help a country move forward.

activities.prompt: An old book gives detailed design rules for artwork. A picture shows planks joined with cords. What do these sources show?
options: Indian knowledge included artistic guidance and ways to build ships.
Indian knowledge included art rules, but shipbuilding methods came from elsewhere.
Indian knowledge included shipbuilding methods, but no artistic guidance.
These sources show that old Indian knowledge was ignored and never added to.

why.Indian knowledge included art rules, but: This wrongly treats the pictured Indian method as a foreign one.
why.Indian knowledge included shipbuilding m: This overlooks the artistic guidance in the śhilpa śāstras.
why.These sources show that old Indian knowl: This ignores how Indian knowledge was passed on and added to.

activities.explanation: The śhilpa śāstras guide artwork, and ancient shipbuilders joined planks with cords.

lessons.title: Capital

activities.prompt: What helps a business grow, operate, and reach its dreams?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is capital?
activities.body: Capital is money that helps a business run. It supports day-to-day work and is essential for manufacturing and service businesses. Durable assets include vehicles, computers, shops, factories and office buildings. Businesses may begin with personal savings or help from family and friends. Large companies can also raise money through the stock market, where shares are bought and sold.
keyPoints: Capital supports day-to-day operations.
Personal savings, family and friends can provide early funding.
Large companies can raise money through the stock market.
activities.explanation: Capital helps businesses start, run and grow.

activities.prompt: Ratna’s other funds were not enough. What did she do next?
steps: Savings, family and friends are often the first source, so start there.
Because her other funds are insufficient, Ratna still needs money.
She takes a bank loan because the lender supplies the missing money.
She pays interest for using it, so the loan has a cost.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which one is an example of a durable asset?
options: A vehicle
A dividend
A bank interest
A personal saving
activities.explanation: Vehicles are examples of durable assets. The other choices are related to business funding.

activities.prompt: _____ is essential for both manufacturing and service businesses.
activities.hint: It helps a business carry out its work.
activities.explanation: Capital supports the work done by both manufacturing and service businesses.

activities.prompt: Match each business term with its correct meaning.
pairs: An early source of business funding
Funding used when her other funds were insufficient
A market where shares are bought and sold
A share of profits offered to the public
activities.explanation: Each choice connects a funding source or market term with its meaning.

activities.prompt: Why did Ratna take a bank loan?
options: Her other funds were insufficient
Her savings covered every cost
Her shop needed a vehicle
Her company offered dividends
activities.explanation: Ratna took the loan because her other funds were not enough.

activities.prompt: What is a stock market?
options: A market for shares
A source of personal savings
A charge on company profits
A lender charging no interest
activities.explanation: A stock market is where shares are bought and sold. Large companies can raise money through it.

activities.prompt: Put Ratna’s funding steps in order.
items: She pays interest on the loan
activities.explanation: Ratna takes the loan when her funds are insufficient. She then uses the money and pays interest.

activities.prompt: An office uses a computer for daily work. What counts as capital?
options: The computer used by the office
The interest paid on a bank loan
The dividend offered to the public
The share sold in the stock market

why.The interest paid on a bank loan: Interest is a payment for borrowed money, not a durable asset.
why.The dividend offered to the public: A dividend is a share of profits, not a durable asset.
why.The share sold in the stock market: A share is bought and sold, not a durable asset.

activities.explanation: A computer is a durable asset that can support business work.

activities.prompt: Personal savings and family help can fund a business. A large company seeks public money to expand. Which path fits it?
options: Use the stock market to raise financial capital.
Rely only on personal savings.
Ask only family and friends for money.
Pay interest to a bank for its money.

Personal savings may come first, but they need not fund a large expansion.
Family and friends may come first, but large firms can use public markets.
Interest is paid for borrowed money; it does not raise capital from the public.

activities.explanation: Large companies can raise financial capital from the public through the stock market.

activities.prompt: A company offers the public a share of profits. A borrower pays interest for loan money. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The company’s offer is a dividend; interest pays for borrowed money.
The company’s offer is interest; dividends pay for borrowed money.
The company’s offer is a bank loan; interest is a share of profits.
The two offers are equal because both come from borrowed money.

why.The company’s offer is interest; dividen: This swaps their roles; dividends do not pay for borrowed money.
why.The company’s offer is a bank loan; inte: This swaps their roles; interest is not a company’s profit share.
why.The two offers are equal because both co: Dividends come from company profits, not from borrowing money.

activities.explanation: A dividend is a share of profits offered to the public, while interest pays for loan use.

lessons.sceneCaption: Indian food shown inside a shop.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship and technology

activities.prompt: How can a new idea and modern technology change people’s lives?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ideas, technology and society
activities.body: Entrepreneurship means starting an enterprise or creating something new to solve a problem. Entrepreneurs develop ideas, take risks, and combine the things needed to make goods and services. Technology applies scientific knowledge. Cameras turn light into electrical signals for digital images. Email helps communication and costs less than posting letters. New ideas can help society and create ways to earn a living.
keyPoints: Entrepreneurship starts an enterprise or creates something new.
Entrepreneurs solve problems and take risks.
Technology applies scientific knowledge.
activities.explanation: Entrepreneurship uses new ideas, while technology applies scientific knowledge.

activities.prompt: How can a young entrepreneur solve a local problem and reach customers cheaply?
steps: Find a real problem, because entrepreneurship starts by solving one.
Combine needed factors, because goods and services require them.
Use email, because it communicates quickly and at lower cost.
This can create jobs and support society, so the idea is entrepreneurial.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is technology?
options: Collecting old objects
Using scientific knowledge
Following oral customs
Making handmade goods
activities.explanation: Technology means applying scientific knowledge.

activities.prompt: Entrepreneurship means starting an enterprise or creating something ______ to solve a problem.
activities.hint: Choose one word from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Creating something new helps an entrepreneur solve a problem.

activities.prompt: Match each entrepreneur’s action with its result.
activities.explanation: Entrepreneurs solve problems, combine factors, take risks, and create opportunities.

activities.prompt: What did J.R.D. Tata believe businesses should do?
options: Earn money and help society.
Make losses and help society.
Save money and avoid helping society.
Earn money and harm society.
activities.explanation: J.R.D. Tata believed that businesses should earn money and also help society.

activities.prompt: How does email help people communicate?
options: Quickly and at higher cost
Slowly and at lower cost
Quickly and at lower cost
Slowly and at higher cost
activities.explanation: Email helps people communicate quickly and at a lower cost than posting letters.

activities.prompt: Put these in the camera’s conversion order.
activities.explanation: A camera converts light into electrical signals for a digital image.

activities.prompt: A young entrepreneur wants customers to hear about a new service quickly. Which choice helps most?
options: Send email, because it communicates quickly and at lower cost.
Post every letter, because posted letters always arrive sooner.
Send email, because it replaces the need for a good idea.
Post every letter, because posting always costs less than email.

why.Post every letter, because posted letter: This reverses email's quick communication compared with posted letters.
why.Send email, because it replaces the need: This confuses a communication tool with the entrepreneur's new idea.
why.Post every letter, because posting alway: This reverses email's lower cost compared with posted letters.

activities.explanation: Email communicates quickly and at lower cost than posted letters.

activities.prompt: An entrepreneur puts money and time into a new business idea. Why is this a risk?
options: The idea may fail, so the entrepreneur may lose money and time.
The idea cannot fail because the entrepreneur has already paid.
Only time is at risk because invested money stays safe.
Neither money nor time is at risk because ideas always succeed.

why.The idea cannot fail because the entrepr: This wrongly assumes that paying money removes the risk.
why.Only time is at risk because invested mo: This forgets that entrepreneurs can also lose their invested money.
why.Neither money nor time is at risk becaus: This confuses taking risks with ideas always succeeding.

activities.explanation: Investing money and time is risky because the new idea may fail.

activities.prompt: A child has an idea for solving a school problem. What should the child do next?
options: Combine the factors needed to make the proposed good or service.
Wait for others because the problem does not need solving.
Change the idea into a problem because change is easier.
Keep the idea private because innovation needs no action.

why.Wait for others because the problem does: This mistakes waiting with taking responsibility for solving the problem.
why.Change the idea into a problem because c: This reverses the process because the idea is meant to solve a problem.
why.Keep the idea private because innovation: This confuses keeping ideas private with developing them innovatively.

activities.explanation: Entrepreneurs combine the factors needed to make goods and services.

activities.prompt: An older shop uses posted letters. A new shop uses email. What can you compare?
options: Email can save time and money compared with posted letters.
Posted letters can save time and money compared with email.
Both methods reach people at the same speed and cost.
Both methods make communication slower and more costly.

why.Posted letters can save time and money c: This reverses the speed and cost advantage of email.
why.Both methods reach people at the same sp: This overlooks that email is quicker and cheaper than posted letters.
why.Both methods make communication slower a: This confuses email's benefits with slower, costlier communication.

activities.explanation: Email helps people communicate quickly and at lower cost.

activities.prompt: An entrepreneur creates a new service in a community. What wider effects can the business have?
options: It can create jobs and support people's livelihoods.
It can remove all work and leave nobody employed.
It can stop innovation because everyone already has work.
It can affect only the owner and nobody else.

why.It can remove all work and leave nobody: This confuses new opportunities with the loss of all work.
why.It can stop innovation because everyone: This mistakes existing work for a reason to stop innovation.
why.It can affect only the owner and nobody: This assumes an entrepreneur's business cannot affect the community.

activities.explanation: Entrepreneurs can create job opportunities and support people's livelihoods.

lessons.title: Connecting factors and using them responsibly

activities.prompt: How can we connect production fairly and sustainably?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How factors work together
activities.body: Production uses factors such as labour, capital and specialised machinery. Labour-intensive work needs more labour. Some industries need more capital and specialised machinery. These factors complement one another, so missing or misused inputs can reduce production. Production inputs are available in different geographical locations. This spread gives businesses access to different kinds of inputs. A supply chain is a network of people, organisations, resources, activities and technology. Responsible production includes fair pay, safe work, sustainable practices and Corporate Social Responsibility.
keyPoints: Labour-intensive work needs more labour.
Some industries need capital and specialised machinery.
Responsible production supports workers, resources and communities.
activities.explanation: These factors work together, so producers must connect them carefully and use them responsibly.

activities.prompt: A factory lacks machine parts. How should it keep production moving?
steps: It should check every supply-chain link, because a disruption can stop production.
It should find inputs elsewhere, because inputs are spread across locations.
It should combine all needed factors, because missing inputs can reduce production.
Finally, it should use resources sustainably, because future production needs them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Connecting inputs across places
activities.body: New techniques can change how much of each factor is used and how much is produced. Production inputs are available in different geographical locations. This spread gives businesses access to different kinds of inputs. A supply chain is a network of people, organisations, resources, activities and technology. If an input is missing or misused, production can fall. A disruption in the supply chain can stop the whole production process.
keyPoints: New techniques can change factors and output.
Different places provide different inputs.
A supply chain disruption can stop production.
activities.explanation: Connecting inputs helps production, but weak links can cause major problems.

activities.prompt: Which group needs more labour?
options: Agriculture, construction and handicrafts
Semiconductor chips and satellites
Corporate Social Responsibility activities
Supply chains
activities.explanation: Agriculture, construction and handicrafts are labour-intensive. They need more labour to carry out their work.

activities.prompt: Semiconductor chips and satellites mainly need more labour than capital.
activities.explanation: They need more capital and specialised machinery. These inputs support their production.

activities.prompt: Match each activity with its correct feature.
pairs: Help use natural resources in the future
Includes reducing pollution and supporting local communities
activities.explanation: Each feature shows how different activities use inputs or act responsibly.

activities.prompt: Why does the geographical spread of inputs help businesses?
options: It gives them access to different kinds of inputs.
It removes the need for specialised machinery.
It makes every industry labour-intensive.
It prevents all supply chain disruptions.
activities.explanation: Inputs are available in different geographical locations. This spread gives businesses access to different kinds of inputs.

activities.prompt: A network of production links is called a ______ chain.
activities.hint: The network includes people, organisations, resources, activities and technology.
activities.explanation: A supply chain connects many parts of production. A disruption in it can stop the whole process.

activities.prompt: What can new techniques change?
options: The proportion of each factor used and the output
Only the geographical locations of inputs
Only the need for fair pay
Only the number of supply chain members
activities.explanation: New techniques can change the proportion of each factor used. They can also change the output.

activities.prompt: India's CSR law required companies to spend 2 per cent of their average profits on such activities.
activities.explanation: This requirement supports activities such as reducing pollution and helping local communities.

activities.prompt: A factory has materials but misses a machine part. What may happen?
options: It may stop, because a supply-chain disruption can stop production.
It may grow, because missing machinery makes workers work faster.
It may stay unchanged, because only workers are needed for output.
It may improve, because fewer parts always make production better.

why.It may grow, because missing machinery m: This mistake wrongly assumes missing machinery makes workers work faster.
why.It may stay unchanged, because only work: This mistake wrongly assumes workers alone are enough for production.
why.It may improve, because fewer parts alwa: This mistake wrongly assumes fewer parts always improve production.

activities.explanation: This is right because a supply-chain disruption can stop the whole process.

lessons.sceneAlt: A bright aerial view shows green agricultural fields, rural houses and dirt roads in Punjab, India.
lessons.sceneCaption: Green farmland and rural homes show how land is used for agricultural production.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Ratna can adopt suitable technology and increase food output without necessarily increasing all her inputs.
Reason (R): Technology helps enterprises produce more goods with the same or fewer inputs.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains how technology can help Ratna increase her output.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between geographical land and natural resources, and how can a business use land?
activities.answer: In economics, land includes geographical land as well as natural resources. Geographical land is the physical location a business uses, such as Ratna’s restaurant site. Natural resources include soil, forests, water, air, sunlight, minerals and oil. Thus, natural resources are included within the wider factor of production called land. A business does not have to own the land it uses: it can buy land or pay rent to use it for a particular period.
points: Defines land as including geographical land and natural resources.
Gives examples of natural resources.
Explains that natural resources are part of land.
Explains that land can be bought or used by paying rent.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A production worker wants to change his career and become a police officer. He already has basic literacy, but he does not yet have the specialised knowledge, skills and decision-making abilities needed to maintain order. His education and training prepare him for the new career. He also works to stay healthy so that he can attend classes regularly, learn better and give his best physically and mentally in his work.
activities.prompt: If the worker regularly misses classes because his health is poor, what is most likely to happen?
options: His learning and preparation for the police career are likely to get worse.
He will already know every required skill, so attending classes will no longer matter.
Maintaining order will improve his health and make the missed classes unimportant.
Physical effort alone will provide all the expertise needed for police work.

why.He will already know every required skil: Suitable knowledge and skills are still needed to perform the job well.
why.Maintaining order will improve his healt: Police work does not remove the importance of learning and health.
why.Physical effort alone will provide all t: Human capital includes specialised abilities, not physical effort alone.

activities.explanation: Poor health can make regular attendance and learning more difficult.

activities.context: A production worker wants to change his career and become a police officer. He already has basic literacy, but he does not yet have the specialised knowledge, skills and decision-making abilities needed to maintain order. His education and training prepare him for the new career. He also works to stay healthy so that he can attend classes regularly, learn better and give his best physically and mentally in his work.
activities.prompt: Suppose the worker develops literacy but receives no expertise in a particular field and no job training. What should be concluded?
options: He may still be unprepared for police duties even though he can read and write.
He must be fully prepared because basic reading is enough for every job.
He can maintain order without gaining suitable knowledge and skills.
He should stop learning because human capital is no longer useful.

why.He must be fully prepared because basic: Basic literacy does not provide every kind of expertise.
why.He can maintain order without gaining su: Maintaining order well requires preparation for the role.
why.He should stop learning because human ca: Continued learning and training remain important for human capital.

activities.explanation: Police work requires suitable knowledge and skills, not literacy alone.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Human capital means only the physical effort used in production.
Reason (R): Human capital means specialised skills, knowledge, abilities and expertise.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion wrongly confuses labour with human capital, while the reason states the correct meaning.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between labour and human capital?
activities.answer: Labour is the physical and mental effort that people use in production. Human capital is the specialised skills, knowledge, abilities and expertise that people bring to their work. A person may provide labour simply by using physical or mental effort, while human capital shows specialised ability developed for a role. Knowledge, decision-making abilities and training are therefore important parts of human capital. Human beings play a key part in economic activities, and both labour and human capital help them perform their jobs well.
points: Defines labour as physical and mental effort in production.
Defines human capital as specialised skills, knowledge, abilities and expertise.
Explains that human capital is more than physical effort.
Connects knowledge, decision-making and training with human capital.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In India, about 65 per cent of the population is below the age of 35. This creates the possibility of a demographic dividend because the country can have many young, working people. A programme is being designed to provide good education, healthcare, training and skilling so that these young people can benefit. It will also promote literacy, punctuality, attention to detail, quality, and Kaizen, the Japanese idea of continuous improvement.
activities.prompt: What is the most likely result if the programme improves literacy among its participants?
options: Their skills and productivity will improve.
Their need for healthcare will disappear.
Training and skilling will become unnecessary.
The country's demographic dividend will end.

why.Their need for healthcare will disappear: Improved literacy does not remove healthcare needs.
why.Training and skilling will become unnece: Education and training remain important for gaining from a demographic dividend.
why.The country's demographic dividend will: Better literacy supports, rather than ends, the country's potential benefit from its young population.

activities.explanation: Literacy is given as a way to improve skills and productivity.

activities.context: In India, about 65 per cent of the population is below the age of 35. This creates the possibility of a demographic dividend because the country can have many young, working people. A programme is being designed to provide good education, healthcare, training and skilling so that these young people can benefit. It will also promote literacy, punctuality, attention to detail, quality, and Kaizen, the Japanese idea of continuous improvement.
activities.prompt: Why is the programme providing education, healthcare, training and skilling to young people?
options: To help India gain from its demographic dividend.
To make punctuality less important in the workplace.
To replace education with healthcare.
To stop young people from becoming workers.

why.To make punctuality less important in th: The programme is intended to promote punctuality, not reduce its importance.
Education and healthcare are both needed, so one should not replace the other.
why.To stop young people from becoming worke: The purpose is to prepare young people to benefit from working, not to keep them out of work.

activities.explanation: These services help people gain from a demographic dividend.

activities.context: In India, about 65 per cent of the population is below the age of 35. This creates the possibility of a demographic dividend because the country can have many young, working people. A programme is being designed to provide good education, healthcare, training and skilling so that these young people can benefit. It will also promote literacy, punctuality, attention to detail, quality, and Kaizen, the Japanese idea of continuous improvement.
activities.prompt: A participant finds a better way of completing a task. What best reflects Kaizen in the programme?
options: Adopt the better method and continue looking for improvements.
Keep the old method because continuous improvement should happen only once.
Wait until the programme ends before suggesting any change.
Avoid changes because good quality means the work must always remain the same.

why.Keep the old method because continuous i: Continuous improvement is an ongoing idea, not a one-time task.
why.Wait until the programme ends before sug: Kaizen encourages people to act on improvements they identify.
why.Avoid changes because good quality means: Valuing quality can support improvement rather than prevent every change.

activities.explanation: Kaizen means continuous improvement, so improvement should continue.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): India has the possibility of gaining a demographic dividend because it has many young people.
Reason (R): About 65 per cent of India's population is below the age of 35.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The large share of young people helps explain India's potential demographic dividend.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): German work culture values punctuality, attention to detail and quality.
Reason (R): Kaizen is a Japanese idea meaning continuous improvement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the Japanese origin and meaning of Kaizen does not explain German work culture.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between Kaizen and German work culture?
activities.answer: Kaizen is a Japanese idea that means continuous improvement. It encourages people to keep improving how they work. German work culture is described by three values: punctuality, attention to detail and quality. Thus, Kaizen focuses on the ongoing process of getting better, while German work culture focuses on how work is carried out. A person following Kaizen would look for further improvements, while a person following German work culture would value punctuality, careful attention and good quality. The two ideas can support each other, but they are not the same.
points: Kaizen means continuous improvement.
Kaizen is a Japanese idea.
German work culture values punctuality, attention to detail and quality.
Kaizen focuses on ongoing improvement.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ratna wanted to start a service business. She first used personal savings and money from family and friends, but these funds were insufficient. She therefore took a bank loan and will pay interest for using the lender’s money. Capital will support her business’s day-to-day operations. She is also considering buying a computer, a durable asset. If her business becomes a large company, she may need much more money to expand.
activities.prompt: Ratna asks why she needs capital besides buying a computer. Which explanation is correct?
options: It is essential only for manufacturing businesses.
It can raise money from the public through the stock market.
It supports the day-to-day operations of a business.
It pays interest on every purchase of a durable asset.

why.It can raise money from the public throu: The stock market is one way for large companies to raise money, not the purpose of capital.
why.It pays interest on every purchase of a: Interest is paid on a loan, not on every purchase of a durable asset.

activities.explanation: This correctly describes an important role of capital.

activities.context: Ratna wanted to start a service business. She first used personal savings and money from family and friends, but these funds were insufficient. She therefore took a bank loan and will pay interest for using the lender’s money. Capital will support her business’s day-to-day operations. She is also considering buying a computer, a durable asset. If her business becomes a large company, she may need much more money to expand.
activities.prompt: If Ratna’s business becomes a large company and needs a lot of money to expand, what can it do?
options: Ask the stock market to lend money to the company without interest.
Sell the company’s computer as a public share.
Offer a dividend as though it were new capital.
Make company shares available for sale to the public through the stock market.

why.Ask the stock market to lend money to th: The stock market is where shares are bought and sold, not a source of interest-free loans.
why.Sell the company’s computer as a public: A computer is a durable asset, not a company share.
why.Offer a dividend as though it were new c: A dividend is a share of profits offered to the public, not money raised for expansion.

activities.explanation: Large companies can raise financial capital from the public through the stock market.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Ratna needed a bank loan because her personal savings and funds from family and friends were insufficient.
Reason (R): Personal savings, family and friends are often the first sources of business funding, so she used them before borrowing.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why Ratna first used other funds and then took a bank loan.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A service business can carry out its day-to-day operations without any capital.
Reason (R): Capital is essential for service businesses and supports their day-to-day operations.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is false, while the reason is true and explains why capital cannot be omitted.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between raising financial capital through the stock market and offering a dividend to the public?
activities.answer: The stock market is a market where shares are bought and sold. A large company can use it to raise financial capital from the public, which helps it obtain money for expansion. A dividend has a different role because it is a share of the company’s profits offered to the public. Raising capital brings money into the business, while a dividend relates to sharing the company’s profits. The two actions therefore serve different purposes.
points: The stock market is where shares are bought and sold.
Large companies can raise financial capital through it.
A dividend is a share of the company’s profits offered to the public.
Raising capital brings in money, while a dividend shares profits.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: J.R.D. Tata believed that a business should earn money and also help society. He took the risk of starting India’s first airline, Tata Airlines, in 1932, by investing money and time. He combined the factors needed to make services and made important decisions about how the business operated. Technology also mattered in daily life: a camera converted light into electrical signals for a digital image, while email helped people communicate quickly and at a lower cost than posting letters.
activities.prompt: If Tata Airlines wanted to communicate more quickly and at a lower cost, which action would best apply technology?
options: Use email instead of relying on posted letters.
Use a camera to turn each letter into a digital image.
Send more posted letters to keep everyone informed.
Replace letters with digital images of handwritten pages.

why.Use a camera to turn each letter into a: A camera creates images; it is not the communication method described.
why.Send more posted letters to keep everyon: Sending more letters would not improve speed or reduce cost.
why.Replace letters with digital images of h: A digital image of a letter would not provide quick, low-cost communication.

activities.explanation: Email is described as quicker and cheaper than posting letters.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Factors of Production

activities.title: Four Factors
activities.prompt: Which group includes all four factors of production?
options: Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship
Land, labour, skills and entrepreneurship
Land, workers, capital and planning
Land, labour, capital and production
activities.explanation: Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship are the four types of factors of production.

activities.title: Better Technology
activities.prompt: Technology helps enterprises produce more goods with the same or fewer inputs.
activities.explanation: Technology helps businesses produce more goods without needing more inputs.

activities.title: Durable Assets
activities.prompt: Durable assets include vehicles, computers, shops, factories and ______ buildings.
activities.hint: These buildings are used for business work.
activities.explanation: Office buildings are durable assets. Such assets help businesses operate.

activities.title: Know the Factors
activities.prompt: Match each factor of production with its meaning.
pairs: Physical and mental effort used in production
Resources that support a business's day-to-day operations
Starting an enterprise or creating something new to solve a problem
activities.explanation: Each factor has a special role in production. Good matches help you spot their uses.

activities.title: How a Camera Works
activities.prompt: Put the stages of a camera's technology in the correct order.
activities.explanation: A camera converts light into electrical signals for a digital image.

activities.title: Learning for Work
activities.prompt: Which activity gives people the skills required for a particular job?
options: Hiring
Training
Borrowing
Planning
activities.explanation: Training gives people job-specific skills. Education and training prepare people for their careers.

activities.title: Supply Chain Trouble
activities.prompt: What can a disruption in a supply chain do?
options: Increase all business output
Remove all technology inputs
Stop the whole production process
Make all inputs fully available
activities.explanation: A supply chain connects many resources and activities. A disruption can stop the whole production process.

activities.title: Email Costs
activities.prompt: Email helps people communicate quickly at a higher cost than posting letters.
activities.explanation: Email helps people communicate quickly and at a lower cost than posting letters.

activities.title: Continuous Improvement
activities.prompt: Kaizen is a Japanese idea meaning ______ improvement.
activities.hint: Improvement happens again and again over time.
activities.explanation: Kaizen means continuous improvement. This idea can help a country move forward.

activities.title: Work and Resources
activities.prompt: Match each example with the factor or role connected with it.
pairs: Need more capital and specialised machinery
Identifies a problem and works to solve it innovatively
activities.explanation: Different activities need different resources. Entrepreneurs also solve problems through new ideas.
