chapters.title: World Geography: Some Glimpses
chapters.summary: In this chapter: mapping the earth; the blue planet; trenches, reefs and waterways; asia’s landforms.

lessons.title: Mapping the Earth

activities.prompt: How do map-makers turn our world into flat maps?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Maps of Our World
activities.body: Maps help us show the round Earth on a flat surface. A map projection is the process of doing this. Every map has some distortion. Every map involves a compromise between different features. Physical maps use colours for land and water. Blue shows water, green shows plains, and yellow or brown shows plateaus. Dark brown shows high mountains, while white shows ice and glaciers.
keyPoints: A map projection shows the round Earth on a flat surface.
All maps contain some distortion.
Physical maps use colours to show different features.
activities.explanation: Map-makers balance different features because the Earth is round.

activities.prompt: How can you choose a world map without pretending it is perfect?
steps: Maps must flatten the round Earth, so some distortion is unavoidable.
Every map balances different features, because one flat view cannot keep all perfect.
Compare several projections, because this gives a fairer view of the world.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Imagine you are colouring a physical map. Which colour shows oceans, seas, lakes and rivers?
options: Blue
Green
White
Light yellow
activities.explanation: Physical maps use blue for oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.

activities.prompt: On a physical map, deserts are shown in light yellow.
activities.explanation: Yes, deserts appear in light yellow on physical maps.

activities.prompt: A physical map uses ______ to show plains.
activities.hint: Look at the colours used for physical map features.
activities.explanation: Physical maps use green for plains.

activities.prompt: Match each physical map feature with its colour.
activities.explanation: These colours help map readers recognise different physical features.

activities.prompt: What is a map projection?
options: Measuring land and water areas
Choosing colours for map features
Showing Earth on a flat surface
Finding the exact size of countries
activities.explanation: A map projection is the process of showing the Earth on a flat surface.

activities.prompt: What should you do to understand the world fairly through maps?
options: Look at only one projection
Look at several projections
Ignore every projection
Use only the largest country map
activities.explanation: Looking at several projections helps us understand the world fairly.

activities.prompt: A map shows the coast of a country with the correct outline. The country looks too small beside another country. What does this map show?
options: It shows correct country shapes but gives wrong sizes.
It shows wrong country shapes but gives correct sizes.
It shows correct country shapes and correct sizes.
It shows wrong country shapes and wrong sizes.

why.It shows wrong country shapes but gives: This confuses shape accuracy with size accuracy.
why.It shows correct country shapes and corr: This assumes that one map can keep both shapes and sizes perfectly.
why.It shows wrong country shapes and wrong: This wrongly says that both shapes and sizes must be wrong.

activities.explanation: This is right because a map can keep shapes while changing sizes.

activities.prompt: Two maps show the same world. One map makes some countries look larger. Why might this happen?
options: Flat maps must compromise between different features.
Map-makers remove every source of distortion.
All maps show country shapes and sizes perfectly.
Using several maps can make one map perfect.

why.Map-makers remove every source of distor: This wrongly assumes that map-makers can remove all distortion.
why.All maps show country shapes and sizes p: This wrongly assumes that every map is perfect.
why.Using several maps can make one map perf: This wrongly assumes that comparing maps can remove distortion.

activities.explanation: Flat maps must compromise, so some features can become distorted.

activities.prompt: A student wants a fair view of the world. The student studies only one map. What should the student do next?
options: Look at several projections before judging the whole world.
Choose the map with the most distorted country sizes.
Use only the map that shows every country shape perfectly.
Draw a new map without looking at any projection.

why.Choose the map with the most distorted c: This wrongly chooses a map because it exaggerates size distortion.
why.Use only the map that shows every countr: This wrongly assumes that one map can show every feature perfectly.
why.Draw a new map without looking at any pr: This wrongly assumes that making one map removes the need to compare.

activities.explanation: Looking at several projections helps the student understand the world fairly.

activities.prompt: Two students study world maps. One trusts one projection. Another checks several projections. Who understands the world more fairly?
options: The second student, because several projections balance different map features.
The first student, because one projection removes all distortion.
The second student, because several projections show every country perfectly.
The first student, because checking maps makes country sizes agree.

why.The first student, because one projectio: This wrongly assumes that one projection can remove all distortion.
why.The second student, because several proj: This wrongly assumes that several projections make every feature perfect.
why.The first student, because checking maps: This wrongly assumes that comparing maps makes all country sizes agree.

activities.explanation: Comparing several projections helps avoid judging the world from one compromise.

lessons.title: The Blue Planet

activities.prompt: Why does our blue planet have so many hidden wonders beneath the waves?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Blue Planet
activities.body: The ocean covers about 71 per cent of Earth's surface. Earth looks blue from space. Oceans contain 97 per cent of Earth's water. Life ranges from tiny plankton to blue whales. The ocean floor has mountains, valleys and plains. Currents move like giant rivers. Warm currents travel from the equator towards the poles. Oceans help regulate climate by absorbing heat and adding moisture. Currents affect climates beside the sea.
keyPoints: Oceans cover most of Earth's surface and hold most of its water.
The ocean floor has land-like features, while currents move like rivers.
Oceans regulate climate and affect climates beside the sea.
activities.explanation: The ocean makes Earth look blue and helps regulate its climate.

activities.prompt: One coast has warm current water. Another coast has cold current water. Which coast has a warmer climate?
steps: The warm current carries warm water from the equator toward the poles.
Because currents affect coastal climates, the warm-current coast gets a warmer climate.
The cold current carries cold water from the poles toward the equator.
So the coast beside the warm current is warmer than the cold-current coast.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement about our blue planet is true?
options: The Earth looks blue from space.
Oceans contain all of Earth's water.
The ocean floor is flat.
Warm currents carry cold water towards poles.
activities.explanation: The Earth looks blue when seen from space.

activities.prompt: Oceans contain ______ per cent of the Earth's water.
activities.hint: This is the share of Earth's water found in oceans.
activities.explanation: Oceans contain 97 per cent of the Earth's water.

activities.prompt: Match each ocean feature or current to its description.
pairs: carry warm water from the equator towards the poles
carry cold water from the poles towards the equator
has mountains, valleys and plains like the land
includes tiny plankton and giant blue whales
activities.explanation: Warm and cold currents travel in opposite directions across the oceans.

activities.prompt: Which statement about ocean currents is true?
options: Warm currents carry cold water towards the poles.
Warm currents carry warm water towards the poles.
Cold currents carry warm water towards the equator.
Cold currents carry cold water towards the poles.
activities.explanation: Warm currents carry warm water from the equator towards the poles.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for a cold current in order.
items: Carries cold water towards the equator
activities.explanation: Cold currents move through oceans from the poles towards the equator.

activities.prompt: Which pair contains two true facts?
options: Earth looks blue from space; oceans support only giant blue whales.
Earth looks blue from space; oceans hold 97 per cent of Earth's water.
Earth looks blue from space; the ocean floor has no valleys or plains.
Earth looks blue from space; warm currents carry warm water towards the equator.
activities.explanation: Earth looks blue from space, and oceans hold 97 per cent of Earth's water.

activities.prompt: One coast has warm current water. Another has cold current water. Which coast has a warmer climate?
options: One coast, because warm currents carry warmer water.
The other, because cold currents carry colder water.
One coast, because currents move like giant rivers.
The other, because cold currents move toward the poles.

why.The other, because cold currents carry c: Cold currents do not make the second coast warmer than the first.
why.One coast, because currents move like gi: Moving like rivers does not explain which coast is warmer.
why.The other, because cold currents move to: Cold currents move from poles to equator, not toward the poles.

activities.explanation: Warm currents warm the coast, so the first coast is warmer.

activities.prompt: A map shows warm water moving from the equator toward poles. What happens to a coast it reaches?
options: That coast will be warmer than a cold-current coast.
That coast will be colder than a cold-current coast.
That coast will be warmer than every other coast.
That coast will be colder than every polar coast.

why.That coast will be colder than a cold-cu: That current carries warm water, so it does not cool the coast.
why.That coast will be warmer than every oth: One warm current cannot make a coast warmer than every coast.
why.That coast will be colder than every pol: A warm current can warm even a coast near the poles.

activities.explanation: That current carries warm water, so it warms the coast.

activities.prompt: The ocean absorbs heat during the day. It releases heat slowly. What happens to nearby air at night?
options: The nearby air stays warm because the ocean releases heat.
The nearby air turns cold because the ocean releases heat.
The nearby air gets wetter because the ocean releases heat.
The nearby air stays dry because the ocean releases heat.

why.The nearby air turns cold because the oc: Heat release warms the air instead of making it colder.
why.The nearby air gets wetter because the o: Moisture comes from the ocean adding it to the air.
why.The nearby air stays dry because the oce: Slow heat release does not mean the air becomes dry.

activities.explanation: Slow heat release keeps the nearby air warm at night.

activities.prompt: A map shows raised and sunken parts of the ocean floor. What can a reader infer?
options: The floor is uneven and may include land-like features.
The floor is flat, with only small surface waves.
The floor has mountains, but never any valleys.
The floor has valleys, but never any mountains.

why.The floor is flat, with only small surfa: Surface waves do not make the ocean floor flat everywhere.
why.The floor has mountains, but never any v: The child forgot that the ocean floor also has mountains.
why.The floor has valleys, but never any mou: The child forgot that the ocean floor also has valleys.

activities.explanation: The floor is uneven and has land-like mountains, valleys, and plains.

activities.prompt: Coastal climates change with nearby currents. A family wants a warmer coast. Which current should it choose?
options: A warm current moving from the equator toward the poles.
A cold current moving from the poles toward the equator.
A warm current moving from the poles toward the equator.
A cold current moving from the equator toward the poles.

why.A cold current moving from the poles tow: Cold currents make coastal climates colder, not warmer.
why.A warm current moving from the poles tow: Warm currents do not move from poles toward the equator.
why.A cold current moving from the equator t: Cold currents do not move from the equator toward poles.

activities.explanation: Warm currents make coastal climates warmer than cold-current coasts.

activities.prompt: Earth looks blue when seen from space. What can a reader infer from this?
options: Ocean water covers most of Earth's surface.
Land covers most of Earth's surface.
Ocean water covers all of Earth's surface.
The ocean floor covers most of Earth's surface.

Most of Earth's surface is ocean, not land.
why.Ocean water covers all of Earth's surfac: Oceans cover most of Earth's surface, but not all of it.
why.The ocean floor covers most of Earth's s: The ocean floor is under the ocean, not covering Earth.

activities.explanation: The blue view fits the ocean covering most of Earth's surface.

lessons.title: Trenches, Reefs and Waterways

activities.prompt: What can we discover beneath the waves in trenches, reefs, and waterways?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Exploring the Deep and Shallow
activities.body: Ocean trenches are very deep, V-shaped seafloor areas. The Mariana Trench is the deepest. Its Challenger Deep reaches over 11,000 metres below sea level. It has near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and complete darkness. Some deep-sea life makes food using chemicals in water for energy. Corals may build reefs. Reefs give food and shelter to about one-quarter of ocean species. Seas, straits, bays, gulfs and canals are smaller water features.
keyPoints: The Mariana Trench has harsh, dark conditions.
Reefs face overfishing, pollution and climate change.
The Suez Canal joins the Red Sea and Mediterranean Sea.
A continent is a large, continuous expanse of land.
activities.explanation: This lesson explores deep trenches, reefs and smaller waterways.

activities.prompt: Why should a community reduce overfishing near a reef?
steps: Reefs may be built by tiny sea animals called corals, so reefs are formed by sea life.
Because reefs provide food and shelter to about one-quarter of all ocean species, many species need them.
Overfishing, pollution and climate change seriously threaten reefs, so these actions can harm that support.
Therefore, reducing overfishing can help protect food and shelter for many ocean species.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which description matches an ocean trench?
options: Deep, V-shaped seafloor area
Natural reef built by corals
Large, continuous expanse of land
Waterway joining two seas
activities.explanation: Ocean trenches are very deep, V-shaped areas of the seafloor.

activities.prompt: Match each place or feature with its correct description.
pairs: Red Sea and Mediterranean Sea connection
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a place with its matching lesson description.

activities.prompt: The Challenger Deep reaches over ______ metres below sea level.
activities.hint: Use the depth stated in your book.
activities.explanation: The Challenger Deep reaches over 11,000 metres below sea level.

activities.prompt: Which set of conditions is found in the Mariana Trench?
options: Near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and darkness
High temperatures, low pressure and darkness
Clear sunlight, low pressure and warmth
Warm water, low pressure and sunlight
activities.explanation: The trench has near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and complete darkness.

activities.prompt: Put these places from the wider place to the place within it.
activities.explanation: The Challenger Deep is inside the Mariana Trench, which is an ocean trench.

activities.prompt: Which sentence explains how some deep-sea life gets food in darkness?
options: It makes food using energy from chemicals in water.
It makes food using energy from sunlight.
It makes food using energy from moonlight.
It eats plants that grow on the deep ocean floor.
activities.explanation: Your book says some deep-sea life makes food using chemicals in water.

activities.prompt: A map marks a deep, V-shaped area of the seafloor. Which kind of place is it?
options: A deep ocean trench
A coral reef
A narrow canal
A large continent

why.A coral reef: A reef may be built by corals, but it is not the deep V-shaped area.
why.A narrow canal: A canal is a smaller water feature, not a seafloor area.
why.A large continent: A continent is continuous land, not part of the seafloor.

activities.explanation: A deep, V-shaped seafloor area is an ocean trench.

activities.prompt: A camera in the Mariana Trench shows complete darkness. What does this tell us?
options: It helps make the trench one of Earth’s harshest environments.
It makes the trench a warm, bright coral reef.
It makes the trench a shallow coastal canal.
It makes the trench a wide, dry continent.

why.It makes the trench a warm, bright coral: This choice confuses a dark, harsh trench with a warm coral reef.
why.It makes the trench a shallow coastal ca: This choice confuses an ocean trench with a smaller water feature.
why.It makes the trench a wide, dry continen: This choice confuses an ocean trench with land.

activities.explanation: Complete darkness helps make the trench one of Earth’s harshest environments.

activities.prompt: A community overfishes near a reef. Why might many species lose their home?
options: Overfishing threatens reefs that support about one-quarter of ocean species.
Overfishing protects reefs and gives every species more shelter.
Overfishing turns reefs into deep, freezing ocean trenches.
Overfishing makes reefs safe from pollution and climate change.

why.Overfishing protects reefs and gives eve: This mistake treats a serious threat as protection for every species.
why.Overfishing turns reefs into deep, freez: This mistake confuses reef damage with the deep shape of an ocean trench.
why.Overfishing makes reefs safe from pollut: This mistake assumes overfishing also removes pollution and climate threats.

activities.explanation: Overfishing is a serious reef threat, and reefs support about one-quarter of ocean species.

lessons.sceneCaption: A colorful coral reef in the Arabian Sea provides food and shelter for ocean life.

lessons.title: Asia’s Landforms

activities.prompt: What shapes Asia’s towering plateaus, sweeping steppes, and vast deserts?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Tibetan Plateau
activities.body: The Tibetan Plateau is a high land area. It is Earth’s highest and largest plateau. The Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze rivers begin in this region. Scientists call the plateau and its mountains the ‘Third Pole’. It holds the largest freshwater reserves outside the polar regions. Snow-melt can enlarge lakes and create new ones.
keyPoints: The Tibetan Plateau is Earth’s highest and largest plateau.
Three great rivers begin in this region.
Scientists call it the ‘Third Pole’.
activities.explanation: The Tibetan Plateau is high, vast and important for rivers and freshwater.

activities.prompt: A map marks a very high region where three rivers begin. Why is it called the ‘Third Pole’?
steps: The region stretches about 2,500 kilometres from east to west, so it is huge.
The Tibetan Plateau fits because it is Earth’s highest and largest plateau.
The rivers fit because the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze begin in this region.
Its large freshwater stores outside polar regions explain the ‘Third Pole’ name.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Deserts, Steppes and Mountains
activities.body: Deserts cover about one-fifth of Earth’s land area. The Gobi Desert lies in Mongolia and part of northern China. The Steppes spread for more than 8,000 kilometres from west to east. They are a global carbon sink because they absorb carbon from the air. The Ural Mountains form a natural boundary between Europe and Asia.
keyPoints: Deserts cover about one-fifth of Earth’s land area.
Steppes absorb carbon from the air.
The Ural Mountains separate Europe and Asia.
activities.explanation: Asia’s deserts, Steppes and mountains each have distinct features.

activities.title: Earth’s Highest Plateau
activities.prompt: Which landform is Earth’s highest and largest plateau?
options: Gobi Desert
Tibetan Plateau
Ural Mountains
Steppes
activities.explanation: The Tibetan Plateau is Earth’s highest and largest plateau.

activities.title: Match the Landforms
activities.prompt: Match each landform with its correct description.
pairs: Highest and largest plateau on Earth
Mongolia and part of northern China
Natural boundary between Europe and Asia
activities.explanation: Each landform has a special place or feature in Asia.

activities.title: The Steppes and Carbon
activities.prompt: What do the Steppes do as a global carbon sink?
options: They release carbon into the air.
They create new lakes.
They absorb carbon from the air.
They form a natural boundary.
activities.explanation: The Steppes absorb carbon from the air. This makes them a global carbon sink.

activities.title: How Far Do the Steppes Spread?
activities.prompt: The Steppes spread for more than ______ kilometres from west to east.
activities.hint: Look for the distance across Asia.
activities.explanation: The Steppes spread for more than 8,000 kilometres from west to east.

activities.title: What Snow-melt Does
activities.prompt: Put the snow-melt sequence in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Snow-melt enlarges existing lakes and creates new ones.

activities.title: Find the True Statement
activities.prompt: Which statement about Asia’s landforms is true?
options: Steppes release carbon into the air.
Gobi Desert lies only in Mongolia.
Ural Mountains separate Europe and Asia.
Deserts cover less than one-fifth of Earth’s land.
activities.explanation: The Ural Mountains form a natural boundary between Europe and Asia.

activities.prompt: Snow has melted on the Tibetan Plateau. Old lakes are now wider, and new lakes have appeared. What explains both changes?
options: The snow-melt water enlarged old lakes and created new ones.
The plateau’s rivers pushed ice into the lake shapes.
The plateau grew wider, and its new parts filled with lakes.
The larger freshwater stores made the snow melt more quickly.

why.The plateau’s rivers pushed ice into the: This mistakes river action for the melting of snow.
why.The plateau grew wider, and its new part: This mistakes the plateau’s width for a process that forms lakes.
why.The larger freshwater stores made the sn: This reverses the link between snow-melt and the lakes.

activities.explanation: This matches the effect of snow-melt on existing and new lakes.

activities.prompt: Scientists call the Tibetan Plateau and its mountains the ‘Third Pole’. It is Earth’s highest, largest plateau and stretches about 2,500 kilometres. What does this name describe?
options: A huge high region with large freshwater stores outside the polar regions.
A small low region with small freshwater stores inside the polar regions.
A dry river source with no freshwater outside the polar regions.
A mountain boundary with freshwater stores inside both polar regions.

why.A small low region with small freshwater: It wrongly makes the highest, largest plateau small and low.
why.A dry river source with no freshwater ou: It wrongly treats a major river source as dry and empty of freshwater.
why.A mountain boundary with freshwater stor: It mixes the Ural boundary and polar regions into the plateau’s features.

activities.explanation: Its height, size, and freshwater stores fit the ‘Third Pole’ name.

activities.prompt: A map measures the Tibetan Plateau at about 2,500 kilometres from east to west. The Steppes measure more than 8,000 kilometres. Which landform spreads farther west to east?
options: The Steppes, because they spread more than 8,000 kilometres.
The Tibetan Plateau, because it spreads about 2,500 kilometres.
The Steppes, because they spread about 2,500 kilometres.
The Tibetan Plateau, because they spread more than 8,000 kilometres.

why.The Tibetan Plateau, because it spreads: The Tibetan Plateau is shorter, at about 2,500 kilometres.
why.The Steppes, because they spread about 2: This uses the plateau’s length for the Steppes.
why.The Tibetan Plateau, because they spread: This gives the plateau the Steppes’ much greater length.

activities.explanation: The Steppes spread more than 8,000 kilometres, so they stretch farther.

activities.prompt: A map shows the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze starting in one region. What does this map suggest about that region?
options: It is the Tibetan Plateau, where all three rivers begin.
It is the Gobi Desert, where all three rivers begin.
It is the Steppes, where all three rivers begin.
It is the Ural Mountains, where all three rivers begin.

why.It is the Gobi Desert, where all three r: The Gobi is a desert, not the shared source of these rivers.
why.It is the Steppes, where all three river: The Steppes are a wide belt, not the source region of these rivers.
why.It is the Ural Mountains, where all thre: The Urals form a boundary, not the source region of these rivers.

activities.explanation: All three rivers begin in the Tibetan Plateau.

activities.prompt: A school map shades a desert across Mongolia and part of northern China. Deserts altogether cover about one-fifth of Earth’s land. What does this show?
options: The Gobi is one desert within the world’s large desert area.
The Gobi is one river source within the world’s large plateau.
The Steppes are one desert within the world’s large desert area.
The Gobi is all the deserts covering Earth’s land.

why.The Gobi is one river source within the: This confuses the Gobi’s desert location with the rivers’ plateau source.
why.The Steppes are one desert within the wo: This wrongly treats the Steppes as part of the world’s deserts.
why.The Gobi is all the deserts covering Ear: This wrongly makes one Gobi equal all deserts on Earth.

activities.explanation: The Gobi lies there, and deserts cover one-fifth of Earth’s land.

activities.prompt: A map marks the Steppes across a wide belt. Another map marks the Ural Mountains. What can we learn from both maps?
options: The Steppes absorb carbon, while the Urals separate Europe and Asia.
The Steppes separate Europe and Asia, while the Urals absorb carbon.
The Steppes and Urals both lie in the Gobi Desert.
The Steppes store freshwater, while the Urals cover one-fifth of Earth.

why.The Steppes separate Europe and Asia, wh: This swaps the roles of the Steppes and the Ural Mountains.
why.The Steppes and Urals both lie in the Go: This wrongly places both landforms in the Gobi Desert.
why.The Steppes store freshwater, while the: This mixes the plateau’s freshwater and the deserts’ land share.

activities.explanation: Steppes absorb carbon, and the Urals are the Europe–Asia boundary.

lessons.title: Europe and Africa

activities.prompt: What secrets do Europe’s plains and Africa’s deserts and rivers hold?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lands, animals and rivers
activities.body: The European Plain is vast and low, with gentle hills. Farmers grow wheat, barley, rye and potatoes there. It holds coal, oil and natural gas. The Alps form a barrier and feed rivers like the Rhine. Africa's Sahara is the world's largest hot desert. Its savannah has grass, scattered trees and seasonal rain. Nomadic tribes herd animals and trade. The Nile supports farms and helped the ancient Egyptian civilisation grow.
keyPoints: The European Plain is large, low and gently rolling.
The Sahara is hot, while the savannah is tropical grassland.
The Nile helps farming and helped ancient Egyptian civilisation grow.
activities.explanation: This card connects the land, people and rivers of Europe and Africa.

activities.prompt: A family crosses south-central Europe and wants water from the Rhine. What should they learn?
steps: The Alps form a natural barrier, so they affect travel routes.
The Alps provide water to the Rhine, so they affect its water supply.
Crops are widely cultivated on the plain, so it supports farming.
Thus, the mountains and plain affect travel, water and farming differently.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The European Plain
activities.prompt: What is the European Plain's terrain like?
options: Low-lying land with rolling hills
High mountains with deep valleys
Hot desert with scattered trees
Grassland with seasonal rainfall
activities.explanation: The Plain has low-lying terrain. Its hills roll gently across the land.

activities.title: A natural barrier
activities.prompt: Which mountain range forms a natural barrier in south-central Europe?
options: Alps
Sahara
Nile
Rhine
activities.explanation: The Alps form a natural barrier in south-central Europe.

activities.title: The largest hot desert
activities.prompt: The Sahara is the largest ______ desert in the world.
activities.hint: Find the word that describes the Sahara's temperature.
activities.explanation: The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert.

activities.title: Places and descriptions
activities.prompt: Match each place with its correct description.
pairs: Major river fed by the Alps
activities.explanation: Each place has a special feature. The Alps feed the Rhine, while the Nile is Africa's great river.

activities.title: African savannah
activities.prompt: Which description fits the African savannah?
options: Tropical grassland with scattered trees
Flat land with gently rolling hills
Natural barrier feeding major rivers
Low plain holding mineral deposits
activities.explanation: The savannah is tropical grassland. It has scattered trees and seasonal rainfall.

activities.title: The Nile's effect
activities.prompt: What did the Nile's waters help create in dry lands?
options: Fertile agricultural areas
A natural mountain barrier
A large hot desert
A tropical grassland
activities.explanation: The Nile turned dry lands into fertile agricultural areas. This supported farming along the river.

activities.prompt: A farm lies on Europe's vast flat plain. Which crops fit there?
options: Wheat, barley, rye and potatoes
Livestock moved across hot desert sand
Food grown beside a long African river
Routes crossing a mountain natural barrier

why.Livestock moved across hot desert sand: This mistake treats hot desert movement as plain farming.
why.Food grown beside a long African river: This mistake uses river growth instead of plain crops.
why.Routes crossing a mountain natural barri: This mistake treats a mountain crossing as low-land farming.

activities.explanation: This is right because these crops are widely cultivated on the plain.

activities.prompt: Low hills and crops describe place A. Scattered trees and seasonal rain describe place B. Which pair?
options: The European Plain; the African savannah
The European Plain; the Sahara hot desert
The Alps; the African savannah
The Alps; the Sahara hot desert

why.The European Plain; the Sahara hot deser: This mistake calls the hot desert a place of scattered trees and seasonal rain.
why.The Alps; the African savannah: This mistake matches the mountain barrier with low hills and crops.
why.The Alps; the Sahara hot desert: This mistake matches neither place with the descriptions given.

activities.explanation: This is right because the first place fits the plain and the second fits the savannah.

activities.prompt: A record shows low land with coal, oil and natural gas. Which region fits it?
options: The vast European Plain
The southern Alps barrier
The Sahara hot desert
The Nile river basin

why.The southern Alps barrier: This mistake matches the mountain barrier with the described deposits.
why.The Sahara hot desert: This mistake treats the hot desert as the recorded deposit region.
why.The Nile river basin: This mistake uses a river basin instead of the described low land.

activities.explanation: This is right because the plain has low land and these deposits.

activities.prompt: A family moves with animals and trades with others. Where does this fit?
options: The Sahara's nomadic tribes
The European Plain farmers
The African savannah herders
The Alps river communities

why.The European Plain farmers: This mistake treats crop farming as moving with animals and trading.
why.The African savannah herders: This mistake assigns herding and trade to the savannah without support.
why.The Alps river communities: This mistake confuses the Alps' river role with nomadic life.

activities.explanation: This is right because Sahara tribes herd livestock and engage in trade.

activities.prompt: A farmer grows food on dry land made fertile by a river. Which river fits?
options: The Nile
The Rhine
The Alps
The Sahara

why.The Rhine: This mistake gives the Rhine a fertilising effect that is not stated.
why.The Alps: This mistake chooses mountains instead of a river.
why.The Sahara: This mistake chooses the hot desert instead of a river.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Nile has turned dry lands into fertile areas.

lessons.title: South America, North America and Australia

activities.prompt: Have you wondered why some deserts hide beneath ice?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Exploring Our World
activities.body: The Andes are South America’s largest mountain range. They supply freshwater for millions. Species losses make them a conservation hotspot. The Amazon is South America’s longest river. Chile’s Atacama Desert is one of Earth’s driest places. The Colorado Plateau is a large southwestern United States highland. The Rocky Mountains exceed 4,800 kilometres. Wolves were introduced at Yellowstone in 1995. Australia has large desert areas. Studying geography helps us manage Earth wisely.
keyPoints: The Andes supply freshwater for millions.
Australia has large desert or arid areas.
Studying world geography helps us manage Earth’s features wisely.
activities.explanation: Studying world geography helps us understand and manage Earth’s features wisely.

activities.prompt: Native species in the Andes are disappearing. Why should the family support protecting the mountains?
steps: The Andes are South America’s largest mountain range.
They provide freshwater for millions of people, so water matters.
Many native species have been lost, so the area is a critical conservation hotspot.
Therefore, the family should support careful protection of this important range.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which place is the largest mountain range in South America?
options: The Andes in South America
The Rocky Mountains in South America
The Colorado Plateau in South America
The Amazon River in South America
activities.explanation: The lesson says the Andes are the largest mountain range in South America.

activities.prompt: The Colorado Plateau is a large highland region in the ______ United States.
activities.hint: Choose the direction word.
activities.explanation: The Colorado Plateau is in the southwestern United States.

activities.prompt: The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the wettest places on Earth.
activities.explanation: The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth.

activities.prompt: Match each place with its detail in the lesson.
pairs: The largest mountain range in South America
The longest river in South America
One of the driest places on Earth
A large highland region in the southwestern United States
activities.explanation: Each place matches the detail given about it in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Why are the Andes a critical conservation hotspot?
options: Many native species have been lost.
The range supplies freshwater for millions.
The range is South America’s largest.
The Atacama Desert is very dry.
activities.explanation: Many native species have been lost in the Andes. This makes the range a critical conservation hotspot.

activities.prompt: The Rocky Mountains stretch for less than 4,800 kilometres.
activities.explanation: The Rocky Mountains stretch for more than 4,800 kilometres, not less.

activities.prompt: The Andes are South America’s largest mountain range. They provide freshwater for millions of people. Many native species have been lost there. What should a local group do?
options: Protect the area because it is a critical conservation hotspot.
Choose wildlife care only, because freshwater needs no attention.
Choose water care only, because wildlife losses do not matter.
Wait and do nothing, because lost species do not affect the mountains.

why.Choose wildlife care only, because fresh: Freshwater for millions also makes water care important.
why.Choose water care only, because wildlife: Lost native species make wildlife care important too.
why.Wait and do nothing, because lost specie: The lost species show that the area needs active protection.

activities.explanation: The facts call the Andes a critical conservation hotspot.

activities.prompt: The Amazon River is the longest river in South America. What should a map comparing its rivers show?
options: The Amazon has the greatest length among those rivers.
The Amazon has the shortest length among those rivers.
The Amazon and every other river have equal lengths.
The Amazon appears outside South America on the map.

why.The Amazon has the shortest length among: This mistake reverses the meaning of longest.
why.The Amazon and every other river have eq: The fact does not say that all rivers have one length.
why.The Amazon appears outside South America: The fact places the Amazon River in South America.

activities.explanation: The fact directly says that the Amazon is the longest.

activities.prompt: The Colorado Plateau is a large highland in the southwestern United States. The Rocky Mountains stretch for more than 4,800 kilometres. What can a map compare?
options: A highland region and a very long mountain range.
A dry desert and a very small mountain range.
A short river and a very large highland region.
Two small coastal islands near the southwestern United States.

why.A dry desert and a very small mountain r: Calling either place a desert mistakes these land features.
why.A short river and a very large highland: Calling either place a river mistakes these land features.
why.Two small coastal islands near the south: Calling either place an island is not supported by either fact.

activities.explanation: The map can compare the plateau’s highland shape and the range’s great length.

activities.prompt: The Atacama Desert is one of Earth’s driest places. Antarctica is Earth’s largest desert. How do these deserts compare?
options: Antarctica is larger, while Atacama is among the driest.
Atacama is larger, while Antarctica is only slightly dry.
Both have exactly the same size and level of dryness.
Neither is dry, because deserts contain lots of water.

why.Atacama is larger, while Antarctica is o: This option swaps the size and dryness facts.
why.Both have exactly the same size and leve: The facts do not show equal size or equal dryness.
why.Neither is dry, because deserts contain: Both facts clearly describe places with very dry land.

activities.explanation: Antarctica has the largest desert, while Atacama is one of the driest.

activities.prompt: A source says wolves were introduced in 1995. It names Yellowstone National Park. What can that source show?
options: The introduction year, but not what happened afterward.
The introduction year and every later change in wolves.
The reason for the introduction and its full effect.
The wolf numbers before and after the introduction.

why.The introduction year and every later ch: One event statement does not give every later change.
why.The reason for the introduction and its: The source does not state the reason or full effect.
why.The wolf numbers before and after the in: The source does not give any wolf numbers.

activities.explanation: The source gives a date and event, but no later results.

lessons.sceneCaption: An astronaut view reveals the Central Andes and young volcanoes near Chile’s Atacama Desert.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A color physical world map shows Earth’s landforms and oceans using the Robinson projection at a scale of 1:35,000,000.
lessons.sceneCaption: This physical world map uses the Robinson projection to show Earth’s oceans and landforms.

sceneCredit.text: CIA World Factbook 2021 physical world map by US Government, Central Intelligence Agency, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: US Government, Central Intelligence Agency

activities.context: A student is preparing a physical map for a class display. The map-maker marks the oceans, seas, lakes, and rivers in blue, the plains in green, and the plateaus in yellow or brown. High mountains appear in dark brown, deserts in light yellow, and ice and glaciers in white. When the student compares the flat map with the round Earth, the student notices that the Earth has been shown using a projection.
activities.prompt: Why might a country look the correct shape but the wrong size on this map?
options: Showing the round Earth on a flat surface involves compromise between map features.
Every feature can be represented equally accurately on one flat map.
Using dark brown for high mountains automatically changes the size of countries.
Using white for ice and glaciers makes neighbouring countries shrink.

why.Every feature can be represented equally: This contradicts the fact that every map involves compromise.
why.Using dark brown for high mountains auto: Map colours do not determine the size of a country.
why.Using white for ice and glaciers makes n: Map colours do not make neighbouring countries shrink.

activities.explanation: Projection requires compromises, so some sizes may be wrong.

activities.context: A student is preparing a physical map for a class display. The map-maker marks the oceans, seas, lakes, and rivers in blue, the plains in green, and the plateaus in yellow or brown. High mountains appear in dark brown, deserts in light yellow, and ice and glaciers in white. When the student compares the flat map with the round Earth, the student notices that the Earth has been shown using a projection.
activities.prompt: What should the student do before claiming that one projection gives the fairest view of the world?
options: Look at several projections and compare them.
Use only one projection and ignore all the others.
Choose the projection that shows every country with perfect shapes and sizes.
Judge projections only by the colours used for physical features.

why.Use only one projection and ignore all t: Looking at only one ignores other projections and their compromises.
why.Choose the projection that shows every c: No map is free from distortion or compromise.
why.Judge projections only by the colours us: Physical-map colours do not determine which projection is fairest.

activities.explanation: Several projections help the student understand the world fairly.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): All maps contain some distortion.
Reason (R): Map-makers try to show the round Earth on a flat surface.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Trying to show a round Earth on a flat surface explains why maps contain distortion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Every map shows the correct shapes and sizes of countries.
Reason (R): Every map involves a compromise between different features.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The claim about every map is false, while the statement about compromise is true.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a physical map and a map projection, and why does a physical map also involve distortion?
activities.answer: A physical map uses colours to represent features of the Earth. Oceans, seas, lakes and rivers are blue; plains are green; plateaus are yellow or brown; high mountains are dark brown; deserts are light yellow; and ice and glaciers are white. A map projection is the process of showing the Earth on a flat surface. Since the Earth is round, making a flat map involves compromise. Therefore, a physical map also contains some distortion.
points: Physical-map colours are identified correctly.
A projection is defined as showing the Earth on a flat surface.
The compromise involved in flattening the Earth is explained.
The answer links these compromises to distortion.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A coastal school studies Earth from space and learns that it looks blue. The class also learns that the ocean covers about 71 per cent of Earth’s surface and contains 97 per cent of Earth’s water. Their project follows a warm current carrying warm water from the equator towards the poles and a cold current carrying cold water from the poles towards the equator. They note that currents affect coastal climates.
activities.prompt: Why can the warm current in the project influence the climate of the school’s coastal area?
options: It moves warm water towards the poles, and such water movement can change a coastal area’s climate.
Ocean-floor mountains stop the current before it can reach any coast.
Warm currents make every coastal area have exactly the same climate.
The current releases all the ocean’s heat at once, changing the climate immediately.

why.Warm currents make every coastal area ha: Ocean-floor features do not stop currents according to the lesson.
why.The current releases all the ocean’s hea: The ocean releases heat slowly rather than all at once.

activities.explanation: Warm currents carry warm water towards the poles.

activities.context: A coastal school studies Earth from space and learns that it looks blue. The class also learns that the ocean covers about 71 per cent of Earth’s surface and contains 97 per cent of Earth’s water. Their project follows a warm current carrying warm water from the equator towards the poles and a cold current carrying cold water from the poles towards the equator. They note that currents affect coastal climates.
activities.prompt: What should a student do to find out whether a coastal area is affected by a warm or cold current?
options: Identify the nearby current and check whether it carries warm or cold water.
Study whether the ocean floor is flat along the coast.
Check whether Earth looks blue from outer space.
Count different kinds of ocean life instead of examining the water.

why.Study whether the ocean floor is flat al: Warm and cold currents carry water with different temperatures.
why.Check whether Earth looks blue from oute: The shape of the ocean floor does not identify current temperature.
why.Count different kinds of ocean life inst: Looking from space or counting ocean life does not show the type of current.

activities.explanation: The student must identify the current near the coast.

activities.context: A class prepares an ocean project. One student suggests studying the Mariana Trench because it is the deepest trench, with near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and complete darkness. Another suggests studying a reef built by corals, which gives many ocean species food and shelter but faces overfishing, pollution and climate change. The class also plans to examine the Suez Canal, which links the Red Sea and Mediterranean Sea, and compare a continent, a large continuous expanse of land.
activities.prompt: For the Mariana Trench part of the project, the team must plan for the environment. Which conditions should it expect?
options: Warm water, high pressure and no sunlight
Extremely cold water, crushing pressure and no sunlight
Extremely cold water, gentle pressure and no sunlight
Warm water, gentle pressure and bright sunlight

why.Warm water, high pressure and no sunligh: The water there is near-freezing, not warm.
why.Extremely cold water, gentle pressure an: The pressure is high, not gentle.
why.Warm water, gentle pressure and bright s: The water is neither warm nor bright, and the pressure is not gentle.

activities.explanation: Near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and complete darkness match these conditions.

activities.context: A class prepares an ocean project. One student suggests studying the Mariana Trench because it is the deepest trench, with near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and complete darkness. Another suggests studying a reef built by corals, which gives many ocean species food and shelter but faces overfishing, pollution and climate change. The class also plans to examine the Suez Canal, which links the Red Sea and Mediterranean Sea, and compare a continent, a large continuous expanse of land.
activities.prompt: The class must label its features correctly. Which description correctly distinguishes the Suez Canal from a continent?
options: The Mariana Trench is a water connection between two seas; a continent is a broad, continuous land area.
The Suez is a water connection between two seas; a continent is a broad, continuous land area.
The Mariana Trench is a broad, continuous land area; a continent is a water connection between two seas.
The Mariana Trench is a deep, V-shaped seafloor; a continent is a water connection between two seas.

why.The Mariana Trench is a water connection: The Mariana Trench is a deep seafloor feature, not a water connection between seas.
why.The Mariana Trench is a broad, continuou: This reverses the correct meanings of a trench and a continent.
why.The Mariana Trench is a deep, V-shaped s: The first description is correct, but a continent is land, not a water connection.

activities.explanation: The Suez is a canal joining the Red Sea and the Mediterranean Sea, while a continent is land.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Some deep-sea life makes food by using energy from chemicals in the water.
Reason (R): The Mariana Trench has near-freezing temperatures and high pressure.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the temperature and pressure do not explain how the life obtains energy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Suez Canal is a continent because it joins two seas.
Reason (R): A continent is a large continuous expanse of land.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The canal is a water feature, while a continent is a large continuous expanse of land.

activities.prompt: Explain how the conditions of the Mariana Trench make it a harsh environment, and how some deep-sea life can make food there.
activities.answer: The Mariana Trench is a very deep, V-shaped area of the seafloor and is the deepest of these trenches. Its conditions are extreme: temperatures are near-freezing, pressure is high, and complete darkness makes it one of Earth’s harshest environments. These three features explain why it is a harsh setting. However, some deep-sea life can make food by using energy from chemicals in the water. Thus, the presence of harsh conditions does not mean that no life exists there; some life can obtain food through chemical energy.
points: The Mariana Trench is the deepest trench.
It is a very deep, V-shaped seafloor area.
It has near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and complete darkness.
Some deep-sea life uses chemical energy to make food.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is preparing a geography report on Asia’s landforms. The student notes that the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze rivers begin on the Tibetan Plateau and that the plateau holds the largest freshwater reserves outside the polar regions. Snow-melt has enlarged existing lakes and created new ones. The student also records that the Steppes absorb carbon from the air. After studying the Gobi Desert, the student plans to compare these landforms by their locations and effects.
activities.prompt: If more snow-melt occurred in the plateau region, what would the student most likely expect to happen to its lakes?
options: Existing lakes would grow larger, and additional lakes would form.
Existing lakes would become smaller, and newly formed lakes would disappear.
Existing lakes would remain unchanged, and no additional lakes would form.
Only existing lakes would change, because new lakes could not be created.

why.Existing lakes would become smaller, and: This reverses the stated effects of snow-melt.
why.Existing lakes would remain unchanged, a: This wrongly denies both enlargement and the creation of lakes.
why.Only existing lakes would change, becaus: This recognises enlargement but wrongly rules out new lakes.

activities.explanation: This follows both stated effects of snow-melt on plateau lakes.

activities.context: A student is preparing a geography report on Asia’s landforms. The student notes that the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze rivers begin on the Tibetan Plateau and that the plateau holds the largest freshwater reserves outside the polar regions. Snow-melt has enlarged existing lakes and created new ones. The student also records that the Steppes absorb carbon from the air. After studying the Gobi Desert, the student plans to compare these landforms by their locations and effects.
activities.prompt: Suppose the Steppes began absorbing less carbon from the air than before. What conclusion would follow?
options: They would take in less carbon, so their global carbon-sink role would be weaker.
They would take in more carbon, so their global carbon-sink role would grow.
They would absorb no carbon at all and therefore lose their carbon-sink role.
Their carbon-absorbing role would stay unchanged because their location had not changed.

why.They would take in more carbon, so their: This contradicts the change described in the question.
why.They would absorb no carbon at all and t: Absorbing less does not mean that no carbon would be absorbed.
why.Their carbon-absorbing role would stay u: The question states a change in absorption, so the role would not remain unchanged.

activities.explanation: Taking in less carbon directly weakens their stated role as a carbon sink.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Tibetan Plateau stretches about 2,500 kilometres from east to west.
Reason (R): The Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze rivers begin in this region.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the rivers beginning there does not explain the plateau’s east-to-west length.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Steppes act as a global carbon sink.
Reason (R): They absorb carbon from the air.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Their absorption of carbon from the air explains why they function as a global carbon sink.

activities.prompt: Explain how the Tibetan Plateau differs from the Ural Mountains.
activities.answer: The Tibetan Plateau is the highest and largest plateau on Earth, stretching about 2,500 kilometres from east to west. The Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze rivers begin in this region, which also contains the largest freshwater reserves outside the polar regions. Scientists call the plateau and its mountains the “Third Pole”. In contrast, the Ural Mountains form a natural boundary between Europe and Asia. Thus, the plateau is a vast high region associated with rivers and freshwater, whereas the Urals mark the separation between Europe and Asia.
points: Identifies the plateau as the highest and largest on Earth.
Gives its east-to-west length of about 2,500 kilometres.
Mentions the rivers, freshwater reserves and “Third Pole” name.
Explains that the Urals separate Europe and Asia.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student visits the European Plain, a vast flat area with low-lying land and gentle hills. Several crops grow there, and deposits of coal, oil and natural gas lie underground. Following the Rhine toward the Alps, the student learns why the river receives water. In Africa, the student sees farms beside the Nile, where dry land has become fertile, and nomadic herders in the Sahara who trade. A final stop is an African savannah with scattered trees and seasonal rainfall.
activities.prompt: Why does the European Plain's landscape suit the cultivation of several crops?
options: Low-lying ground and gentle hills make cultivation possible across the plain.
The Alps form a barrier around the plain and create its farmland.
Seasonal rainfall and scattered trees make it a tropical grassland.
The Nile's fertile basin extends across the European Plain.

why.The Alps form a barrier around the plain: The Alps are a natural barrier, not the reason crops grow on the plain.
why.Seasonal rainfall and scattered trees ma: Those features describe the African savannah, not the European Plain.
why.The Nile's fertile basin extends across: The Nile is in Africa and does not explain farming conditions on the plain.

activities.explanation: The plain's low-lying terrain and gently rolling hills support crop cultivation.

Green

options: Low-lying ground and gentle hills
High peaks and deep trenches

chapters.title: India’s Long Road to Independence
chapters.summary: In this chapter: royal control and early reform; congress, discontent and national awakening; revolutionaries and the move for home rule; gandhi, non-cooperation and national uniting.

lessons.title: Royal Control and Early Reform

activities.prompt: How did India change after the 1857 uprising?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Royal Rule and Early Reform
activities.body: After 1857, Queen Victoria began ruling India directly. A Secretary of State and a Viceroy governed British India in her name. Heavy land taxes brought famines and widespread discontent. Indian industries struggled against cheap British goods. Reformers challenged child marriage, the low status of widows and caste discrimination. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Anandamath. Rabindranath Tagore set Bande Mataram to music.
keyPoints: Queen Victoria began direct rule after 1857.
Heavy taxes harmed people and Indian industries.
Bankim wrote Anandamath, and Tagore set Bande Mataram to music.
activities.explanation: These points connect royal rule, hardship and early reform.

activities.prompt: A student asks why Indians wanted reform after 1857.
steps: After 1857, Victoria ruled directly, so the East India Company lost power.
The Viceroy and Secretary of State kept power in the Queen's name.
Heavy taxes caused famine, while cheap British goods hurt Indian industry.
Reformers opposed child marriage and caste unfairness, so they sought broad reform.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Ruled India Directly?
activities.prompt: Who began ruling India directly after 1857?
options: Queen Victoria
A Secretary of State
A Viceroy
The East India Company
activities.explanation: After 1857, Queen Victoria ruled India directly instead of using the East India Company.

activities.title: A Popular Bengali Novel
activities.prompt: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay published ______ in 1882.
activities.hint: It is the title of his popular Bengali novel.
activities.explanation: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay published Anandamath in 1882.

activities.title: The Effect of Land Taxes
activities.prompt: Heavy land taxes removed widespread discontent among Indians.
activities.explanation: Heavy land taxes caused severe famines and widespread discontent.

activities.title: Governing in the Queen's Name
activities.prompt: Who governed British India in the Queen's name?
options: Secretary of State and Viceroy
Viceroy and Company secretary
Local ruler and Governor
Company agent and Secretary
activities.explanation: British India was governed in the Queen's name by both officials.

activities.title: People, Works and Organisations
activities.prompt: Match each item with its detail from the lesson.
pairs: Published in 1882 by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
Set to music by Rabindranath Tagore
activities.explanation: These details link the song, novel and organisation with the people connected to them.

activities.title: A Challenge for Indian Industries
activities.prompt: What made British goods difficult for Indian industries to match?
options: British goods had low prices.
British goods had high prices.
British goods were made in India.
Indian goods were made in Britain.
activities.explanation: Indian industries could not compete with cheap goods made in Britain.

activities.prompt: A farmer pays a very heavy land tax. What may result?
options: Famine and strong anger may spread.
Cheap British goods may enter India easily.
Bande Mataram may become India's National Song.
Indian industries may sell more goods.

why.Cheap British goods may enter India easi: Cheap British goods relate to industry, not heavy land taxes.
why.Bande Mataram may become India's Nationa: Bande Mataram's adoption came later and did not result from this tax.
Indian industries did not gain sales merely because farmers paid heavy tax.

activities.explanation: This is right because heavy land taxes caused famine and discontent.

activities.prompt: A buyer chooses a cheap British shirt over a similar Indian shirt. Why can this hurt Indian industry?
options: British goods are cheap, so Indian makers struggle to compete.
Indian factories pay heavy land taxes, so every shirt becomes costly.
British shops pay more tax, so their shirts cost less.
Indian makers sell novels, so their shirts cannot reach buyers.

why.Indian factories pay heavy land taxes, s: This links land taxes to factory costs, but taxes caused famines.
why.British shops pay more tax, so their shi: This reverses the trade problem, since British goods were cheap.
why.Indian makers sell novels, so their shir: This confuses popular novels with goods made in industries.

activities.explanation: This is right because cheap British goods made Indian competition difficult.

activities.prompt: Between 1896 and 1950, how did Bande Mataram's role change?
options: It changed from a Congress performance into India's National Song.
It changed from a novel publication into India's National Song.
It changed from founding a Mission into India's National Song.
It changed from collecting land tax into India's National Song.

why.It changed from a novel publication into: This confuses Bankim's novel publication with the song's 1896 performance.
why.It changed from founding a Mission into: This mistakes Vivekananda founding the Mission for the song's earlier role.
why.It changed from collecting land tax into: This mistakes a cause of famine for an event in the song's history.

activities.explanation: This is right because 1896 was a performance and 1950 was adoption.

lessons.title: Congress, Discontent and National Awakening

activities.prompt: Why did people across India begin to unite against colonial rule?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Congress and National Awakening
activities.body: Allan Octavian Hume brought together like-minded Indians. The Indian National Congress began in Bombay in 1885. At first, Congress expressed full faith in British rule and loyalty to the Crown. The colonial government mostly ignored Congress resolutions. People later opposed colonial authority and partition. Swadeshi and boycott encouraged Indian-made products. Congress declared Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education as aims in 1906.
keyPoints: Congress began in Bombay in 1885.
Congress resolutions were mostly ignored by the colonial government.
Swadeshi and boycott encouraged Indian-made products.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how Congress developed from loyalty to opposition.

activities.prompt: A group asks the government for changes, but the government ignores every request. What should the group do next?
steps: Congress began in Bombay in 1885, showing that like-minded Indians could organise together.
It first trusted British rule, so members expected loyal requests to bring change.
When the government ignored resolutions, members saw that continued loyalty was not enough.
Congress then declared Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education in 1906, giving people stronger ways to act.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who worked to bring together a group of like-minded Indians?
options: Allan Octavian Hume
Birsa Munda
Rabindranath Tagore
Curzon
activities.explanation: Allan Octavian Hume worked to bring together like-minded Indians.

activities.prompt: The Kuka Movement was also called the ______ Movement in Punjab.
activities.hint: This was another name for the Kuka Movement.
activities.explanation: The Kuka Movement was also called the Namdhari Movement in Punjab.

activities.prompt: At first, what did Congress express?
options: Loyalty to the British Crown and faith in British rule
Support for Curzon’s partition of Bengal
Plans for Swadeshi and boycott movements
A demand for National Education in 1906
activities.explanation: At first, Congress expressed full faith in British rule and loyalty to the Crown.

activities.prompt: Match each person or movement with the matching information.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a person or movement with its matching action or name.

activities.prompt: What policy did Curzon’s partition of Bengal apply?
options: The policy of Swadeshi trade
The policy of divide and rule
The policy of National Education
The policy of boycott
activities.explanation: Curzon’s partition of Bengal applied the colonial policy of divide and rule.

activities.prompt: Put these Congress-related events in order by their years.
items: Congress declared Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education as its aims in 1906
The Surat session divided Congress in 1907
activities.explanation: The years 1885, 1906 and 1907 give the order shown.

activities.prompt: The colonial government mostly ignored Congress resolutions. What would this most likely cause?
options: They would keep full faith in British rule.
They would feel peaceful requests had failed.
They would divide Bengal into two parts.
They would stop seeking any political change.

why.They would keep full faith in British ru: This mistakes ignored requests for continued trust.
This confuses political dissatisfaction with the partition of Bengal.
why.They would stop seeking any political ch: This assumes ignored requests would end all political action.

activities.explanation: Ignored resolutions can make members feel that peaceful requests failed.

activities.prompt: Congress began in Bombay in 1885. In 1906, it declared four aims. What does this change show?
options: It had moved from loyalty to active demands.
It had always opposed British rule from its start.
It had stopped holding any meetings altogether.
It had changed only its main meeting city.

why.It had always opposed British rule from: This treats early loyalty as constant opposition.
why.It had stopped holding any meetings alto: New aims do not mean that Congress stopped meeting.
why.It had changed only its main meeting cit: The change concerned its aims, not mainly its meeting city.

activities.explanation: The change from loyalty to declared aims shows growing demands.

activities.prompt: Curzon’s partition of Bengal applied divide and rule. People later united against it. What would a map of divided Bengal help explain?
options: Why people were angry about Bengal's partition.
Why Bengal was joined to Bombay in 1885.
Why Congress first began in Bombay city.
Why people rejected all Indian-made products.

The map concerns partition, not Bombay's Congress beginning.
The map concerns partition, not the beginning of Congress.
why.Why people rejected all Indian-made prod: The map concerns partition, not the Swadeshi boycott.

activities.explanation: A divided map helps show the partition that people opposed.

activities.prompt: The government mostly ignored Congress resolutions. Which response best fits this situation?
options: Wait longer and keep trusting the same system.
Organise people and use Swadeshi and boycott methods.
Divide Bengal and seek support from one side.
Leave all political work to other leaders.

why.Wait longer and keep trusting the same s: This assumes ignored requests will suddenly receive a response.
why.Divide Bengal and seek support from one: This confuses resistance to rule with dividing Bengal.
why.Leave all political work to other leader: This assumes political action should be left to others.

activities.explanation: Swadeshi and boycott offered people a way to act together.

lessons.sceneCaption: Delegates gather at the first Indian National Congress meeting in Bombay in 1885.

lessons.title: Revolutionaries and the Move for Home Rule

activities.prompt: What inspired revolutionaries to unite and fight for Home Rule?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways of Challenging British Rule
activities.body: Many Indians challenged British rule. Yugantar, a Bengali newspaper, called for open revolt. Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki threw bombs at a carriage. They thought it carried a British judge. Tilak and Annie Besant launched the Home Rule Movement in 1916. The Ghadar Movement tried to start a mutiny in the British Indian Army during World War I. A mutiny is a revolt by soldiers.
keyPoints: Yugantar called for open revolt.
Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki threw bombs at a carriage.
Tilak and Annie Besant launched Home Rule in 1916.
activities.explanation: Revolutionaries used newspapers, direct action and united movements.

activities.prompt: Yugantar tells readers to openly resist British rule. Why might some readers join?
steps: Yugantar openly called for revolt against British rule.
Its message did not hide what the newspaper wanted.
Readers may then see that others also oppose British rule.
So Yugantar could encourage open resistance, without guaranteeing that everyone joined.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Unity and Decisions at Lucknow
activities.body: Tilak reunited the two Congress factions at Lucknow in 1916. This completed his first task. The Lucknow Pact was an agreement between Congress and the All-India Muslim League. In the Alipore Bomb trial, Aurobindo Ghose was acquitted. Acquitted means found not guilty. Barindra Ghose was sentenced to death in the same trial.
keyPoints: Tilak reunited the two Congress factions at Lucknow.
The Lucknow Pact joined Congress and the All-India Muslim League.
The Alipore Bomb trial gave Aurobindo Ghose and Barindra Ghose different outcomes.
activities.explanation: Notice the unity at Lucknow and the different outcomes in the Alipore Bomb trial.

activities.title: The Newspaper for Open Revolt
activities.prompt: Which newspaper called for open revolt against British rule?
options: Yugantar
Cellular Jail
Lucknow Pact
Alipore Bomb trial
activities.explanation: Yugantar was a Bengali newspaper. It called for open revolt against British rule.

activities.title: Tilak's Jail Sentence
activities.prompt: Tilak was sentenced to ______ years in jail in Mandalay.
activities.hint: Tilak received this sentence in Mandalay.
activities.explanation: Tilak was sentenced to six years in jail in Mandalay.

activities.title: The Lucknow Pact
activities.prompt: Who made the Lucknow Pact?
options: Cellular Jail and the British government
Congress and the All-India Muslim League
British Indian Army and the Ghadar Movement
Yugantar and the Alipore Bomb trial
activities.explanation: The Lucknow Pact was an agreement between Congress and the All-India Muslim League.

activities.title: People and Actions
activities.prompt: Match each name with its action from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a person or group with an action described in the lesson.

activities.title: Events in Your Book
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they appear in your book.
items: Rani Gaidinliu begins fighting British rule
Bagha Jatin organises a weapons reception
Tilak and Annie Besant launch Home Rule
activities.explanation: The events appear on pages 54, 57, 59 and 60.

activities.title: Tilak's Achievement
activities.prompt: What did Tilak achieve at Lucknow in 1916?
options: He ended the Home Rule Movement.
He started a mutiny in the army.
He reunited the two Congress factions.
He released all political prisoners.
activities.explanation: At Lucknow in 1916, Tilak reunited the two Congress factions. This completed his first task.

activities.prompt: A Bengali newspaper calls for open revolt against British rule. What effect is most likely on readers?
options: Readers may feel ready to join public resistance together.
Readers must learn every secret plan before joining resistance.
Every reader will surely stop supporting British colonial rule.
Readers may decide to hide all their demands for change.

why.Readers must learn every secret plan bef: It mistakes a public call for a complete secret plan.
why.Every reader will surely stop supporting: One call cannot guarantee that every reader changes support.
why.Readers may decide to hide all their dem: The call supports open revolt, not hiding demands.

activities.explanation: An open call to revolt can encourage people to join resistance.

activities.prompt: Tilak serves six years in Mandalay. The Cellular Jail isolates revolutionaries. What does this show about colonial punishment?
options: Colonial punishment included both long sentences and isolation.
All political prisoners stayed in one shared colonial prison.
Both places were used mainly for public political meetings.
Tilak served all six years inside the Cellular Jail.

why.All political prisoners stayed in one sh: The facts show two places with different prison roles.
why.Both places were used mainly for public: The facts describe imprisonment, not public meetings.
why.Tilak served all six years inside the Ce: They place Tilak's sentence in Mandalay, not the Cellular Jail.

activities.explanation: Mandalay held Tilak, while the Cellular Jail isolated revolutionaries.

activities.prompt: A court record names Aurobindo Ghose and Barindra Ghose. It gives them different results. What does this show?
options: The Alipore Bomb trial treated both defendants differently.
The Alipore Bomb trial punished both defendants equally.
The Alipore Bomb trial released both defendants completely.
The Alipore Bomb trial gave both men prison sentences.

why.The Alipore Bomb trial punished both def: The outcomes were different, not equal punishments.
why.The Alipore Bomb trial released both def: Only Barindra Ghose was sentenced; Aurobindo Ghose was acquitted.
why.The Alipore Bomb trial gave both men pri: It wrongly assumes both men received prison sentences.

activities.explanation: Aurobindo Ghose was acquitted, but Barindra Ghose received death.

activities.prompt: Tilak and several Nationalist leaders are jailed by the colonial government. What does this show about its method?
options: It used prison terms to control Nationalist leaders.
It used public meetings to control Nationalist leaders.
It used newspaper calls to control Nationalist leaders.
It used military alliances to control Nationalist leaders.

why.It used public meetings to control Natio: It mistakes public meetings for the imprisonment described.
why.It used newspaper calls to control Natio: It confuses Yugantar's newspaper call with government punishment.
why.It used military alliances to control Na: It confuses the Ghadar army plan with the government's response.

activities.explanation: The government's response was to jail Tilak and other leaders.

activities.prompt: Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki thought a carriage carried a British judge. What does the source's wording suggest?
options: They believed it, but the facts do not confirm it.
They knew it with complete certainty before throwing bombs.
The carriage certainly carried the British judge they expected.
British officials had already checked that carriage before the attack.

why.They knew it with complete certainty bef: It mistakes belief for complete certainty about the target.
why.The carriage certainly carried the Briti: It treats their belief as proof of the judge's identity.
why.British officials had already checked th: It adds an unsupported official check before the bombing.

activities.explanation: “Thought” shows belief, not confirmed knowledge of the judge's identity.

activities.prompt: At Lucknow in 1916, Tilak reunited two Congress factions. Also in 1916, he and Annie Besant launched Home Rule. What connection is best supported?
options: He supported both political unity and Home Rule in 1916.
He opposed political unity while supporting Home Rule in 1916.
He supported prison unity and Home Rule from Mandalay.
He supported Congress unity but opposed the Lucknow Pact.

why.He opposed political unity while support: He reunited the factions, so this wrongly says he opposed unity.
why.He supported prison unity and Home Rule: It wrongly turns political unity into prison unity in Mandalay.
why.He supported Congress unity but opposed: The Lucknow Pact was an agreement, not something he opposed.

activities.explanation: He reunited Congress factions and launched Home Rule with Annie Besant.

lessons.sceneCaption: An outside view of the Cellular Jail, a major landmark connected with India’s revolutionary history.
