lessons.title: Gandhi, Non-Cooperation and National Uniting

activities.prompt: Could one person’s peaceful ideas help unite an entire nation?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Gandhi and Non-Cooperation
activities.body: Racial discrimination in South Africa led Gandhi to develop satyagraha, his peaceful method of resistance. He used satyagraha against low wages and land revenue. The Rowlatt Act of 1919 let police detain anyone without trial. At Jallianwala Bagh, Dyer’s troops blocked the main exit and fired on the unarmed crowd. Congress launched the Non-Cooperation Movement at Nagpur in 1920. Gandhi withdrew it after policemen were killed at Chauri Chaura.
keyPoints: Gandhi developed satyagraha after facing racial discrimination in South Africa.
Congress launched Non-Cooperation at Nagpur in 1920.
Gandhi withdrew the movement after the Chauri Chaura killing.
activities.explanation: These events show how Gandhi used and then withdrew Non-Cooperation.

activities.prompt: What should citizens do when police can detain people without trial?
steps: The Rowlatt Act let police detain people because no trial was required.
Without a trial, people could not answer the case against them.
Gandhi used satyagraha because it opposed injustice without violence.
So citizens should use peaceful satyagraha against such a law.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Gandhi’s Beginning
activities.prompt: Where was Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi born?
options: Nagpur
Porbandar
Jallianwala Bagh
Chauri Chaura
activities.explanation: Porbandar in Gujarat was Gandhi’s birthplace.

activities.title: Gokhale’s Advice
activities.prompt: Gandhi joined Congress on ______’s advice.
activities.hint: Use the adviser’s surname.
activities.explanation: Gokhale advised Gandhi to join Congress.

activities.title: Match Events
activities.prompt: Match each event with its date or name.
pairs: Police could detain people without trial
activities.explanation: These pairs connect key events with their dates or names.

activities.title: Police Power
activities.prompt: What did the Rowlatt Act allow the police to do?
options: Detain people without trial
Release every arrested person
End the Non-Cooperation Movement
Launch the Nagpur session
activities.explanation: The Act allowed police to detain people without trial.

activities.title: Place Events in Time
activities.prompt: Put these events in date order.
items: Gandhi used satyagraha against local grievances
The Rowlatt Act allowed detention without trial
activities.explanation: The events run in order from 1915 to 1920.

activities.title: Public Trust
activities.prompt: Which event permanently damaged public trust in the British government?
options: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre
The Chauri Chaura killing
The Rowlatt Act of 1919
The Nagpur Congress session
activities.explanation: Dyer’s troops blocked the main exit and fired on the unarmed crowd.

activities.prompt: A rule lets officers hold a shopkeeper for days without any trial. What can we infer?
options: Officers can punish people without giving them a chance to answer.
Every child who breaks a rule must receive a court trial.
The rule makes it easier for children to reach a court.
People must stop all courts from working at once.

why.Every child who breaks a rule must recei: This wrongly assumes the rule guarantees every accused person a trial.
why.The rule makes it easier for children to: This wrongly assumes detention without trial makes courts easier to reach.
why.People must stop all courts from working: This wrongly uses one bad law to justify boycotting all courts.

activities.explanation: This is right because detention without trial denies a chance to answer.

activities.prompt: Gandhi faced racial discrimination in South Africa. Why did he later use satyagraha in India?
options: He wanted to challenge injustice through peaceful resistance.
He wanted to copy South African customs in Indian life.
He wanted to punish unfair rules through violent attacks.
He wanted to ignore all unfair treatment of people.

why.He wanted to copy South African customs: This wrongly assumes satyagraha meant copying customs from another place.
why.He wanted to punish unfair rules through: This wrongly assumes Gandhi’s response to injustice was violence.
why.He wanted to ignore all unfair treatment: This wrongly assumes Gandhi avoided unfair treatment instead of challenging it.

activities.explanation: This is right because satyagraha challenged injustice without violence.

activities.prompt: Police were killed at Chauri Chaura during Non-Cooperation. Why did Gandhi withdraw?
options: He wanted the movement to remain based on nonviolence.
He thought violence had made the movement stronger.
He wanted the boycott of schools and courts to end.
He believed police killings had made British rule fair.

why.He thought violence had made the movemen: This wrongly treats violence as a reason to strengthen the movement.
why.He wanted the boycott of schools and cou: This wrongly assumes ending the movement meant ending every local struggle.
why.He believed police killings had made Bri: This wrongly treats police killings as proof that British rule was fair.

activities.explanation: Gandhi withdrew after the killings because the movement was nonviolent.

activities.prompt: After World War I, Indians still had no freedom. Why did Congress launch Non-Cooperation?
options: It gave them a peaceful way to oppose British rule.
They expected freedom to follow automatically after the war.
They wanted to stop all schools and courts from working.
They planned to welcome more foreign goods into India.

why.They expected freedom to follow automati: This wrongly assumes freedom would come without organised resistance.
why.They wanted to stop all schools and cour: This wrongly turns a boycott into stopping every school and court.
why.They planned to welcome more foreign goo: This wrongly reads the foreign-goods boycott as support for importing more.

activities.explanation: This is right because Non-Cooperation offered a peaceful boycott of British rule.

lessons.sceneCaption: Gandhi at the spinning wheel, representing the Swadeshi movement and the boycott of foreign goods.

lessons.title: Mass Protests and the Demand for Purna Swaraj

activities.prompt: How did ordinary people and young leaders demand complete independence?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different Paths to Independence
activities.body: Many groups and leaders challenged British rule in different ways. Some marched peacefully, while revolutionaries also took up arms. The Simon Commission faced public protests. Congress demanded Purna Swaraj, or complete independence, at Lahore in December 1929. Gandhi began the Salt March in 1930. Women joined processions and broke the salt law during Civil Disobedience.
keyPoints: Peaceful marches, rallies and slogans challenged British rule.
Congress demanded Purna Swaraj at Lahore in December 1929.
Women and younger leaders joined the struggle for independence.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the main events and ideas in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Two school groups ask for different political goals. How can they understand Purna Swaraj?
steps: The Motilal Nehru Report asked for Dominion status, so one group wanted that status.
Another group supports younger leaders because they wanted complete independence.
Congress demanded Purna Swaraj at its Lahore session in December 1929.
Therefore, Purna Swaraj meant complete independence and became a Congress demand.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Meeting the Simon Commission
activities.prompt: Which response met the Simon Commission?
options: Public rallies and marches
A long march to Dandi
A separate territory proposal
A government train robbery
activities.explanation: Rallies, marches and the slogan “Simon Go Back!” met the Commission.

activities.title: The Demand of Congress
activities.prompt: What did Congress demand at its Lahore session in December 1929?
options: Complete independence
Dominion status
A separate territory
A new train robbery
activities.explanation: Congress passed a resolution demanding Purna Swaraj, meaning complete independence.

activities.title: People and Their Actions
activities.prompt: Match each person with what they did.
pairs: Was badly injured by a police lathi charge
Was among the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association's leaders
Led the Salt March to Dandi
Proposed a separate territory for Muslims in northwestern India
activities.explanation: Each pairing links a person with an action or proposal from the lesson.

activities.title: A Separate Territory
activities.prompt: Who proposed a separate territory for Muslims in northwestern India?
options: Muhammad Iqbal
Gandhi
Bhagat Singh
Lala Lajpat Rai
activities.explanation: This was Muhammad Iqbal's proposal for a separate territory.

activities.title: The Peaceful March
activities.prompt: Put these events from the peaceful march in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The peaceful march was followed by a lathi charge, which badly injured Lala Lajpat Rai.

activities.title: Different Forms of Struggle
activities.prompt: Which pair shows a public protest and a revolutionary activity?
options: Marching and train robbery
Rallies and a report
Processions and picketing
A march and a massacre
activities.explanation: A peaceful march was a public protest, while the HRA train robbery funded revolutionary activities.

activities.prompt: A town follows a salt law. People hear about Gandhi’s march to Dandi. What may happen next?
options: Many women may break the salt law and join processions.
Many women may join processions but obey every law.
Many women may break the law but avoid all processions.
Many women may avoid both law-breaking and public processions.

why.Many women may join processions but obey: This mistakes peaceful participation for refusing to break the law.
why.Many women may break the law but avoid a: This separates breaking the law from taking part in processions.
why.Many women may avoid both law-breaking a: This overlooks how many women joined the movement.

activities.explanation: This matches women’s actions during the Civil Disobedience Movement.

activities.prompt: One report describes a peaceful Lahore march. Another describes the Peshawar massacre. What difference do the reports show?
options: Lahore had a police lathi charge; Peshawar had a massacre.
Lahore had a massacre; Peshawar had only a lathi charge.
Both places had the same peaceful police response to protest.
Neither place shows any harm during political protest.

why.Lahore had a massacre; Peshawar had only: This swaps the two events and changes the Peshawar massacre’s scale.
why.Both places had the same peaceful police: This wrongly treats both reports as showing the same kind of harm.
why.Neither place shows any harm during poli: This ignores the injured marcher and the Peshawar massacre.

activities.explanation: Lahore’s peaceful march was met with police violence; Peshawar had a massacre.

activities.prompt: The Report supports one demand. Younger leaders support another. Which demand did each group support?
options: Dominion status; complete independence.
Complete independence; Dominion status.
Simon Go Back; complete independence.
Separate territory; complete independence.

This swaps Dominion status and Purna Swaraj between the two groups.
Simon Go Back was a slogan against the Simon Commission.
why.Separate territory; complete independenc: Separate territory was Iqbal’s proposal, not the Report’s demand.

activities.explanation: The Report called for Dominion status; Purna Swaraj meant complete independence.

activities.prompt: A group needs money for activities against British rule. It wants HRA methods. What should it do?
options: Rob a government train to raise money for the activities.
Lead a peaceful march to collect money for the activities.
Demand Dominion status at a public meeting.
Picket shops after breaking the salt law.

why.Lead a peaceful march to collect money f: This confuses HRA fund-raising with peaceful public protest.
why.Demand Dominion status at a public meeti: This confuses HRA methods with the Motilal Nehru Report’s demand.
why.Picket shops after breaking the salt law: This confuses HRA methods with Civil Disobedience actions.

activities.explanation: The HRA robbed a government train to raise money for its activities.

activities.prompt: A report says even schoolgirls joined the armed struggle. What can we safely conclude?
options: Young people also took part in the armed struggle.
Only adult leaders took part in the armed struggle.
Schoolgirls became the leaders of the HRA.
Schoolgirls made the Congress demand at Lahore.

why.Only adult leaders took part in the arme: This ignores the fact that even schoolgirls joined.
why.Schoolgirls became the leaders of the HR: This mistakes taking part for leading the HRA.
why.Schoolgirls made the Congress demand at: This mistakes taking part for making the Congress demand.

activities.explanation: Even schoolgirls joined, so young people were participants too.

activities.prompt: A map marks a separate area for Muslims in northwestern India. Which historical idea does it represent?
options: Muhammad Iqbal proposed a separate territory for Muslims.
Bhagat Singh proposed a separate territory for Muslims.
Gandhi proposed a separate territory for Muslims.
The Simon Commission proposed a separate territory for Muslims.

why.Bhagat Singh proposed a separate territo: This confuses the HRA leader with the person who made the proposal.
why.Gandhi proposed a separate territory for: This confuses the Salt March leader with the proposal’s author.
why.The Simon Commission proposed a separate: This confuses the Simon Commission with the proposal’s author.

activities.explanation: The map matches Iqbal’s proposal for Muslims in northwestern India.

lessons.title: World War II, Quit India and Independence

activities.prompt: How did India find its way to freedom amid war, resistance, and painful division?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Key Ideas
activities.body: World War II pulled India into the conflict without asking the Indian people. Subhas Chandra Bose escaped house arrest in 1941. He formed the Indian National Army and declared the Azad Hind, or Free India, government. The Cripps Mission offered dominion status, allowing provinces to choose whether to join. Gandhi started Quit India in August 1942. Partition meant painful splitting. India became independent on 15 August 1947.
keyPoints: Bose formed the Indian National Army and the Azad Hind government.
Gandhi started the Quit India Movement in August 1942.
Partition caused sorrow, but India became independent in 1947.
activities.explanation: Read each clue, then use the matching event from your book.

activities.prompt: A government joins a world war without asking its people. What should it do differently?
steps: World War II pulled India into the conflict without consulting the Indian people.
This meant that the people did not choose whether their country would join.
If their views are asked only after the decision, their choice cannot guide it.
Therefore, people should be consulted before their country enters a war.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Formed the Army?
activities.prompt: Who formed the INA with Indian prisoners of war and volunteers?
options: Subhas Chandra Bose
Mahatma Gandhi
Muhammad Ali Jinnah
Aruna Asaf Ali
activities.explanation: The book says Bose formed the INA from Indian prisoners of war and volunteers.

activities.title: The Free India Government
activities.prompt: Which name did Bose give to the Free India government?
options: Quit India Movement
Direct Action Day
Azad Hind
Cripps Mission
activities.explanation: Bose declared the Azad Hind, or Free India, government.

activities.title: A Choice After the War
activities.prompt: What choice did the Cripps Mission allow after the war?
options: Each province could choose to opt out.
Each soldier could choose to opt out.
Each province could choose to opt in.
Each merchant could choose to opt out.
activities.explanation: The Cripps Mission offered dominion status, but provinces could opt out.

activities.title: Complete the Choice
activities.prompt: After the war, provinces could opt ______.
activities.hint: Complete the phrase from your book.
activities.explanation: The offer allowed provinces to opt out after the war.

activities.title: Match the People and Events
activities.prompt: Match each person or event with its matching detail.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a leader or event with its matching detail from your book.

activities.title: Events in Time Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: February 1946: Royal Indian Navy mutiny begins
activities.explanation: These dates are in the order given in your book.

activities.prompt: World War II pulls India into conflict without asking the people. What should a fair government do before joining a war?
options: Ask the people before joining the war.
Choose war partners without telling the people.
Wait until the war ends before deciding.
Ask only a few leaders before joining the war.

why.Choose war partners without telling the: This ignores the people whose country is entering the war.
This treats a decision to join as one that can wait.
why.Ask only a few leaders before joining th: A few leaders cannot speak for everyone in India.

activities.explanation: Consulting the people gives them a say in the war decision.

activities.prompt: The Cripps Mission offers dominion status after the war. It lets provinces opt out. If Bengal wants a different choice, what can it do?
options: Bengal must accept the plan with all provinces.
Bengal can choose to stay outside the plan.
Bengal must wait until after the war to decide.
Only Britain's government can let Bengal opt out.

why.Bengal must accept the plan with all pro: This wrongly treats the plan as compulsory for every province.
why.Bengal must wait until after the war to: This confuses dominion after the war with the power to opt out.
why.Only Britain's government can let Bengal: This denies provinces the choice allowed by the Cripps Mission.

activities.explanation: The Cripps Mission allows provinces to choose whether to opt out.

activities.prompt: In August 1942, Gandhi launches the Quit India Movement. His call is “Do or Die.” On 16 August 1946, Jinnah calls for Pakistan. What do these two calls show?
options: The leaders wanted exactly the same final result.
Both calls wanted only a small change for India.
Jinnah sought delay, while Gandhi sought quick action.
The leaders wanted different changes in India.

why.The leaders wanted exactly the same fina: Quit India and the demand for Pakistan had different goals.
why.Both calls wanted only a small change fo: Both calls sought major political change, not small changes.
why.Jinnah sought delay, while Gandhi sought: Jinnah called for Direct Action rather than further delay.

activities.explanation: Gandhi sought to end British rule, while Jinnah demanded Pakistan.

activities.context: In an Indian village, a student sees families suffering after heavy land taxes bring severe famine and widespread discontent. Local handloom workers also struggle because cheap British goods are difficult to compete with. At a Congress session, the student hears Rabindranath Tagore sing “Bande Mataram,” a song praising the motherland. Nearby, reformers are challenging child marriage, the low status of widows, and caste discrimination.
activities.prompt: If the government reduced the heavy land tax burden, what would most likely happen?
options: Severe famine and widespread discontent would probably be reduced.
Famine and widespread discontent would probably become worse.
British-made goods would probably become more expensive in the village.
The competition faced by Indian industries would probably disappear.

why.Famine and widespread discontent would p: Reducing the tax burden could ease that suffering.
why.British-made goods would probably become: The change in tax would not directly alter the price of British goods.
why.The competition faced by Indian industri: Tax reduction and industrial competition are separate issues.

activities.explanation: Heavy land taxes were a cause of the suffering.

activities.context: In an Indian village, a student sees families suffering after heavy land taxes bring severe famine and widespread discontent. Local handloom workers also struggle because cheap British goods are difficult to compete with. At a Congress session, the student hears Rabindranath Tagore sing “Bande Mataram,” a song praising the motherland. Nearby, reformers are challenging child marriage, the low status of widows, and caste discrimination.
activities.prompt: Which action best follows the example of the reformers in the case?
options: Help challenge child marriage, the treatment of widows, and unfair caste rules.
Ask the reformers to stop questioning these customs.
Believe that only cheaper imported cloth can solve the village's problems.
Avoid the reformers because social issues do not affect family life.

why.Ask the reformers to stop questioning th: The student should support their efforts rather than silence them.
why.Believe that only cheaper imported cloth: Buying imported cloth would not address the social problems described.
why.Avoid the reformers because social issue: These customs affect families and the wider society.

activities.explanation: The reformers were challenging these harmful customs.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay published Anandamath in 1882.
Reason (R): Rabindranath Tagore wrote and published Anandamath in 1882.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Anandamath was published by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, not Rabindranath Tagore.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Constituent Assembly adopted Bande Mataram as India’s National Song in 1950.
Reason (R): Rabindranath Tagore set it to music and sang it at the 1896 Congress session.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Tagore’s earlier performance is related, but the given facts do not say that it caused the Assembly’s decision.

activities.prompt: How did the system of British control over India change after 1857?
activities.answer: After 1857, Queen Victoria began ruling India directly instead of allowing the East India Company to govern it. British India was then governed in the Queen’s name by a Secretary of State and a Viceroy. This meant that direct royal control replaced rule through the Company. The change affected both who held supreme authority and how British India was governed under that authority.
points: Before 1857, the East India Company governed India.
After 1857, Queen Victoria began ruling directly.
A Secretary of State and a Viceroy governed in the Queen’s name.
Company rule was replaced by direct British royal control.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After the colonial government mostly ignored Congress resolutions, Indian leaders sought stronger methods. In 1906 Congress adopted Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education as aims. When Curzon partitioned Bengal, Rabindranath Tagore, Surendranath Banerjee and Bipin Chandra Pal united people against it. The situation also raised the question of how ordinary people could respond.
activities.prompt: If the colonial government continued to mostly ignore Congress resolutions, which response best fits the movement's later direction?
options: Make political self-rule, rejection of foreign goods, use of Indian-made products and national education central aims
Continue making loyal appeals and rely on resolutions alone
Adopt Swadeshi but leave national education and political self-rule outside the programme
Oppose the partition but avoid organising people around any common programme

why.Continue making loyal appeals and rely o: Loyal appeals and resolutions had already been mostly ignored.
why.Adopt Swadeshi but leave national educat: The 1906 programme included both economic resistance and national education.
why.Oppose the partition but avoid organisin: The leaders' united opposition shows the importance of a common programme.

activities.explanation: This paraphrases the stronger aims Congress declared in 1906.

activities.context: After the colonial government mostly ignored Congress resolutions, Indian leaders sought stronger methods. In 1906 Congress adopted Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education as aims. When Curzon partitioned Bengal, Rabindranath Tagore, Surendranath Banerjee and Bipin Chandra Pal united people against it. The situation also raised the question of how ordinary people could respond.
activities.prompt: If a shopkeeper wanted to act on the boycott, which purchasing decision would be most consistent with it?
options: Stop buying foreign goods and choose Indian-made goods instead
Continue buying foreign goods while encouraging others to do the same
Reject foreign goods but replace them with products from other countries
Avoid buying any goods so that the distinction between foreign and Indian products is unnecessary

why.Continue buying foreign goods while enco: This choice continued the practice that the boycott opposed.
why.Reject foreign goods but replace them wi: Goods from other countries were also foreign goods.
why.Avoid buying any goods so that the disti: The boycott distinguished between foreign and Indian-made goods rather than rejecting all buying.

activities.explanation: Boycott required rejecting foreign goods and using Indian-made products.

activities.context: After the colonial government mostly ignored Congress resolutions, Indian leaders sought stronger methods. In 1906 Congress adopted Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education as aims. When Curzon partitioned Bengal, Rabindranath Tagore, Surendranath Banerjee and Bipin Chandra Pal united people against it. The situation also raised the question of how ordinary people could respond.
activities.prompt: If disagreement over methods arose at the 1907 Surat session, what result would the case support?
options: The gathering would split into moderate and nationalist groups
Congress would remain one unified camp because its goals had already been settled
The gathering would divide into a camp for Swadeshi and a separate camp for Boycott
Congress would divide into a loyal camp and a camp seeking further colonial control

why.Congress would remain one unified camp b: The session actually produced two separate camps.
why.The gathering would divide into a camp f: Swadeshi and Boycott were both part of the programme and did not define the two camps.
why.Congress would divide into a loyal camp: The division was between Moderate and Nationalist approaches, not between these groups.

activities.explanation: The 1907 Surat session did divide Congress into Moderate and Nationalist camps.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): By 1906, Congress's declaration of Swaraj represented a stronger response to colonial rule than its early cooperation.
Reason (R): The colonial government mostly ignored the resolutions passed by Congress.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The government's disregard helps explain why Congress moved from loyal appeals to stronger aims.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The All-India Muslim League was founded in Dhaka in 1906.
Reason (R): It was founded at the 1907 Surat session of Congress because that session divided Congress into two camps.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The League was founded in Dhaka in 1906, not at the Surat session in 1907.

activities.prompt: How did people respond to Curzon's partition of Bengal, and how did Swadeshi and boycott add to that response?
activities.answer: Curzon's partition of Bengal was an application of the colonial policy of divide and rule. In response, Rabindranath Tagore, Surendranath Banerjee and Bipin Chandra Pal united people against the partition. Swadeshi and boycott added a practical form of participation: people were encouraged to reject foreign goods and use Indian-made products. Thus, opposition to the partition was supported not only by political unity but also by everyday economic action.
points: Curzon's partition applied the policy of divide and rule
Tagore, Banerjee and Pal united people against the partition
Swadeshi encouraged the rejection of foreign goods
Boycott encouraged the use of Indian-made products
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Tilak’s first task of reuniting the two Congress factions was achieved at Lucknow in 1916, where the Lucknow Pact brought the Congress and the All-India Muslim League together. In the same year, Tilak and Annie Besant launched the Home Rule Movement. The colonial government had jailed Tilak and several other Nationalist leaders, showing that it viewed their political work as a serious challenge to British rule.
activities.prompt: If the Lucknow Pact had not brought Congress and the All-India Muslim League together, what would most likely have happened to Tilak’s effort to reunite the Congress factions?
options: The two factions would probably have found unity harder to reach.

Tilak would probably have been able to avoid political work.

why.The Home Rule Movement would probably ha: A missing agreement would reduce cooperation.
why.Tilak would probably have been able to a: Political work would still be needed.

activities.context: Tilak’s first task of reuniting the two Congress factions was achieved at Lucknow in 1916, where the Lucknow Pact brought the Congress and the All-India Muslim League together. why.It would help the colonial government co: The reception supported revolutionaries, not colonial authorities.

activities.prompt: Explain how unity between political groups was important to the Home Rule Movement launched by Tilak and Annie Besant.
activities.answer: Tilak’s effort to reunite the Congress factions was important because the Lucknow Pact brought the Congress and the All-India Muslim League together at Lucknow in 1916. The colonial government’s decision to jail Tilak and several other Nationalist leaders shows that their work was a serious challenge to British rule. Thus, unity and organisation helped the Home Rule cause gain strength.
points: The Lucknow Pact brought the Congress and Muslim League together.
Tilak had reunited the two Congress factions at Lucknow.

Unity strengthened the wider nationalist cause.

Organize a violent attack on police stations.

why.Organize a violent attack on police stat: This contradicts the instruction to act without violence.
why.Continue cooperating with the same insti: Passive waiting does not apply satyagraha to the injustice.
why.Encourage people to use threats and forc: Threats and force are contrary to the peaceful method described.

chapters.title: A Journey through Indian Architecture
chapters.summary: In this chapter: architecture begins: cities, drainage and stupas; rock-cut caves and sacred sites; water structures; classical temple architecture.

lessons.title: Architecture Begins: Cities, Drainage and Stupas

activities.prompt: How did ancient Indian cities handle water, and how did Buddhism change their buildings?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Cities, drains and dome-shaped buildings
activities.body: Architecture means the art and techniques of designing and building things. Harappan towns planned drainage, water management and civic organisation. Most Harappan cities used bricks. Mohenjo-daro had wide streets, narrow lanes and drains. Dholavira used local stone. As Buddhism began to rise, new architectural forms spread across India. Stupas were dome-shaped buildings that held relics of the Buddha or revered monks. Larger stupas became ritual centres with railings for worship.
keyPoints: Architecture includes design and construction.
Harappan towns valued drainage and civic organisation.
Stupas were dome-shaped buildings for sacred relics.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect early city planning with the later rise of Buddhist architecture.

activities.prompt: A Harappan town has used water collecting in its streets. What should builders do, and why?
steps: Architecture includes design and construction, so builders planned the whole town.
Harappan towns valued drainage because used water needed a clear way out.
Drains carried used water out of Mohenjo-daro, serving the whole city.
Therefore, drainage was central to Harappan architecture and civic organisation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What is architecture?
activities.prompt: What does architecture include?
options: Designing and constructing things
Growing and harvesting crops
Collecting and trading coins
Painting and singing songs
activities.explanation: Architecture combines the art of design with construction techniques.

activities.title: Building with bricks
activities.prompt: Most Harappan cities were built with bricks.
activities.explanation: Most Harappan cities were built with bricks.

activities.title: Used water leaves the city
activities.prompt: Mohenjo-daro used drains to carry used ______ out of the city.
activities.hint: Look for the word after “used”.
activities.explanation: The drains carried used water out of Mohenjo-daro.

activities.title: Local stone for building
activities.prompt: Which city used local stone for extensive construction?
options: Mohenjo-daro
Dholavira
Sanchi
activities.explanation: Dholavira used local stone for extensive construction.

activities.title: Places and their features
activities.prompt: Match each place or building with its feature.
activities.explanation: Each feature comes from the lesson about early cities and Buddhist architecture.

activities.title: The size of Dholavira
activities.prompt: Dholavira was a small Harappan settlement.
activities.explanation: Dholavira was another large Harappan city.

activities.title: Sanchi's place in history
activities.prompt: What does Sanchi show in India's architectural history?
options: The earliest phase of monumental religious stone architecture.
The earliest known tradition of urban planning.
The earliest phase of Harappan civic organisation.
The earliest use of bricks in Indian cities.
activities.explanation: Aśhoka supported Sanchi's main stupa. Sanchi shows India's earliest monumental religious stone phase.

activities.prompt: Harappan towns valued water management and civic organisation. Why did this matter?
options: Used water could flow away through drains.
Used water could stay near homes and streets.
Every street could become wider and straighter.
Brick buildings could replace stone construction.

why.Used water could stay near homes and str: This confuses management with leaving water in streets.
why.Every street could become wider and stra: This mixes street layout with water management.
why.Brick buildings could replace stone cons: This confuses building materials with town services.

activities.explanation: This matches the Harappan emphasis on water management.

activities.prompt: A map shows Mohenjo-daro's wide streets and narrow lanes. What should the map suggest about its planning?
options: The streets pointed towards the cardinal directions.
The streets ignored the cardinal directions completely.
Every lane was as wide as the wide streets.
Every street curved in the same unknown direction.

why.The streets ignored the cardinal directi: This wrongly denies the stated cardinal direction pattern.
why.Every lane was as wide as the wide stree: This confuses wide streets with equally wide narrow lanes.
why.Every street curved in the same unknown: This mistakes planned streets for unknown curved streets.

activities.explanation: This matches Mohenjo-daro's planned street directions.

lessons.title: Rock-Cut Caves and Sacred Sites

activities.prompt: How did people turn solid rock into homes, temples, and sacred spaces?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rock-cut architecture
activities.body: Rock-cut architecture gave religious communities an efficient, durable way to build. Builders carved caves directly into rock for worship, living, and assembly. Udayagiri–Khandagiri caves began in the 2nd century BCE, with royal support. Most were homes for Jain monks. At Ellora, builders removed thousands of tonnes of rock. Cave 10 has a huge seated Buddha beside a stupa. Pradakṣhiṇa means walking clockwise around a sacred object.
keyPoints: Builders carved caves directly into rock.
Most Udayagiri–Khandagiri caves were homes for Jain monks.
Pradakṣhiṇa means walking clockwise around a sacred object.
activities.explanation: Rock-cut caves were useful places for worship, living, and assembly.

events.label: Rājarāja Chola I built the Bṛihadīśhvara Temple
The Hidimba Devi Temple was built
Humayun’s chief wife, Bega Begum, commissioned his

Go forward to the last event.

activities.prompt: A religious community needs spaces for worship, living, and meeting. It wants a method that lasts well.
steps: Rock-cut builders carve caves directly into solid rock.
This method gives religious communities efficient, durable construction.
The caves can serve worship, residence, or assembly.

activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How did builders make rock-cut caves?
options: Carved directly into rock
Built with bricks
Painted rock walls
Covered caves with cloth
activities.explanation: Builders made caves by carving directly into rock.

activities.prompt: Most caves at Udayagiri–Khandagiri served as homes for Jain monks.
activities.explanation: Most of these caves were homes for Jain monks.

activities.prompt: Pradakṣhiṇa means walking ______ around a sacred object.
activities.hint: This word tells you which way to walk.
activities.explanation: Pradakṣhiṇa means walking clockwise around a sacred object.

A place of worship for Sikhs

options: It was efficient and durable
It was quick to paint

activities.explanation: Rock-cut architecture provided an efficient and durable method of construction.

activities.prompt: Which statement matches Sharada Peetha?
options: It was a famous centre of learning.
It was a place of worship for Sikhs.
It contained a huge seated Buddha.

activities.explanation: Sharada Peetha was a famous centre of learning.

activities.prompt: A religious community needs an efficient, durable building method. Which method best fits?
options: Carve caves directly into solid rock
Build using separate movable pieces
Use a small shelter that can move
Make a temporary shelter with cloth

why.Build using separate movable pieces: This mistake treats movable pieces as the stated rock-cut method.
why.Use a small shelter that can move: This mistake assumes a movable shelter is the durable method.
why.Make a temporary shelter with cloth: This mistake treats a temporary shelter as the durable method.

activities.explanation: This is right because carving into rock is efficient and durable.

activities.prompt: At Udayagiri–Khandagiri, carving began in the 2nd century BCE. Royal support helped it. What building work could this support?
options: Caves for worship, residence, or assembly
Caves only for the seated Buddha
A centre with about 124 stone temples
A royal palace inside the caves

why.Caves only for the seated Buddha: This mistake turns one cave's Buddha into every cave's purpose.
why.A centre with about 124 stone temples: This mistake mixes in Jageshwar's temple count.
why.A royal palace inside the caves: This mistake imagines a royal use not given in the facts.

activities.explanation: This is right because builders made caves for these three uses.

activities.prompt: One visitor wants a Jain monk's home. Another wants a seated Buddha beside a stupa. Which stops fit?
options: Udayagiri–Khandagiri, then Ellora Cave 10
Ellora Cave 10, then Udayagiri–Khandagiri
Jageshwar, then Ellora Cave 10
Sharada Peetha, then Udayagiri–Khandagiri

why.Ellora Cave 10, then Udayagiri–Khandagir: This mistake reverses the order of the two matching stops.
why.Jageshwar, then Ellora Cave 10: This mistake uses Jageshwar for the Jain monks' home.
why.Sharada Peetha, then Udayagiri–Khandagir: This mistake uses a learning centre for the Jain monks' home.

activities.explanation: It is right: Jain homes match Udayagiri–Khandagiri; Buddha matches Cave 10.

activities.prompt: From a clock's top, a visitor walks right. This circles a sacred object. Which path is it?
options: Clockwise around the sacred object
Counterclockwise around the sacred object
Straight across the sacred object
Away from the sacred object

why.Counterclockwise around the sacred objec: This mistake reverses the direction defined for pradakṣhiṇa.
why.Straight across the sacred object: This mistake crosses the object instead of walking around it.
why.Away from the sacred object: This mistake walks away instead of circling the sacred object.

activities.explanation: It is right: pradakṣhiṇa means clockwise walking around a sacred object.

activities.prompt: Ellora's builders removed thousands of tonnes of rock. What does this show about their work?
options: The builders carved the temples from rock.
The builders moved all the rock away.
The builders used only tiny stone pieces.
The builders did not carve temple buildings.

This mistake thinks the rock was moved rather than carved away.
why.The builders used only tiny stone pieces: This mistake thinks only small pieces were used, not carved rock.
why.The builders did not carve temple buildi: This mistake ignores that the removed rock was carved into temples.

activities.explanation: It is right because rock was removed to carve Ellora's temples.

lessons.title: Water Structures

activities.prompt: How did ancient India turn water into wonder?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different Water Structures
activities.body: India’s monsoon-driven climate led people to build many kinds of water structures. Their designs differed because India’s geological, climatic and environmental conditions varied. Harappan wells used trapezoid-shaped bricks that locked firmly together. Shringverpur had large interconnected reservoirs. Stepwells were useful and beautiful places. Temples often had attached reservoirs called puṣhkariṇīs.
keyPoints: Different conditions led to different water structures.
Harappan wells and Shringverpur had special features.
Stepwells and temple reservoirs served people.
activities.explanation: These features show how water structures served practical, artistic and social needs.

activities.prompt: Why did water structures in different parts of India look different?
steps: India’s monsoon-driven climate made people create many water structures.
Different geological, climatic and environmental conditions changed local needs.
Builders therefore made different designs for different places.
Conclusion: varied local conditions explain the differences.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why Designs Differed
activities.prompt: Why did water structures differ across India?
options: India’s conditions varied.
People wanted matching designs.
Every region had the same climate.
All rivers stayed dry.
activities.explanation: India’s varied conditions made different designs suitable in different places. These conditions included geological, climatic and environmental differences.

activities.title: The Name in the Rāmayaṇa
activities.prompt: Shringverpur was known as ______ in the Rāmayaṇa.
activities.hint: Use the spelling shown in your book.
activities.explanation: Śhringaverapura was the name of Shringverpur in the Rāmayaṇa. Shringverpur is in Uttar Pradesh.

activities.title: Water from the Ganga
activities.prompt: When did a channel from the Ganga supply water?
options: Before any flood arrived.
After every monsoon season.
During the river’s seasonal flooding.
While the river stayed dry.
activities.explanation: The channel supplied water during the river’s seasonal flooding. This is exactly what the lesson states.

activities.title: Places and Their Features
activities.prompt: Match each place or structure with its feature.
pairs: trapezoid-shaped bricks that locked firmly together
several pillared levels and hundreds of magnificent statues
a cool social space for sitting and talking together
activities.explanation: These pairs match each site or structure with its described feature. Every pair follows the lesson directly.

activities.title: Uses of Puṣhkariṇīs
activities.prompt: Which uses are given for puṣhkariṇīs?
options: Making statues and building pillared temple levels.
Collecting water and performing water-based rituals.
Repairing wells and locking trapezoid bricks together.
Creating social spaces and supplying seasonal floodwater.
activities.explanation: Puṣhkariṇīs collected water and were used for water-based rituals. Temples often had these reservoirs attached to them.

activities.title: Identify the Temple Reservoir
activities.prompt: A temple has an attached reservoir. People collect water there for rituals. What is this reservoir called?
options: stepwell
Harappan well
Shringverpur
puṣhkariṇī
activities.explanation: An attached temple reservoir is called a puṣhkariṇī. It collects water and supports water-based rituals.

activities.prompt: Two families live in Indian places with very different weather and land. Why might their water structures differ?
options: Varied local conditions led to different designs.
Every family wanted the same ancient shape.
Monsoon rain was absent in both places.
Water structures were made only for decoration.

why.Every family wanted the same ancient sha: This ignores how local conditions changed the structures.
This wrongly assumes monsoon rain was absent everywhere.
why.Water structures were made only for deco: This mistakes water structures for only decorative works.

activities.explanation: Different conditions led builders to use different designs.

activities.prompt: Archaeologists see linked reservoirs at Shringverpur and a Ganga channel. What does this suggest?
options: Water came from a channel during seasonal flooding.
Water depended only on stored rainwater.
Each reservoir was separate from every other.
People carried all water from faraway rivers.

This ignores the channel found at Shringverpur.
why.Each reservoir was separate from every o: This mistakes linked reservoirs for separate ones.
why.People carried all water from faraway ri: This assumes water came from distant rivers without evidence.

activities.explanation: The Ganga channel supplied water during seasonal flooding.

activities.prompt: A child sees pillared levels and hundreds of statues at Rani ki Vav. What does this show?
options: A stepwell could be both engineering and beautiful art.
A stepwell was built only to store extra grain.
A stepwell had no useful purpose beyond decoration.
A stepwell was designed mainly as a royal palace.

why.A stepwell was built only to store extra: This misses the useful engineering shown by pillared levels.
why.A stepwell had no useful purpose beyond: This treats a water structure as only decoration.
why.A stepwell was designed mainly as a roya: This mistakes a stepwell for a palace.

activities.explanation: Stepwells were engineering marvels and also works of art.

activities.prompt: Traditional structures face shortages, damage, pollution and rubbish. Why might environmentalists, local people and NGOs work together?
options: To protect structures facing serious problems.
To make every traditional structure disappear quickly.
To stop local people from caring for their water.
To replace all water structures with new ones.

why.To make every traditional structure disa: This wrongly treats old structures as only harmful.
why.To stop local people from caring for the: This suggests protection would reduce local care.
why.To replace all water structures with new: This assumes the goal was to remove old structures.

activities.explanation: The structures face serious problems and need protection.

lessons.title: Classical Temple Architecture

activities.prompt: What secrets might a temple’s shape and rooms reveal about its builders and beliefs?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Classical Temples
activities.body: Classical temples first emerged during the Gupta era. They supported worship, learning, literature and art. Builders followed śhilpaśhāstra, written guides for design. Temples were planned like the human body. A gopuram is a south Indian entrance. Some north Indian temples have a toraṇa. A maṇḍapa is a pillared hall. The garbhagṛiha is the innermost chamber for the deity’s image. The tower above it is a śhikhara in north India and vimāna in south India.
keyPoints: Temples followed śhilpaśhāstra and represented the human body.
A maṇḍapa is a pillared hall.
The garbhagṛiha holds the deity’s image.
activities.explanation: This lesson names the parts and shows their purposes.

activities.prompt: Two builders make temple plans. One follows written rules, while the other imitates the human body. How should they combine both ideas?
steps: Begin with the garbhagṛiha, because it is the innermost chamber for the deity.
Place a śhikhara or vimāna above it, because both name the tower there.
Use śhilpaśhāstra’s principles, because builders followed that written guidance.
Their plan should also be body-like, because temples represent the human body.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Life Inside a Temple
activities.prompt: Which activities happened in temples?
options: Worship, learning and art
Only farming and hunting
Only shipping and trade
War planning and trading
activities.explanation: Temples were centres of worship, learning, literature, art and social life.

activities.title: When Classical Temples Emerged
activities.prompt: Classical temples first emerged during the Gupta era.
activities.explanation: The Gupta era was the time when classical temples first emerged.

activities.title: Temple Building Guides
activities.prompt: Builders followed principles and methods given in treatises called ______.
activities.hint: These were written guides for temple building.
activities.explanation: Temple builders followed principles and methods given in these treatises.

activities.title: Temple Plans
activities.prompt: What was a temple planned to represent?
options: The human body
A local market
A royal court
A mountain peak
activities.explanation: Temple planning represented the parts of the human body.

activities.title: From Entrance to Inner Chamber
activities.prompt: Put these parts in order from the entrance to the innermost chamber.
activities.explanation: The gopuram is the entrance. The maṇḍapa is the pillared hall. The garbhagṛiha is the innermost chamber.

activities.title: Changes in Temple Size
activities.prompt: From the 10th century onward, temples grew smaller and lost facilities.
activities.explanation: From the 10th century onward, temples grew larger and gained more shrines and facilities.

activities.title: Famous Temple Groups
activities.prompt: Match each temple group with its description.
pairs: built by Rājarāja Chola I around 1010
five finely carved Jain temples built between the 11th and 13th centuries
brick buildings decorated with carved square panels
activities.explanation: Rājarāja Chola I built the Bṛihadīśhvara Temple around 1010. The other pairs match the given descriptions.

activities.prompt: A north Indian temple has a śhikhara. A south Indian temple has a vimāna. Where are both towers placed?
options: Both stand above the garbhagṛiha in each temple.
Both stand beside the entrance in each temple.
Both stand above the maṇḍapa in each temple.
Both stand inside the chamber holding each deity.

why.Both stand beside the entrance in each t: This mistake puts the towers beside entrances instead of above the chamber.
why.Both stand above the maṇḍapa in each tem: This mistake confuses the tower’s place with the pillared hall.
why.Both stand inside the chamber holding ea: This mistake puts the tower inside the chamber instead of above it.

activities.explanation: This is right because both towers rise above the garbhagṛiha.

Toward the left side of this map
Toward the upper edge of this map
Toward the lower edge of this map

why.Toward the left side of this map: This mistake reverses the direction shown for east.
why.Toward the upper edge of this map: This mistake treats east as the upper edge instead of the right.
why.Toward the lower edge of this map: This mistake treats east as the lower edge instead of the right.

lessons.title: Mosques, Forts and Palaces

activities.prompt: What stories can we discover in mosques, forts, and palaces?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Buildings with important purposes
activities.body: Mosques are Islamic places for prayer, education, meetings, lectures and discussions. A mosque’s prayer hall faces Mecca. Larger mosques often have domes. Jama means gathering, while masjid means mosque. Ahmedabad’s Jama Masjid mixes Hindu and Islamic design. Islamic design can include domes, arches and floral patterns. Delhi’s Jama Masjid is India’s largest mosque. Forts often stood near important land or sea routes.
keyPoints: Mosques serve prayer and community activities.
Buildings have matching names, places and features.
Forts often stood near important routes.
activities.explanation: The examples connect buildings with their uses, designs, locations and important features.

activities.prompt: A class visits Ahmedabad’s Jama Masjid and a fort shown beside an important route. What can they learn?
steps: They can explain that jama means gathering and masjid means mosque, because these are the words’ meanings.
They can expect mixed architectural elements, because Ahmedabad’s Jama Masjid combines Hindu and Islamic styles.
They can look for domes, because larger mosques often contain one or more domes.
They can connect the fort with travel routes, because forts were often placed near important land or sea routes.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which building is an Islamic place of prayer?
options: A mosque
A fort
A palace
A dome
activities.explanation: Mosques are Islamic places used for prayer, education, meetings, lectures and discussions.

activities.prompt: The word ______ means gathering or assembly.
activities.hint: This word names a gathering.
activities.explanation: “Jama” means gathering or assembly, while “masjid” means mosque.

activities.prompt: A mosque’s prayer hall faces the direction of Mecca.
activities.explanation: The prayer hall of a mosque faces the direction of Mecca.

activities.prompt: What do larger mosques often contain?
options: One or more domes
One or more forts
One or more palaces
One or more routes
activities.explanation: Larger mosques often contain one or more domes.

activities.prompt: Match each place or building with its matching detail.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a place or building with the detail given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Forts were often placed far from important land or sea routes.
activities.explanation: Forts were often placed near important land or sea routes, not far from them.

activities.prompt: Which mosque is India’s largest?
options: Delhi’s Jama Masjid
Ahmedabad’s Jama Masjid
Mehrangarh Fort
Mysuru Palace
activities.explanation: Delhi’s Jama Masjid is India’s largest mosque.

activities.prompt: A mosque’s prayer hall faces Mecca. What does this help worshippers do?
options: Face Mecca while they pray.
See the road outside while they pray.
Meet in a hall for a lecture.
Find the mosque near a sea route.

This confuses facing Mecca with seeing outside.
This confuses a mosque’s hall with a meeting hall.
This confuses prayer direction with fort location.

activities.explanation: This is right because the prayer hall faces Mecca.

activities.prompt: A map shows a fort beside an important land route. What can we reasonably say?
options: The fort was placed near an important route.
The fort was built mainly for sea travel.
The fort must contain a large prayer hall.
The fort was built beside the direction of Mecca.

why.The fort was built mainly for sea travel: This confuses a land route with sea travel.
why.The fort must contain a large prayer hal: This confuses a fort with a mosque.
why.The fort was built beside the direction: This confuses fort placement with prayer direction.

activities.explanation: This matches the common placement of forts near routes.

lessons.title: Tombs, Houses, Churches and Colonial Architecture

activities.prompt: What can buildings tell us about the people who built them?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Look closely at buildings
activities.body: A mausoleum is a grand building for one tomb or many tombs. Tombs and their gardens followed strict symmetry. Humayun’s chief wife, Bega Begum, commissioned his tomb in 1558. The Taj Mahal combines styles from three cultures. Richer homes had rooms around central courtyards. Chettinadu houses suit local climates. Shekhawati havelis have central courtyards and decorations. Some churches copied classic European styles. Indo-Saracenic architecture mixes Islamic, Hindu and Gothic elements.
keyPoints: Mausoleums are grand buildings for tombs.
Tombs and their gardens follow strict symmetry.
Architectural styles include blends of Islamic, Hindu and Gothic elements.
activities.explanation: These are the main features you will spot in the lesson.

activities.prompt: A richer family wants a traditional home. Where should the rooms go?
steps: Traditional houses for richer families often had a central courtyard.
The rooms went around that courtyard because it was the traditional layout.
This layout is part of the shared architectural heritage.
People should therefore feel responsible for and appreciate this heritage.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What is a mausoleum?
activities.prompt: Which description fits a mausoleum?
options: A small house for gardens
A market for old stones
A grand building for tombs
A church with one tower
activities.explanation: A mausoleum can house one tomb or a group of tombs. You found the correct meaning.

activities.title: Find the year
activities.prompt: Bega Begum, Humayun’s chief wife, commissioned his tomb in ______.
activities.hint: Think about the year in your lesson.
activities.explanation: The year is 1558. You can find this detail in your book.

activities.title: When was the tomb commissioned?
activities.prompt: Bega Begum commissioned Humayun’s tomb after 1558.
activities.explanation: Bega Begum commissioned the tomb in 1558. It was not after that year.

activities.title: Match buildings with features
activities.prompt: Match each home or building with its lesson feature.
pairs: Houses one or a group of tombs
Well adapted to local climate and surroundings
activities.explanation: Match each home or building with its feature. Courtyard, climate and style clues help you.

activities.title: Styles of the Taj Mahal
activities.prompt: What does the Taj Mahal combine?
options: Central courtyard rooms
Styles from three cultures
European church styles
Local climate features
activities.explanation: The Taj Mahal combines architectural styles from three cultures. This is an important clue.

activities.title: Responsibility for heritage
activities.prompt: What should citizens feel for architectural heritage?
options: Careless about architectural heritage
Afraid of architectural heritage
Angry at architectural heritage
Responsible for architectural heritage
activities.explanation: Citizens must feel responsible for architectural heritage. They should also appreciate it.

activities.prompt: Industrial pollution affects the Taj Mahal area. What action can help?
options: A ban on industrial activity can help reduce that pollution.
A ban on all visitors can help reduce industrial pollution.
More industrial activity can help reduce industrial pollution nearby.
More gardens around it can help reduce industrial pollution nearby.

why.A ban on all visitors can help reduce in: It mistakes visitors for the industrial cause of the pollution.
why.More industrial activity can help reduce: The fact links a ban, not more industry, with less pollution.
why.More gardens around it can help reduce i: It confuses gardens with the industrial activity addressed by the ban.

activities.explanation: This uses the ban that reduced industrial pollution around the Taj Mahal.

activities.prompt: Two traditional homes have different designs. Which comparison best fits the facts?
options: Richer homes can have a courtyard; Chettinadu homes suit local conditions.
Richer homes suit local conditions; Chettinadu homes can have a courtyard.
Both home types can have a central courtyard with rooms around it.
Neither home type has a courtyard or a climate-based design.

why.Richer homes suit local conditions; Chet: It swaps the features assigned to the two house types.
why.Both home types can have a central court: It wrongly gives the courtyard detail to Chettinadu houses.
why.Neither home type has a courtyard or a c: It denies both the courtyard and the local climate design.

activities.explanation: Richer homes can have courtyards, and Chettinadu houses suit local conditions.

activities.prompt: A school compares an Indian church with Indo-Saracenic architecture. Which comparison fits?
options: The church may copy Europe; Indo-Saracenic mixes three kinds of elements.
The church may mix three kinds; Indo-Saracenic copies only Europe.
Both styles copy only classic European building styles.
Both styles use only one kind of cultural element.

why.The church may mix three kinds; Indo-Sar: It swaps the features of the two architectural styles.
why.Both styles copy only classic European b: It wrongly makes both styles copies of classic European styles.
why.Both styles use only one kind of cultura: It wrongly reduces both styles to one cultural element.

activities.explanation: Some churches copy Europe, while Indo-Saracenic blends three elements.

activities.prompt: A guide compares two styles. Which explanation fits the facts?
options: The Taj joins three cultures; Indo-Saracenic names three elements.
The Taj names three elements; Indo-Saracenic joins three cultures.
Both styles use the same three cultures and elements.
The Taj uses one culture; Indo-Saracenic uses three cultures.

why.The Taj names three elements; Indo-Sarac: It swaps the details given for the two styles.
why.Both styles use the same three cultures: It ignores the difference between cultures and listed elements.
why.The Taj uses one culture; Indo-Saracenic: The fact does not limit the Taj Mahal to one culture.

activities.explanation: The fact joins cultures for the Taj and names elements for Indo-Saracenic.
