lessons.title: Rights and Fundamental Rights

activities.prompt: What helps us decide if something should be everyone’s right?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Rights
activities.body: Rights are what people need to live with dignity, safety and respect. A wish does not automatically become a right. Actions that harm ourselves or others cannot be rights. Fundamental rights are protections listed in the Constitution. They can be enforced through law. Equality gives equal opportunities and ends discrimination. Freedom has reasonable restrictions. Exploitation means taking an unfair advantage and denying basic rights.
keyPoints: Rights support dignity, safety and respect.
A wish is not automatically a right.
Fundamental rights can be enforced through law.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand rights and use them fairly.

activities.prompt: A town has clean water and equal chances at school. One child cannot find work, attend school, or stay healthy. Is the child’s right to life protected?
steps: Clean water protects the environment part of the right to life.
Work, school, and health are also parts of this right.
Equal chances help, but they cannot replace these basic needs.
So the child’s right to life is not fully protected.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is true about a wish?
options: It may become a right without checking
It cannot become a right automatically
It is always a right at once
It must always harm other people
activities.explanation: A wish cannot automatically be treated as a right.

activities.prompt: The Constitution lists ______ broad categories of fundamental rights.
activities.hint: Think about the number of categories listed in the Constitution.
activities.explanation: The Constitution lists six broad categories of fundamental rights.

activities.prompt: How can fundamental rights be enforced?
options: Through enforceable law
Through personal wishes
Through secret choices
Through silent agreement
activities.explanation: Fundamental rights can be enforced through law.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: Equal opportunities in jobs and education
Taking an unfair advantage and denying basic rights
activities.explanation: Equality gives equal opportunities. Freedom has reasonable restrictions. Exploitation takes an unfair advantage.

activities.prompt: Which set is fully included in the right to life?
options: Livelihood, education, health, clean environment
Religion, equality, culture, freedom, law
Untouchability, discrimination, jobs, safety, respect
Religion, education, culture, equality, freedom
activities.explanation: A livelihood, education, health and a clean environment are all included.

activities.prompt: Which action cannot be considered a right?
options: Hurting another person
Choosing a religion
Getting an education
Finding a livelihood
activities.explanation: Actions that harm ourselves or others cannot be considered rights.

activities.prompt: Ravi’s family has no work or school place. Water near home is dirty. What should be provided to protect them?
options: Livelihood, education, health, and a clean environment
Only equal chances at work and school
Only freedom to choose a religion
Only fair cultural and school rights

why.Only equal chances at work and school: Equal chances help, but they do not cover every basic need.
why.Only freedom to choose a religion: Religious freedom is not part of this family’s missing needs.
why.Only fair cultural and school rights: Cultural rights do not cover work, health, or a clean environment.

activities.explanation: Work, education, health, and a clean environment are parts of the right to life.

activities.prompt: In one village, all children share water equally. Elsewhere, some are refused water for being untouchable. What should the second village do?
options: End untouchability and give every child equal chances.
Keep separate water rules for those families.
Give them work but still refuse school access.
Allow the refusal only after local agreement.

why.Keep separate water rules for those fami: This mistake treats untouchability as a fair exception to equality.
why.Give them work but still refuse school a: This mistake separates rights to work from the right to education.
why.Allow the refusal only after local agree: This mistake thinks local agreement can make discrimination fair.

activities.explanation: Refusing water because of untouchability is discrimination, and equality ends this practice.

activities.prompt: A group can meet and speak freely. Shouting that harms others is stopped. Why is this fair?
options: Freedom needs reasonable limits to stop harm.
Every wish should become a right.
Harmful actions can also be rights.
All people may harm others freely.

This mistake treats every wish as a right.
This mistake allows harm because rights need no limits.
This mistake thinks freedom should never be restricted.

activities.explanation: The limit is reasonable because it stops freedom from harming others.

activities.prompt: A law can stop a person from unfairly taking workers’ rights. Why does this help protect fundamental rights?
options: Law can enforce rights against unfair treatment.
Law can turn every wish into a right.
Law can make harmful actions into rights.
Law can remove all reasonable limits.

This mistake thinks law turns wishes into rights.
why.Law can make harmful actions into rights: This mistake thinks harmful actions deserve rights.
This mistake thinks rights need no reasonable limits.

activities.explanation: Law can enforce fundamental rights when people face unfair treatment.

activities.prompt: A person pays workers very little and takes their fair share. What is happening to these workers?
options: Exploitation and denial of basic rights
Equal chances in work and education
Religious freedom with reasonable limits
Protection of cultural diversity and schools

why.Equal chances in work and education: This mistake sees equality in work, but the workers’ rights are denied.
why.Religious freedom with reasonable limits: This mistake mentions religion, but the situation is about unfair treatment.
why.Protection of cultural diversity and sch: This mistake mentions culture, but the situation is about workers’ rights.

activities.explanation: Taking an unfair advantage and denying basic rights is exploitation.

activities.prompt: Local traditions are protected, but one faith is told to hide. What has been taken away?
options: Freedom to choose and practise religion
Equal chances in work and school
Access to a basic livelihood
Access to cultural education

why.Equal chances in work and school: This mistake connects hiding a faith with unequal job or school chances.
why.Access to a basic livelihood: This mistake connects hiding a faith with lost work or income.
why.Access to cultural education: This mistake connects hiding a faith with blocked school access.

activities.explanation: Being told to hide stops free religious choice and practice.

lessons.title: Duties

activities.prompt: How can you help your country, your community, and the planet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Fundamental Duties
activities.body: Fundamental duties are responsibilities that citizens should follow. Citizens must respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem. They should follow freedom struggle ideals and protect India’s unity, integrity and sovereignty. They must defend the nation, help during emergencies and promote harmony. They should respect women, preserve culture and heritage, protect public property and avoid violence. Parents and guardians must ensure education for children aged 6 to 14.
keyPoints: Respect the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem.
Protect unity, public property, culture, heritage and the environment.
Defend the nation, help during emergencies, respect women and show compassion.
activities.explanation: Learning these duties helps you act responsibly as a citizen.

activities.prompt: A student finds a broken bench and a scared dog near school. What should she do, and why?
steps: She should report the broken bench because public property must be protected.
She should not hurt the dog because citizens must show compassion.
She should speak calmly because citizens must avoid violence.
Together, these choices show how fundamental duties guide daily life.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which action is a fundamental duty?
options: Respect the Constitution
Replace the National Flag
Ignore the National Anthem
Break public property
activities.explanation: The Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem must be respected.

activities.prompt: You help keep school property safe. Which duty does this show?
options: Protect public property
Protect national sovereignty
Follow freedom struggle ideals
Preserve culture and heritage
activities.explanation: Citizens should protect public property and avoid violence.

activities.prompt: Match each action with the duty it shows.
pairs: Defend the nation and help during emergencies
Protect public property and avoid violence
activities.explanation: Each action matches a duty listed in your lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these duties in the order shown on page 157 of your book.
items: Follow the ideals of the freedom struggle
Protect India’s unity, integrity and sovereignty
Defend the nation and help during emergencies
Preserve the country’s culture and heritage
activities.explanation: Page 157 presents these duties in this order.

activities.prompt: Citizens should protect India’s ______, integrity and sovereignty.
activities.hint: This means keeping the country together.
activities.explanation: Protecting India’s unity, integrity and sovereignty is a fundamental duty.

activities.prompt: At a community event, citizens preserve traditions, avoid fights and care for animals. Which actions show duties?
options: Preserve culture, avoid violence and show compassion
Preserve culture, harm animals and use violence
Protect property, promote conflict and ignore emergencies
Respect women, damage heritage and abandon animals
activities.explanation: The duties include preserving culture, avoiding violence and showing compassion towards animals.

activities.prompt: During a flood, neighbours carry an elderly person to safety. What fundamental duty should guide their action?
options: They should help the person because emergencies require citizen help.
They should protect public property first because property matters more.
They should respect the Constitution instead because people need not help.
They should preserve culture because helping people is not a duty.

why.They should protect public property firs: This mistake thinks property needs more care than people in danger.
why.They should respect the Constitution ins: This mistake replaces the emergency duty with respect for the Constitution.
why.They should preserve culture because hel: This mistake wrongly treats culture as a duty during emergencies.

activities.explanation: This is right because citizens must help during emergencies.

activities.prompt: One school’s children clear litter from a park. Another school’s children break plants there. Which school better follows the fundamental duty to protect the environment?
options: Children who clear litter because protecting nature is their duty.
Children who stay away because parks do not belong to them.
Children who break plants because plants block the path.
Children who only watch because adults must protect nature.

why.Children who stay away because parks do: This mistake assumes citizens have no duty to care for parks.
why.Children who break plants because plants: This mistake treats damage to plants as harmless.
why.Children who only watch because adults m: This mistake thinks only adults can protect the environment.

activities.explanation: This is right because citizens should protect and improve the environment.

activities.prompt: A child is six years old. A parent says school is optional. What fundamental duty must the parent follow?
options: The parent must ensure the child receives an education.
The parent may let the child work because school is optional.
The parent may wait because school begins after fourteen.
The parent may stop lessons if school feels difficult.

why.The parent may let the child work becaus: This mistake thinks the child’s sixth year does not need schooling.
why.The parent may wait because school begin: This mistake moves the starting age to after fourteen.
why.The parent may stop lessons if school fe: This mistake thinks school difficulty removes the duty to educate.

activities.explanation: This is right because parents must ensure children aged six to fourteen receive education.

activities.prompt: People from different states work together to clear roads and help families. Which fundamental duty does their joint action show?
options: They work as citizens of one country, so unity and integrity matter.
They should help only their own state because unity is weak.
They should keep separate because different states cannot trust each other.
One state should lead because India should not remain united.

why.They should help only their own state be: This mistake limits responsibility to one state.
why.They should keep separate because differ: This mistake thinks separation will protect India.
why.One state should lead because India shou: This mistake confuses protecting sovereignty with letting one state control India.

activities.explanation: This is right because citizens should protect India’s unity and integrity.

activities.prompt: Two children argue during a group project. One says girls should not lead. What should the speaker do to follow a fundamental duty?
options: Apologise, listen to everyone, and include girls fairly.
Ask the boys to choose a leader and leave girls out.
Tell the group that only boys may make decisions.
Choose the louder child and keep the girls quiet.

why.Ask the boys to choose a leader and leav: This mistake keeps girls out of shared decisions.
why.Tell the group that only boys may make d: This mistake gives boys alone the power to decide.
why.Choose the louder child and keep the gir: This mistake uses loudness instead of harmony and fair respect.

activities.explanation: This is right because citizens should promote harmony and respect women.

lessons.title: Rights and Duties: Two Sides of the Same Coin

activities.prompt: How do rights and duties help us build a fair and peaceful community together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rights and Duties
activities.body: Rights are the freedoms and benefits that every citizen enjoys. Duties are the responsibilities that citizens must follow as community members. They are not opposites, because they work together. Rights help us live with dignity. Duties remind us to use our freedom wisely and respectfully. The law protects citizens’ rights. A person can approach the court for help if the government violates them.
keyPoints: Rights give citizens freedoms and benefits.
Duties guide citizens’ actions in the community.
Rights and duties work together.
activities.explanation: Your freedom includes a responsibility to use it well.

activities.prompt: A student wants to share an opinion at a class meeting. What should the student do when others disagree?
steps: The student may share their opinion, because every citizen has this right.
The student should listen to others, because free expression creates a duty to listen.
The student should respect classmates, because being respected creates a duty to respect.
Therefore, the student should speak and listen respectfully, because rights and duties work together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What are rights?
options: Freedoms and benefits
Responsibilities to follow
Rules made by courts
Help from the government
activities.explanation: Rights are the freedoms and benefits that every citizen enjoys.

activities.prompt: Match each idea to its partner.
pairs: remind us to use freedom wisely
can help when rights are violated
activities.explanation: Rights support dignified life, while duties guide our use of freedom.

activities.prompt: Duties are moral and social responsibilities.
activities.explanation: Duties are the responsibilities that citizens must follow as community members.

activities.prompt: Why should you not enjoy a right while ignoring duties?
options: Because rights and duties work together.
Because citizens should ignore their duties.
Because the law removes every freedom.
Because duties cancel all rights.
activities.explanation: One should not fulfil a right while ignoring the other.

activities.prompt: Fulfilling duties protects everyone’s ______ and keeps society fair and peaceful.
activities.hint: Think about what every citizen enjoys.
activities.explanation: Fulfilling duties protects everyone’s rights and keeps society fair and peaceful.

activities.prompt: At a community meeting, what should you do?
options: Express your view and listen to others.
Express your view and ignore replies.
Listen only and hide your view.
Ask everyone to follow you.
activities.explanation: The right to express opinions freely creates a duty to listen to other people’s views.

activities.prompt: A student shares an opinion. Others disagree. What should the student do?
options: They listen to the other students’ views too.
They ignore everyone who disagrees with them.
They stop speaking so no one can disagree.
They demand that everyone accept only their view.

why.They ignore everyone who disagrees with: This mistake mistakes free speech for freedom from listening.
why.They stop speaking so no one can disagre: This mistake mistakes self-expression for refusing others’ rights.
why.They demand that everyone accept only th: This mistake mistakes one right for control over others.

activities.explanation: This is right because free expression creates a duty to listen.

activities.prompt: A citizen fails a duty without legal action. What does this show?
options: The duty is not important to others.
The duty still helps protect everyone’s rights.
The court must ignore every duty completely.
The citizen may ignore all duties from then on.

This mistake thinks no legal action means no social importance.
why.The court must ignore every duty complet: This mistake treats every moral duty as something courts must punish.
why.The citizen may ignore all duties from t: This mistake treats one unpunished failure as permission to ignore all duties.

activities.explanation: This is right because duties protect rights even without legal action.

activities.prompt: One meeting values different views. Another ignores them. Which result is likely?
options: The first meeting can help rights and duties work together.
The second meeting must lead to a court case.
The first meeting removes everyone’s right to speak.
The second meeting makes rights more important than duties.

why.The second meeting must lead to a court: This mistake assumes every ignored view must cause legal action.
why.The first meeting removes everyone’s rig: This mistake says listening removes the right to speak.
why.The second meeting makes rights more imp: This mistake thinks rights matter without their matching duties.

activities.explanation: This is right because listening helps rights and duties work together.

activities.prompt: A child is treated disrespectfully. Which response best respects rights and duties?
options: They respect others while expecting respect for themselves.
They insult others so everyone knows they are upset.
They avoid all people to stop feeling disrespected.
They demand respect but never show respect to others.

why.They insult others so everyone knows the: This mistake thinks hurting others protects the right to respect.
why.They avoid all people to stop feeling di: This mistake thinks avoiding people respects their rights.
why.They demand respect but never show respe: This mistake treats respect as a right without its duty.

activities.explanation: This is right because mutual respect matches a right with a duty.

lessons.title: Discrimination and Inclusion

activities.prompt: What can we do when someone is treated differently from everyone else?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Fairness and belonging
activities.body: Discrimination means mistreating someone because of their identity or background. It is unethical and legally prohibited. It can be subtle, such as leaving a classmate out of a group project. It may also work indirectly and be hard to prove or penalise. Inclusion means making everyone feel welcomed and respected. Examples include braille books, ramps and classroom support. Inclusive actions also remove barriers so everyone can take part.
keyPoints: Discrimination is mistreating someone because of their identity or background.
Discrimination is unethical and legally prohibited.
Inclusion welcomes, respects and supports everyone.
activities.explanation: Fair treatment helps everyone feel safe, respected and able to take part.

activities.prompt: A classmate is left out of a group project because of their background. What should the class do?
steps: This is discrimination because the classmate is mistreated because of their background.
It can create barriers because subtle exclusion can still block participation.
The class should include them because everyone must feel welcomed and respected.
That is right because discrimination breaks core values of respect and unity.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Seeing and removing barriers
activities.body: Discrimination may be visible, but it can also be invisible and work indirectly. Invisible discrimination is difficult to prove and difficult to penalise. Inclusion means making everyone feel welcomed and respected, especially groups that have faced exclusion. It means more than reservations. Providing braille books, ramps and classroom support helps. Removing barriers helps everyone take part.
keyPoints: Invisible discrimination can work indirectly.
Inclusion supports groups that have historically been excluded.
Inclusion means more than providing reservations.
activities.explanation: Inclusion helps people join in, even when discrimination is hidden or barriers remain.

activities.title: Understanding discrimination
activities.prompt: What does discrimination mean?
options: Mistreating someone because of their identity
Mistreating someone for choosing another game
Helping someone join a classroom activity
Respecting a group's different needs
activities.explanation: Discrimination means mistreating a person or group because of their identity or background.

activities.title: Fill the idea
activities.prompt: Inclusion means creating an environment where everyone feels ______ and respected.
activities.hint: This means everyone is welcomed.
activities.explanation: Inclusion creates an environment where everyone feels welcomed and respected.

activities.title: Ideas and examples
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: Excluding a classmate from a group project
activities.explanation: These pairs show examples of discrimination and inclusion. They help us understand how barriers can be reduced.

activities.title: Choose an inclusive action
activities.prompt: Which action best shows inclusion?
options: Providing braille books, ramps and support
Giving reservations and no other help
Leaving classroom barriers unchanged
Making only excluded groups welcome
activities.explanation: Providing braille books, ramps and classroom support are inclusive actions.

activities.title: Order the chain
activities.prompt: Put the chain of effects and response in order.
items: Barriers stop people enjoying fundamental rights
activities.explanation: Discrimination creates barriers that stop rights. Inclusion removes these barriers so everyone can take part.

activities.title: Why is it difficult?
activities.prompt: Why can invisible discrimination be difficult to deal with?
options: Hard to prove and penalise
It is easy for everyone to see
It is allowed in every public place
It affects only one person
activities.explanation: Invisible discrimination is difficult to prove and difficult to penalise.

activities.prompt: A student is left out of a group project because of their background. What effect can this have?
options: It can create social barriers that block the student's fundamental rights.
It can make school life fair because every project stays peaceful.
It can remove a barrier and make the student feel included.
It can change the project only, without affecting the student's rights.

why.It can make school life fair because eve: This is wrong because peaceful projects do not remove unequal treatment.
why.It can remove a barrier and make the stu: This is wrong because exclusion removes a barrier instead of creating one.
why.It can change the project only, without: This is wrong because social barriers can still affect the student's fundamental rights.

activities.explanation: This is right because identity-based mistreatment can create barriers to fundamental rights.

activities.prompt: Class A has a ramp, braille books, and support for every learner. Class B has steps and no support. Which class shows more inclusion?
options: Class A, because barriers are removed and people can take part.
Class B, because having no support makes every learner equal.
Class A, because every learner must receive exactly the same help.
Class B, because reserved places alone make people feel accepted.

why.Class B, because having no support makes: This is wrong because equal treatment without support can leave barriers in place.
why.Class A, because every learner must rece: This is wrong because inclusion does not mean giving everyone exactly the same help.
why.Class B, because reserved places alone m: This is wrong because reservations alone do not create acceptance and support.

activities.explanation: This is right because these actions remove barriers and help people take part.

activities.prompt: A school map shows a ramp into the classroom. What can the map tell us?
options: It suggests a barrier is removed so more people can take part.
It proves that all discrimination has ended and everyone feels included.
It shows that reserved places alone make every person feel accepted.
It shows that every learner must remove barriers alone.

why.It proves that all discrimination has en: This overreaches, because one map detail cannot prove complete inclusion.
why.It shows that reserved places alone make: This confuses seats with inclusion, because acceptance and support are also needed.
why.It shows that every learner must remove: This misunderstands support, because inclusion requires removing barriers for everyone.

activities.explanation: This is right because a ramp removes a barrier to taking part.

activities.prompt: Two classmates receive different project tasks because one is from another background. Which response follows the Constitution?
options: Stop the mistreatment, because discrimination violates respect and unity.
Allow it, because teachers may choose any project task.
Ignore it, because unequal treatment can be hard to prove.
Accept it, because school projects matter more than constitutional values.

why.Allow it, because teachers may choose an: This is wrong because choosing tasks by background is discriminatory mistreatment.
why.Ignore it, because unequal treatment can: This is wrong because difficulty proving harm does not make discrimination allowed.
why.Accept it, because school projects matte: This is wrong because project needs cannot outweigh respect and unity.

activities.explanation: This is right because discriminatory mistreatment breaches the Constitution's core values.

activities.prompt: A student is quietly given less help because of their background. Why may this unfairness remain unnoticed?
options: It may work indirectly, so it is difficult to notice or prove.
It may be visible to everyone, so it is easy to notice.
It may be lawful, because unequal help is allowed at school.
It may affect only work, so rights and values stay safe.

why.It may be visible to everyone, so it is: This is wrong because indirect mistreatment is not always visible to everyone.
why.It may be lawful, because unequal help i: This is wrong because discrimination is legally prohibited, not allowed at school.
why.It may affect only work, so rights and v: This is wrong because identity-based mistreatment can still block fundamental rights.

activities.explanation: This is right because indirect mistreatment can be hard to notice and prove.

activities.prompt: Reserved seats are provided for a group that was excluded before. Many members still feel unwelcome. Has inclusion been achieved?
options: No, because acceptance and support must go beyond reservations.
Yes, because reservations alone give every person enough support.
No, because reservations harm the group that was excluded before.
Yes, because providing places removes every possible barrier.

why.Yes, because reservations alone give eve: This misses support, because reserved places alone do not make people accepted.
why.No, because reservations harm the group: This reverses the issue, because reservations support a group that was excluded.
why.Yes, because providing places removes ev: This overstates the result, because reserved places do not remove every barrier.

activities.explanation: This is right because inclusion needs more than reserved seats.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: Indian politician CH. Dillu Ram appears at a community meeting in Karnal.

activities.context: A citizen of India lives in another country and attends a local school. In class, the student learns that citizenship includes legal membership and taking an active part in society. When the class discusses equal rights, a newcomer is left out because of where they come from. The student suggests including everyone and reminds the group that citizens must respect others, obey the law, pay taxes, and help keep society safe.
activities.prompt: Suppose the student had only lived in the second country and had no legal tie to it. What would this show about becoming a citizen there?
options: A legal tie and membership in the political community are required.
Living in the country automatically creates citizenship.
Citizenship ends whenever a person lives abroad.
Any resident can vote in a democracy.

why.Living in the country automatically crea: Residence by itself does not create citizenship.
why.Citizenship ends whenever a person lives: A citizen may live in another country.
Voting is a right of citizens, not every resident.

activities.explanation: Citizenship requires a legal and political connection.

activities.context: A citizen of India lives in another country and attends a local school. In class, the student learns that citizenship includes legal membership and taking an active part in society. When the class discusses equal rights, a newcomer is left out because of where they come from. The student suggests including everyone and reminds the group that citizens must respect others, obey the law, pay taxes, and help keep society safe.
activities.prompt: If the student joins a discussion about the country’s future and offers a reasoned view, which citizenship idea is being applied?
options: Making a deliberate contribution to decisions about the country.
Only following rules without joining public decisions.
Relying on residence instead of legal membership.
Keeping citizenship entirely private and separate from society.

why.Only following rules without joining pub: Following rules alone misses active participation.
why.Relying on residence instead of legal me: Residence does not replace legal membership.
why.Keeping citizenship entirely private and: Citizenship includes responsibility towards the country.

activities.explanation: The student is helping shape the country’s future.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Simply living in a country does not automatically make a person a citizen.
Reason (R): Citizenship requires a legal tie to the country and membership in its political community.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why residence alone does not establish citizenship.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Legal membership by itself is the whole meaning of citizenship.
Reason (R): Citizenship also includes social responsibility towards the country.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but the claim wrongly treats legal membership as sufficient.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between being a citizen and merely living in a country.
activities.answer: Citizenship is a legal tie to a country and membership in its political community. It is not the same as merely living there, because residence by itself does not automatically create citizenship. A citizen may live in another country and still hold citizenship. Citizenship also carries rights and responsibilities. In a democracy, rights can include voting and free speech, while duties include obeying the law, paying taxes, respecting others, and helping keep society safe. Therefore, citizenship is both legal membership and social responsibility.
points: Citizenship requires a legal and political connection.
Residence alone does not create citizenship.
A citizen may live in another country.
Citizenship includes both rights and responsibilities.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school, a student asks to join a debate with everyone else, although a rule requires students to respect others and avoid harm. The teacher says equal opportunities should prevent discrimination and freedom needs reasonable restrictions. A parent objects, saying equal treatment means giving this student special attention. Another parent argues that removing discrimination must not remove the rule against harm. The teacher says students should be free in matters of religion and that education must remain accessible.
activities.prompt: If the teacher follows the second parent’s argument, what is the most likely result?
options: The student gains fair access, while protection against harmful participation remains.
The student receives a special privilege, so equal treatment becomes unequal opportunity.
The rule against harm disappears, because removing discrimination requires unrestricted participation.
The student stays excluded, since established practices cannot change after one request.

why.The student receives a special privilege: Special preference would make equal treatment unequal.
why.The rule against harm disappears, becaus: Removing discrimination does not require ending all restrictions.
why.The student stays excluded, since establ: Keeping the student out could continue discrimination and deny fair opportunity.

activities.explanation: Equal access removes unfair exclusion, while limits against harm remain.

activities.context: At a school, a student asks to join a debate with everyone else, although a rule requires students to respect others and avoid harm. The teacher says equal opportunities should prevent discrimination and freedom needs reasonable restrictions. A parent objects, saying equal treatment means giving this student special attention. Another parent argues that removing discrimination must not remove the rule against harm. The teacher says students should be free in matters of religion and that education must remain accessible.
activities.prompt: During the debate, one student uses the activity to insult others. How should the teacher respond?
options: The teacher should allow the insult because equal participation means every behaviour must be accepted.
The teacher may enforce the rule, because freedom does not include actions that harm others.
The teacher should remove all restrictions so that every student can speak without limits.
The teacher should treat the insult as a right because the student has equal access to the activity.

why.The teacher should allow the insult beca: Equal access does not make harmful behaviour acceptable.
why.The teacher should remove all restrictio: Removing all limits could allow freedom to harm others.
why.The teacher should treat the insult as a: A request for equal access does not make harmful conduct a right.

activities.explanation: Harmful actions cannot be considered rights, and freedom has reasonable limits.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A school can provide equal opportunities while keeping reasonable restrictions against harmful conduct.
Reason (R): Freedom without reasonable restrictions may be misused to harm others.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why fair freedom needs limits that prevent harm while equal access is maintained.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A harmful wish becomes a fundamental right as soon as a person asks for it.
Reason (R): Rights protect dignity, safety and respect, and actions that harm ourselves or others cannot be considered rights.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because requests are not automatically rights, while the reason correctly states that harmful conduct cannot be a right.

activities.prompt: How does the Constitution protect rights, and how is a wish different from a right?
activities.answer: The Constitution lists six broad categories of fundamental rights to protect people’s freedom, and they can be enforced through law. A right is something people need in order to live with dignity, safety and respect, while a wish is simply what someone wants. A wish cannot automatically become a right. For example, a wish for education may support equal opportunities, but a wish to harm another person cannot be a right because actions that harm ourselves or others cannot be considered rights. Equality prevents discrimination and ends practices such as untouchability.
points: The Constitution lists six broad categories of fundamental rights.
Fundamental rights can be enforced through law.
A right is based on dignity, safety and respect, not merely on wanting something.
Harmful actions and wishes cannot automatically be treated as rights.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a school activity, a student notices that some students are disrespecting the National Flag. Another student suggests that people from different communities should be treated equally and that the school grounds should be kept clean. A third student refuses to join an argument and says that public property must be protected. The group discusses how citizens can support the country and other people.
activities.prompt: What should the students do after noticing that some students are disrespecting the National Flag?
options: They should stop the disrespect and follow the citizen duty of respecting the flag.
They should continue the activity while leaving the disrespect unchallenged.
They should punish the students by using violence.
They should respect the flag only when someone is watching.

why.They should continue the activity while: Ignoring disrespect would not fulfil the duty.
why.They should punish the students by using: Violence is wrong and should be avoided.
why.They should respect the flag only when s: Respect should not depend on whether people are watching.

activities.explanation: This follows the duty to respect the National Flag.

activities.context: During a school activity, a student notices that some students are disrespecting the National Flag. Another student suggests that people from different communities should be treated equally and that the school grounds should be kept clean. A third student refuses to join an argument and says that public property must be protected. The group discusses how citizens can support the country and other people.
activities.prompt: If students from different communities begin arguing, what is the best response?
options: They should calm the disagreement and promote harmony among all people.
They should ask one community to leave the activity.
They should encourage both sides to use stronger words.
They should decide the argument by insulting the other group.

why.They should ask one community to leave t: Excluding people would not promote harmony.
why.They should encourage both sides to use: Stronger arguments could increase the disagreement.
why.They should decide the argument by insul: Insults would harm respect and harmony.

activities.explanation: Promoting harmony is a fundamental duty.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A citizen can show a fundamental duty by respecting the National Anthem.
Reason (R): Citizens must respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly states that respecting the National Anthem is a citizen duty.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Parents and guardians must ensure that children aged 6 to 14 years receive an education.
Reason (R): This responsibility is placed only on schools, not on parents and guardians.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because the duty is also on parents and guardians.

activities.prompt: How does the duty of parents and guardians differ from the duties of citizens?
activities.answer: The duty of citizens is broad. Citizens should respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem, follow the ideals of the freedom struggle, protect India’s unity, integrity and sovereignty, defend the nation, and help during emergencies. They should also promote harmony, respect women, preserve culture and heritage, protect the environment, show compassion towards animals, protect public property and avoid violence. The duty of parents and guardians is more specific: they must ensure that children aged 6 to 14 years receive an education.
points: Explains that citizens have many responsibilities.
Includes duties about the nation and emergencies.
Includes social, cultural and environmental duties.
Identifies the specific duty of parents and guardians.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student believes that everyone should be free to express opinions and treated with respect. At a community meeting, the student shares personal views but refuses to listen when neighbours offer different opinions. A neighbour asks the student to respect everyone’s right to speak. The student realises that expressing an opinion freely also creates a duty to listen to other people’s views. The student apologises and agrees to listen respectfully.
activities.prompt: What should the student do after the neighbour asks for respect?
options: The student should consider other people’s views as well.
The student should continue speaking without listening.
The student should leave the meeting and ignore everyone.
The student should ask only the people who agree to speak.

why.The student should continue speaking wit: Refusing to listen ignores a duty linked to expressing opinions freely.
why.The student should leave the meeting and: Leaving the meeting does not fulfil the duty to respect others.
why.The student should ask only the people w: Only accepting agreement prevents the student from respecting others’ rights.

activities.explanation: The student should listen to other views respectfully.

activities.context: A student believes that everyone should be free to express opinions and treated with respect. At a community meeting, the student shares personal views but refuses to listen when neighbours offer different opinions. A neighbour asks the student to respect everyone’s right to speak. The student realises that expressing an opinion freely also creates a duty to listen to other people’s views. The student apologises and agrees to listen respectfully.
activities.prompt: If the student later says that a government decision has taken away a right protected by law, what can happen?
options: The student can approach a court for help.
The student must give up the right altogether.
The student should ignore the decision and break the law.
The student should rely only on personal opinion and take no action.

why.The student must give up the right altog: Giving up the right is not required when it is violated.
why.The student should ignore the decision a: Ignoring the law does not protect the right.
why.The student should rely only on personal: Personal opinion alone may not provide a way to challenge the violation.

activities.explanation: A court can help when the government violates a citizen’s right.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Rights and duties work together rather than oppose each other.
Reason (R): Duties remind citizens to use their freedom wisely and respectfully.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason explains why rights and duties work together.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Citizenship: Rights and Duties

activities.prompt: What connects a citizen to a country?
options: A legal tie and political membership
A shared hobby and travel plan
A private promise to stay
A payment for public services
activities.explanation: Citizenship joins legal membership with responsibility towards the country.

activities.prompt: Simply living in a country automatically makes someone a citizen.
activities.explanation: Living in a country does not by itself give someone legal membership.

activities.prompt: Which pair shows rights citizens enjoy in a democracy?
options: Voting and free speech
Loyalty and payment of taxes
Harmony and public safety
Heritage and excellence
activities.explanation: Voting and free speech are rights that citizens enjoy in a democracy.

activities.prompt: A citizen may live in a country different from the one whose __________ they hold.
activities.hint: Name the legal membership that stays with the person.
activities.explanation: A citizen can live in another country while holding citizenship elsewhere.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: Freedoms and benefits enjoyed by every citizen
Equal opportunities in jobs and education
Choosing, practising and sharing religion freely
Making everyone feel welcomed and respected
activities.explanation: These ideas help citizens gain freedom, accept others and live together fairly.

activities.prompt: Which result shows equality in action?
options: Equal chances and less discrimination
Separate chances for each group
Fewer chances for some people
No shared public rules
activities.explanation: Equality gives people equal opportunities and prevents discrimination.

activities.prompt: Freedom should have reasonable restrictions so it cannot harm others.
activities.explanation: Reasonable restrictions stop freedom from being misused or harming others.

activities.prompt: Put these effects of discrimination in order.
items: A person is mistreated because of identity.
The person cannot enjoy fundamental rights.
activities.explanation: Mistreatment can create barriers that stop people from enjoying their fundamental rights.

activities.prompt: If the government violates your rights, you can approach the ______ for help.
activities.hint: This place helps people when their rights are violated.
activities.explanation: The law protects rights, and courts can help when the government violates them.

activities.prompt: Which action is a fundamental duty for citizens?
options: Respect the Constitution, flag and anthem
Keep citizenship details private
Choose only one religion
Skip duties during emergencies
activities.explanation: Fundamental duties are responsibilities citizens should follow for their country.

chapters.title: Dynamics of Population
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is demography?; population at a glance; what determines a country’s population?; how countries experience population change.

lessons.title: What Is Demography?

activities.prompt: What can we learn about people by studying how populations grow and change?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Demography
activities.body: Demography studies the size, structure and changes of human populations. It also examines population composition, patterns and trends. Births, deaths and movement can change population characteristics. Governments use this information to plan schools, hospitals, roads and housing. The census gives an official count of people living in a country.
keyPoints: Demography studies human populations.
Births, deaths and movement change population characteristics.
A census officially counts a country's people.
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas you will use in this lesson.

activities.prompt: A town has many young children. The government is deciding what to build next. What should it build first?
steps: Demography studies population size and structure.
The town has many young children, so many people are young.
Many young children create a need for more schools.
Therefore, the government should plan more schools first.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Using Population Information
activities.body: Population information helps people make useful plans. Many young children mean a need for more schools. A high proportion of elderly people means more healthcare facilities. A large population of young working-age people means more jobs are needed. Businesses also study customers’ characteristics to create suitable products. Census information includes age, gender, education, religion, family size and occupation.
keyPoints: Young children create a need for schools.
Elderly people create a need for healthcare facilities.
Businesses study customers' characteristics.
activities.explanation: Population information helps planners and businesses make suitable choices.

activities.prompt: What does demography study?
options: Their size, structure and changes
Their products and business plans
Their schools, hospitals and roads
Their customers and suitable products
activities.explanation: Demography studies the size, structure and changes of human populations.

activities.prompt: In India, a census is generally conducted every ______ years.
activities.hint: Think about the gap between each census.
activities.explanation: The census is generally conducted in India every ten years.

activities.prompt: Population characteristics can change because of births, deaths and movement.
activities.explanation: Births, deaths and movement can change population characteristics.

activities.prompt: Match each population idea to its meaning.
activities.explanation: Demography studies populations, while a census counts people and records details.

activities.prompt: A place has many young children. What does it need?
options: More healthcare facilities
More schools
More jobs
More suitable products
activities.explanation: A place with many young children needs more schools.

activities.prompt: Which list shows only census information?
options: Schools, hospitals and roads
Births, deaths and movement
Age, education and occupation
Size, structure and changes
activities.explanation: Census information includes age, education and occupation.

activities.prompt: Place A has many young children. Place B has many elderly people. What does each place need most?
options: Place A needs schools; Place B needs healthcare.
Place A needs healthcare; Place B needs schools.
Place A needs jobs; Place B needs more schools.
Place A needs housing; Place B needs more roads.

why.Place A needs healthcare; Place B needs: This swaps the needs linked to children and elderly people.
why.Place A needs jobs; Place B needs more s: Children need schools, while working-age people need jobs.
why.Place A needs housing; Place B needs mor: These options do not match the needs of young or elderly people.

activities.explanation: Young children need schools, while elderly people need healthcare.

activities.prompt: Families move into a town from another place. What may change in that town?
options: The size and structure of its population
The number of the town's schools
The number of local births and deaths
The age and occupation of each person

why.The number of the town's schools: Schools may need to grow, but they are not a population characteristic.
why.The number of local births and deaths: Movement can change population, but births and deaths are separate causes.
why.The age and occupation of each person: Movement does not change each person's age and occupation details.

activities.explanation: Movement can change population size, structure and composition.

activities.prompt: Government census data shows many children and elderly residents. What planning choice follows?
options: Plan more schools and healthcare facilities
Plan more jobs and suitable products
Plan more census counts for residents
Plan more housing for all workers

why.Plan more jobs and suitable products: Working-age numbers point to jobs; businesses study customer characteristics.
why.Plan more census counts for residents: Census information helps planning, but it does not call for more counts.
why.Plan more housing for all workers: Housing is planned too, but these age groups point to other services.

activities.explanation: Children point to schools, while elderly residents point to healthcare.

activities.prompt: A business wants products that suit its customers. What should it study first?
options: The customers' age, family size and occupation
The country's census count every ten years
The government's plans for schools and roads
The country's deaths and movements of people

why.The country's census count every ten yea: This is census timing, not customer information.
why.The government's plans for schools and r: Governments use population information for schools, roads and other planning.
why.The country's deaths and movements of pe: These are population changes, not customer characteristics.

activities.explanation: Businesses study customers' characteristics to create suitable products.

lessons.title: Population at a Glance

activities.prompt: Why is the world’s population changing in such surprising ways?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: World Population Facts
activities.body: India became the world's most populous country in 2023. Indians make up around 17 per cent of the world's population. The world population grew from 2.5 billion in 1950 to 8.2 billion in 2025. It is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050. Better healthcare has helped people live longer. Growth has slowed, but population is projected to peak at 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s.
keyPoints: India became the world's most populous country in 2023.
Indians make up around 17 per cent of the world's population.
The world population is expected to peak at 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s.
activities.explanation: These facts show India's place and the world's population journey.

activities.prompt: Why might schools need more space now if world population will later fall?
steps: The world population is already high because it grew to 8.2 billion in 2025.
Some schools need more space because several African nations still grow rapidly.
More space is still needed because growth has slowed but is expected to continue.
Later decline does not remove today's need, because decline comes after the peak as birth rates fall.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Growth, Peak and Decline
activities.body: Population growth means the number of people is increasing. World population growth has slowed over time. However, several African nations, including Nigeria and Ethiopia, continue to grow rapidly. China, Japan and Italy already have shrinking populations. A peak is the highest point reached. Population decline is expected after the peak as birth rates fall.
keyPoints: World population growth has slowed over time.
Nigeria and Ethiopia continue to grow rapidly.
Population decline is expected after the peak.
activities.explanation: This card explains growth, peak and decline in simple words.

activities.prompt: When did India become the world's most populous country?
activities.explanation: The lesson says India became the world's most populous country in 2023.

activities.prompt: India became the world's most populous country in ______.
activities.hint: This was the year of the population milestone.
activities.explanation: India became the world's most populous country in 2023.

activities.prompt: What is expected after the world population reaches its peak?
options: Faster growth
Population decline
Constant population
Rapid birth-rate growth
activities.explanation: Population decline is expected to follow the peak as birth rates fall.

activities.prompt: Match each year with its population figure.
activities.explanation: The world population was 2.5 billion in 1950. It was 8.2 billion in 2025 and is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050.

activities.prompt: Put these population milestones in order.
items: India became the world's most populous country in 2023
World population is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050
World population is projected to peak at 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s
activities.explanation: The dates show population milestones from 1950 to the mid-2080s.

activities.prompt: Which statement about population change is correct?
options: China, Japan and Italy have shrinking populations.
Nigeria and Ethiopia have shrinking populations.
The world population will peak before 2050.
World population growth has sped up.
activities.explanation: China, Japan and Italy already have shrinking populations. Nigeria and Ethiopia continue to grow rapidly.

activities.prompt: A village gets better healthcare. Which change is most likely there?
options: More people may live to old age.
Births must rise faster than deaths.
Young people must all leave the village.
Population must fall very quickly.

It wrongly links better healthcare with a sudden rise in births.
It wrongly links better healthcare with young people leaving.
It wrongly assumes that better healthcare quickly causes population decline.

activities.explanation: Better healthcare has enabled people to live longer.

activities.prompt: Two maps use arrows. Japan's arrow points down. Nigeria's arrow points up. What do the arrows show?
options: Different population trends in the two countries.
Equal population size in the two countries.
Falling birth rates in both countries.
Rapid population growth in both countries.

why.Equal population size in the two countri: An arrow shows the direction of change, not the population size.
Nigeria is growing rapidly, so falling birth rates do not explain both arrows.
why.Rapid population growth in both countrie: Japan is shrinking, so both places are not growing rapidly.

activities.explanation: Japan is shrinking, while Nigeria continues to grow rapidly.

activities.prompt: A poster shows 8.2 billion beside 2025 and 9.7 billion beside 2050. The future line is dotted. What does that line mean?
options: The 9.7 billion figure is an expectation.
The 9.7 billion figure has already happened.
The 8.2 billion figure is only an expectation.
The two figures must be exactly equal.

why.The 9.7 billion figure has already happe: It mistakes a future expectation for a fact that has happened.
why.The 8.2 billion figure is only an expect: It mistakes the 2025 figure for a future expectation.
It wrongly treats two different figures as equal.

activities.explanation: The facts give 8.2 billion for 2025 and only an expected 9.7 billion for 2050.

activities.prompt: A chart compares 1950 with 2025. Which change best explains the population rise?
options: Major medical advances helped population growth.
Falling birth rates caused all the growth.
The world reached its peak in 1950.
Healthcare changes had no effect on growth.

why.Falling birth rates caused all the growt: Falling birth rates explain later decline, not earlier rapid growth.
The population peak is expected in the mid-2080s, not 1950.
why.Healthcare changes had no effect on grow: Better healthcare helped people live longer, so it did affect growth.

activities.explanation: Rapid world population growth followed major medical advances.

activities.prompt: World population growth has slowed. The population is expected to peak in the mid-2080s. What should happen before the peak?
options: Population should keep growing, but more slowly.
Population should fall below 1950 levels.
Population should stay exactly at 8.2 billion.
Population should stop changing at once.

why.Population should fall below 1950 levels: The expected peak is higher than today's population, not below 1950.
why.Population should stay exactly at 8.2 bi: The 8.2 billion figure is for 2025, and growth continues toward the peak.
Slowing growth is not the same as population staying still.

activities.explanation: Slowed growth still leads to a higher population before the peak.

lessons.title: What Determines a Country’s Population?

activities.prompt: What makes a country’s population grow, shrink, or change?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How populations change
activities.body: The birth rate counts live births in a year per 1,000 people. Many babies being born means the birth rate is high. Fewer babies being born means it is low. The death rate counts deaths during a year. Migration is movement of people from one place to another. The fertility rate shows the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime.
keyPoints: Live births are counted per 1,000 people in a year.
Deaths during a year help show the death rate.
Movement of people between places is migration.
activities.explanation: These measures help you understand how a country’s population changes.

activities.prompt: Each town has the same population. One town has more live births each year. What can we say about their birth rates?
steps: One town has more live births in one year.
The birth rate counts those births per 1,000 people.
Because both towns have the same population, more births mean a higher rate.
So the town with more babies has the high birth rate, while the other has the low birth rate.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which measure counts live births in a year per 1,000 people?
options: Birth rate
Death rate
Fertility rate
Migration rate
activities.explanation: The birth rate counts live births in a year per 1,000 people. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: The mortality rate counts live births during a year.
activities.explanation: The mortality rate counts deaths during a year, not live births.

activities.prompt: Movement of people from one place to another is called ______.
activities.hint: Think about people moving between places.
activities.explanation: Migration means the movement of people from one place to another.

activities.prompt: Match each population measure with its meaning.
pairs: Live births in a year per 1,000 people
Average children a woman would have in her lifetime
Deaths in a population during a year
Movement of people from one place to another
activities.explanation: You matched each measure with the population change it counts.

activities.prompt: What is 2.1 called in population studies?
options: Replacement level fertility rate
Recorded population death rate
Average children birth rate
Highest movement rate
activities.explanation: The number 2.1 is called the replacement level fertility rate. Great work!

activities.prompt: China introduced the One-Child Policy in 1979.
activities.explanation: China introduced the One-Child Policy in 1979. You got it right!

activities.prompt: Put these China population events in time order.
items: China introduced the One-Child Policy in 1979
activities.explanation: These events are ordered by the years 1963, 1979 and 2025.

activities.prompt: China’s fertility rate was 1 in 2025. What may happen over time?
options: Its population may shrink over time
Its population must grow quickly
Its fertility rate becomes 2.1
Its death rate must fall
activities.explanation: A fertility rate below 2.1 may cause the population to shrink over time.

activities.prompt: Each town has the same population. One has more live births each year. Which town has the higher birth rate?
options: The town with more live births each year.
The town with fewer live births each year.
Both towns must have the same birth rate.
The town with more people moving away.

why.The town with fewer live births each yea: Fewer births mean a lower rate, not a higher one.
why.Both towns must have the same birth rate: Equal populations do not remove the difference in live births.
Movement of people is migration, not the birth rate.

activities.explanation: With equal populations, more live births give the higher birth rate.

activities.prompt: A country's fertility rate is below the replacement level of 2.1. What may happen to the population over time?
options: The population may shrink over time.
The population is likely to grow quickly.
The population will have no people moving.
The population will keep every family large.

why.The population is likely to grow quickly: A rate below 2.1 does not point to quick growth.
why.The population will have no people movin: This rate describes fertility, not whether people migrate.
why.The population will keep every family la: A below-2.1 rate does not mean every family stays large.

activities.explanation: A fertility rate below 2.1 may cause the population to shrink.

lessons.title: How Countries Experience Population Change

activities.prompt: Why do some countries’ populations grow quickly while others change more slowly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Population Change
activities.body: Population changes through births, deaths and migration over years. Demographic characteristics are population features affected by birth and death rates. Demographic transition has three stages. Stage 1 has high birth and death rates, so growth is slow. Stage 2 brings better healthcare and rapid growth. Stage 3 has low death rates while birth rates fall. Urbanisation, income, education and women’s work lower birth rates. Fertility means birth levels. Very low fertility can make a population shrink.
keyPoints: Population change comes from births, deaths and migration over years.
Three stages show how birth and death rates change.
Very low fertility can make a population shrink.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect population change with the three stages of demographic transition.

activities.prompt: A village gets better healthcare, but families still have many babies. Why is its population growing fast?
steps: Because better healthcare is present, Stage 2 has a lower death rate.
Fewer deaths mean more people survive each year.
High birth rates also mean many babies are born each year.
So population grows rapidly because births are high and deaths are low.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Changes Population?
activities.prompt: Which changes shape a country's population over many years?
options: Births, deaths and migration
Rainfall, soil and sunshine
Schools, roads and hospitals
Jobs, farms and markets
activities.explanation: A country's population results from changes in births, deaths and migration.

activities.title: The Effect of Better Healthcare
activities.prompt: In Stage 2, better healthcare brings down the ______ rate.
activities.hint: Think about the rate connected with healthcare.
activities.explanation: Better healthcare brings down the death rate in Stage 2.

activities.title: Why Growth Becomes Rapid
activities.prompt: Why does population growth become rapid in Stage 2?
options: Birth rates remain high.
Death rates remain high.
Migration stops completely.
Healthcare becomes poor.
activities.explanation: High birth rates cause rapid population growth in Stage 2.

activities.title: Match Each Stage
activities.prompt: Match each stage with its population pattern.
pairs: High birth and death rates; very slow growth
Low death rates; birth rates begin to fall
activities.explanation: Each stage has a different pattern of birth rates, death rates and growth.

activities.title: Order the Stages
activities.prompt: Put the three demographic transition stages in order.
activities.explanation: The stages run from Stage 1 to Stage 2 and then Stage 3.

activities.title: When Fertility Becomes Very Low
activities.prompt: What can happen when fertility becomes very low?
options: A population can start shrinking.
A population must grow quickly.
Birth rates always rise sharply.
Death rates must become high.
activities.explanation: Very low fertility can make a population start shrinking.

activities.prompt: Imagine a country enters Stage 2, but birth rates stay high. What will most likely happen?
options: Population will grow fast because death rates fall and births stay high.
Population will grow slowly because birth rates also fall quickly.
Population will stop growing because better healthcare means fewer births.
Population will shrink quickly because better healthcare lowers death rates.

why.Population will grow slowly because birt: The scenario says birth rates stay high, not that they fall.
why.Population will stop growing because bet: Better healthcare lowers deaths, not births.
why.Population will shrink quickly because b: Lower death rates with high births cause growth, not shrinking.

activities.explanation: Stage 2 has lower deaths, while high births keep growth rapid.

activities.prompt: Stage 1 has high birth and death rates. Stage 2 has high birth rates but lower death rates. Which grows faster?
options: Stage 2, because lower deaths and high births cause faster growth.
Stage 1, because high birth rates always produce faster population growth.
Stage 2, because a lower death rate always makes birth rates fall.
Neither, because high birth and death rates always cause rapid growth.

why.Stage 1, because high birth rates always: High births matter, but Stage 1 also has high deaths.
why.Stage 2, because a lower death rate alwa: Lower deaths do not automatically make birth rates fall.
why.Neither, because high birth and death ra: Stage 1 grows slowly because both birth and death rates are high.

activities.explanation: Stage 1 grows slowly, while Stage 2 grows rapidly.

activities.prompt: A map shows people moving from one village to one city. What can this movement do to population size?
options: It can lower the village population and raise the city population.
It can lower both populations because every moving person disappears.
It can raise both populations because every moving person arrives twice.
It cannot change population because only births and deaths matter.

why.It can lower both populations because ev: Migration does not remove everyone from both populations.
why.It can raise both populations because ev: Each moving person is counted in only one new place.
why.It cannot change population because only: Population changes through births, deaths, and migration.

activities.explanation: Migration can lower one population and raise another.

activities.prompt: A government wants birth rates to fall. Which plan best supports lower birth rates?
options: Raise income, expand education, and support women’s workforce participation.
Improve healthcare only, because healthcare directly lowers birth rates.
Expand education only, but stop women from joining the workforce.
Raise income only, because money always makes families have more children.

why.Improve healthcare only, because healthc: Better healthcare mainly brings down the death rate.
why.Expand education only, but stop women fr: Education helps, but stopping women’s work removes a reason.
why.Raise income only, because money always: Higher income is linked with lower, not always higher, birth rates.

activities.explanation: Education, income, and women’s work help lower birth rates.

activities.prompt: A family moves to a city, earns more, and gets more education. Why might they have fewer children?
options: City living, higher income, and education can lower birth rates.
City living, higher income, and education always stop all births.
City living raises death rates, so families choose to have more children.
Paid work takes women away, so families cannot have any children.

why.City living, higher income, and educatio: These factors may lower births, but do not stop all births.
why.City living raises death rates, so famil: Urbanisation helps lower birth rates, not raise them.
why.Paid work takes women away, so families: Women’s workforce participation can help lower birth rates.

activities.explanation: Urbanisation, higher income, and education help lower birth rates.

activities.prompt: A report says India’s fertility rate is below replacement level. What may happen to its population?
options: Its population may start shrinking because fertility is very low.
Its population must grow faster because birth rates are very high.
Its population will stay unchanged because migration no longer matters.
Its population will shrink at once, without any time to change.

why.Its population must grow faster because: Below replacement level means low fertility, not high birth rates.
why.Its population will stay unchanged becau: Migration still matters because population change includes migration.
why.Its population will shrink at once, with: The fact says shrinking may start, not that it happens at once.

activities.explanation: Very low fertility can make a population start shrinking.
