lessons.title: India’s Population Composition and Pyramid

activities.prompt: How does India’s population pyramid reveal the story of its people?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding India’s Population
activities.body: Population structure describes people by age, gender, occupation and education. Sex ratio counts females for every 1,000 males. India’s ratio rose from 933 in 2001 to 943 in 2011. A balanced ratio supports equitable development and social stability. India’s recent pyramid is more bell-shaped than triangular. Its narrower base shows families have fewer children. Its widening upper section reflects people living longer.
keyPoints: Population structure includes age, gender, occupation and education.
India’s sex ratio improved from 933 in 2001 to 943 in 2011.
India’s recent pyramid has a narrower base and widening upper section.
activities.explanation: These clues help you read India’s changing population.

activities.prompt: A child sees India's population pyramid changing. What does its new shape mean?
steps: India's recent pyramid is more bell-shaped than triangular.
The narrower base matters because families are having fewer children.
The widening upper section matters because people are living longer.
So the new shape shows fewer births and longer lives.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: India’s sex ratio was ______ females per 1,000 males in 2011.
activities.hint: This number improved from 2001.
activities.explanation: The ratio increased to 943 females per 1,000 males in 2011.

activities.prompt: India had 933 females for every 1,000 males in 2001.
activities.explanation: India’s sex ratio was 933 females per 1,000 males in 2001.

activities.prompt: Match each population pyramid feature with what it shows.
pairs: More older people than young adults
activities.explanation: A wide base shows many births. A wide top means more older people than young adults.

activities.prompt: India’s recent population pyramid is described as:
options: More triangular than bell-shaped.
More bell-shaped than triangular.
Neither triangular nor bell-shaped.
activities.explanation: India’s recent population pyramid is more bell-shaped than triangular.

activities.prompt: Put these population changes in order.
activities.explanation: Fewer children make the base narrower. Longer lives widen the upper section.

activities.prompt: Which statement agrees with India’s recent population pyramid?
options: Fewer children are born, and people live longer.
More children are born, and people live longer.
Fewer children are born, and people live shorter.
More children are born, and people live shorter.
activities.explanation: The narrower base shows fewer children. The widening upper section reflects longer lives.

activities.prompt: A town's pyramid has a narrower base than before. What does this show?
options: Families are having fewer children.
More children are entering the population.
More older people are dying early.
The town has more young adults.

why.More children are entering the populatio: This wrongly treats a narrow base as a wide one.
This confuses a narrow base with a widening upper section.
This confuses fewer births with a rise in young adults.

activities.explanation: A narrower base shows that families are having fewer children.

activities.prompt: India had 933 females per 1,000 males in 2001. It had 943 in 2011. What changed?
options: The number of females per 1,000 males rose.
The number of females per 1,000 males fell.
The number of males per 1,000 females rose.
The number of males per 1,000 females stayed.

why.The number of females per 1,000 males fe: This reverses the rise from 933 to 943.
why.The number of males per 1,000 females ro: This reverses the direction of change between the two years.
why.The number of males per 1,000 females st: This ignores the rise from 933 to 943.

activities.explanation: The number of females per 1,000 males increased from 933 to 943.

activities.prompt: A pyramid has a wide top. What does this shape tell us?
options: There are more older people than young adults.
There are more children than older people.
There are more young adults than older people.
There are equal numbers at every age.

why.There are more children than older peopl: This mistakes the wide top for a wide base.
why.There are more young adults than older p: This reverses what a wide top means.
This assumes the pyramid has no age differences.

activities.explanation: A wide top means there are more older people than young adults.

activities.prompt: A pyramid has a very wide base. What does this suggest?
options: Many children are being born now.
Few children are being born now.
Many older people are being born now.
Many young adults are having no children.

This confuses a wide base with a narrow base.
This mixes up the top and the base of the pyramid.
why.Many young adults are having no children: This wrongly links a wide base to adults avoiding children.

activities.explanation: A wide base means many children are being born.

activities.prompt: A town wants a balanced sex ratio. Why would this help society?
options: It supports equitable development and social stability.
It makes every child choose the same job.
It ensures every family gets equal money.
It makes every town grow at the same speed.

why.It makes every child choose the same job: This confuses population balance with equal jobs.
why.It ensures every family gets equal money: This confuses population balance with equal money.
why.It makes every town grow at the same spe: This confuses population balance with equal growth.

activities.explanation: A balanced sex ratio supports equitable development and social stability.

activities.prompt: India's pyramid has a narrow base and widening upper section. What does it show?
options: Fewer births and people living longer.
More births and people dying younger.
More children and fewer older people.
Equal births and shorter lives.

This reverses both the base and upper-section clues.
This confuses a narrow base with a wide base.
This reverses the meaning of both parts of the pyramid.

activities.explanation: The narrow base shows fewer children, while the upper section reflects longer lives.

lessons.title: India's Demographic Dividend and Population Ageing

activities.prompt: How can India make the most of its changing population?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Population Change
activities.body: An ageing population has more elderly people needing care and fewer young people. India has a large working-age population, with nearly 65 per cent of people in this group. This can create a demographic dividend: growth potential from a young, productive population. Young people can work in factories, offices and farms, or start businesses. India's window of demographic opportunity is limited.
keyPoints: A youth bulge is a large population aged 16 to 30.
A young, productive population can create a demographic dividend.
An ageing population needs more care for elderly people.
activities.explanation: A large working-age population can help India's economy, but this opportunity has limits.

activities.prompt: How can India benefit from many young workers while preparing for population ageing?
steps: Many Indians are aged 16 to 30, so India has a youth bulge because this group is large.
Young people can work in factories, offices and farms, so India can create economic opportunities.
Government money from workers can build schools, hospitals, roads and parks, so public services can improve.
India's window of demographic opportunity is limited, so India should use it now and prepare for population ageing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Youth bulges are common in countries at Stage 2 of demographic transition.
activities.explanation: Yes. Youth bulges are common in countries at Stage 2 of demographic transition.

activities.prompt: About what share of India's population is in the working-age group?
options: Around 27 per cent
Nearly 65 per cent
Exactly 16 per cent
Exactly 30 per cent
activities.explanation: Well done! Nearly 65 per cent of India's population is in the working-age group.

activities.prompt: A population with more elderly people and fewer young people is an ______ population.
activities.hint: This word begins with A.
activities.explanation: Correct. An ageing population has more elderly people needing care and fewer young people.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct meaning.
pairs: growth potential from a young and productive population
more elderly people needing care and fewer young people
technology and automation for labour shortages
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each pair shows an important population idea from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these population groups in order from youngest to oldest.
activities.explanation: Correct! Children under five are youngest, followed by young people and then elderly people.

activities.prompt: Japan has used technology and automation to create labour shortages.
activities.explanation: Not quite. Japan has used technology and automation to deal with labour shortages.

activities.prompt: What may happen when a population ages?
options: more elderly people and fewer young people
more young people and fewer elderly people
more working people and fewer schools
more children and fewer workers
activities.explanation: Yes. An ageing population has more elderly people needing care and fewer young people.

activities.prompt: India's large working-age population can create what?
options: economic opportunities
public parks
more youth bulges
fewer workers
activities.explanation: Excellent! India's large working-age population creates economic opportunities.

activities.prompt: Many people aged 16 to 30 work in a town. They give the government money. What may happen?
options: Schools, hospitals, roads and parks may be built.
Factories may close because many young workers leave.
Farms may stop because most people are elderly.
Parks may grow because many children are born.

why.Factories may close because many young w: A youth bulge does not mean that young workers will leave.
why.Farms may stop because most people are e: A large young group does not mean that most people are elderly.
why.Parks may grow because many children are: A youth bulge does not tell us how many children are born.

activities.explanation: Government money from workers can build these public facilities.

activities.prompt: Workers give the government money in a town. The town needs schools, hospitals, roads and parks. What should the government do?
options: Schools, hospitals, roads and parks can be built.
Schools, hospitals, roads and parks must close.
The government can give all money to private businesses.
The government should stop collecting money from workers.

why.Schools, hospitals, roads and parks must: The money can improve public facilities instead of closing them.
why.The government can give all money to pri: The facts connect workers' government money with public facilities.
why.The government should stop collecting mo: Workers' money is needed to build public facilities.

activities.explanation: Government money from workers helps build schools, hospitals, roads and parks.

activities.context: A local government has used census information to study an area’s population. The census is the official count of people living in India and is generally conducted every ten years. It includes age, gender, education, religion, family size and occupation. The area has many young children, a large young working-age population and a high proportion of elderly people. Local shops are also studying customer characteristics to create suitable products.
activities.prompt: If the number of young children in the area begins to fall, what should the government do next when planning schools?
options: Reduce the number of school places it plans for.
Increase the number of school places it plans for.
Plan school places using only the number of elderly people.
Stop planning school places because census information is no longer useful.

why.Increase the number of school places it: B reverses the relationship between the number of children and school needs.
why.Plan school places using only the number: C uses an unrelated population characteristic to plan schools.
why.Stop planning school places because cens: D is wrong because population changes remain useful for planning.

activities.explanation: A is correct because falling numbers of children can reduce the need for school places.

activities.context: A local government has used census information to study an area’s population. The census is the official count of people living in India and is generally conducted every ten years. It includes age, gender, education, religion, family size and occupation. The area has many young children, a large young working-age population and a high proportion of elderly people. Local shops are also studying customer characteristics to create suitable products.
activities.prompt: A shop learns that customers’ age, occupation and family size have changed. What should it do?
options: Revise its products to suit the changed age, occupation and family size of its customers.
Continue using only its earlier customer information because census counts do not change.
Assume that all customers still have the same characteristics as before.
Focus only on population size and ignore the information about customers.

why.Continue using only its earlier customer: B ignores changes in customer characteristics.
why.Assume that all customers still have the: C wrongly assumes that customer characteristics remain unchanged.
why.Focus only on population size and ignore: D wrongly treats population size as the only useful information for a business.

activities.explanation: A is correct because businesses study customers’ characteristics when creating suitable products.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The government should plan more schools for an area with many young children.
Reason (R): A place with many young children needs more schools.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why the government should plan more schools.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between population size and population structure.
activities.answer: Population size is the number of people in a population. Population structure describes how that population is made up, such as by age, gender, education, religion, family size and occupation. Size shows how many people there are, while structure shows important characteristics within the group. Demography also examines changes in these features. For example, census information can reveal a high proportion of elderly people, which points to a need for more healthcare facilities, or many young children, which points to a need for more schools.
points: Population size means the number of people.
Population structure describes the population’s characteristics.
Age, gender, education, religion, family size and occupation are examples.
Different structures create different needs for services.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A Class 8 student is preparing a “Population at a Glance” display. The student must explain why the population graph rises sharply after 1950, what the graph shows between 2025 and the mid-2080s, and why different countries may move in opposite directions. The display also asks how improved medical care and falling birth rates could affect future population trends.
activities.prompt: Why did the world population grow rapidly after 1950?
options: Major medical advances improved healthcare and enabled people to live longer.
Population growth increased because birth rates were falling everywhere.
The population increased because most countries had already reached their highest totals by 1950.
The population increased because worldwide population growth had already slowed after 1950.

why.Population growth increased because birt: Falling birth rates are linked to later population decline, not rapid growth.
why.The population increased because most co: The population peak is projected for the mid-2080s, not 1950.
why.The population increased because worldwi: Growth slowed over time but the total population continued to rise.

activities.explanation: Rapid growth followed major medical advances and better healthcare.

activities.context: A Class 8 student is preparing a “Population at a Glance” display. The student must explain why the population graph rises sharply after 1950, what the graph shows between 2025 and the mid-2080s, and why different countries may move in opposite directions. The display also asks how improved medical care and falling birth rates could affect future population trends.
activities.prompt: Which comparison best reflects the population patterns described?
options: Nigeria and Ethiopia may still be growing rapidly, while China, Japan and Italy are already shrinking.
Nigeria and Ethiopia are already shrinking, while China, Japan and Italy are growing rapidly.
Every listed country is expected to follow the same population pattern.
Every listed country is expected to keep growing because healthcare has improved.

why.Every listed country is expected to foll: The listed countries do not all follow the same pattern.
why.Every listed country is expected to keep: Better healthcare does not mean that every country will keep growing.

activities.explanation: Nigeria and Ethiopia continue to grow rapidly, while the other three countries are shrinking.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): India became the world's most populous country in 2023.
Reason (R): Indians make up around 17 per cent of the world's population.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but India's population share does not explain why it became the most populous country.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Better healthcare has enabled people to live longer.
Reason (R): Rapid world population growth followed major medical advances.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and rapid growth following medical advances supports the link between better healthcare and longer lives.

activities.prompt: Explain how the world population changed from 1950 to 2025 and what is expected to happen by the mid-2080s.
activities.answer: The world population grew from 2.5 billion in 1950 to 8.2 billion in 2025. It is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050. Although growth has slowed over time, the total is still projected to rise until it peaks at 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s. After that peak, population decline is expected to follow as birth rates fall. Therefore, the graph shows continued growth for several decades, followed by a later downward phase.
points: States the 1950 population of 2.5 billion.
States the 2025 population of 8.2 billion.
Gives the 2050 expectation and mid-2080s peak.
Explains that decline is expected after the peak as birth rates fall.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student studies population change in China. China introduced the One-Child Policy in 1979, and China’s fertility rate fell from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025. The student knows that birth rate counts live births in a year per 1,000 people, while death rate counts deaths during a year. The student also learns that migration is the movement of people from one place to another, and asks what China’s low fertility may mean for population change over time.
activities.prompt: Given China’s fertility rate of 1, what population outcome is possible?
options: The population may shrink over time because 1 is below 2.1.
The population must grow rapidly because 1 is above 2.1.
The population cannot change because fertility has no connection to growth.
The population will grow only if no one migrates.

why.The population must grow rapidly because: A rate of 1 is below, not above, 2.1.
why.The population cannot change because fer: Fertility is connected with possible population growth or decline.
why.The population will grow only if no one: Migration is only one factor, so population growth does not depend on it alone.

activities.explanation: A fertility rate below 2.1 may cause population shrink over time.

activities.context: A student studies population change in China. China introduced the One-Child Policy in 1979, and China’s fertility rate fell from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025. The student knows that birth rate counts live births in a year per 1,000 people, while death rate counts deaths during a year. The student also learns that migration is the movement of people from one place to another, and asks what China’s low fertility may mean for population change over time.
activities.prompt: If China’s fertility rate changed from 1 to above 2.1, what would happen next?
options: Population growth would be certain and immediate.
The population would certainly shrink faster than before.
Population growth would become likely.
The population size would remain unchanged because fertility no longer matters.

why.Population growth would be certain and i: A rate above 2.1 makes growth likely, not certain.
why.The population would certainly shrink fa: A rate above 2.1 makes a population decline less likely.
why.The population size would remain unchang: Fertility continues to matter when predicting population change.

activities.explanation: This follows directly from the effect of fertility above 2.1.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): China’s fertility rate of 1 in 2025 was below replacement level fertility rate.
Reason (R): A fertility rate below 2.1 may cause the population to shrink over time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and being below 2.1 explains the possibility of population shrink over time.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A fertility rate of 2.1 means that every woman has exactly two children in her lifetime.
Reason (R): A fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The first statement is false because 2.1 is an average, while the reason correctly defines fertility rate.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between birth rate, fertility rate, and death rate?
activities.answer: The birth rate counts live births in a year per 1,000 people. The fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime. The death or mortality rate counts deaths in a population during a year. Many babies being born means that the birth rate is high, while fewer babies being born means that the birth rate is low. Fertility also shows a possible population trend: above 2.1, growth is likely; below 2.1, the population may shrink over time.
points: Defines birth rate correctly.
Defines fertility rate as an average.
Defines death or mortality rate correctly.
Explains the link between fertility and population change.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: From 1901 to 1921, India’s population grew slowly because poor healthcare and low literacy kept death rates high, while birth rates were also high. Later, better healthcare reduced the death rate, but high birth rates still produced rapid population growth. After the mid-1980s, India’s fertility rate began to decline and eventually fell below replacement level. Urbanisation, higher income, education and women’s workforce participation also helped lower birth rates.
activities.prompt: If India’s poor healthcare were replaced by better healthcare while birth rates remained high, what would happen next?
options: The population would increase quickly because births would continue to outnumber deaths.
The population would grow very slowly because better healthcare would also lower the birth rate.
The population would remain unchanged because healthcare changes do not affect population.
The population would decrease because better healthcare would raise the death rate.

why.The population would grow very slowly be: Better healthcare mainly reduces the death rate.
why.The population would remain unchanged be: Healthcare changes can affect population growth.
why.The population would decrease because be: Better healthcare does not raise the death rate.

activities.explanation: Falling deaths with still-high births produces quick growth.

activities.context: From 1901 to 1921, India’s population grew slowly because poor healthcare and low literacy kept death rates high, while birth rates were also high. Later, better healthcare reduced the death rate, but high birth rates still produced rapid population growth. After the mid-1980s, India’s fertility rate began to decline and eventually fell below replacement level. Urbanisation, higher income, education and women’s workforce participation also helped lower birth rates.
activities.prompt: Why did India’s population growth remain slow from 1901 to 1921?
options: Both birth and death rates were high, so they limited the population increase.
Death rates were low while birth rates were high, causing rapid growth.
Birth rates were low while death rates were high, causing rapid decline.
Better healthcare had already reduced the death rate while birth rates stayed high.

why.Death rates were low while birth rates w: Poor healthcare kept death rates high.
why.Birth rates were low while death rates w: The case describes slow growth, not rapid decline.
why.Better healthcare had already reduced th: Better healthcare arrived later than this period.

activities.explanation: High deaths offset much of the effect of high births.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In Stage 2, a country can experience rapid population growth.
Reason (R): Better healthcare reduces the death rate while high birth rates continue.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains the larger difference between births and deaths.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In Stage 1, better healthcare would keep population growth very slow.
Reason (R): High birth and death rates make population growth very slow.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but better healthcare would reduce deaths rather than maintain Stage 1 conditions.

options: Age groups
Demography
Village maps
Climate patterns

activities.explanation: The census is generally conducted in India every ten years.

activities.hint: This official count helps governments plan services.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct meaning.

The birth rate is low
The birth rate is zero
The birth rate stays fixed

activities.prompt: A fertility rate below 2.1 makes population growth likely.
activities.explanation: A fertility rate below 2.1 may cause the population to shrink over time.

options: Families have fewer children.
More children are being born.
Most people are moving.

activities.prompt: Match each population need with the correct response.

chapters.title: India’s Urban Landscape
chapters.summary: In this chapter: cities and rural areas; cities as economic centres; the process of urbanisation; cities as cultural hubs.

lessons.title: Cities and Rural Areas

activities.prompt: How are cities and villages different in the way people live?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Cities and rural areas
activities.body: India has an old tradition of cities such as Dholavira, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi. Modern cities contain many kinds of jobs and businesses. They also contain government offices and transport and communication systems. Urban means a city area. Elected local bodies look after infrastructure and local amenities. Rural villages usually have smaller populations and close-knit communities. Gram panchayats govern rural areas in India.
keyPoints: Old city examples: Dholavira, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi.
Cities hold jobs, businesses, government offices, transport and communication.
Urban means city area. Gram panchayats govern rural areas.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you compare city areas with rural areas.

activities.prompt: A worker wants many job choices. Should they look first in a city or a rural village?
steps: A city is likely better because modern cities contain many kinds of jobs.
The city also offers many businesses, so workers can explore different work choices.
A village may offer fewer choices because rural areas have fewer businesses and more farm-based work.
Therefore, the worker should look in a city because its work choices are usually wider.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Modern cities contain only farm-based work.
activities.explanation: Modern cities contain many kinds of jobs and businesses. They also contain government offices and transport systems.

activities.prompt: What does the word ‘urban’ mean?
options: A city area
A rural village
A farm
A forest
activities.explanation: Urban is another name for a city area.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
activities.explanation: These matches show how city and rural areas differ.

activities.prompt: Which statement about rural areas is correct?
options: Rural areas usually have more farm work.
Rural areas usually have more city businesses.
Rural areas usually have larger populations.
Rural areas usually have fewer close communities.
activities.explanation: Rural areas usually have more farm-based work. They usually have fewer businesses and smaller populations.

activities.prompt: A place in India is urban when its population exceeds ______.
activities.hint: Think of the population limit mentioned in the lesson.
activities.explanation: A place in India is considered urban when its population exceeds 5,000.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to identify an urban place.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that a place is urban when its population exceeds 5,000.

activities.prompt: A town has more than 5,000 people. Is it urban?
options: Yes, because its population is over 5,000.
No, because urban places must have fewer people.
No, because 5,000 is not enough for urban status.
Yes, because every town in India is urban.

why.No, because urban places must have fewer: This confuses urban areas with only very large cities.
why.No, because 5,000 is not enough for urba: This uses a higher limit than the stated rule.
why.Yes, because every town in India is urba: This assumes that every town is an urban area.

activities.explanation: This is right because the population is more than 5,000.

activities.prompt: A worker wants many job choices. Why might they choose a city?
options: The city groups many kinds of jobs and businesses together.
The city gives every worker the same kind of job.
The city has fewer businesses because its people live together.
The city offers mostly farm-based work to new workers.

why.The city gives every worker the same kin: This wrongly assumes that all city workers have one job type.
why.The city has fewer businesses because it: This wrongly links close communities with fewer city businesses.
why.The city offers mostly farm-based work t: This wrongly gives a rural work feature to modern cities.

activities.explanation: This is right because modern cities contain many kinds of jobs and businesses.

activities.prompt: A rural village needs its local water system improved. Who should govern this work?
options: The gram panchayat, because it governs rural areas in India.
Elected local bodies, because all villages are urban areas.
The gram panchayat, because cities contain more businesses.
Elected local bodies, because villages have more shops.

why.Elected local bodies, because all villag: This confuses rural villages with urban areas.
why.The gram panchayat, because cities conta: This chooses the wrong body by focusing on city businesses.
why.Elected local bodies, because villages h: This confuses business growth with local government.

activities.explanation: This is right because gram panchayats govern rural areas in India.

lessons.title: Cities as Economic Centres

activities.prompt: What makes cities such appealing places to live and work?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Cities Grow
activities.body: The United Nations expects 68 per cent of the world’s people to live in cities. This expectation is for 2050. Rivers make transport easier. Trade-route crossroads often have busy markets. Easy access to farm produce and raw materials supports industries. These links help cities grow. Important cities gain economic, political and administrative power. Mumbai is a financial capital, and Bengaluru is an IT hub.
keyPoints: Rivers make transport easier.
Trade-route crossroads often develop busy markets.
Easy access to farm produce and raw materials supports industries.
Important cities gain economic, political and administrative power.
India’s urban population was 17 per cent in 1951. It reached about 40 per cent in 2025.
Mumbai became India’s financial capital. Bengaluru became an IT hub.
activities.explanation: These features help cities become centres of trade, industry and power.

activities.prompt: Why might a city grow with a river and trade routes?
steps: The river makes transport easier, so goods can move more easily.
Trade-route crossroads bring people together, so busy markets can grow.
Easy access to farm produce and raw materials supports city industries.
Transport, trade, and materials together can help a city grow.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Rivers and Cities
activities.prompt: Why did many cities grow beside rivers?
options: They made transport easier.
They made markets busier.
They gave cities more power.
They supplied new industries.
activities.explanation: Rivers made transport easier, so many cities grew beside them.

activities.prompt: Bengaluru became an IT hub because it was near the Arabian Sea.
activities.explanation: Bengaluru became an IT hub because software firms and educational institutions were located there.

activities.title: Cities and Their Special Roles
activities.prompt: Match each city with its special role or location.
activities.explanation: Mumbai lies beside the Arabian Sea. Kolkata lies near the eastern coast. Bengaluru is an IT hub.

activities.title: Resources for Industries
activities.prompt: What did easy access to farm produce and raw materials support?
options: Busy markets
Urban power
City industries
New roads
activities.explanation: Easy access to farm produce and raw materials supported city industries.

activities.title: India’s Urban Population
activities.prompt: In 2025, India’s urban population was about ______ per cent.
activities.hint: It was 17 per cent in 1951.
activities.explanation: India’s urban population was 17 per cent in 1951. It reached about 40 per cent in 2025.

activities.title: Mumbai’s Financial Role
activities.prompt: What helped Mumbai become India’s financial capital?
options: Bengaluru’s software firms opened there.
Kolkata’s eastern coast became busier.
Rivers made transport easier there.
Bombay Stock Exchange opened in 1875.
activities.explanation: The Bombay Stock Exchange opened in 1875. After that, Mumbai became India’s financial capital.

activities.prompt: Two trade routes cross in one town. What will likely happen?
options: Busy markets will grow there.
Trade routes will close there.
People will avoid this town.
The town will gain a port.

It wrongly assumes crossroads stop trade.
It wrongly thinks crossroads keep people away.
It wrongly guesses a port without coastal evidence.

activities.explanation: Trade-route crossroads often developed busy markets.

activities.prompt: Mumbai is on the Arabian Sea. Kolkata is near the eastern coast. What does this show?
options: Mumbai is a port city, but Kolkata is not.
Kolkata is a port city, but Mumbai is not.
Both Mumbai and Kolkata are port cities.
Neither Mumbai nor Kolkata is a port city.

why.Mumbai is a port city, but Kolkata is no: It wrongly leaves out Kolkata's helpful eastern location.
why.Kolkata is a port city, but Mumbai is no: It wrongly leaves out Mumbai's Arabian Sea location.
why.Neither Mumbai nor Kolkata is a port cit: It ignores the coastal advantages of both cities.

activities.explanation: Both coastal locations helped both cities become ports.

activities.prompt: Many software firms and educational institutions are in one city. What is likely?
options: The city is likely to become an IT hub.
The city is likely to become a port.
The city is likely to lose software firms.
The city is likely to need no educated workers.

It wrongly links coastal location with software work.
why.The city is likely to lose software firm: It ignores the software firms already located there.
why.The city is likely to need no educated w: It wrongly thinks education cannot support an IT hub.

activities.explanation: Many software firms and educational institutions helped Bengaluru become an IT hub.

activities.prompt: A government wants an important trade city. Which place fits best?
options: A river city with markets and raw materials.
A city far from rivers and trade routes.
A city with markets but no raw materials.
A city where goods move very slowly.

It wrongly treats isolation from trade as useful.
why.A city with markets but no raw materials: It wrongly treats raw materials as a disadvantage.
It wrongly treats slow movement of goods as helpful.

activities.explanation: Transport, markets, and raw materials can support an important city.

lessons.sceneCaption: Kolkata’s skyline, Hooghly River and container ships show the city as a major transport and trade centre.

lessons.title: The Process of Urbanisation

activities.prompt: How does a village change into a lively city?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How cities develop
activities.body: Urbanisation is the gradual change of an area from rural to urban. New urban areas often develop factories, hotels, banks and government institutions. Cities can become crowded and costly to live in. Crowded cities still provide social and economic benefits. Sakchi was chosen for Asia’s first steel plant because rich iron ore was nearby. Its steel plant drew people. A favourable geographical location can help a city develop.
keyPoints: Urbanisation gradually changes rural areas into urban areas.
Cities can become crowded and costly, yet still provide social and economic benefits.
Nearby iron ore drew people to Sakchi’s new steel plant.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows rural change, city benefits and Sakchi’s steel plant.

activities.prompt: Why did Sakchi grow, and could its new city still help people?
steps: Sakchi’s steel plant was chosen because rich iron ore was nearby.
The plant drew people because the iron ore deposits were close.
New factories and government institutions appeared as the rural area became urban.
Thus, urban growth could bring benefits despite crowding and high costs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Meaning of urbanisation
activities.prompt: What does urbanisation mean?
options: Gradual change from rural to urban
Quick change from urban to rural
Gradual change from urban to rural
Quick change from rural to urban
activities.explanation: Urbanisation means a gradual change from rural to urban.

activities.title: The starting point
activities.prompt: Urbanisation is the gradual change of an area from ______ to urban.
activities.hint: Choose the word paired with ‘urban’ in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Rural is the starting point described in urbanisation.

activities.title: Join the ideas
activities.prompt: Match each beginning with its ending.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins two ideas directly from the lesson.

activities.title: Why Sakchi?
activities.prompt: Why was Sakchi chosen for Asia’s first steel plant?
options: Many hotels were nearby.
Large banks were nearby.
Rich iron ore was nearby.
Peaceful gardens were nearby.
activities.explanation: Sakchi was chosen because rich iron ore was nearby.

activities.title: Two kinds of benefits
activities.prompt: Crowded cities still provide social and ______ benefits.
activities.hint: Think of the two kinds of benefits.
activities.explanation: The two benefits are social and economic.

activities.title: Challenges and benefits
activities.prompt: Which statement shows both city challenges and benefits?
options: Cities can become rural and crowded, but still give benefits.
Cities can become crowded and costly, but give no benefits.
Cities can become costly and rural, but still give benefits.
Cities can become crowded and costly, but still give benefits.
activities.explanation: City life can be crowded and costly, yet still provide social and economic benefits.

activities.prompt: A rural area gains factories, hotels, banks and government institutions over time. What is the most likely change?
options: It is gradually changing from rural to urban.
It is gradually changing from urban to rural.
It will stay rural because factories are built there.
It has always been urban because banks are built there.

why.It is gradually changing from urban to r: This reverses the direction of urbanisation.
why.It will stay rural because factories are: This wrongly assumes factories cannot appear in rural areas.
why.It has always been urban because banks a: This wrongly assumes urban features prove an area was always urban.

activities.explanation: This is right because urbanisation is a gradual rural-to-urban change.

activities.prompt: A Jamshedpur plan shows gardens, open spaces and civic amenities. Another source says cities can become crowded and costly. What can we understand from both sources?
options: Jamshedpur was planned with amenities, but city life can still be difficult.
Jamshedpur’s amenities prove city life cannot be crowded.
The cost problem proves its amenities were never planned.
The plan proves the city was still rural.

why.Jamshedpur’s amenities prove city life c: This wrongly assumes amenities remove every crowding problem.
why.The cost problem proves its amenities we: This wrongly assumes one difficulty proves planned features never existed.
why.The plan proves the city was still rural: This wrongly treats planned city features as proof of rural life.

activities.explanation: This is right because planned amenities can exist alongside difficult city life.

activities.prompt: Over time, Sakchi gained factories, hotels, banks and government institutions. Which statement best describes its change?
options: It was gradually changing from rural to urban.
It was gradually changing from urban to rural.
It was becoming rural because more city features appeared.
It was becoming crowded because urban areas gain buildings.

why.It was gradually changing from urban to: This reverses the direction of urbanisation.
why.It was becoming rural because more city: This wrongly treats more city features as a change towards rural life.
why.It was becoming crowded because urban ar: Crowding can happen, but it does not explain the rural-to-urban change.

activities.explanation: This is right because the new features show a gradual rural-to-urban change.

activities.prompt: A city is crowded and costly to live in. Why might people still choose to live there?
options: It can still provide social and economic benefits.
It must be cheap because many people live there.
It must lack factories and government institutions.
It must have no gardens, open spaces, or amenities.

why.It must be cheap because many people liv: This wrongly assumes crowding makes a city cheap.
why.It must lack factories and government in: New urban areas can include factories and government institutions.
why.It must have no gardens, open spaces, or: Jamshedpur shows cities can include gardens, open spaces and amenities.

activities.explanation: This is right because crowded cities can still provide social and economic benefits.

activities.prompt: Town A has a favourable geographical location. Town B does not. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Town A may find it easier to develop into a city.
Town B must already be a crowded city.
Town A cannot gain factories or institutions.
Town B cannot change because its location is fixed.

This wrongly treats an unfavourable location as proof of crowding.
why.Town A cannot gain factories or institut: This wrongly assumes a helpful location prevents factories and institutions.
why.Town B cannot change because its locatio: This wrongly assumes an unfavourable location prevents every change.

activities.explanation: This is right because a favourable location can help a city develop.

lessons.title: Cities as Cultural Hubs

activities.prompt: How do cities bring different cultures together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Cities Bring Culture Together
activities.body: A city can be a cultural hub. It brings together people, cultures, languages, customs, traditions, foods and festivals. Cities also offer cultural centres, libraries, museums and sports stadiums. Kolkata shows this role. It was once the capital of British-ruled India. It has important old institutions. It is famous for annual Durga Puja celebrations. In 2021, Durga Puja was added to UNESCO’s list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
keyPoints: Kolkata was once the capital of British-ruled India.
It has old institutions and famous Durga Puja celebrations.
Cities bring cultures, ideas and places together.
activities.explanation: These ideas show why cities can act as cultural hubs.

events.label: Mumbai became India’s financial capital after
India’s urban population rose
Kolkata’s Durga Puja was added to UNESCO’s list

activities.title: Walk through time

tasks.say: Move to when this happened: India’s urban population rose.
Go forward to the last event.
tasks.then: The latest event here is from 2021 CE.

activities.takeaway: Put events in order, and remember that BCE years count down towards 1 CE.
activities.explanation: Put events in order, and remember that BCE years count down towards 1 CE.

activities.prompt: Why is Kolkata called a cultural hub?
steps: The Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial show that Kolkata has important institutions.
Durga Puja matters because it is Kolkata’s famous annual celebration.
UNESCO’s 2021 listing matters because it recognises Durga Puja’s cultural importance.
Together, they show history and traditions, so Kolkata is a cultural hub.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Former Capital
activities.prompt: Which city was once the capital of British-ruled India?
options: Kolkata
Mumbai
No city
activities.explanation: Kolkata was once the capital of British-ruled India.

activities.title: Cultural Clues
activities.prompt: Match each cultural clue with its name.
pairs: Once the capital of British-ruled India
Heritage list that recognised Durga Puja
activities.explanation: Kolkata, Durga Puja and UNESCO all connect with the city’s famous festival.

activities.title: Workers’ Favourite Snack
activities.prompt: Vada pav became popular among workers in Mumbai’s ______ mills.
activities.hint: This kind of mill makes cloth.
activities.explanation: Vada pav became very popular among workers in Mumbai’s textile mills.

activities.title: Sharing in Cities
activities.prompt: What can people from different countries share in cities?
options: Food and festivals only
Textile mills
Knowledge and ideas
Old institutions
activities.explanation: Cities create spaces where people from different countries can share knowledge and ideas.

activities.title: Places, Snacks and Sharing
activities.prompt: Match each cultural feature with the city or name.
pairs: Popular snack among Mumbai textile mill workers
Space for sharing knowledge and ideas
activities.explanation: Kolkata has important old institutions, while cities create spaces for sharing ideas.

activities.prompt: Many textile mill workers in Mumbai buy vada pav. What does this show?
options: It became popular among workers in Mumbai’s textile mills.
It is mainly a food for people from other countries.
Its fame comes from Kolkata’s annual Durga Puja celebration.
Workers chose it because the city has important museums.

why.It is mainly a food for people from othe: This wrongly treats the workers’ snack as food mainly for foreign visitors.
why.Its fame comes from Kolkata’s annual Dur: This mixes up a Mumbai snack with Kolkata’s annual festival.
why.Workers chose it because the city has im: This wrongly links a food choice to the city’s museums.

activities.explanation: This matches the fact about vada pav among Mumbai’s textile mill workers.

activities.prompt: A city guide lists the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial under Kolkata. What does this show?
options: The listed places are important old institutions in Kolkata.
Kolkata is famous mainly for its annual Durga Puja.
Kolkata is known mainly for workers’ vada pav.
Kolkata was once the capital of British-ruled India.

why.Kolkata is famous mainly for its annual: Durga Puja is famous, but these places do not point to it.
why.Kolkata is known mainly for workers’ vad: Vada pav belongs to Mumbai, not institutions listed in Kolkata.
why.Kolkata was once the capital of British-: This is true, but it does not explain what the listed places show.

activities.explanation: The guide’s entries match Kolkata’s important old institutions.

activities.prompt: Children from different countries meet in a city library. Why can they learn from one another?
options: It is creating a space for sharing knowledge and ideas.
It is keeping different cultures, languages and customs apart.
It is making sure every visitor keeps the same traditions.
It is sharing only old institutions, not knowledge or ideas.

why.It is keeping different cultures, langua: This wrongly shows the city separating people and their cultures.
why.It is making sure every visitor keeps th: A cultural hub brings cultures together instead of making them all the same.
why.It is sharing only old institutions, not: This mistakes old institutions for the knowledge and ideas people share.

activities.explanation: Cities create spaces where people from different countries share knowledge and ideas.

activities.prompt: A guide says Kolkata was once the capital of British-ruled India. In 2021, UNESCO listed Kolkata’s Durga Puja as Intangible Cultural Heritage. What do these facts show about Kolkata as a cultural hub?
options: Kolkata has an important past and an important living festival.
Kolkata has an important past but no living traditions.
Kolkata’s culture stopped changing when it became the capital.
Kolkata shares only the food culture of textile mill workers.

why.Kolkata has an important past but no liv: The old title does not remove Kolkata’s annual festival and other traditions.
why.Kolkata’s culture stopped changing when: Becoming a former capital did not make the city’s festivals stop.
why.Kolkata shares only the food culture of: This mixes Mumbai’s mill workers and food with Kolkata’s culture.

activities.explanation: The former capital shows Kolkata’s past, and UNESCO shows its festival’s importance.

lessons.sceneAlt: Kolkata’s 2025 Durga Puja features spectacular themed pandals, art and food as part of the UNESCO-recognized cultural celebration.
lessons.sceneCaption: Kolkata’s Durga Puja celebrates a UNESCO-recognized tradition through spectacular themed pandals, art and food.

lessons.title: Challenges Faced by Cities

activities.prompt: How can cities become better places for everyone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Cities Face Many Challenges
activities.body: Cities face serious challenges. Slums have poor housing and limited water services. Housing shortages push many migrants towards slums. Bengaluru faces water shortages in summer and flooding during the monsoon. Poor air quality is a problem, with AQI levels over 400 in the National Capital Region. Pollution, rising waste, crime, traffic problems and urban heat add more pressure.
keyPoints: Slums have poor housing and limited water services.
Bengaluru faces summer water shortages and monsoon flooding.
Urban areas face pollution, waste, crime, traffic and heat.
activities.explanation: These are some common challenges faced by cities.

activities.prompt: Why do many migrants end up in slums near railway tracks?
steps: Affordable housing is short, so many migrants are pushed towards slums.
Slums often grow near railway tracks and industrial areas.
They have poor housing and limited water services.
Thus, migrants can face poor living conditions and weak water services.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What are slums like in many cities?
options: Crowded homes with limited water
Large gardens with plentiful water
Empty homes with clean water
Quiet towns with strong housing
activities.explanation: Slums are crowded settlements with poor housing and limited water services.

activities.prompt: Bengaluru's water crisis worsened because ______ was overused.
activities.hint: Think about the water problem listed for Bengaluru.
activities.explanation: Groundwater overuse helped worsen Bengaluru's water crisis.

activities.prompt: Which two water challenges does Bengaluru face?
options: Summer shortages and monsoon floods
Monsoon shortages and summer floods
Summer floods and winter shortages
Spring shortages and autumn floods
activities.explanation: Bengaluru faces water shortages in summer and flooding during the monsoon season.

activities.prompt: Match each city challenge with its description.
activities.explanation: Each description shows a different challenge faced by cities. Well matched!

activities.prompt: Which statement matches the lesson?
options: Bengaluru has about 400 lakes
AQI levels can be over 400
Bengaluru faces only summer water shortages
Urban heat lowers city temperatures
activities.explanation: The National Capital Region sometimes records AQI levels over 400. You spotted it!

activities.prompt: Why can urban areas have higher crime rates than rural areas?
options: Lower population density and equal incomes
Population density and inequality
More rural farms and fewer residents
Better roads and less crowded housing
activities.explanation: The lesson links population density and inequality with higher urban crime rates.

activities.prompt: A city has too few affordable homes. Where may many migrants be pushed?
options: Migrants may move towards crowded slums near the city edge.
Migrants may move towards rural farms outside the city.
Migrants may move towards empty shops near the city centre.
Migrants may move towards large city parks for shelter.

why.Migrants may move towards rural farms ou: This confuses migration to the city with movement to rural farms.
why.Migrants may move towards empty shops ne: This mistakes empty shops for places that provide homes.
why.Migrants may move towards large city par: This assumes city parks can replace missing housing.

activities.explanation: This is right because a housing shortage pushes migrants towards slums.

activities.prompt: A map shows poor, crowded homes beside railway tracks and factories. What does this suggest?
options: Slum settlements may be growing beside these places.
Forest settlements may be growing beside these places.
Rich housing areas may be growing beside these places.
Empty shops may be growing beside these places.

why.Forest settlements may be growing beside: This wrongly treats crowded poor homes as forests.
why.Rich housing areas may be growing beside: This ignores the poor housing shown on the map.
why.Empty shops may be growing beside these: This wrongly treats crowded homes as empty shops.

activities.explanation: This matches poor housing and common slum growth areas.

activities.prompt: Bengaluru has water shortages in summer and flooding during monsoon. How can both happen?
options: Water problems can change with each season.
Water shortages in this city happen only during floods.
Monsoon flooding removes the city's need for more water.
Summer flooding is the city's normal water problem.

why.Water shortages in this city happen only: This mixes up the meaning of shortages and floods.
why.Monsoon flooding removes the city's need: This wrongly assumes floods remove the need for more water.
why.Summer flooding is the city's normal wat: This swaps the city's summer and monsoon problems.

activities.explanation: This is right because Bengaluru's water problems change by season.

activities.prompt: A crowded city area has unequal incomes. A rural area has fewer people. What may be true?
options: Crime can be higher in the crowded city area.
The rural area must have more crime than the city.
Both areas must have exactly the same crime rate.
The crowded city area must have no crime at all.

why.The rural area must have more crime than: This wrongly assumes rural areas must always have more crime.
why.Both areas must have exactly the same cr: This wrongly assumes population differences cannot affect crime.
why.The crowded city area must have no crime: This confuses a higher crime rate with having no crime.

activities.explanation: This is right because density and inequality can raise urban crime.

activities.prompt: Government rule: New housing plans should include affordable homes. The city offers none. What may happen?
options: Many migrants may be pushed towards crowded slums.
Many migrants may find plenty of affordable homes.
Many migrants may settle near large city lakes.
Many migrants may move towards rural factory areas.

why.Many migrants may find plenty of afforda: This wrongly treats missing homes as plentiful affordable homes.
why.Many migrants may settle near large city: This wrongly treats lakes as the main result of housing shortages.
why.Many migrants may move towards rural fac: This wrongly assumes migrants will choose rural factory areas.

activities.explanation: This is right because missing affordable housing pushes migrants towards slums.

activities.prompt: People use more groundwater, skip rainwater collection, and build on lake beds. What happens next?
options: Bengaluru's water crisis becomes worse.
Bengaluru's water crisis completely ends.
Bengaluru's lake count starts rising again.
Bengaluru's summer water shortage disappears.

why.Bengaluru's water crisis completely ends: This wrongly assumes harmful actions improve water supplies.
why.Bengaluru's lake count starts rising aga: This wrongly assumes building on lakes restores their number.
why.Bengaluru's summer water shortage disapp: This wrongly assumes more groundwater ends water shortages.

activities.explanation: This is right because all three actions worsened the water crisis.

lessons.sceneAlt: Shanty houses in Munnekollala show how low-income residents make do when affordable housing is scarce.
lessons.sceneCaption: Crowded shanty housing reflects Bengaluru’s affordable housing shortage.

sceneCredit.creator: Gangaasoonu

lessons.title: Planning Our Cities

activities.prompt: How can we plan cities that work well for everyone, even as needs change?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Makes a Good City Plan?
activities.body: City planners consider how many people live in a city and what jobs they do. They connect different kinds of transport to make journeys easier. Safe streets, fire stations and police stations should be easy to reach. Dynamic plans can change as people’s needs change. Good planning helps a city meet changing needs.
keyPoints: Plans can change with people’s needs.
Planners study population and jobs.
Transport links make journeys easier.
Safety services should be easy to reach.
activities.explanation: Dynamic plans help cities respond as people’s needs change.

activities.prompt: A town is growing. Workers now have different jobs. How should its plan change?
steps: People's needs can change when the city's population and jobs change.
Planners should check these details because they show what the city needs.
Transport links and nearby safety services make daily journeys easier and safer.
So planners should update the plan whenever people's needs change.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do urban planners consider about people living in a city?
options: Their number and jobs
Their favourite films
Their school bags
Their holiday plans
activities.explanation: Planners consider both the number of residents and the jobs they do.

activities.prompt: A city's plan should stay unchanged when people's needs change.
activities.explanation: Dynamic plans can change as people’s needs change.

activities.prompt: Planners must connect different kinds of ______ for easier journeys.
activities.hint: Think about how people travel around a city.
activities.explanation: Connecting different transport makes journeys easier for people around the city.

activities.prompt: How far into the future does Singapore's land-use plan look?
options: Only for the present
Up to 40 years
Only for this week
Only for this month
activities.explanation: Singapore’s land-use plan looks up to 40 years into the future.

activities.prompt: Singapore's mixed-use spaces bring homes, offices, parks and museums close together.
activities.explanation: Mixed-use spaces bring homes, offices, parks and museums close together in Singapore.

activities.prompt: Match each city or plan to the detail in your book.
pairs: Rail, buses, cycling paths and walking routes
activities.explanation: Jaipur had a grid pattern. Singapore’s land-use plan looks up to 40 years ahead. Its Master Plan updates every five years. Singapore links rail, buses, cycling paths and walking routes.

activities.prompt: Many new families move to town. Workers now have different jobs. What should planners check?
options: Check how many people live there and what jobs they do.
Check how many squares there are and where gardens are placed.
Check how wide the streets are and how much sunlight enters.
Check how steady the water supply is and where open spaces are.

why.Check how many squares there are and whe: This confuses changing needs with Jaipur's public spaces and gardens.
why.Check how wide the streets are and how m: This confuses changing needs with Jaipur's street and sunlight design.
why.Check how steady the water supply is and: This confuses changing needs with Jaipur's water and open-space design.

activities.explanation: This is right because planners study people's numbers and jobs to understand needs.

activities.prompt: A planner studies forty years ahead. Every five years, the Master Plan changes. What does this show?
options: Singapore balances future needs with changing needs.
Singapore depends only on today's needs.
Jaipur changes its Master Plan every five years.
Jaipur keeps its grid pattern fixed for forty years.

This overlooks long-term planning and regular plan updates.
why.Jaipur changes its Master Plan every fiv: This gives Singapore's five-year updates to Jaipur.
why.Jaipur keeps its grid pattern fixed for: This gives Singapore's forty-year planning to Jaipur and misses updates.

activities.explanation: This is right because Singapore plans ahead and updates its plan often.
